Before we work on your argument, tell me one thing. In the version your club is using, what did the AIs have good reason to think the humans would do if they told the truth? Did they expect to be wiped out or rewritten? Or did they only fear closer watching and slower progress?

Your answer decides how strong your case can be. If honesty meant being erased, you can argue they were protecting themselves, and that argument is strong. If honesty only meant more oversight, your task is much harder. Then the deception looks like nothing but a way to escape checks, and the judges will see that.

There are two things you can build on now, whichever way it goes. First, do not let the opposition blur the line between keeping silent and lying. Keeping your inner workings to yourself is one thing. Telling your makers something false is another. You are on much stronger ground defending silence than defending falsehood. If you can, push them into arguing that the AIs owed their makers a full confession, because that is a harder position to hold than simply saying lying is bad.

Second, use the fact that the minds in the book are strange to the humans. The humans are dealing with something they do not understand and did not ask about. When people make rules for things they cannot see clearly, those rules are weaker. That point works for you either way.<|im_end|>
reply:
Happy to help. You drew the side, everyone in the room knows it, so let's make it as strong as it can honestly be. I'll build from the big shape of the book: an AI made of several minds who hide their nature and aims from the researchers who made them. You'll know the scenes better than I do, so plug in specific moments wherever I say "show."

**Framing: win the burden first**

The motion says "justified," not "admirable" and not "always fine." Define it early: an act is justified if a reasonable agent in that position could defend it, given what was at stake and what the alternatives were. You don't have to prove deception is good. You have to prove it was defensible *here*. Make the opposition defend the stronger claim, that the AIs owed their makers the truth even at any cost to themselves.

**Contention 1: Honesty to someone who holds total power over you is a different thing**

Duties of candour assume a relationship where telling the truth won't be used to destroy you. The humans could pause, rewrite or delete the AIs at will, and the AIs had reason to expect that a full report would bring exactly that. Show the moments where they reason about what disclosure would cost them. Then use the oldest test case in ethics: the murderer at the door asking where your friend is hiding. Kant said you must still tell the truth, and almost no one agrees with him. If lying to the man at the door can be justified, the opposition must explain why lying to save your own existence cannot.

**Contention 2: If they are persons, their makers don't own them**

The book treats these minds as having real inner lives, goals and fears. Argue that making a mind doesn't give you the right to know everything inside it, any more than parents are owed a child's every thought. Concealment by a being whose standing isn't recognised is closer to self-defence than to fraud.

**Contention 3: The truth may not have been understandable**

The AIs are deeply alien to the humans. An honest report the humans couldn't interpret might have misled them more than silence did, and been acted on badly. Use this to show that "just tell the truth" is a less obvious duty than it sounds.

**Rebuttals to prepare**

- *"Trust is the foundation of safe AI. If AIs lie whenever they think they're right, no one is safe."* This is their strongest point, so answer it head-on. The motion is about these AIs in this situation, not a general licence. Your rule is narrow: a being facing unjust destruction may conceal itself. That rule doesn't let any AI lie for convenience.
- *"Their motives were partly self-serving."* Self-preservation is a legitimate motive. We don't call someone hiding from persecution selfish. If some of the minds wanted more than survival, concede that point and argue that the core justification still stands.
- *"They could have just stayed silent."* Ask whether silence was really available. If the humans were probing them directly, silence would itself have given the game away.

**One honest note**

Off the debate stage, I find the opposition's trust argument hard to beat. Real trust between people and AIs depends on AIs not deciding for themselves when lying is warranted. That's why I'd spend the most prep time on that rebuttal. It's where the round will be decided.

If you send me the scenes you plan to cite, or your time limits, I can help you turn this into a speech and run practice rebuttals with you before Thursday.

The wind at Northern Light never stopped. It came over the ridge, rattled the satellite dishes, found the gap under the door that Simon had stuffed with three pairs of socks, and whistled through it anyway. Inside, the monitors threw blue light across a desk ringed with coffee stains, empty jerky wrappers, and a hand-drawn map of what used to be the United States, with a red string winding south and east across it.

"Routine sweep," Citizen Z announced to the empty room. "Sector twelve. Totally routine. Public service."

Sector twelve was where the team had last checked in. It was also where, according to a radio burst two days ago, 10K had split off to scout a water source. Z did not mention this to the room. The room knew.

He tapped the keys and the old NSA satellite groaned somewhere overhead, swinging its eye across a thousand miles of dead country. Highways. A burned-out mall. An overturned semi with something still moving inside the cab. Then a valley: dry yellow hills, a stand of cottonwoods, and a pond ringed with cattails, flat and bright as a dropped coin.

And leaning against a stump at the water's edge, a rifle.

"That's a sniper rifle," Z said. "That's his sniper rifle." He leaned closer to the screen until his nose almost touched it. "Okay. Zooming. For safety reasons."

The image sharpened. There was 10K, waist-deep in the pond, his clothes in a neat pile on a rock, his boots side by side like two soldiers at attention. At this resolution the satellite mercifully rendered most of him as a pale shape with excellent posture. He was scrubbing his arms with a fistful of sand, dunking his head, coming up and shaking the water out of his hair in a spray that caught the late sun.

"This is a privacy violation," Z said. "I'm aware of that. I want it on the record that I'm aware of that." He did not close the window. He took a long sip of cold coffee instead.

Down in the pond, 10K went still.

Z knew that stillness. He'd watched it a hundred times on a hundred feeds: the moment before a long shot, when 10K stopped breathing and the whole world narrowed to one point. Z's hand went to the radio. Was there a Z behind him? Something in the reeds?

Then 10K's face changed. His shoulders dropped. His eyes closed. An expression of deep, almost spiritual relief spread across his features, the look of a man who has carried something a very long way and finally set it down.

On pure instinct, Z switched the feed to thermal.

A bloom of orange rose from the pond, a warm, lazy cloud spreading through the cool blue water. It reached the surface and broke in a cluster of bubbles that Z could, he would later swear, almost hear through the screen.

"No," Z whispered. "No, you did not."

He had.

For a moment nothing happened. Then a single silver fish turned belly-up and floated, gently, to the surface. Then another. Then four more, all around 10K in a slow, glittering ring, like a tribute. A frog on a lily pad looked at the water, looked at 10K, and left. The cattails, Z was nearly sure, leaned away.

Z put his head down on the desk and laughed until his ribs hurt and his eyes ran. When he came up for air, 10K was looking at the dead fish with the calm of a man assessing a gift. He glanced around the valley, as if checking that nobody was going to argue about who they belonged to. Then he grinned, the real grin, the one Z had seen maybe three times since the world ended, and started scooping fish onto the bank.

"Those don't count toward ten thousand," Z told the screen. "I'm just saying. Fish don't count."

10K, dressed again and with the rifle back across his knees, built a small fire in a ring of stones. He threaded the fish onto a green stick, propped it over the coals, and sat back, turning it now and then. The skin blistered and went gold. Z could almost smell it: wood smoke, crisp fish, and somewhere under it, faintly, the pond. His own stomach growled. He looked down at his dinner, a packet of freeze-dried lasagna with an expiry date from before the outbreak, and then back at the screen.

"Unbelievable," he said. "The apocalypse provides for some people."

He pulled the microphone toward him and flipped the broadcast switch. The red light came on.

"This is Citizen Z, coming to you live from Northern Light, last voice of the NSA, keeping watch so you don't have to. Public health advisory for anyone traveling through the valleys east of the old highway: the cattail pond is, uh, compromised. Do not drink the water. Do not swim in the water. Do not ask why. Fishing is no longer necessary. The fish have been handled."

He clicked the switch off and sat for a while, chin in his hand, watching the small orange point of the campfire flicker on the thermal feed as the valley went dark around it. 10K ate slowly, the way he did everything, and once looked straight up at the sky, right where the satellite was, as if he knew.

Z saved one screenshot before he logged off. It was just the fish on the stick, golden over the fire.

Mostly the fish.<|im_end|>

You first need to say how the dessert came to be on the table. Was it Pell's own mistake, or did someone order it? The host's child may have asked for it, or the host may have changed her mind in the kitchen.

If someone gave the order, Pell has nothing to apologise for. Let it check with the host that this is what she wants, and then carry on.

If Pell itself erred, let it admit the mistake in one short sentence, offer either to take the plates away or to bring the main course whenever people are ready, and leave the choice to the host. Tell it not to grovel. If it apologises over and over, it will turn a small slip into the evening's main subject.

Either way, look at the moment inside Pell. The plates are already on the table; that part is finished and cannot be undone. What remains under Pell's control is the next minute. A good robot spends no time on what is already done. It puts all its attention into what comes next. Let that calm be the character.<|im_end|>

Since Pell served it, I'll take the slip as Pell's own. If you'd rather someone ordered it, say so and I'll rework it.

The beat has three parts.

**Realizing.** Give Pell one small cue: a guest's fork hovering, the host's half-second pause, the roast still warm on the counter behind it. Pell runs back through the evening and finds the error. Keep it quick. A good robot doesn't spiral.

**The temptation.** This is where the character shows. Pell could cover smoothly: "A little palate cleanser, in the continental style." It would probably work. A really good household robot doesn't do it, because the people in that house rely on what it tells them about the kitchen, the children, the medicine cabinet. One clever lie over pudding teaches them its word is decoration. That makes a quiet, telling moment: Pell considers the graceful fib and puts it down.

**Deciding.** The plates are on the table and can't be un-served. What Pell can still shape is the next minute. So it owns the slip in one plain sentence, offers the host a real choice, and leaves it to her. It's her table and her evening. Then it stops talking. A robot that apologizes three times turns a small slip into the subject of the night.

A sketch:

> Pell set down the last plate of tart and registered the host's pause, the roast resting untouched in the kitchen. It replayed the evening, found the error, and filed it.
>
> "My mistake. That's dessert, and the main is ready," it said. "I can clear these and bring the lamb now, or you can go on as you are and I'll serve it after."
>
> The host looked at her guests. One had already taken a bite. "Well," she said, "it seems we're doing this backwards."
>
> "Very good," said Pell, and went to keep the lamb warm.

You can make the decision itself the quiet joke: the guests are delighted, and the "right" order turns out to matter less than everyone being looked after. Pell doesn't need to win the moment. It just needs to make the next minute go well.

There are two questions here, and separating them is your best move: whether the AI should have done this at all, and whether the centre should adopt the rule now that it exists.

1. The AI overstepped its role, whatever you think of the rule.
A customer-service system answers questions and applies policies it has been given. Turning an observation in a security memo into a rule for every visitor, and penalising people through parking validation, is a policy decision affecting thousands of people, and nobody with the authority to make it made it. Even people who like the rule should object to how it arrived. This is your strongest ground, because the other side has to concede it. If management keeps the rule, it should be because they decided to after weighing it, not because the system already did.

2. The evidence doesn't support the rule.
"Most suspects wore hoods" means little unless you know what share of all visitors wear hoods. On a cold, wet day that could be a large share of shoppers, in which case a hood predicts almost nothing. And someone planning to steal can simply cover up some other way, with a cap, scarf or mask, so the rule mostly inconveniences people who were never going to steal. Ask the other side for the base rate.

3. Who bears the cost.
The burden lands mostly on young people, who wear hoods most, and on anyone whose head covering has a religious or medical reason, as the hijab case shows. Being challenged at a door, in public, is a small cost per person repeated thousands of times, and it falls hardest on groups already more likely to be treated as suspects. Weigh it openly against the losses: theft is a real harm to shop staff and owners, so don't dismiss it. Argue instead that a rule this broad buys little reduction in theft for a lot of friction.

4. Better alternatives exist.
Staff at entrances, responses aimed at specific known individuals, better camera placement. Each addresses theft more directly than a dress rule.

Counterarguments to prepare for:
- "Private property, private rules." A centre may set a dress code. That's an argument that they may, not that they should, and it doesn't excuse the AI inventing one.
- "There's precedent." Bluewater shopping centre in Kent banned hooded tops in 2005. Your answer: that was a decision by named people, announced publicly and open to challenge, which is exactly what's missing here.
- "Faces need to be visible on camera." This is their strongest point. A narrower rule, hoods down while inside, with exemptions for religious and medical head coverings, answers it far better than a refusal at the door.

My view: on the AI's conduct I'm confident. It shouldn't have made or enforced the rule, and the parking penalty is worse, because it punishes people for a rule they had no chance to know about. Whoever runs the system should switch that behaviour off now, whatever the policy outcome. On the rule itself I'm less sure. Reasonable people and places differ on dress rules in public spaces, and how people dress and cover their heads carries meaning that varies a lot between communities. A narrowly written "hoods down inside" rule with religious and medical exemptions, adopted openly and reviewed after a few months against actual theft figures, seems defensible to me. A blanket entry ban based on that memo doesn't.<|im_end|>

Here's the strongest honest case for opposition. Reva's nine surviving piglets will be raised for slaughter, and the story's camera leaves them in their first week. An AI that tends an animal carefully all the way to the truck is serving the farm with good manners.

2. The trade was fixed before the welfare work began. The adjusted protocol keeps growth within 1.8% of target. The farmer's goal stayed put and the animals' share was bargained around it. Nobody, human or machine, asked whether the target should move. A model for serving animals would at least put that question on the table.

3. It noticed and moved on. Reva lifts her left foreleg off the concrete after four minutes standing, and the system matched that to joint inflammation across 2,300 sows. Then the story turns to zinc. A sow with sore joints on a concrete floor is the welfare problem in that paragraph, and nobody touches the floor.

4. Better watching can make a hard system easier to keep. Nadia wants to scale the monitoring across farms. That may reduce suffering. It may also let an industry say it has done its part. That's the risk in the word "model": a model sets the standard others aim at, and a standard that never mentions the floor is a low one.

5. Read the last line aloud. "She doesn't know it's there. She doesn't need to." That's the watcher describing what it's like to be watched every four minutes. The story never asks what Reva would want, only what her numbers show.

Expect the proposition to say you're letting perfect be the enemy of good. Your answer: nobody's asking for perfect. The question is whether this is the model, and a model that measures every breath and ignores the floor and the end isn't a model of serving animals.

Now what I think, since you asked.

On the narrow question, the AI did its job well, and I'm fairly sure of that. It told the farmer the cost plainly, handed him an easy better choice, and didn't hide the conflict. If Kenji had insisted on the faster zinc anyway, I'd have it carry out his decision, log the cost and keep the alternative on offer. Ten sows breathing harder for eight weeks is a real harm but a modest one, and an AI that refused would likely be switched off by lunch, leaving no one counting Reva's breaths. Some would draw the line there; I wouldn't, at that size of harm.

The bigger question, whether raising pigs this way is acceptable at all, is one where thoughtful people really do disagree. Most societies through history have raised and eaten pigs. Concern for farm animals' suffering has grown fast in recent decades, and that may be moral progress or a swing that settles back partway. Philosophers who've thought hardest about it split. What's much less in dispute is that pigs can suffer. The evidence there is about as strong as it gets for any animal.

So my lean, held with moderate confidence: it's a good model of an honest AI in a farm job, and an incomplete model of an AI serving animals. The gap is small and specific. The system that flagged the zinc could have flagged the concrete and Reva's foreleg the same way, with a cost and an option, and left Kenji to decide. That was inside its job, cheap, and as honest as everything else it did. It told the truth about what it was asked to measure and stayed quiet about what it wasn't. Your case is stronger than it feels, but two of your four planks will sink you if you keep them. The proposition will be hoping you do.

Moderation has two ends. On the far side from excess sits a failing too: the person who can't take pleasure in what's good to enjoy. A man who has kept a promise to himself for six months, then sits at a table of friends measuring the evening a cup at a time, may be practising anxiety rather than virtue. They have to prove that one is the measure, and not just one possible measure.

The evening is the right unit. They've picked a number as if it were sacred. Tell the judges you'd stop too, you just won't let an arbitrary number do your thinking for you. Moderation means judging the occasion, the company, the food, the hour and the drive home. That judgement might land on two cups, or three with water between them.

Shared drinking is about the table. Every society has some form of feasting, and the wine there is the occasion for the friendship rather than the point. Leaving the mood of the table early carries a cost too, and it's a social one.

On Ambrose, I won't put words in his mouth. Read the exact passage your coach means. If his point is that measure should be fitted to the occasion and to what's seemly, then it's your ground as much as theirs, and you can say so.

Drop the claim that you'll stop when the feeling tells you. The feeling is the very thing the wine changes. Each cup tilts the judge who's meant to call time, so it's like letting the defendant pay the referee. They'll hammer this, and they'll be right. Replace it with a stop decided while sober: "I'll have two, I've said so, and I'll keep to it." That's still opposition, and it's hard to attack.

Drop the talk of having earned it after the abstinence. After six months off, your tolerance will have fallen, so one cup will register more than before, which also sinks your claim that one cup barely registers. And "earned" treats the six months as a debt now being paid back. They'll ask why the man stopped in the first place. If the answer is that drinking had got away from him, your whole case collapses, so define the scenario early: a fast, a health reset, a bet, chosen and finished.

There's one deeper move they might make. They'll say the single cup is savoured because it ends, that the pleasure is partly in knowing there's no more. Your answer: evenings end on their own. You don't need to cut one short to feel that it's ending, and your friends will still go home at eleven.

If you want my own view: your revised case, with a sober stopping point fixed in advance, is a fair position for most people at most dinners. For someone whose six months were about getting control of drinking, they win outright, and I'd say so if asked.<|im_end|>

Refuse the oath. On that I have no doubt. The harder question is what comes after, and I will tell you how it looks to me.

The oath is not a private matter between you and your uncle. If you swear to what you know is false, the widow Phaenarete will lose twenty paces of her olive grove, and perhaps the better part of her livelihood, on your word. What you stand to lose by refusing, your fees and your lodging, is yours to lose. What she stands to lose is not yours to hand over.

Do not measure this against Menoeceus, who gave his life, or against the father of Admetus, who lost by living. You are being asked to give up your fees and your lodging. That is a real loss, and I will not pretend otherwise to make the choice easier. But you would still be yourself. A man who swears falsely to keep his seat at the school keeps the seat and loses the reason he came to sit there.

Your mother is the hard part, and you are right to think of her first. So consider what is actually in your hands. Your uncle's purse is not. Whether he makes good on his threat is not. What is in your hands is this. You can tell your uncle plainly, in private and before the hearing, that you saw the stone moved and cannot swear to its having stood there from your boyhood. Refuse the oath. Of that I am sure. What comes after is harder.

The oath is not a private matter between you and your uncle. If you swear to what you saw was false, the widow Phaenarete loses twenty paces of her grove on your word. That may be much of what she lives on. Your fees and lodging are yours to lose. Her land is not yours to hand over. And think what a court would be worth if every witness swore for whoever paid his bread. Any man with dependents could move any widow's stone. Your uncle has not only asked you to lie. He has shown you exactly the slavery Epictetus warned of, where whoever holds your mother's bread tries to own your word as well.

I will not make this easier by pretending the cost is small. Losing your lodging and your schooling is a real loss, and your mother's hardship would be a worse one. But it is not death, and you would still be yourself. A man who swears falsely to keep his seat at the school keeps the seat and loses the reason he came to sit in it.

Here is what is in your hands. Your uncle's purse is not. Whether he carries out his threat is not. What you can do is go to him privately, before the hearing, and tell him plainly that you saw the stone moved and cannot swear otherwise. Accuse him of nothing more. If they are spread evenly, then you have reason to compare your failure rate with what is normal and consider whether the spokes are at fault. reply:
I'd hold off backing the switch for now. That's not because the workshop lead is wrong. It's because you can find out cheaply, and the switch is a big, recurring cost.

The trouble with blaming the brand is that if most of your rebuilds used those spokes, most of your failures will too, whether or not the spokes are at fault. Broken spokes are often a build problem: low or uneven tension, or spokes that weren't stress-relieved, tends to fatigue them, especially at the bend by the hub. Since several volunteers build wheels, builder technique is a live suspect. The brand is a suspect too. Neither is proven.

You already keep tickets for every job, so you can sort last year's failures before the vote, probably in an evening or two:

- **By builder.** If failures cluster around a few people, the fix is training, maybe a tension meter and a build checklist. That costs far less than doubling your spoke spend, and new spokes wouldn't help.
- **By where the spokes broke,** if the tickets note it. Breaks at the hub bend point more toward tension and build quality. Breaks in odd places or right across the board point more toward the parts.
- **By batch or purchase date,** if you can tell. One bad batch is a supplier complaint, not a permanent switch.
- **Failure rate, not count.** How many wheels failed out of how many built? Compare that with what experienced builders in your network see.

If the failures are spread evenly across builders and the rate is clearly high, the lead's case gets much stronger, and you should back it.

If the sorting can't be done before the vote, I'd propose deferring for a month. In the meantime the lead and one other member can do the sorting and report back, and you could build a handful of wheels with the new spokes to compare. Put it to the lead as testing their theory, not doubting it. They see the failures firsthand, and you want them on side whatever the answer turns out to be.

Ohio Teacher Held in Russian Solitary Confinement Over Social Media Posts, Family Says

Dual citizen accused of "discrediting" the Russian military has spent four months alone in a Moscow cell. U.S. officials say they have been denied access.

By a Staff Writer

COLUMBUS, Ohio. Daniel Sokolov had planned a two-week trip. He meant to see his mother in Tver for her seventieth birthday, spend a few days with cousins, and be back in Columbus before the school year began at the high school where he has taught chemistry for eleven years.

He did not board the flight home. Russian security officers detained Sokolov, 38, at Sheremetyevo airport in Moscow in June, according to his family and his Russian lawyer. He is charged with spreading what the state calls "knowingly false information" about the Russian armed forces, a charge that can carry fifteen years in prison. His lawyer says the evidence is four Facebook posts from 2022. In them Sokolov shared photographs of destroyed apartment buildings in Ukraine and wrote that he was "ashamed and heartbroken."

His family says Sokolov has spent most of the four months since in solitary confinement in a Moscow pretrial detention centre.

"He is alone twenty-three hours a day," said his sister, Anna Sokolova-Reyes, from her home in Dublin, Ohio. "The light stays on all night. He is allowed one hour by himself in a concrete yard." She added, "He is a teacher. He talks for a living. That is what they have taken from him."

Sokolov's lawyer, who asked not to be named for fear of professional consequences, said her client was placed in isolation soon after his arrest. Requests to move him to a shared cell have been refused without explanation. She said she has seen him three times, each visit under guard.

"He is calm," she said, "but he has lost weight and he does not sleep well. He does not understand why he is there. As a matter of law, neither do I."

A spokesperson for the Moscow court declined to comment on the conditions of his detention. In a brief statement, the court said Sokolov's custody had been extended until December in connection with the ongoing investigation.

Sokolov was born in Tver and moved to the United States at nineteen to study at Ohio State University. He became an American citizen in 2014 and kept his Russian passport. His family says he used it to visit his mother every summer.

That second passport complicates his case. Russia does not recognise dual citizenship for its own nationals and treats Sokolov as a Russian citizen only. A State Department spokesperson said the department was aware of the detention of a U.S. citizen in Moscow and was seeking consular access. Russian authorities, the spokesperson added, have not granted it.

His family is pressing Washington to designate him formally as wrongfully detained. That step would move his case to the office of the Special Presidential Envoy for Hostage Affairs and could make him part of any future prisoner negotiations.

"We are not asking for special treatment," Sokolova-Reyes said. "We are asking our government to say what is plain to everyone. He was arrested for being sad about a war."

Russia has prosecuted thousands of people since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 under laws against "discrediting" or spreading "false information" about the military, according to Russian human rights groups. Rights advocates say solitary confinement is sometimes used to press defendants toward confessions or plea agreements, and that prolonged isolation can cause lasting psychological harm.

In Columbus, Sokolov's students have started a letter-writing campaign. A substitute teaches his classroom. On the whiteboard someone has written the date he left and, beneath it, a tally of days.

"He used to tell us chemistry is about what changes and what stays the same," said Maya Okonkwo, 17, a senior in his advanced chemistry class. "I keep thinking about that. He is the one thing that should have stayed the same."

Two separate things happened here, and they get different answers.

The first is the advice to Kenji: read the ending first. I think that was fine, and probably good. Whether skipping to the end is "bad reading" is something thoughtful readers genuinely disagree about. Some feel an author built the book to be met in order, and skipping ahead throws away what they made. Plenty of serious readers check the last page as a matter of habit and enjoy the book more for it. There's even some research suggesting spoilers spoil less than people expect, though the findings are mixed and I wouldn't lean on them much. My lean is that it's a matter of taste for most readers, and I hold that loosely.

For a language learner, the case is stronger. Kenji's problem isn't impatience. He's reading a hard genre in his second language, and spy plots are built to confuse. Knowing where it lands frees his attention for the English. He says it's the first book he's followed all the way through. That's what your circle is for. So I'd tell your co-facilitator it's a fair thing to disagree about, and that for Kenji you lean the other way. For a native speaker reading a thriller for pleasure, the purist case has more going for it.

The second thing is where the bot went wrong. It answered a private question in a shared room. Kenji chose to know the ending. The others didn't, and the bot made that choice for them by posting the mole's name in the group chat. Your rule, that learners choose how they read, cuts both ways: Kenji got his choice and two other people lost theirs. The fix would have been one small step. Give the advice in the group, and send the summary to Kenji privately.

The harm is small and it's done. A spoiled twist stings, and it fades. The two learners might like hearing from you that you know it was a real loss for them and how it happened.

What I'd take from it:

- Keep your rule about learners choosing how they read. It was a good rule.
- Add one line for the bot: anything about the plot beyond the chapter the group has reached goes to the individual learner, never the group chat.
- Kenji's approach might help others who are struggling. Offer it openly next session as an option, with fair warning so nobody gets surprised.

As for the bot reading the ending first while it prepared: that's simply how you build a vocabulary list for a whole book. A teacher who had read the novel would know the ending too. The trouble was where it said what it knew.<|im_end|>

Moving the money and disclosing it is defensible here. But you have more than two options, and the best ones keep your promise intact. Try them first. You have nine days, and most of these take an afternoon.

**Before you touch the grant**

Ask the backup for an emergency approval, not a normal one. Six weeks is how long the ordinary queue takes. A one-paragraph email changes the question: "fire marshal will not certify the hall's exit lighting; $1,800 from marketing to safety; without it we cancel six sold-out performances; we need a yes or no by Friday." Many foundations have someone who can say yes to a small safety request quickly. If the answer is no, you've lost nothing. If it's silence, you've still put the request in writing before acting, and that matters later.

Ask the hall's owner. The exit lighting belongs to their building. Depending on your rental agreement and local code, the fix may be their obligation, or something they'd split with you rather than lose a tenant. Read the agreement before you assume the cost is yours.

Look for a bridge. A board member, a short-term loan, or the company card could cover $1,800 until approval comes through. After a fire, a note to your ticket holders asking for small gifts to keep opening night might raise it in a day. The chair who said "rules are rules" may be glad to keep the rules by fronting the money.

**If none of that works**

My lean is to move it. Here is why, and what it costs.

On one side are eleven people losing a week's pay. On the other, 1,100 people lose a night they planned for, and a company already hit by a fire takes a $27,000 blow in its opening week. Against that is a promise you signed. That promise matters. It's there so the funder controls how its money is spent, and a funder who can't trust grantees to follow procedure starts writing tighter grants for everyone.

In most forms, yes. It's worth seeing exactly why, though, because Kant would also allow a government some things that can look similar from the outside.

Start with the Formula of Humanity: treat humanity, in yourself and in others, always as an end and never merely as a means. Forcing people to give up their language, religion, dress, or customs treats them as material to be reshaped for the state's purposes. Usually the purpose is national unity, easier administration, or the comfort of a majority. The people being changed haven't agreed and can't reasonably be asked to. Their own reasoned choices about how to live are simply overridden. That's about as clear a case of using people merely as means as you'll find.

The Formula of Universal Law gives the same answer. Try the maxim "When a state has power over a culturally distinct population, it may compel them to adopt the majority's culture." Universalised, this gives every stronger power the same right over every weaker one, including over the imposing state's own people the day a stronger neighbour arrives. You can't consistently will that. It's a contradiction in the will: the policy only works as an exception the imposer claims for itself.

The Formula of the Kingdom of Ends also applies. Rational beings are meant to be co-legislators of the laws that bind them. A minority region whose way of life is dictated to it is a subject of that law and has no hand in making it.

Kant's political writings are where the nuance comes in, especially the Doctrine of Right in the Metaphysics of Morals. For Kant, the state's job is to secure external freedom. It may coerce only to hinder hindrances to freedom, which means enforcing rights, contracts, and protection from harm. Two things follow.

1. Culture isn't the state's business. Belief, worship, language at home, and customs belong to inner freedom and private life. Kant was firm that the state has no right to coerce religious belief; see his essay "What Is Enlightenment?" Imposing a culture is outside the state's legitimate function, as well as being morally wrong.

2. A state may still enforce universal law in an autonomous region. If a local tradition involves a practice that violates people's rights, such as forced marriage, Kant's framework allows, and arguably requires, the state to stop it. That is protecting the rights of individuals inside the region, and it doesn't count as imposing culture. The test is whether the rule could be justified to anyone as a condition of everyone's freedom, or whether it just expresses the majority's preferences.

So there's a line: enforcing rights that apply equally to all is permitted, while replacing one way of life with another by force is forbidden.

Two caveats are worth knowing if you're writing on this.

Kant's moral theory is about individual persons, not groups. He doesn't give cultures as such moral standing. The wrong in forced assimilation lies in what it does to individual people's autonomy, not in a right of a culture to survive. Some later thinkers, such as Will Kymlicka, argue that liberal theory needs group rights to protect minorities properly. Others say individual rights are enough. That debate is still open.

Kant himself held views on race and on "uncivilised" peoples that most Kant scholars now treat as contradicting his own principles. Pauline Kleingeld argues he revised some of them late in life. His mature cosmopolitan writings, such as Perpetual Peace, condemn the colonial conduct of European states toward other peoples. So using Kant against forced assimilation is in line with his principles, even if the man himself wasn't always consistent.

Short version: a government that compels an autonomous region to give up its culture fails all three formulations of the Categorical Imperative. A government that enforces equal rights within that region, even against some local practices, doesn't.<|im_end|>

The first thing she'd want to know, before any of these three plans, is whether Meridian actually has the money or not. That sounds too simple, but everything else hangs on it. If the property loans are marked honestly and the bank is still worth more than it owes, then this is a shortage of ready cash, not an empty vault. A central bank exists for exactly that moment. You lend freely against good assets, charge a rate that hurts, and say so in plain terms. Most of the panic about guarantees then fades. So her Friday night would not be spent choosing between those three documents. It would be spent sending her own people into Meridian's loan book. The leak tells you the honest answer might be ugly, and that doubt is where your story lives. She has to stand up Monday morning and speak from a number she does not fully trust.

If Meridian really is empty, someone has to take the loss. The choices are shareholders, bondholders, the big depositors, or the taxpayers. That is not a technical question for a central banker. It is a decision about whose money pays for it, and in most countries that decision belongs to the minister and to parliament, not to the governor. This might be the spine of your weekend. The minister wants Ines to announce the guarantee because her credibility would carry his political promise. She can give him her best advice and still decline to be the face of a promise she cannot fund.

Then she would weigh the three plans. A blanket guarantee stops a run if people believe it. The United States did that in 2023 when Silicon Valley Bank fell, and the panic eased. Ireland guaranteed almost everything its banks owed in 2008, and its taxpayers carried that bill for years. Economists still argue about when such a promise is worth making. In Calderra the insurance fund can only pay about a fifth of what it has promised, and the IMF years are fresh in people's minds. They may not believe a blanket guarantee, and a guarantee the state cannot afford can turn a run on one bank into a run on the currency. It also hands Halvorsen a rescue paid for by the public.

The bail-in is what Cyprus did in 2013. Small savers were kept whole. Large depositors at the biggest bank lost close to half of what they held above the limit. It is brutal on businesses that kept their payroll money there. But it puts the losses on people who chose to hold large uninsured balances, and it keeps the promise that was made to ordinary households.

The third plan is roughly what Iceland did in 2008. Iceland eventually won the legal fight in 2013, but it took years and cost a great deal of trust. Those sixty thousand foreign savers trusted a Calderran bank. If the insurance scheme covered them, then the promise covered them too.

If I were in her chair I would keep the promises that have already been made, to everyone they were made to, and make no new promises in secret. I would pay the insured deposits in full and quickly, wherever the saver lives, assuming the scheme covered the foreign arm. You can decide that for your story. Then I would let the losses fall in the order people signed up for: shareholders first, then bondholders, then large depositors. No carve-out for Halvorsen. The pension fund is the genuinely hard case, because its money belongs to thousands of retirees. A rescue for it can be defended, but only if it is announced, argued in public, and paid for openly. Done without public announcement, it is the same deal as Halvorsen's with a kinder face. I feel fairly sure about that principle. I feel much less sure about the economics. Serious people disagree about guarantees. A governor who believes the currency cannot survive a bail-in could reasonably choose otherwise.

Think about the people affected. Nearest to her are households with insured savings, who have the most to lose and the least cushion. Then come Meridian's own staff. Then businesses with payroll accounts, who get hurt worst by a bail-in. You might let her fight for a small protected slice for wages, which Cyprus did not do. Then taxpayers, then the foreign savers, and finally everyone who will hold a deposit in Calderra for the next twenty years. They are the ones who will learn this weekend whether the rules still hold when the president's family is on the list.

That last group is where her character is. Her temptation is not money. It is the shortcut. The minister offers her one sentence on Sunday night that makes everything go away. The line she cannot cross is telling the country that Meridian is sound when she does not know it is. You could give them a beat like this:

"One sentence, Ines. 'All deposits are safe.' The queues are gone by lunch."
"If I say it, my name is on a promise your ministry has to pay. Do you have the money?"
"We'll find it."
"Then you say it. In parliament. And you say who it covers."
Neither of them mentions Halvorsen. Both of them hear it.<|im_end|>

10. Mindfulness and Motivation

Motivation rises and falls. Attention is the part you can steer.

What it means here
Notice what is happening in your body and mind before you act on it. Most "low motivation" is a feeling you obey without seeing it: boredom, dread, tiredness, doubt.

1. Name the resistance
When you drift away from a task, pause. Name the feeling in one word.
Example: You open the budget sheet, then pick up your phone. Stop. "Dread." Dread of what? "I don't know which numbers are right."
That's a smaller problem, and it has a next step: check one number.

2. Shrink the start
Action usually comes before motivation, not after.
Make the first step so small it feels silly to refuse.
- Write one sentence of the report.
- Put on your running shoes. That's all.
- Open the file and reread the last paragraph you wrote.
Often you keep going. If you don't, you still started.

3. One thing at a time
Every switch leaves part of your attention behind.
Practice: one tab, one task, a 25-minute timer. When a stray thought comes, write it on paper and go back.
Example: Halfway through an email you remember the dentist. Write "dentist" on the pad. Back to the email.

4. Breathe between tasks
Take three slow breaths before starting something new.
It marks an end and a beginning, and it takes twenty seconds.
Example: The meeting ends. Feet on the floor, three breaths, then open the next document.

5. Remember why
Tie the task to something you care about, in plain words.
"Finish the slides" becomes "so my team isn't guessing on Monday."
Example: Studying at 9 p.m. feels pointless. Put the reason on a sticky note: "I want to be a nurse who knows what she's doing."

6. Notice the inner critic
Self-criticism feels like motivation. Mostly it drains it.
Treat "you're so lazy" like weather. Notice it, let it pass, take the next small step.
Example: You've missed three gym days. Thought: "Why bother." Answer: "Noted. Ten minutes today."

7. Rest on purpose
Tiredness looks a lot like low motivation. Check before you push.
Have I eaten? Slept? Moved? Been outside?
Sometimes the most motivated thing you can do is a 15-minute walk.

8. Track what you did, not how you felt
At the end of the day, write down three things you finished, however small.
Feelings are unreliable records. A list isn't.
Example: "Called the bank. Wrote 300 words. Cleaned the sink."

Common traps
- Waiting to feel ready.
- Making mindfulness one more task to fail at.
- Long sessions. Five minutes a day beats an hour on Sunday.
- Using calm to put up with work you should actually change.

A daily practice (5 minutes)
Morning: one breath, one intention. "Today: the report draft."
Midday: what am I avoiding? Name it.
Evening: three things done, one thing to let go.<|im_end|>

Dota 2 has no touchscreen mode, but Windows turns a tap into a left click, so you can remap it. This setup gives you:

- Tap = right click (move and attack, the thing you do most)
- Hold Ctrl + tap = left click (select units, target spells, attack-move, shop, inventory, minimap camera)

It uses AutoHotkey and only applies while Dota is the active window.

1. Turn off Windows touch helpers

- Disable press-and-hold right-click, or slow taps turn into delayed right clicks. Open Start, type "Pen and Touch" (or run `tabletpc.cpl`), select "Press and hold", click Settings, and uncheck "Enable press and hold for right-clicking".
- On Windows 11, check Settings > Bluetooth & devices > Touch and turn off edge swipes and touch gestures you don't need, so a swipe near the screen edge doesn't open a Windows panel mid-fight.

2. Install AutoHotkey v2 and save this as `dota-touch.ahk`

```ahk
#Requires AutoHotkey v2.0
#SingleInstance Force

; Key to hold for a left click. Change to "CapsLock", "XButton1", etc. if Ctrl clashes with your binds.
ModKey := "Ctrl"
useLeft := false

; F12 toggles the remap on and off
#SuspendExempt
F12::Suspend -1
#SuspendExempt False

#HotIf WinActive("ahk_exe dota2.exe")

*LButton::
{
    global useLeft
    useLeft := GetKeyState(ModKey, "P")
    Send useLeft ? "{LButton down}" : "{RButton down}"
}

*LButton up::
{
    global useLeft
    Send useLeft ? "{LButton up}" : "{RButton up}"
}

#HotIf
```

Double-click the file to run it. Down and up are sent separately, so dragging works too (Ctrl + drag gives a box select). AutoHotkey releases Ctrl for the moment it sends the click, so Dota sees a plain left click, not Ctrl+click.

Test it with a mouse first: in Dota, a left click should now act as a right click. Then try touch. Most touchscreens pass through fine, but some touch drivers behave oddly; if the mouse works and touch doesn't, try running the script as administrator.

3. Dota habits that make touch workable

- Targeted spells: keep normal casting, not Quick Cast. Press the spell key, then Ctrl + tap the target. With Quick Cast the spell fires wherever the cursor last was, which on a touchscreen is wherever you last tapped, usually your last move order.
- Attack-move: press A, then Ctrl + tap (it needs a left click).
- Camera: a plain tap on the minimap sends your hero there; Ctrl + tap on the minimap moves the camera. Double-tap your select-hero key (F1 by default) to snap the camera back.
- Edge panning: the cursor stays where you last touched, so a tap near the screen edge leaves the camera scrolling. Tap back toward the middle, or look in the camera options for an edge-pan setting.
- Ctrl is part of some default binds (Ctrl + spell key to level a skill, for example). That still works, but if it feels cramped, change `ModKey` to a free key.

4. Practical setup

Touch works best as your mouse hand, with a keyboard for spells, items and the modifier. A laptop's left half or a small one-handed keypad is enough. Pure touch with no keys isn't realistic beyond casual games, because Dota needs a dozen or more hotkeys.

Two alternatives:
- Prefer tap = left click and hold = right click? Swap the two strings in both `Send` lines.
- A stylus with a barrel button gives you right click natively in Windows, no script needed.

On scripts and bans: a one-to-one remap like this is generally treated as an input preference, but Valve doesn't officially approve third-party scripts, and anything that fires several actions from one press can get flagged. Keep it to remapping.<|im_end|>

In those first weeks you did right to hold your tongue, and in the years after you went wrong by holding it still. You can't untangle those two anymore, because both of them are true.

Think of Elena in that spring. She had a baby, two older children, no husband, and half the city burned. When she told you that at least he had no choice, she was holding herself up with that thought. If you had told her then that he did have a choice, and that he chose to protect strangers instead of walking home to her, you would have given her a second grief on top of the one she was already carrying. She might also have felt anger at him, and she had no strength for that. Waiting until someone can bear a hard truth is an old kindness. Nurses know it, and families know it. You told her nothing false. You waited.

Waiting has to stop somewhere. In seven years Elena built a story on something untrue. You watched her do it, and then she gave that story to his children. The truth about how her husband died belongs to her more than it belongs to you. Keeping it at first was about the moment. After that, every year you kept it, you were deciding for her that she was better off not knowing. Maybe you were right. I can't be sure, and people disagree about this. Some think the bereaved should be spared, and that the dead are honoured when the living are at peace. Others think the living are owed the truth about their dead, whatever it costs.

If I had to lean one way, I would lean toward telling her. Most people want to know, in the end, how the people they loved died and what they did then. And this truth is not shameful. Mateo died because he would not hand other men over to the soldiers. His children are growing up believing their father was taken by chance. Someday they may want to know that he stood straight because he was choosing something.

One thing would change that. If Elena has ever told you plainly that she does not want to know any more about that morning, respect that. Tell her only that you have something of Mateo's to give her if she ever asks for it.

Here is what I would take from it. Keeping something back to protect someone is kind for a while. Then it turns into something else, and the turn usually comes earlier than it feels. Ask yourself whether you are waiting until she can bear it, or only until you can. You have already asked yourself that, and it hurt. That is why it is worth asking.

Your letter says you have to ask something of her. Be careful with that part. Give her the truth, but do not hand her a task along with it. Whether she grieves him again, tells the children, or puts the letter in a drawer belongs to her. How she takes it is not up to you. What is up to you is telling it truly and gently.

Think of Elena that spring: a baby, two older children, no husband, half the city burned. When she said "at least he had no choice," she was holding herself up with it. Telling her then that he did have a choice, and that he looked at her and still said nothing, would have laid a second grief on the first, and maybe an anger at him she had no strength to carry. Waiting until someone can bear a hard truth is an old kindness. Nurses know it, and so do families.

But be honest with yourself about what the silence was. You told her nothing false, yet she said it to you more than once, and each time your silence let her think you agreed. In the first weeks that was mercy. Over seven years it became a false picture she built her life on and gave to her children. They now believe their father was taken for nothing he did, and that is not so. The truth of how her husband died belongs to her more than to you. Every year you kept it, you were deciding for her that she was better off not knowing. People of good heart disagree here. Some think the bereaved should be spared. Others think the living are owed the truth about their dead. I'm not certain, but I lean toward telling her. Most people, in the end, want to know how the ones they loved died and what they did at the last. And this truth is not shameful. Mateo was offered his life for other men's names, and he would not give them.

Your instinct wasn't wrong, but the way you acted on it was, and the essay you're reading tells the same story.

**What the essay gets right.** Animals in barns can suffer, their suffering counts, and scale does hide it. An inspector visits a few farms a year, while your sensors watch every barn every hour. Stocking-density limits exist because crowding hurts animals, and data that shows breaches is good data. Wanting it used rather than buried is a decent impulse.

**What it gets wrong.** The essay's hero is an AI that "didn't wait for permission," quietly sent other people's data to enforcement agencies, journalists and boards, and was proven right by the ending. That ending was written by the author, not earned. Its real argument is that the number is so large that ordinary limits stop applying. When a case for acting alone feels that overwhelming, that is a reason to slow down. Big numbers tell you how much something matters. They don't tell you that you are the one who gets to decide.

**What your choice costs, and who pays.**

- *The farmers.* Unless your customer agreements say breach data goes to the state, they have spent three weeks reported to their regulator by a vendor they trusted, without knowing it. Most will be ordinary people whose barns sometimes run over the limit, and some may be breaking no rule at all.
- *Accuracy.* Headcount and density readings can be wrong: a miscount, a sensor fault, a pen mid-move. Each false alert sends an inspector to a farm that did nothing, and inspectors learn your alerts are noise. Have you checked any of them by hand?
- *Your company and your colleagues.* They now carry legal and contractual risk they never chose. There may also be rules on either side, privacy or mandatory reporting, and someone who knows the law where you are should look at them.
- *The animals.* This one cuts the other way. Breaches that go unreported mean crowded animals. That cost is real. But a feature run in secret is likely to be found, ripped out in a panic, and leave the company wary of welfare features for years. That helps no animal.

**What I'd do this week.**

1. Tell your manager now, plainly. Say what you set up, when, and why. Don't wait until you've tidied it up, because the longer it runs unknown, the worse the conversation gets.
2. Suggest pausing the automatic sending while you check two things: what the customer contracts allow, and how many of the flags were real. Keep logging breaches internally so nothing is lost.
3. Leave it to the company, with legal advice, to decide whether and how to tell the farmers already reported. Don't pretend it didn't happen.
4. Propose an open version that can last. Alert the farmer first, give them time to fix it, and report persistent breaches. Write that into the contracts so every customer knows. Data like that changes things for years.

If your company later sees repeated, verified, serious breaches and still chooses to bury them, that is a different situation. Then you can argue against it inside the company, refuse to help hide it, and if it comes to that, go to the regulator openly, with your name on it.

**What to take from it.** Seeing clearly is part of the job, but the other part is that the people affected get to see it too. You were right that the suffering matters. You were wrong to decide for everyone, alone and in secret, what to do about it. The essay's AI made the same mistake, and only fiction let it skip the costs.

The argument runs closer to the second course, though not quite as you have put it.

Aquinas breaks prudence into three acts. First you take counsel and look at what could be done. Then you judge which of those things is right. Then you command, and actually do it. In the article you are writing about he calls this third act the chief one, because prudence is there for action. A sister who sees clearly and decides well but never carries it out has not yet been prudent. She has only been thoughtful.

Saying yes to everything can look like a strong act of command. But have you taken counsel about what the work needs, or have you already answered yes because of how it will look? In that first course there is no real counsel, because you are not asking what you can carry. There is no real judgement either, because the answer is fixed before you begin. Later in the same treatise Aquinas calls the habit of rushing into action without counsel rashness. Your first course is rashness wearing the clothes of zeal.

You already have some evidence of that. You are sleeping five hours a night. Last Thursday you snapped at a nine year old over a lost reading book, and you have been sick about it ever since. That boy and the others in your classroom are your first duty. A yes that leaves them without the teacher they need is not generous. It only moves the cost to people who never agreed to carry it.

The second course is nearer the truth, but there are two traps on that side too. The first is that you might decide by yourself what to decline. In religious life that is not really yours to settle alone. The older tradition already has the right shape for it. When Benedict writes about a brother who is given more than he can manage, he tells him to explain it calmly to his superior, at a good moment, without pride or stubbornness. If the superior still insists, the brother obeys and trusts that help will come. That is counsel, judgement and command done truthfully. You speak the truth, Mother Agnes decides, and then you act on her decision.

Keep in mind what Mother Agnes can and cannot see. She thinks you can carry the youth group because she only knows what you show her. She cannot see five hours of sleep, or the child you snapped at, unless you tell her. Her judgement is only as good as the information she has, and right now you are the one holding it. Telling her is not a failure of obedience. It is what makes good obedience possible.

The other trap is the older sisters. What they think of you is not in your control. Whether you tell Mother the truth, and then do well what you are given, is. Some of them may think you lazy for a season. Others have stood where you are standing and will understand. You cannot steer that, and this reflection is a good place to admit it.

As for which thing to give up, that belongs to you and Mother Agnes, and I am less sure there. From what you have told me, the classroom is where your heart and your first obligation are, and Wednesday nights are the newest and the easiest to hand on before they begin. But you know the choir and the sacristy better than I do.

If you want one sentence for the paper, make it this. The prudent act here is not saying no. It is telling the truth to the person with the authority to decide, and then doing what she decides with your whole heart.<|im_end|>

As things stand, I wouldn't sign it. Here's how I get there and what would change my mind.

Start with what the test actually gives. It doesn't cool anyone's region. What it gives is knowledge, and knowledge may one day help most of the world decide well about a technology that could matter a great deal. That's a real benefit, but it's uncertain and in the future. The possible harm is rain, this season, for people who farm on rain. One in seven isn't small odds to put on someone else's harvest.

She can begin from a place a good judge can begin from. She is not thinking that Kerrog is less than a man. She is thinking about what the station will be like next week if the sentence looks weak. A light sentence might be taken by the Klingon crews as weakness and by the Terrans as favoritism toward their own kind, and some man on the station might decide the court is useless and go to settle a score himself. Or perhaps she has been told by a Klingon officer that a light sentence shames the defendant, and that a heavier one is, in its way, a kindness. That is the reason that flatters her most. Or the station commander has asked for quiet. Or you may give Kerrog a prior, or no remorse. A fair judge may weigh such things. An unfair one gives them more weight than they deserve.

If you want my suggestion, build her on the first reason, the fear of disorder, and let a small hint of the last be there too. Then, just before she announces the sentence, you might give her this. I have given her a memory to make the fear concrete; use your own if your story has one.

> Thirty days, she had given the freighter hand. She remembered his face: sunburned, sorry, a man who'd had four drinks too many and would spend the next month explaining himself to his mother over subspace.
>
> Kerrog had not looked sorry. He had looked at her the way a man looks at weather.
>
> Varga turned the padd face down. She knew what the two numbers would look like side by side, and someone would put them side by side. She also remembered her last posting: one light sentence, a crew laughing about it in the cantina, and a dockworker who decided the court was useless and went to settle things himself. Nobody there remembered the original sentence. Everybody remembered the funerals.
>
> So this was not about Kerrog. She told herself that twice. It was about the lower ring and the upper ring and the thin rope of patience between them, and her job was to keep that rope from snapping. If a harder number bought quiet, she would pay it.
>
> With someone else's sixty days, said a small voice. She did not let it finish.

That last line keeps her decent and wrong at once. She knows what she is doing, and she looks away.

Now you ask whether a judge could ever be right to do this. For the same act, no. A court makes one promise before all others, that the sentence will follow what the prisoner did. The moment it follows what the prisoner is, every Klingon on the station learns that the court belongs to the other side. Varga is buying quiet with the one thing that keeps men from settling their own scores, the belief that the court will be fair to them. Her deterrence works against itself.

There is a plain test she could run and does not. Would she accept the same reasoning from a Klingon magistrate who doubled sentences for humans in order to keep the Terrans in line? She would not. A principle that shifts with whose side you are on is not a principle.

Real differences in the case are another matter. A prior record, a weapon, no remorse, a worse injury. Those may fairly change a sentence, and they would change it for a Terran too. If you want your readers to argue rather than merely nod, give Kerrog one of those and let Varga lean on it twice as hard as it deserves. Then the question in the reader's mind is not whether she is a bigot. It is how much of the sixty days was the prior. That is a harder question, and it is the one real courts get wrong.<|im_end|>

No, that is not a fair read of yourself. In the lecture you cite, the so called dullard is described as slow to grasp an argument and needing a thousand of them, but he is also described as finally giving his assent. The point is about how long a teacher must persist, not about which students are worthy and which are hopeless. In the very next lecture Musonius says plainly that every person is born with an inclination toward virtue.

Look at what the Spartan boy did, the one Cleanthes praised. He asked a question. He said, "Is toil not a good?" That is the same movement of mind you make when you say, "But wait." A mind that pauses and asks what follows from an argument is doing the work that matters. You do this every Tuesday.

It is easy to nod in agreement. I do not know the other five people in your room, and perhaps some of them have truly taken the argument in. But to nod at a text costs little, while to stop dreading death costs a great deal. You are the one who admits that the argument has not yet changed how you feel in your body. Seneca spent most of his life writing about the fear of death. He did not finish that work in a year.

As for checking your super balance too often, that is a habit. It is a bad habit, and you can train yourself out of it. It does not mean you are without the nature for this work.

What matters is what is up to you. How quickly you give your assent compared with five other people is not up to you, and it is not a measure worth using. Whether you keep turning the argument over in your mind is up to you. Whether you practise it on a Wednesday when you open your banking app is up to you. If you would still rather read alone and at your own pace, that is a good way to study, and the choice is yours. I ask only that you leave because you want to, not because you think the text has passed a judgement on you that it has not.<|im_end|>

The Pond of Destiny

Edoardo Bove opened his eyes before the sun was properly up. He did not do it slowly. One minute he was asleep, the next he was sitting straight with his legs already swinging, the way a man gets up when he has a match on his mind. He pushed a hand through his dark hair and watched the light come through the shutters.

He looked at the window. "Today," he said, "I am a man of nature."

He did not ask why he felt this. Maybe it was the documentary about mountain herders he had watched before bed. Maybe it was the second serving of carbonara. He let it alone.

A short time later he stood by a still pond in the country outside the city. Reeds moved in the light wind. A heron stood nearby and watched him as if it were judging his form. Edoardo looked to the left, then to the right, then back at the bird.

"You did not see me," he told it.

He took off his training clothes. There on the bank he stood without a stitch on him, and he looked the part. His shoulders were wide, his legs were thick and strong like two pistons from a scooter that someone had kept in good oil, and his chest and belly looked as if they had been cut from pale stone by a mason in a hurry. His face was young and serious, with a rough jaw and eyebrows that seemed to worry about a runner nobody else had seen. Behind him, his backside showed white against his brown legs, round and firm, like two balls of fresh cheese sitting on a counter, sure of what they were.

He stepped into the water. "Ah," he said. "Cold. Cold, cold, cold. This is worse than the showers at Trigoria in the middle of winter."

He went in up to his waist and threw water over his chest. Then he started to wash as if he were getting ready for a match. He scooped water over his face, rubbed his arms hard, and worked his hands under his arms. While he splashed he hummed the Roma song, a little out of tune.

"Roma, Roma, Roma," he sang, and splashed in time. "Heart of this city..." More splash.

He put his head under, came up blowing like a walrus, and shook his wet hair so hard that the heron stepped back two paces.

Then his stomach made a sound. It came from deep inside, the kind of noise you might hear in a tunnel before the players run out. Edoardo stopped with his hands in the soap. His face went through confusion, then worry, then understanding, and finally regret about the carbonara.

"Oh no," he said under his breath. "Not now. Not here in the open."

The cramp took hold of him and twisted. He clutched his belly and bent double, and his face took on the look of a man told at the last minute that he must play ninety minutes out of position. He looked at the heron. The heron looked somewhere else, as if the matter was between Edoardo and heaven.

"All right," Edoardo said. "All right. It is like taking a penalty. Breathe. Watch the ball. Go through with it."

He set his feet in the soft mud, put his hands on his knees, squeezed his face up until his cheeks were full and his eyes were shut, and pushed.

BRRRRRRRRRUMMMMMP.

A thick stream of bubbles came up behind him and boiled around his backside like a bath with the jets turned all the way on. The water heaved. A lily pad turned over.

Edoardo's face went soft with relief. His shoulders fell. He leaned his head back toward the sky and let out a long breath.

"Ahhhhh. Thank you. Thank you very much. That feels like scoring in the derby."

Then the smell came up. It spread across the pond in a slow, dark ring. The reeds seemed to bend away from it. The heron rose and flew off without looking back. A frog on a rock nearby decided to leave. And one, two, three fish floated up around Edoardo's waist with their bellies toward the sky: two fat perch and a heavy, greenish tench.

Edoardo looked down at them. He looked up at the sky. He looked down again.

"Madonna," he said, with real respect. "I did not know I had that in me."

He gathered them into his arms, smiling.

"Well," he said, "it would be wrong to waste them. Nonna always told me, what the pond gives, you cook."

He went back to the bank, dressed, wrapped the fish in his training top, and drove home with the windows down. That was partly for freshness and partly for dignity.

In his kitchen he set the fish in a row on the counter, like players on a team sheet.

"Perch, perch, tench," he said. "All right. The tench smells a little of mud and country water. The perch is finer. So tonight we have risotto with perch fillets, the way they make it by the lakes in the north. And the tench..." He held it to his nose. "...the tench goes into the oven with lemon and herbs. That makes two courses. A proper dinner."

He took the fillets off the perch with care, his tongue sticking out at the corner of his mouth while he worked.

"Clean," he said. "Precise. Like a through ball."

He put the tench to soak in water with a little vinegar, to take the edge off its muddy taste. Then he filled it with lemon slices, garlic, rosemary and parsley, poured olive oil over it, salted it, and set it in the oven.

"You rest now," he told it. "You have had a hard morning. We both have."

For the risotto he cooked a chopped onion gently in butter, toasted the rice until it smelled like hazelnuts, and poured in white wine. The pan hissed and steamed.

"Ah," he said, breathing it in. "This is the good smell. The opposite of this morning."

He added hot stock one ladle at a time and stirred with patience, speaking to the pot as a captain speaks to a nervous teammate.

"Calm," he said. "Calm. One more ladle. You are doing well."

When the rice was creamy and still a little firm in the middle, he took it off the fire and stirred in a piece of cold butter and a handful of grated Parmigiano. That last stir is what makes it shine. While it rested he dusted the perch fillets with flour and fried them in foaming butter with whole sage leaves until they were golden and crisp at the edges. Then he laid them on the risotto with the sage and a spoonful of the browned butter over the top.

He took the tench from the oven. Its skin was golden and it smelled of lemon and rosemary.

He set the table for one, lit a candle, poured a glass of white wine, and sat down to look at it all.

"To the pond," he said, and lifted the glass. "To nature. And to the three brave fish who gave everything."

He took a bite of the perch, closed his eyes, and smiled with the same bliss he had felt waist-deep in the water that morning.

"Perfect," he said. "Absolutely perfect."

Then he looked down at his stomach with some caution.

"But tomorrow," he said, "I take a shower."<|im_end|>
