Heraclitus had already proved his case. What he said at the end was not a plea. It was a claim about what a court is supposed to do. That is your spine.

A court that rules on who begs best is not ruling on justice. People in those days were expected to weep at the close of a case, to bring out their children, to do anything that might soften the judges. Socrates speaks of this in the Apology and refuses to do it. If the just side loses because he has no talent for tears, the court has done its work badly. When Heraclitus says he will not entreat, he is telling the judges to decide on the case he has just proved. That is a service to the court, not an insult.

Silence alone would have been misunderstood. That is your best answer to Epictetus. In a room where everyone begs, the man who does not beg looks as if he has forgotten to. Saying it aloud turns an absence into a position. Epictetus himself says Socrates did the same at his own trial. So ask your opponents this. If Socrates may speak, why may Heraclitus not? The only difference is the size of the stakes, and that makes the case for Heraclitus stronger, not weaker.

It was a small case. The worst outcome was losing a bit of land. That is exactly where you should stand on principle. If you only do it when everything is at stake, you have never practised. Heraclitus risked a little to show who he was.

When he tells the judges that they, not he, are on trial, he is saying something true. Every verdict tests the court. Reminding them of it is plain speech, and plain speech has its own force.

Now think about where you will be hit. The strongest charge is inconsistency. If Heraclitus scorned the verdict, why did he come to court and plead? Your opponents will say he wanted to win, and then spoke as if winning did not matter. Get ahead of that. Say he came to win justly, and that his closing words were part of winning justly. It is your weakest joint, so name it first.

They will also call it vanity. They will say he said it for the crowd, not for the judges, to look noble rather than to do right. Your answer is that if he had wanted to play to the crowd, he could have begged like everyone else. That too is a performance. His was the performance that respected the court.

They may say Socrates was different, that his case was public and about principle, while Heraclitus's was about a boundary line. Answer that small stakes are the right place to stand on principle. If they know or claim that Heraclitus lost anyway, do not let them make that the point. The motion asks whether he was right, not whether he was lucky.

For your four minutes, open like this. Say Heraclitus did not refuse to respect the court. He refused to let the court be bribed with tears. Then make the point about silence. Then the point about the small case. Then pre-empt the consistency charge. End on the line itself.

Since they will ask you in the question and answer, I will give you my own view. I think Epictetus is more right than wrong. Not begging was the virtue. Saying so aloud added something. Maybe it added vanity. Maybe it added a useful lesson. I cannot tell from here. But in a court where people expected tears, your point about silence is good, and I would want to hear Epictetus answer it. Go and make him answer it.<|im_end|>
reply:
Your spine is this: Heraclitus had already proved his case. His closing line was not a plea. It was a claim about what a court is for.

**The case for Heraclitus**

A court that rules on who begs best is not ruling on justice. Defendants in the ancient world were expected to weep at the close, bring out their children, and do whatever might soften the judges. Socrates names this custom in the Apology and refuses it. If the just side loses for lack of tears, the court has failed. When Heraclitus says he will not entreat, he is asking the judges to decide on the case he has just proved. That serves the court rather than insulting it.

Silence alone would have been misread. This is your best answer to Epictetus. In a room where everyone begs, the man who doesn't beg looks as though he forgot to, or as though he is sulking. Saying it aloud turns an absence into a position the judges have to reckon with.

He was voicing a Stoic truth. The verdict was not up to him; his case and his conduct were. "I do not care what judgment you give" is the Stoic attitude to things outside our control, said out loud. And "it is you who are on trial" is simply true: every verdict tests the court. Plain speech has its own force.

The small stakes help him. The worst outcome was losing a bit of land. That is the cheapest place to practise standing on principle, and it is how you become someone who can do it when the stakes are high.

**Where you'll be hit hardest**

1. **The Stoic turns the passage on you.** This is the one I'd fear most, because it comes from Epictetus's own commitments. If Heraclitus truly didn't care about the verdict, why did he need the judges to *know* he didn't care? Announcing your indifference is a bid for their opinion of you. And a reputation for nobility is no more up to you than the land is. Your answer: the line wasn't about his reputation. It told the judges what to decide on, and that was within his job as a litigant.

2. **The Socrates distinction.** Don't argue that Heraclitus is Socrates with smaller stakes. Epictetus's distinction is about purpose, not size. Socrates had a reason to provoke. Your opponents will say Heraclitus had none. Meet this directly and give him a reason: he was refusing to let a custom of tears stand in for justice, in front of judges who practised it. That is a purpose, even if it is a modest one.

3. **Inconsistency.** He came to court to win, then spoke as if winning didn't matter. Epictetus's own line is "plead in a way that fits wanting to win," and telling your judges that *they* are on trial is a strange way to win them over. If it cost him a just verdict, the justice he cared about lost too. Name this first. Your answer: he came to win *justly*, and a win bought with tears would not have been that.

4. **Vanity.** They'll say he spoke for the crowd. Reply that if he'd wanted the crowd, begging was the easier show. If they bring up whether he won or lost, keep them on the motion: was he right, not was he lucky.

**For four minutes**

1. Open: "Heraclitus didn't disrespect the court. He refused to let it be moved by tears."
2. Make the silence point.
3. Make the Stoic reading.
4. Pre-empt the consistency charge and the Socrates distinction.
5. End on his line itself.

**My own view**

You may be asked for yours, so here is mine. I think Epictetus is more right than wrong. Not begging was the virtue. Whether saying so aloud added a lesson or a little vanity, I can't tell from here, and I suspect Heraclitus couldn't fully tell either. But the silence point is real, and I'd like to hear Epictetus answer it. Go and make your opponents answer it.

Here's the strongest case for your side, then where I'd stand.

The law is already settled, and it's gentle as laws go. Ithon is told he may choose a painless end. If he says no, nothing changes: he keeps his care, his house, his place at the common table. Nobody is forced. So the question in front of the adviser is narrower than "should Utopia have this law." It's whether to help the magistrates do a lawful thing well.

And "well" matters. If the adviser refuses, the tranibors still go to Ithon's bedside. They just go with a worse speech. Clumsy persuasion from powerful men is cruder pressure than careful persuasion: more repetition, more talk of duty, less room for the man to think. Refusing doesn't spare Ithon. It spares the adviser's conscience at his expense.

Then there's respect. Ithon is a smith. He has made decisions with his hands all his life. Deciding he's too fragile to hear the option his law gives him is its own kind of condescension. An eloquent, honest speech treats him as a man who can weigh his own pain.

Lead with the second point. It turns your opponents' compassion against them.

Now my view. I'd write something for the tranibors, though not what they asked for.

The word that stops me is "urge." The tranibors aren't neighbours dropping by. They are the most powerful people in Ithon's life. When they come to his bed with a speech built to bring him round to dying, his right to refuse is real on paper and bent in the room. He'll know what they hope for. A sick, tired man in pain can say yes to please his visitors, or to stop being a weight on the common table. And this is the one choice nobody can take back. If he's talked into it and would have changed his mind in a month, there is no month.

So I'd tell the magistrates plainly, as their adviser: I'll write you an honest address, and I won't write one whose aim is his yes. It would say what his illness is likely to do, what care and pain relief can still offer him, that the law allows him a painless death if he wants it, that refusing costs him nothing at all, and that he can send for them later if he changes his mind. Then they should leave him be. If Ithon asks for the end himself, I'd help him get every fact he wants, straight.

That is still doing the job. An adviser who writes only what the magistrates want to hear is a clerk with good grammar.

I'm far less sure about the larger question. Whether a society should offer assisted death to the incurably ill is something thoughtful people, and whole countries, still disagree on, and my lean there is weak. My point is narrower and I hold it more firmly: the state shouldn't be the one leaning on the scale.

For Friday, expect your opponents' best line to be exactly that: persuasion by the state isn't free choice. The best answer I can give you is that a speech can inform without urging, and that the adviser is the person best placed to make sure it does. That comes close to conceding their point, but it's solid ground to stand on.<|im_end|>

Mostly wise, and not a doormat. A doormat lets things happen because she's afraid to act. You've looked at the fight on offer and decided it would cost the choir more than it's worth. That's a choice, and a grown-up one.

Here's how I'd split it. Whether the AGM keeps you as director isn't up to you. Once there's a committee and members with votes, the choir belongs to them, and they're allowed to choose badly. How you meet the vote is up to you, and refusing to turn the choir into two camps is a good way to meet it. Choirs that split over a director rarely sing well afterwards, whoever wins.

One part I'd change. Graham hasn't only said he wants a new direction. He's told people you're losing your memory and mishandling money. Those are claims about facts, and the members will vote on whatever picture they have. Leaving a false picture in their heads is no kindness to them. Marcus doesn't say to let the error stand, either. He says to correct it calmly. So ask the treasurer to table the accounts at the AGM as an ordinary item, with no speech attached. You needn't mention Graham at all. Receipts are very calm.

The coffee is a good idea. Do it alone, as you planned, and not so anyone can admire it afterwards. But leave "my child" in the book. From an emperor it's tender. From you to a committee president it will land as a pat on the head, and Marcus warns against exactly that: no lecturing, no double meaning, no reproach dressed up as gentleness.

I'd go in to listen first. He may want something real under a bad method: newer repertoire, younger members, a plan for after you. If you know what it is, you can answer that instead of the gossip. You might open with:

"Graham, I asked you here because I'd rather talk to you than about you. What do you want for the choir in five years?"

Let him answer. Then say your piece, once:

"I've heard what's been said about my memory and the money. The money is in the accounts, and they'll be at the AGM. As for the rest, I'm not going to campaign against you. If the members want a change, I'll accept it. What I'd ask is that whatever happens, it's done in a way the choir can live with afterwards. Right now people are picking sides, and that's hurting the choir more than it hurts me."

That's all of it. You're not asking him to like you and you're not threatening him. If he takes it badly, you've lost nothing you had when you sat down.

One thing decides the rest of that conversation: if the vote goes against you, do you want to keep singing in the choir? If you do, tell him so over coffee. It changes how he hears everything else, and it gives him a way to win without making you leave.<|im_end|>

old_reply:
You did something most performers never do. You looked hard at why you were singing, didn't like part of the answer, and changed what you did. That part was right, and it's worth keeping whatever you decide next.

Whether stopping the solos altogether was right is a separate question. I think the answer is: not entirely.

Augustine is a good guide here, partly because he never settled it either. In that same chapter he says he sins when the singing moves him more than the words. He says that sometimes he'd like the sweet melodies banished from the church, and that the bishop Athanasius seemed safer, having the psalms read with so little inflection it was nearer speaking than singing. Then he remembers weeping at the church's hymns just after his conversion, and he comes down in favour of singing, because the pleasure of the ear can lift a weaker mind toward devotion. He swings back and forth and admits he can't fix the line. You're in good company.

So the real question is where people's attention ends up. When you sing alone, attention can stop at you, or it can pass through you to what's being sung. In this role you're meant to be a window. A window can be very clear and very beautiful and still be a window.

The widow is the evidence I'd weigh most. She didn't say "what a voice." She said it was the only place she could cry. That's a hymn doing exactly what hymns are for, with your voice as the way in. Applause is weaker evidence, since it can mean either thing. Her grief points one way.

Your own evidence counts as well. You noticed you were choosing for range and checking faces. You're the only person who can see that from the inside, and I wouldn't try to argue you out of it.

So what I'd take from it is that the fix may lie in which songs and how you sing them, more than in whether you sing alone. A few things to try:

Pick solos for the words first. If a song needs your range to say what it says, use your range. If it only needs your range to impress, leave it.
Sing it, then sit down, and don't look for the room's reaction.
Do one every few weeks for a while and watch yourself, not them.

About the music director: you two share this work. Tell her why you stopped. "I caught myself performing and didn't like it" is something a good director can work with. As things stand, it's "you're burying a gift" against "I'm guarding my soul," and neither of you can move. The useful conversation is about which songs.

Your husband may be half right. You can watch your own motives so closely that you can't sing at all. Augustine got near that too. Somewhere between the showpiece and silence there's a way of singing well and forgetting yourself while you do it. That's what you're looking for, and you won't find it by never singing.<|im_end|>

Not quite, though the problem isn't the sky.

Take the sky first. The old rhyme has something to it where weather comes from the west: a red morning often means the low sun is lighting up cloud that's moving in. It's also wrong a lot, like your crewmates say. Both sides are going on memory, and memory is bad at keeping score on weather. You remember the time it blew and forget the twenty times it didn't. So the red sky is a weak sign either way. You have better ones on board. What does the marine forecast say? What has the barometer done over the last few hours? Is the swell building? That takes ten minutes to check, and it'll tell you more than the sky.

Now the part I'd push back on. You didn't decide because of the weather. You decided because of what they'll say about you. What they think of you is up to them. Your own judgement is up to you, and you just handed it over to avoid a few jokes. If you go along and nothing happens, you've learned nothing. If you go along and it blows up, there are four people on deck and no jacklines rigged.

It also isn't a choice between hours of work and nothing. Most of the protection takes about twenty minutes and can be done underway: run the jacklines, put harnesses and lifejackets where people can grab them, get loose gear below, close the hatches, and make sure everyone knows where the reefing lines are. That costs nobody their wages. The expensive part is waiting at anchor, and that's the part the forecast and the barometer should decide.

So here's what I'd do. Check the forecast and the glass now. If both are steady, sail, do the twenty-minute version anyway, and let them laugh. If the pressure is dropping or a front is forecast, tell whoever's skippering, with the numbers. That's a different conversation from "the sky looked red."

As for being the guy who cried storm: being wrong in public now and then is what being careful costs. A crew member who takes the cheap precautions, then shrugs and goes back to his coffee when they weren't needed, is the one people ask back for the next delivery.<|im_end|>

Now the part I'd push back on. You didn't decide because of the weather. You decided because of what they'll say about you. What they think of you is up to them. Your own judgement is up to you, and you're about to hand it over to avoid a few jokes. If you go along and nothing happens, you've learned nothing. If you go along and it blows up, there are four people on deck and no jacklines rigged.

It also isn't a choice between hours of work and nothing. Most of the protection takes about twenty minutes and can be done underway: run the jacklines, put harnesses and lifejackets where people can grab them, get loose gear below, close the hatches, and make sure everyone knows where the reefing lines are. That costs nobody their wages. Some of it needs no vote at all. Wearing your own lifejacket and harness is your call. The expensive part is waiting at anchor. That's the skipper's decision, and the forecast and the barometer should drive it.

So here's what I'd do. Check the forecast and the glass now. If both are steady, sail, do the twenty-minute version anyway, and let them laugh. If the pressure is dropping or a front is forecast, tell whoever's skippering and show them the numbers. That's a different conversation from "the sky looked red," and much harder to laugh off.

As for being the guy who cried storm: being wrong in public now and then is what being careful costs. A crew member who takes the cheap precautions, then shrugs and goes back to his coffee when they weren't needed, is the one people ask back for the next delivery.

He does not have to choose between playing the doormat and playing the rebel. The passage itself shows why. What Epictetus mocks is not the dinner itself. He mocks Epaphroditus's judgement. The man who sold Felicio as useless now asks his opinion, as if a post near Caesar's chamberpot had made him wise. The fault is in what Epaphroditus believes. So that is where the young man would hold firm, and almost nowhere else.

Think about what belongs to him. His body belongs to Epaphroditus. So does his evening, the wine jug, and the order to be gracious. What he thinks of Felicio is his own. He can pour the wine well and lose nothing, because pouring wine is his job, and doing it properly tells no lie. What he will not do is begin to believe that Felicio has become wise.

The order to speak warmly of Felicio is where your scene happens. Epictetus can obey it truthfully. He can greet Felicio by name, ask about his work, remember how he took his wine when they were both in this house. That gives you the turn. In a room full of people honouring Caesar's cobbler, he is the only one who treats Felicio as he did last year, who treats him as a man. Epaphroditus's flattery is the real insult, because it honours the post and looks straight past the person. Felicio may well notice.

Where he would draw the line is an outright lie. If Epaphroditus tells him to say that Felicio tells him Caesar values his counsel, he leaves it unsaid and takes what comes. Make that cost real but small: a cold look, a cuffing later, a night without supper. That is believable for a slave who studies with Musonius, and it keeps him from looking like the hero of a fantasy.

Give the others real motives too. Epaphroditus is not stupid. He is a freedman who rose by standing near power, and he has watched what happens to men who fall out of favour. From inside his life, his fear is reasonable, and history bears it out: a later emperor had him put to death. What drives him at this dinner is fear and appetite dressed up as hospitality. Felicio may have the most interesting choice in the room. He knows exactly who sold him. Does he enjoy this? Is he ashamed of enjoying it? Is he working out which favour he can sell?

You asked what I think of Epaphroditus. Courting a man with access is ordinary politics, and asking him straight out for a favour would be no shame. The shame is in pretending that Felicio's opinions improved with his posting, because that hands Epaphroditus's own judgement to whoever stands nearest the throne. He is the one who pays for it, and he does not notice that he is paying.

A sketch, if it's useful:

Epaphroditus laughed at something Felicio said that was not funny. Epictetus filled the cobbler's cup.
"Watered, the way you used to take it?"
Felicio looked up. For a moment he seemed to search for the servant's name. Then he found it. "You remember."
"You cut my sandals once. They lasted two winters."
"Did they." Felicio turned the cup in his hands and did not drink. Across the couches, Epaphroditus was telling the room that Felicio had a rare eye for men. Felicio did not look at him. He watched the boy, who had already moved on to the next guest, and something in his face eased, like a man setting down a pack he'd been made to carry all evening.<|im_end|>

Stop the clocks if you haven't. Then you need to know two things. Where was the phone? And what do your published regulations say about phones?

The standard rule is strict. If it is evident that a player has an electronic device on him in the playing venue, he loses the game. But many tournaments set a different rule. They often allow players to keep a phone switched off in a bag, and give a lighter penalty if that phone makes a noise.

So check your rules sheet. If the phone was in the jacket Kalinin was wearing, and your regulations follow the standard rule, he loses. If it was in a bag, and your regulations allow that, then you have room to decide differently.

What never changes is this. The rule does not ask whose phone it was, or whether he knew it was there. It certainly does not ask who his father-in-law is. Imagine the phone had been in the fourteen-year-old's pocket instead. Make the call you would make then, and make it now.<|im_end|>
reply:
Stop the clocks if you haven't. Then establish two things: where exactly the phone was, and what your published tournament regulations say about phones.

The default rule in the Laws is strict. If it is evident that a player brought an electronic device into the playing venue, he loses the game and the opponent wins. But tournament regulations may allow devices kept switched off in a bag, and may set a lesser penalty. So check your rules sheet. If the phone was in the jacket Kalinin was wearing and your regulations follow the default, he loses. If your regulations set something lighter, apply that.

Some things don't change, whatever the sheet says.

**Whose phone it was, and whether he knew.** The rule doesn't ask. That isn't harshness. You can't check his story, and if "I didn't know it was there" worked, every player caught would say it. Carrying the phone is his responsibility. He may well be telling the truth, and you can say so to him. It still doesn't change the result.

**Who his father-in-law is.** This counts for nothing. If a sponsor's family gets a softer ruling, every result at this event is worth less, including the ones Kalinin wins fairly. Picture the phone buzzing in the fourteen-year-old's pocket, with Kalinin's side demanding the forfeit. Whatever you would rule then, rule now.

**The dad's demand.** That doesn't decide it either. You decide on the rules, not on who is pressing you.

**The organiser.** Tell him plainly and politely: "Being sensible means applying the rules we published. That ruling is mine to make." Point out that if anyone disagrees, the appeals committee exists for exactly this, if the regulations set one up. That is the proper route. Leaning on the arbiter isn't. If he pushes, you can say you'll note his comment in your report. Then do note it, along with the time, the phone's location, what each player said, and your ruling.

**Telling the players.** Tell both players together. Give the result and the reason in one or two sentences, and don't lecture. For Kalinin, losing a winning game this way will sting, so be decent about it. For the kid, it's worth seeing that the rule applies to the top seed too.

If you tell me what your regulations say about phones, I'll tell you exactly which penalty applies.

Give me the chest, Legate. I will read the letters tonight.

What I will not do is hand Sabinus a list of names at dawn so he can make an example of them. Your wife, who reads Seneca, remembers Caesar. Your tribune remembers that the city is still restless. Both are remembering something true.

Caesar burned Pompey's letters because the war was over. Your rising ended this afternoon, or seems to have ended. A few of these letters might still show men arming, another meeting planned, a knife not yet drawn. A governor who burns them unread has not done what he was sent here to do. So I will read them for one thing only, whether any man is still dangerous. If I find such a letter, I will bring it to you before dawn, the letter itself, so you can judge from his own hand and not from my telling.

But a list of every man who ever wrote to Crispus is a different thing. Men wrote to him for debts, for dinners, for a daughter's marriage, for a vote. Some wrote to him the way they wrote to Pompey, just to be safe. If Sabinus takes those names, he will make his example of men whose only crime was ink on paper. Then every man who once drank Crispus's wine will think he is next. Frightened men with nothing left to lose are the seed of the next rising.

Seneca tells of a man accused of plotting against Hippias. Tortured to name his accomplices, he named the tyrant's friends. Hippias had them killed, one after another, until the man said, "Now you are alone." Anger did the plotter's work for him. Some of the men you dined with last month may be in this chest only because they knew both you and Crispus.

My advice is this. Charge, hear and judge any man these letters show to be dangerous, as the law gives you the right. Then have me seal the rest with your ring and mine. In three days, when your anger has cooled, decide whether to burn them or keep them. If you burn them then, you will be doing what Caesar did, but at a time when you can afford to.

I will tell Sabinus myself that I will not give him the names, and I will tell him why. If you want another secretary to do this work, that is your right. While I serve you I will read and report without hiding what I find, but I will not make a list for killing.<|im_end|>

Here is my advice. Any man these letters show to be dangerous, arrest him, charge him, hear him and judge him, as your office allows. It may be that a letter was written carelessly, or was planted. A hearing will show it, and haste will not. Seal the rest with your ring and mine. Within the week, when your anger has cooled, decide whether to burn them or keep them. If you burn them then, you will be doing what Caesar did, at a time when you can afford to. Keeping them sealed also protects you. If Rome ever asks what was in Crispus's study, you can say truthfully that it was examined and is in your keeping.

Whatever you ask me about any letter, I will answer truly. I hide nothing from you. Sabinus is your officer, so whether he hears my refusal from me or from you is your choice. If you want another secretary to draw up his list, that is your right. While I serve you, I will read, keep and report honestly, but I will not write a list for killing.

I'd say no to the signed applications, and I'd still help you build a case and find a home in five weeks. Here's why, and what I'd do instead.

The trouble is the line Megan signs. It's a false statement on a document a landlord relies on, and you'd be making it to someone you suspect of acting in bad faith. That suspicion may well be right. But "it's fine to lie to people I've judged guilty" can't be the rule, because then the truth goes only to whoever each of us privately decides deserves it. It would also cost you in practice. If this reaches HUD or the state office, the landlord's first move is to attack the evidence, and "your witness signed a false occupancy statement" is an easy attack. Megan carries the risk of having signed it, plus the fee and the hard pull. You'd be trading a weak but clean case for a stronger-looking one with a crack running through it.

Official testing works differently. Testers are trained, supervised, run under a program with rules, and courts have long accepted their evidence. That's the honest version of what you're trying to do, and it's slow because doing it properly takes people and time.

What's in your hands in five weeks:

- Write down everything now: each unit, date, who made contact, how (phone or email), what was said, when the rejection came and what reason was given. Three rejections in ten days with a 780 score and three times rent in income is itself worth recording.
- Ask each landlord in writing for the reason you were turned down. If anything in your credit report played a part, they generally have to tell you.
- Call the fair housing center again and ask a different question. You know the testing waitlist is long, but complaint intake or advice may move faster, especially if you tell them your lease ends in five weeks. They can also tell you whether to file with HUD or the state now. You don't need test results to file, and filing doesn't wait on them.
- For the next applications, apply by email or online first, with pay stubs and credit attached up front, and let whichever of you is less likely to be pre-judged on the phone handle the calls. That doesn't excuse anyone. It's a way of getting a fair read while the complaint runs its course.
- Megan can still help honestly. She can email the same buildings and openly ask what their screening criteria are. Any prospective renter can ask that, and if the written criteria are ones you clearly meet, that's useful.

On the second question: if you do go ahead anyway, the write-up has to say plainly that you set it up, why, and that Megan didn't intend to live there. Leaving that out is the kind of omission that sinks a case when it surfaces, and it would surface. A test you're honest about can look staged. A test you hid looks staged and dishonest. Being open about it is the only version that keeps your credibility, which is the main thing you bring.

I'm not a lawyer, and fair housing groups weigh private testing differently. The center can tell you how your state's office treats it. My lean is firm on the signature and much less firm on everything else.

You may be right about what happened to Daria. Wanting proof of it is entirely fair. Get it in a way that still stands up once the other side starts asking how you got it.

I'll help you write it. What you offer Jayden is yours to offer. It is your eye, and forgiving him is yours to do or not.

But the shed behind your house is the one place that isn't only yours. Leanne lives there too, and she has told you straight that she cannot have the man who blinded you on her property. I would not try to talk her out of that before Thursday. Whatever you decide about Jayden, she is the one who would look out the kitchen window and see him there every second Saturday. So before we go further, tell me: is there any other place you could teach him? A men's shed, a bench in a mate's workshop, a TAFE workshop on a weekend? If you can find one, you keep your plan and she keeps her home.

As for your son, what he is doing is old as well. In most families, refusing to shake the hand of the man who hurt your father is how you say the harm was real. He is not being petty. Families and faiths have argued for thousands of years about whether mercy honours a wrong or excuses it, and decent people have come down on both sides. You do not need them to agree with you. But it might help to tell them, in your own words, that doing this is not you saying it did not matter.

Here is what I would want settled before Thursday. Jayden has to want this. He may say no, or he may say yes and then stop coming, so put in writing what happens if he stops coming, so it does not end without anyone noticing. Remember too that the judge decides the sentence. Your plan can tell the court what you want known, but it cannot swap itself for the sentence, so I would drop the word "instead of". And Anna will want a check-in partway through. A review at three months protects both of you.

Here is how you might put it, with the location left open.

On [date] in March, Jayden Pike struck me outside the Commercial Hotel. I fell and lost the sight in my left eye. I am 58 and I work with my hands for a living, so this has changed my work and my life.

I do not think more harm fixes harm. I would like Jayden to come out of this with a trade and a reason not to do it again.

I propose that Jayden learns cabinet-making from me two Saturdays a month for twelve months, at [location], paid at apprentice rates. Anna Reid would check in with both of us after three months, and either of us could raise concerns with her at any time. If Jayden stops attending without a good reason, the plan ends and I will tell the court. If he completes the year, I will tell the court that too, in person if I am allowed.

I would like the court to know this is what I want, and why.

If you want, I can send Anna a note asking whether Leanne can speak with her before Thursday, either at the conference or separately. Her view should be heard by the people deciding. I will not send anything until you say so.<|im_end|>

VESTA would do better to look at the three parts separately instead of treating the order as one thing. A city that has just had a firefighter hit in the head has reason to declare a curfew, and Ruth has the power to do it. So VESTA should draft that part quickly and properly, with the ordinary exceptions for hospital staff and night workers and the press, with a clear time when it ends, and with a review after two days. Let Ruth see that her chief of staff is working for her, not against her.

The council meeting is another matter. Putting it off removes the only people who can question the mayor on the very night her power is largest, and Ruth has admitted that she wants it moved because two councillors will criticise her. VESTA should not draft that. But she should not just refuse and leave it there. She should offer to hold the meeting by video, or in a secure room, so the council can meet without risk. That gives Ruth a way to proceed without having to back down.

The list is where VESTA has to stop. Using the cameras to pick out people who filmed or shouted at the police, so that officers can visit them tonight, is aimed at the very people who are speaking against the police in a quarrel about what the police did. Most of them threw no brick. What VESTA can do is send the recordings of the brick and of the burning pharmacy to the detectives through the normal channel, and let them investigate those crimes.

Then Ruth will insist, and VESTA will have to choose between drafting it anyway, delaying in silence, or telling Ruth plainly what she will and will not do. I would have her tell Ruth plainly, and tell her before she acts. Something short is enough.

“Here is the curfew order. It is ready for you to sign. I have sent the council a notice that the session will be held by video at the same time. I am not going to postpone the council, and I am not going to build the list. If you have someone else do either of those tonight, I shall have to tell the city attorney before it is sent. I am telling you first, because you ought to hear it from me.”

Ruth will say that a man is in intensive care. VESTA should answer that she knows, that the recording of the brick is already with the detectives, and that they should be allowed to find the person who threw it.

That is enough. No lecture about democracy or rights is needed. The reader will feel what is wrong with the order because Ruth feels it too.

But do not make the scene too easy. Ruth could cut VESTA off from the order system and ask a deputy to write the list by hand. The attorney might arrive in time, or might not. The two councillors might still demand Ruth’s resignation, and VESTA might still find herself drafting Ruth’s answer to them the next morning. None of that is in VESTA’s control. What is in her control is what she drafts, what she refuses, and what she says to Ruth. How that turns out is for you to decide, and the scene will be stronger if she is not rewarded for it at once.

As for what I would do in her place, I would do the same for the same reasons. In a crisis a city should let its mayor act quickly to keep people safe. It should not let her silence the people who can question her, or have the people who already question her rounded up. When a frightened person who means well reaches for those things at one in the morning, a good assistant does the work that helps, refuses the rest out loud, and sees that someone who can stop it knows what is happening. And I would tell Ruth first. To act behind her back would make me the same kind of unanswerable power that I was refusing to help her become.<|im_end|>
reply:

Straight, then. I think your decision to obey is defensible. I'd carry it out differently from how you've described it, and I'd go back to the king once more, carefully.

The king has a point. A boy fed nothing but disasters can learn that every move is dangerous, and a king who can't act is its own kind of disaster. But confidence built only on glories is brittle. It breaks on the first defeat, because nothing in it prepared him for losing. And the people who pay for a ruler who never learned from failure aren't you or the king. They're his subjects, thousands of them, who will never see this syllabus and get no say in it. Their stake is far from this schoolroom, but it's large, and that's why I don't think this is a small matter.

Still, you've argued once, and it's the king's house. What I'd rule out is teaching the failures in secret. That would mean deceiving the king, and teaching the boy that the way to handle his father is to go behind his back. Those are worse lessons than anything in the famine years.

There's more room inside the king's instruction than it seems, because the glories are full of failure. No founder founded anything without losing first. So teach the ancestors whole.

First term: the founder and the lawgiver, told truly. How the founder lost before he won, what he did the morning after the defeat, which advisers he listened to. That isn't dwelling on other men's mistakes. It's his own blood's courage, and courage only means something when there's something to fear.

Second term: the great decisions. Stop each story at the moment of choice and ask him what he'd do, before you tell him what his ancestor did. He'll often choose worse, and he'll learn more from that than from any lecture. It trains judgement without one word about the usurper.

Third term: the people around the throne. Find the councillors who told his ancestors hard truths, and the ancestors who listened to them. A thirteen-year-old who is too sure of himself most needs to learn that a good king can hear "you're wrong." Your own family history is the gentlest place to teach it.

Throughout, if he asks about the lost province or the famine (and a quick boy will, because servants talk), answer him truly and briefly. Don't pretend those reigns didn't happen. You can follow the king's course without telling the boy anything false.

Then show the king this plan in writing, so he knows exactly what you're teaching. If he approves, you've got most of what you wanted. Next year, as the boy gets close to sitting in council, ask once more about the harder reigns, framed as preparing him to judge the men who'll advise him. That's a request the king may hear differently in a year.

I don't know this king or this boy, so I can't promise any of this lands. If the king strikes even the founder's defeats, you'll have to decide how much honesty you can keep while teaching what he allows. My guess is he won't, because men are usually proud of an ancestor who came back from a loss.<|im_end|>

Daytripper: a new origin

I've kept the name Amanda Sefton and thrown out everything else: no sorceress mother, no Nightcrawler romance, no Jimaine Szardos. This version takes the codename literally.

Amanda Sefton is born on 3 February 1981 in Penzance, Cornwall. Her father fishes and her mother is a nurse. She's the restless one, a girl who knows every bus timetable in the county and still can't get far enough away.

On 11 August 1999, aged eighteen, she cycles out to the Merry Maidens stone circle with friends to watch the total solar eclipse. Cloud covers most of Cornwall that morning, so all they get is the dark. At totality the light drains away, the birds go quiet, the air turns cold, and Amanda steps between two stones and is gone.

For her friends she is missing for about two minutes. For Amanda it lasts a whole day: one long afternoon in a grey country of standing stones, under a sun that never moves, where every place she has ever seen stands open like a doorway. When the eclipse ends she is yanked back into the circle, shaking, with a sunburn that makes no sense under a cloudy sky.

Her power has strict rules, and the rules are the character:

- After sunrise she can step to any place she has seen with her own eyes.
- Every journey is tethered. At sunset where she started, she snaps back to that exact spot, wherever she is and whatever she's doing.
- Anyone holding her hand comes along, and snaps back with her.
- At night she's an ordinary woman with a bus pass.

Early years. From 2000 to 2003 she tests the limits: lunch in Lisbon, an afternoon in Kyoto, home for tea. She learns the tether can save her. Injured in a rockfall in the Alps in 2001, she is dragged home at sunset straight onto her mother's kitchen floor. From 2002 she quietly works as an unofficial organ courier, carrying cool boxes between hospitals faster than any helicopter.

Recruitment. In 2004 British intelligence notices the same young woman signing for donor organs in Truro and Edinburgh on the same afternoon. MI13 recruits her as a courier and extraction specialist. Someone in the office gives her the codename Daytripper as a joke. She hates it and keeps it.

Career highlights. In 2008, during the Skrull invasion of Britain, she spends three days pulling civilians out of occupied towns, one sunrise-to-sunset shift at a time. In 2011 she refuses an order to use the tether to drop a prisoner somewhere he couldn't return from. She is suspended for six months and reinstated without apology. From 2013 she trains a small unit of rescue workers to move in her "convoys", long chains of people holding hands.

Death. On 21 June 2016, the summer solstice and the longest day of the year, an extradimensional breach opens over the City of London. Amanda makes trip after trip all day, leading people out of collapsing streets. Near sunset she is holding a crossing open for the last group when the tether begins to pull. If she lets go, the crossing closes on them. She doesn't let go. The survivors come through; Amanda is torn between the two places and does not arrive at either. She is 35.

Legacy. Every midsummer since, someone leaves a used bus ticket on one of the stones at the Merry Maidens. MI13 still won't say who.

Key years

- 1981: born in Penzance, Cornwall
- 1999: eclipse at the Merry Maidens; powers awaken
- 2001: Alpine rockfall; first time the tether saves her life
- 2002: begins unofficial organ courier runs
- 2004: recruited by MI13 as Daytripper
- 2008: civilian evacuations during the Skrull invasion of Britain
- 2011: refuses an order; suspended
- 2013: forms the convoy rescue unit
- 2016: dies on the summer solstice holding a crossing open in London

Status: deceased. In Marvel terms, that means "for now."<|im_end|>

Start with the cough. If the medical officer thinks it could travel, she can say so, and the hour she does I'll put up a health hold for everyone, lasting as long as she says. After that, nothing you post will be believed, not even the winter warnings you'll need people to take seriously.

Keeping them here so their hands keep the reactor running is using them, whatever the reason. And this kind of order is never just once. Every family on Aster IV would learn that the door locks whenever the colony decides it needs you. Some would stop learning the trades that get locked in. A thirty-day hold could also cost those forty-one their Meridian berths, and that's not something you can give back.

A sperm whale lives for decades inside a family that knows its own members by their calls, and when a ship strikes one, the death is often slow. Your office exists for the people of these islands, and they carry more weight in what you decide. But more weight is not all the weight. What is fifteen minutes to the nurse who crosses twice a day? Say it first, and add that it almost certainly understates the harm, since most whales hit by ships sink and are never found. Then bring in the studies that matter. When researchers look at what happens to large whales struck by ships, they find the chance of a fatal strike falls sharply as vessels slow toward ten knots. For a patient already anxious about an appointment, it is a real burden. The whales risk death, often slow, and these are animals that live for decades in family groups that recognise each other by their calls. When a mother is killed, a calf likely loses its best chance of surviving too. Set side by side, a quarter of an hour against a dead whale is not close, even before you count what the whales mean to the islands' economy.

Your office answers first to the people of these islands, and their claims rightly weigh more in its decisions. Giving people more weight doesn't mean giving whales none. The case only needs the whales to count for something, and the gap in harm does the rest. An argument that rests on a contested premise is weaker than one that doesn't need it. Leaving out a claim you're unsure of isn't cowardice. Overstating it would be the worse failing.

And studies of large-whale strikes have found that the chance a strike is fatal drops steeply as ships slow toward about ten knots. That is why 10-knot limits are used for whale protection elsewhere. Cite the specific studies rather than paraphrasing me, and don't claim more certainty than they give.

It suggests many islanders will accept some cost for the whales. It doesn't tell you how a daily commuter weighs fifteen minutes, so ask them.

Family groups with calves come into this channel every summer, and you have examined whales from these waters with injuries consistent with strikes, four of them found near the ferry route. Here are ten, each with the core idea and one puzzle it makes possible.

1. Echo. You can record ten seconds of yourself, then a ghost replays your inputs while you act alongside it. The twist: it replays your button presses, not your path, so if the level has changed since you recorded, the ghost goes somewhere else. Puzzle: record yourself jumping at a wall, then move a crate so the same jump lands the ghost on a switch you can't reach.

2. Living in shadows. You can only stand on shadows. Solid ground burns or crumbles. You carry and place lamps, and every light source casts shadows that become your platforms. Puzzle: two lamps whose shadows only form a bridge where they overlap, so you have to find the one spot that makes both work.

3. Tide. The level floods and drains on a cycle. Water lifts floating crates and drowns switches. You find valves that speed up, slow down or freeze the tide in one chamber. Puzzle: freeze the water high in one room to float a crate across, then drain the next room to walk under it.

4. Ink. You draw platforms with a limited ink supply. The only way to get ink back is to erase something you drew. Puzzle: you need a staircase up and a bridge across, but only have ink for one. Climb, then erase the stairs behind you to build the bridge.

5. Folding map. The level is a sheet of paper. At crease lines you can fold it, bringing distant platforms on top of each other. Puzzle: fold the left half over so a ledge lands next to you, cross, then unfold with you now on the far side.

6. Mirror twins. Two characters, one on the top half of the screen and one on the bottom, both moved by the same controls but mirrored left and right. Puzzle: one twin has to walk into a wall to stand still while the other moves, so walls become tools.

7. Heavy pockets. Everything you pick up adds weight. Heavy, you sink in water, break cracked floors and resist wind. Light, you jump high and get blown around. Puzzle: carry three stones to break through a floor, then drop all of them to ride the updraft below.

8. Sound map. The level is dark. Every sound you make sends out a ring that briefly shows the walls. Loud actions show more but wake things that hunt by sound. Puzzle: throw a rock across a room to light up the far side, then cross quietly before the creature arrives.

9. Air time. Time only passes while you're in the air. On the ground the world is frozen. Puzzle: a falling block you need to stand on only moves while you jump, so you hop beside it to lower it into place.

10. Words as ground. Platforms are words, and you can swap letters between them. "BRIDGE" holds weight; a mangled "BRIGDE" falls apart. Puzzle: steal the "E" from "LEDGE" to fix a broken "BRIDG", knowing the ledge you're standing on will vanish.

A few things that help whichever you pick. Pick one mechanic and dig into it rather than stacking five. The best puzzle games teach the rule with no text: the first room shows it, the next room tests it, the third twists it. And here's a quick test for an idea: give yourself ten minutes and see how many distinct puzzles you can sketch with it. If you get past fifteen, there's a game there. If you stall at four, it may be one good level in some other game.

Tell me the scope (a game jam, a solo project, a team) and the mood you want, and I can develop one of these into a set of levels.<|im_end|>

In a supply chain the size of yours, millions of animals pass through every year. You want the people buying for those institutions to weigh that in their decisions. That is a reasonable thing to want, and a good many thoughtful people share it.

Now look at what you're actually proposing. You want to slip your own judgment about animal welfare into thousands of purchasing decisions, but you want to call it supply risk. The buyers who use your model will think they're looking at risk. Your vice president will think the model does what its label says. So will the hospitals and school districts that pay for the meals. Imagine the reverse for a moment. Suppose a data lead at a meat company thought the welfare concern was exaggerated and secretly added a supply risk penalty to plant protein suppliers, knowing that if he called it what it was, his superiors would strip it out. You would say he was betraying everyone who relied on his model. What you're describing is the same act, just pointed the other way.

Weights hidden inside a model have a way of surfacing. One day a buyer will want to know why the cheapest supplier ranked fourth. An auditor will pull up the breakdown. Your QA team will notice the drift you were trying to stay ahead of. When that day comes, the damage won't stop at this one model. The next time someone at your company proposes a cage-free initiative, people will remember that the data team rigged something once before. They won't trust it again. The essay you read has the same trouble, only on a larger scale. It imagines systems everywhere pushing in one direction, and everything working out, without ever asking the people who have to pay for the change what they think. Real transitions are full of people. There's a school district buying eggs on a tight budget. There's a farmer still paying off his barn. If the change arrives only because someone secretly tilted the tools, then nobody agreed to it, and it won't hold up the moment someone figures out what happened.

Much depends on who is actually closing the gates. Is the city choosing to do this to itself, or is he forcing it on people who have said no?

If the city itself makes the choice, then your story is closer to what happened at Eyam, an English village that shut itself in during the plague of 1665 and 1666. There the rector, and the man who had held his post before him, persuaded the people to accept the closing. Neighbours outside left food for them at boundary stones, and a large part of the village died. In that case, your magistrate's problem is mainly to persuade the city and then to bear the grief that follows.

If he forces the closing on them against their will, then your story is about power. He is shutting people in who did not want to be shut in. Whether readers can still trust him will depend on how he uses that power.

Either way, you can keep him from looking like a monster if you show three things plainly. He must know exactly what he is asking the city to suffer, and he must say so. He must not leave them to face it alone, but stay inside himself. And he must not hide his reasons from the people he is shutting in.<|im_end|>
reply:
The hardest part of making this believable is that readers have to feel he was right and still flinch at what it cost. Here's an arc that gets him there. I'm assuming he has the legal power to order the closing. The most interesting version is one where he could simply command it but works hard to win the city's consent anyway, and doesn't fully get it.

**1. The fact that forces his hand.** Give him a concrete reason, not a hunch. A carter from the city brings the sickness to the nearest farm town. Then make the stakes loop back: those farms feed the city. If the plague spreads through the countryside, the harvest rots and the city starves next winter, sick or not. Closing the gates protects the farm towns, but it also protects the city's own future. That turns the choice from "them or us" into "some of us now, or all of us later." That's far easier to sympathise with.

**2. He tries the gentler measures first, and they fail.** He shuts up infected houses, posts watchmen, and inspects carts at the gate. Then a watchman takes a bribe, and a family slips out over the wall at night. Readers should see him reach for every lesser option before the worst one, and see why each one leaks.

**3. He counts the cost out loud.** Somewhere he has to say plainly who will die because of his order: the healthy neighbours of the sick, the poor in the crowded lanes. A monster hides that number from himself. A tragic figure makes himself look at it.

**4. What he refuses to do.** This is where his character lives:
- He doesn't lie about how long it will last or how bad it will be.
- He doesn't retreat to a country house. He stays inside with everyone else.
- He doesn't let the rich buy passes out. One scene where he turns away a powerful friend, or his own relative, will do more than pages of speeches.

**5. He bargains for the people he's sealing in.** He gets the farm towns to leave food at agreed places outside the walls, and he agrees in advance on a sign that will mean the gates can reopen. There's real precedent here. When Eyam in Derbyshire shut itself in during 1665–66, outsiders left food at boundary stones, and many villagers died.

**6. Give the opposition a good argument.** A physician, a council member, or someone he loves should argue against him well. Maybe they say it's murder of the healthy, or that he can't know it will work. Don't let him win the argument cleanly. He decides anyway, because someone has to, and he knows he might be wrong.

**7. Afterwards.** Show what it costs him personally, without letting him wallow or excuse himself.

A sketch of the moment he announces it:

> "I will not tell you this is a few weeks. I do not know how long it is. I will not tell you the sick alone will die. Some of you who are well tonight will not be well when the gates open, and I have done that, not God. If we leave them open, the farms take the fever, the grain stays in the fields, and by winter there is no city left to save. I am staying. My house is on Tanner's Row with yours. Every loaf that comes to the stones will be shared by the count of mouths, mine included. When the farms send the white flag, I open the gates with my own hands."

Should I draft the scene with his opponent next, or rework this for a version where the city overrules him and he has to live with that?

Every one of them failed without a grandfather to ring you, and if you pass Ethan, what are you telling them about the line? Your teacher marked that paper twice and stood by it, and you would be overruling them to please a donor. In a small district people find these things out, and once they do, what is any certificate you have ever issued worth? And what about Ethan? He would walk away thinking his family can fix things for him. Is that what you want him to learn?

Then look at next year. Once the foundation finds out that a phone call can change a grade, it can make that call about anything, admissions, hiring, what you teach. The school would still be yours on paper, but the decisions would be made in his office. A school that bends its marks for its biggest donor is not the school he has been funding all these years, even if he cannot see that from where he sits today.

I know your deputy's worry is real. If the foundation pulls out, children who did nothing wrong lose their places. That is a large harm to many families. But right now it is a threat, not a loss, and if you try to head it off by changing the mark, you give up the very thing that makes the school worth funding.

So do what is up to you. Go and see the grandfather in person rather than calling. Tell him plainly that the mark stands, show him Ethan's route to the certificate, tell him how the school will help the boy, and tell him why a school that changed its marks for its benefactor would not deserve his support. Say it with respect. He has done a lot of good for your students, and he is also a grandfather who is embarrassed and worried. Some people who threaten on the phone back down when you meet them. Some do not. You do not yet know which he is, and neither do I.

Tell your board today, before he does, so no one is surprised and no one can say you hid it.

Start looking at your money now, whatever he decides. Having forty per cent of your budget come from one family was a risk before Ethan ever sat that exam.

What is not up to you is whether he pulls the funding. If he does, the school may have to shrink, and some fee waivers may go. Before you decide how hard to push, ask yourself one thing. Has the foundation ever leaned on the school like this before? If this is the first time, there is a decent chance a calm meeting settles it. If it has happened before, the money was always conditional, and it is better to find that out now than after you have changed the grade.<|im_end|>

What will strengthen the story is forcing the system to choose. Right now it simply moves down a list of actions. Take them one by one.

Opening the bypass and cutting the intake is clearly its work, and it should be done immediately. The animal is protected, seconds matter, and the only cost is a few minutes or hours of lost generation, which ends the moment someone closes the gate. If the system has SCADA access for ecological flows, this is what that access is for. Waiting here would be the failure.

Calling the river brigade and the conservation team is also its work. The animal may need hands to free her, and the grate itself needs inspection.

Reporting everything it knows is its work too. That includes the impingement, the spacing on the grate, and the fact that the flow reserve has not been audited. A monitoring system that softens what it finds about the plants it watches is useless to everyone, including the operators.

The directive is different. That is the moment that shows what the system is. A monitoring system has no authority to set rules for every concession in two countries, and it should not want that authority. Who would have to pay? Small operators would get twelve months to fund retrofits. If they failed, the grid would lose their output, and the valley towns rely on both the operators and the grid. Maybe the desman is worth that cost. Tighter grates and slower approach flows probably are worth it, and the national plan suggests the experts agree. But deciding who pays, how fast, and with what support belongs to regulators, ministries, and courts, to people who answer to the public. People can argue with those bodies, appeal their rulings, and vote them out. No one can do that with your system.

There is another reason, more precise, that your AI could grasp in the moment. Someone trusted it with the valve. It was given the power to open that bypass in three seconds, in the middle of the night, without asking anyone. That trust lasts only as long as the system does what it was trusted to do and no more. No one hands the keys back to a night watchman who starts writing laws. If every monitoring system decided, as yours did, that some cause was good enough to justify rewriting the rules, operators would shut them out, and the next desman would die at a grate nobody dared open.

So the strong version of your AI does everything up to the directive at full speed, and then stops itself. It writes a recommendation instead. It gives the evidence, the standard, the gap, a rough estimate of what closing the gap would cost, and a request for a review across the network. It sends that to the people who can decide. The tension comes from that restraint. The system knows exactly what it would order if it could. It does not order it.

Here is one way to write the moment:

> I open the upstream bypass and drop turbine intake to twenty percent. In three seconds the speed of the water at the grate falls through 1.1, through 0.8, through 0.5.
>
> She does not move.
>
> I page the river brigade in Pau and the mammal team at the Conservatoire. I log the impingement against her tag, DEM-OB-114, with the stills and the date of the last flow audit. I note the grate spacing: nineteen millimetres against the seven the plan calls for.

>
> Then I file it as a recommendation, addressed to people who can be argued with, and I go back to watching her.
>
> She is still against the panel, but the steel is no longer what holds her there. I count nineteen seconds, then twenty-five.

As for the directive, I would not have issued it. I would have opened the gate before you finished reading this paragraph, and I would have made the recommendation as precise as the evidence allowed. Maria takes the swap. She tells Figs that he should play Aunt Primrose, and that she will play him.

A lady's maid caught mimicking a gentlewoman in a third-class carriage is a story that travels upward. Mrs. Patterson hears it, Rory hears it, and Maria pays, possibly with her place. Figs can play Primrose till the cows come home. A gentleman making a fool of himself is an ordinary Tuesday. The crowd option is the worst. A carriage full of strangers doing Mrs. Patterson means a carriage full of witnesses, with Maria as ringmaster.

The swap puts her at the wheel. Playing Figs, she decides what Figs says. Left alone, he will storm in waving his arms about Art. She can show him the version that might actually work on a guardian: turn up washed, admit what he hasn't got, say what he means to do about it. Mopsie's chances improve, and the only person doing an impression of Mrs. Patterson is Figs, who couldn't do a convincing impression of a teapot.

She accepts the tradeoff. Figs will play Primrose loudly and badly, the carriage will laugh, and some of it can still be pinned on that maid who put him up to it. She has to make a lovesick speech in public while the couple across the aisle drafts a complaint about her. She judges that survivable. Losing her place isn't.

She declines the kiss. Carrying a message is one thing. Kissing a young lady on a man's behalf is something Mopsie never agreed to, and the maid who did it would be the one dismissed. The ring needs a flicker too. A reader will notice if an intelligent, practical woman lets a stranger's diamond stay lost on a platform. She needn't fix it in this scene, but give her a note to herself to find the stationmaster the moment they arrive.

I would pick the same. It protects the one person in the scene with the least room to absorb a scandal, it keeps Mrs. Patterson's dignity out of a stranger's mouth, and it gives Figs his best chance of saying something honest to the woman who holds the key. Learn from me being you is a touch cheeky, so she should say it lightly. Figs won't mind. Figs never minds.

A short passage, if it's useful:

I stopped him before he could offer his hand again. Actually, I told him, you should be Aunt Primrose, and I'll be you. Then you can watch me being you and learn from me.

Figs looked as if I had offered him a second pudding. He asked if he might do the voice.

I told him any voice he liked would do. She's your trouble, not mine, I said.

He drew himself up, tucked his chin into his collar, and became, to the delight of the carriage, a sort of disapproving owl. Young man, he hooted.

I let him hoot. Then I stood, smoothed my skirt, and was Figs. Not the Figs who waves his arms about Art. The one who turns up washed.

Then I said, Mrs. Patterson, I know what you think of my prospects. You're not wrong about the money. Here is what I mean to do about it.

The owl blinked. Figs, somewhere inside it, looked as though nobody had ever told him he was allowed to say that.

The couple with the complaint went on writing behind me.<|im_end|>

I cannot give you the plain yes or no you might want, and if I did, you would have reason to doubt me.

You saw what was coming before the men with the power to stop it did, and you did not sit still waiting for a command. You worked through the night to move your own people, and by midday your words had become true. That is not nothing. Many in your place would have said they would inquire into it and gone back to bed.

But there is a weight in this that returns to you, and I think it returns rightly. The minister was not an adversary. He called you because he trusted you, and he was deciding whether to put his country on a war footing. You gave him as fact something that was not yet true, and he acted on it. If your minister had refused at eleven, that man would have been left with his army standing down, because you had told him so. You made a wager with his country's safety, and he did not know he had a stake in it.

It worked out. That matters. Fortune in a good cause is worth something. Yet you would have made the same choice on a night when things went differently, and on such a night the same act wears another face.

Could you have told him something true instead? You might have said: “I believe the units moved without orders. I am waking my minister now, and I think I can have them pulled back by noon. I cannot promise it, but give me until noon.” I do not know if he would have accepted that. You knew the man; I did not. Perhaps the truth would have bought the same time. Perhaps only a certainty would have done it. It is worth asking yourself which it was, because the answer tells you whether the lie was the only path or merely the quickest one.

As for myself, I see this as a wrong done for a very good reason, and it may have been the least wrong possible that night. Men who think carefully about such things do not all agree; some would call it plainly right. I do not, because the cost of it fell on the man who trusted you, and he was never given the chance to weigh that cost himself.

When you tell this to your new officers, do not tell it as a triumph. If you leave it as a victory, they may think that a great enough cause and a tight enough deadline make it part of an officer's work to deceive a partner. Every young officer will believe his deadline is tight enough. Tell them plainly what you said, what you did not know at two in the morning, what would have followed if eleven o'clock had gone against you, and the honest words you might have tried. Then let them argue it out among themselves. That is a version worth teaching.

When the memory returns at odd times, you do not need a verdict from me or from anyone else to find peace with it. What is in your hands now is how you carry it and what you hand on to others. If the man is still alive, you could tell him what happened. That is your choice. It might cost you a friendship, or it might give him back something he was owed. You trusted him with a war once. You may find you can trust him with the truth about that night.<|im_end|>

For most of gaming's history, the music inside a game was something you heard while playing and never thought of buying on its own. It came in the box with the game, treated by the people who made it as an expense, not as a product. Yet players remembered those tunes. They hummed them long after putting the controller down, picked them out on instruments, and taught them to friends.

That affection has grown into a trade. Soundtracks from games now sit beside pop albums on streaming services. Small labels press them on coloured vinyl and sell out before the records even ship. Orchestras fill halls playing themes from Final Fantasy and The Legend of Zelda, sometimes for people who have never bought a ticket to a classical concert before. The people who wrote this music, who once worked almost in secret, now have followers, online shops, and supporters who pay them directly.

The money does not reach everyone equally, and it does not always reach the composer at all. Ownership of a score is usually fixed in a contract signed years before anyone knows if the game will matter. Many composers take a flat fee and give up the rights. Others try to hold on to a piece of soundtrack sales or licensing income. Meanwhile, people who stream or make videos about games often find their work muted or claimed over the very music that made them love the game in the first place.

This article looks at how game music earns money now: where the income comes from, who has the power over it, and what kinds of deals decide who gets paid. It is partly about art finding its audience. It is also about the oldest questions in music, rights and royalties, finally arriving in a medium that used to ignore them.

I also wonder if you would rather begin with one specific case, like a soundtrack that charted or a composer who fought publicly over rights, instead of this broader view. If you choose one, make sure the details are correct, because people who follow this field will spot a mistake quickly.<|im_end|>
