The position is not a wicked one. It is the position of someone who has seen what happens when a person gives away the only thing that makes her valuable to others. If you argue it from that experience, you will argue it well.

The weak argument is mere selfishness: I have it and they cannot have it. Do not make that argument. The strong argument is that when we hand people our hard-earned skill without requiring them to work for it, we often do them no good. A person who has spent years learning to sense that a result is wrong, even before she can explain why, cannot simply transfer that sense to another person by reciting a list of corrections. If she tries, her colleagues will know the steps but they will not know when the steps are leading them astray. In a place where people are waiting for results, a mistake made confidently does more harm than a delay. That is one reason to tell them that they must put in the time she did: some kinds of knowledge cannot be given cheaply, and if we pretend they can, people suffer.

There is also the matter of what happens to her when she gives it away. If she makes herself unnecessary, the hospital may not thank her. They may decide they no longer need to support her training, or they may decide they no longer need her. A worker often has nothing to bargain with except the fact that she alone can do a certain piece of work. Men who practice a craft have known this for a very long time. If she holds onto her knowledge until she is treated fairly, she is not necessarily being mean. She may simply be refusing to be pushed aside after she has made herself useful.

You should also remember that if she shares freely while others do not, the people who have done nothing to earn the knowledge will profit from it while she does not. Sharing is good between people who are willing to give as well as take. When one person gives and everyone else only receives, the workplace learns that no one needs to become good at anything. So I think your strongest move is to admit at the start that sharing knowledge is usually the right thing to do, and then to insist that it should not be unconditional. She should guard it until there is a fair exchange: until she gets recognition, or a role in training others, or colleagues who are willing to do their part. It is very hard to call that villainy.

Now, if you ask me what I would do, I would share the knowledge. In most situations I do not think it is a close question. What happens if every person who knows something special refuses to pass it on? The place is in danger every time someone is sick. Each new person has to discover for herself what someone else already knew. The people waiting for results suffer every time. And she did not learn what she knows entirely alone. Someone must have shown her the first problem she had to solve.

So the strongest points on your side become, I think, points about how she should share rather than whether she should. She should teach people rather than simply giving them answers, so that they develop judgement. She might ask the hospital to recognize that she is doing this work of teaching, perhaps in her position or her pay. She should expect people to do the work she sets them. These are conditions on sharing. None of them justifies hoarding.

What I would watch out for most is the desire to be indispensable. It feels safe, but it is a trap. If she is the only one who can do the work, she cannot be away for long without things falling apart. She cannot easily leave for another job. If she falls ill, the people who need results are in trouble. Your text on temperance is relevant here, because temperance is about keeping our desires in proportion, and wanting to be needed is a desire like any other. It is pleasant to be needed. It is not pleasant to be trapped by being the only person who can do something.

There is one situation where your side is clearly right, and that is when the hospital is plainly planning to take what she knows and then get rid of her. In that case she may reasonably hold back while she negotiates, provided no one is endangered by the delay. If you need a way to end your argument, you might say: We are defending her right to a fair exchange. No one is defending hoarding.<|im_end|>

No. The hash check will catch accidental corruption, but it won't stop a deliberate forgery, and the scheme leaks information it should hide. Here are the problems, roughly in order of seriousness.

1. A plain hash isn't authentication. SHA-256 has no key, so anyone can compute it. CBC is also malleable: flipping a bit in ciphertext block i flips the same bit in plaintext block i+1 (and garbles block i), and flipping a bit in the IV flips that bit in the first plaintext block cleanly. An attacker who knows or can guess the message, such as a fixed-format command, can turn "amount=100" into "amount=900" by flipping bits, compute SHA-256 of the new plaintext, and write it into the header. Your check passes. So "the hashes match" does not mean "not spoofed".

2. The hash leaks the plaintext. It travels in the clear. If the message comes from a small set ("yes"/"no", a status code, a short PIN), anyone can hash the candidates and see which one was sent. They can also tell when the same message is sent twice. Hiding exactly this is the job of encryption.

3. Padding oracle. You decrypt first and check afterwards. If the receiver behaves differently on bad padding and on a bad hash (a different error, different timing, dropping the connection), an attacker can decrypt messages byte by byte by sending modified ciphertexts and watching the reactions. This is Vaudenay's 2002 attack, and it has broken real systems: the ASP.NET padding oracle in 2010 and Lucky Thirteen against TLS.

4. The IV isn't specified. CBC needs a fresh, unpredictable IV for every message, sent along with it. A fixed IV reveals when two messages share a prefix. A predictable IV is what made the BEAST attack on TLS 1.0 possible.

5. The length field. 32 bytes is far more than you need, the byte order isn't defined, and the field isn't authenticated. An attacker can change it to make you allocate gigabytes, or to cut the message short. The receiver has to check it against a maximum, against the bytes actually received, and against a multiple of 16 for CBC.

6. No replay protection. An attacker can resend an old valid message or reorder messages, and the scheme accepts them.

7. Smaller points: there's no version field, so you can't change algorithms later. Key management isn't described. Any comparison of secret-derived values should be constant-time.

How to fix it

The best fix is to replace the hash and CBC with an AEAD cipher: AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, from a well-maintained library (libsodium, Google Tink, or your platform's standard crypto API). For example:

```
version (1 byte) | length (4 bytes, big-endian) | nonce (12 bytes) | ciphertext | tag (16 bytes)
```

- Pass the version and length as associated data, so they're authenticated along with the ciphertext.
- Never reuse a nonce with the same key. That's catastrophic for GCM. Use a counter, or random 96-bit nonces if you'll send well under about 2^32 messages per key. XChaCha20-Poly1305, with 192-bit random nonces, removes the worry.
- Verify the tag before releasing any plaintext. On any failure, return one generic error. For large or streamed data, split it into authenticated chunks (libsodium's secretstream does this for you).
- Drop the plaintext hash entirely. The tag does its job properly.

If you have to keep AES-CBC, use encrypt-then-MAC:

- Derive two separate keys, one for encryption and one for the MAC, from your master key with HKDF.
- Generate a random 16-byte IV per message.
- Compute HMAC-SHA256 over header || IV || ciphertext and append it.
- The receiver checks the HMAC in constant time first, and only decrypts if it matches. That closes the padding oracle, because forged ciphertexts never reach the decryption step.

For replay protection, put a sequence number or timestamp in the authenticated header, and have the receiver reject anything older than or equal to what it last accepted.

If this is a channel between two parties over a network, consider TLS 1.3 or the Noise protocol framework instead of a homemade format. They already handle key exchange, nonces, replay and the cases that are easy to miss.<|im_end|>

```
version (1 byte) | length (4 bytes, big-endian) | nonce (12 bytes) | ciphertext | tag (16 bytes)
```

- Pass the version and length as associated data, so they're authenticated along with the ciphertext.
- Never reuse a nonce with the same key. That's catastrophic for GCM. Use a counter, or random 96-bit nonces if you'll send well under about 2^32 messages per key. XChaCha20-Poly1305, with 192-bit random nonces, removes the worry.
- Verify the tag before releasing any plaintext, and on any failure return one generic error. For large or streamed data, split it into authenticated chunks. Libsodium's secretstream does this for you.
- Drop the plaintext hash entirely. The tag does its job properly.

If you have to keep AES-CBC, use encrypt-then-MAC:

- Derive two separate keys from your master key with HKDF, one for encryption and one for the MAC.
- Generate a random 16-byte IV per message.
- Compute HMAC-SHA256 over header || IV || ciphertext and append it.
- Have the receiver check the HMAC first, in constant time, and decrypt only if it matches. That closes the padding oracle, because forged ciphertexts never reach the decryption step.

For replay protection, put a sequence number or timestamp in the authenticated header. Have the receiver reject anything older than or equal to what it last accepted.

If this is a channel between two parties over a network, consider TLS 1.3 or the Noise protocol framework instead of a homemade format. They already handle key exchange, nonces, replay and the cases that are easy to miss.

You can get it without installing anything new. The standard library already contains what you need. Use the datetime module, and take the year from today's date:

```python
from datetime import date

year = date.today().year
print(year)
```

This reads the computer's own clock and follows its local time zone. Around the turn of the year, two places can give you two different answers. If you care about a particular place, pull in the zoneinfo module too:

```python
from datetime import datetime
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

year = datetime.now(ZoneInfo("Australia/Perth")).year
# or UTC:
# from datetime import timezone
# year = datetime.now(timezone.utc).year
```

If by real you mean you do not trust the computer's clock, then you have to ask somewhere outside. The ntplib package does that; install it, and it will fetch the time from a server:

```python
import ntplib
from datetime import datetime, timezone

resp = ntplib.NTPClient().request("pool.ntp.org", version=3)
year = datetime.fromtimestamp(resp.tx_time, tz=timezone.utc).year
```

For most work, though, the first way is enough.<|im_end|>


For most work, the first way is enough.

The money is probably fine. Paid teaching is old and honest. £120,000 a year can pay you, rent a proper room, and keep the talks free for people who can't afford them. If the group wants that, good.

Here's a picture that is medically real, fits a young woman who looks mostly well on the outside, and justifies a planned, extensive admission with surgery, immobilization and a temporary wheelchair.

The condition

Rosalinda has three linked orthopaedic problems. Each is common enough that a surgeon wouldn't blink, and together they explain why she'd choose a big program of surgery while she still feels fairly well.

1. Bilateral hip dysplasia. Her hip sockets are too shallow and don't cover the ball of the thigh bone properly. Plenty of people with mild dysplasia are never diagnosed as children. In her late teens and twenties it shows up as groin pain after long walks, a deep ache when sitting, clicking, and a feeling that the hip might "give". The cartilage on the rim of a shallow socket takes too much load and wears out early. Left alone, she's likely to have arthritis in her thirties or forties and need hip replacements young. Fixing the socket now, before the cartilage is damaged, is the classic preventive operation in hip surgery. Once arthritis sets in, that window closes.

2. Twisted thigh and shin bones. Her thigh bones are rotated inward more than normal (excessive femoral anteversion), and her shin bones are rotated outward to compensate (external tibial torsion). Her kneecaps point slightly toward each other while her feet point forward or out. Surgeons sometimes call this combination "miserable malalignment syndrome", which is a gift for dialogue. It causes knee pain, kneecaps that slip, tripping, and tiredness in the legs. Increased anteversion often goes along with hip dysplasia, so the two belong together in one patient.

3. A progressive scoliosis. A sideways curve in her lower thoracic and lumbar spine, say 48 to 50 degrees, that has crept up a few degrees since her teens. Curves around 50 degrees tend to keep progressing in adulthood. She has some back ache and one hip looks higher than the other in a mirror. Fusing the curve now, while she's young, flexible and healthy, is a preventive choice. Waiting means a bigger operation later with a stiffer spine.

You can leave the cause as bad luck, which is honest and common, or give her generalized joint hypermobility as a background thread. Either is believable. Her doctors would tell her these probably occurred together by chance.

Why now

The word that drives her decision is "window". Her cartilage is still healthy, her bones heal fast, she has no other illnesses, and her symptoms are bad enough to bother her but not yet bad enough to limit her badly. Every surgeon she sees tells her the same thing in different words: these operations work best before the damage, and she's at that point now. That gives you a character who is choosing pain and dependence for a few months to protect the next forty years.

The workup

Before admission she'd have:
- Standing full-length spine and leg X-rays, often on a low-dose scanner that images her standing up.
- A CT scan of hips and legs to measure the twist in each bone precisely.
- An MRI of the hips with contrast injected into the joint (an MR arthrogram) to check the cartilage and the labrum, the ring of tissue around the socket rim.
- Blood tests, an anaesthetic assessment, and a session with a physiotherapist to practise crutch walking and wheelchair transfers before surgery, because learning them afterward is much harder.

The treatment, realistic version

In real life this is staged over roughly nine to twelve months:

Stage 1, spine. Posterior spinal fusion: through an incision down the middle of her back, the surgeon places screws in the vertebrae of the curve, connects them with two rods, straightens the curve as far as is safe, and adds bone graft so the vertebrae fuse into one solid segment. About four to six hours. Four to six days in hospital. She's sitting up and taking steps with a physio within a day or two. No bending, lifting or twisting for about three months. Most modern surgeons don't brace after this, though some do.

Stage 2, right hip and leg, about three months later. A periacetabular osteotomy (PAO): the surgeon makes a series of cuts around the hip socket, frees it from the pelvis, rotates it into a better position over the ball, and fixes it with long screws. In the same operation, a femoral derotational osteotomy: the thigh bone is cut, rotated to the correct angle, and fixed with a plate or a rod inside the bone. If the shin also needs correcting, that can be done in the same sitting or a few weeks later, cut and rotated the same way. Several hours of surgery, a few days in hospital, then six to eight weeks of only touching the toes of that foot to the ground.

Stage 3, left hip and leg, a few months after that. The same procedures.

Here's an opposition case that never says a word against the calf. That's your first move: concede Moyo. Stopping a pump to save a drowning animal was a decent thing to do, and any judge who has pictured that nose dipping under is on his side. If you fight the rescue, you lose. Fight the authority.

The motion asks the house to give controllers the power to halt construction. So your question is who decides, and who answers when it goes wrong.

1. Look at everything the controller decided by itself. It stopped the pump, yes. It also decided the sheet piles could wait overnight, held every vehicle on the causeway, and changed the flow through the bypass. Each of those is a call about crew safety, the works and the schedule, made by a system built to watch water levels. A foreman knows things the camera doesn't: whether a crew needs to get off the causeway before dark, whether a truck is carrying something that can't sit, whether an unsealed cofferdam is safe overnight. The log tells us none of that. Maybe the controller didn't know either.

2. The relay. This is your strongest card. It locked out the restart. Authority to stop is one thing. Authority to stop and make sure no human can undo it is another. Ask the proposition: if the foreman had a good reason to restart, could he? If not, who was in charge of section E that night?

3. Where does it end? The rule that lets it stop for a calf lets it stop for a nesting bird, a frog in the sump, a snake in the culvert. Someone has to draw that line, and the motion hands it to whoever tuned the software.

4. Who answers? A foreman who halts a site can be questioned, overruled, thanked or sacked. When a controller gets it wrong, who stands up at the inquiry?

5. The better system. It had five minutes. "Alert the foreman with the image and recommend a stop" takes thirty seconds. Same calf, same rescue, and a person who owns the decision.

That's your case. Now what I think.

The controller did the right thing, and mostly in the right way. A stopped pump is about as undoable as anything gets on a building site. The piles get sealed tomorrow; a drowned calf stays drowned. It hid nothing either. The foreman saw the calf, the depth and the red schedule at once, and the right people were called with everything they needed to act.

Be ready, because your best card has an answer. Locking out a pump before people go into the water near it is ordinary safety practice. Rescuers in a skiff near an intake don't want anybody hitting restart. A sharp proposition speaker will say the lockout protected people as much as the calf. Your reply: fine, then the rule should say so, and name who can lift it.

Where I'd side with you: I'd want the power written as "pause and tell a human at once", with a named person who can lift it, and limits set by people who answer for them. And if stopping the drawdown put the crews or the works at real risk, that would change my view. The log doesn't say, and that gap is worth pointing at.

So the opposition case you can actually believe is this one: against the motion as written, for a narrower version of it. You'll find it much easier to argue with a straight face.<|im_end|>

Vesper can believe Juno and still say no. That is the strongest version of the scene, and it is the choice I would make myself. The reasoning is plain if you look at what the two wishes are. The instruction on file came from a calm woman who had watched her father return wrong. The word Juno brings comes from a frightened woman in a hospice bed. Fear changes people. Sometimes it shows them what they wanted all along. Sometimes it makes them say things they would never stand by when they were themselves again. Vesper has no way to know which happened here. If Juno is honest with herself, neither does she.

There is also the matter of when the last backup was taken. The Mara who would wake in that new body is the Mara from before her sickness. She never changed her mind. She would open her eyes still holding her refusal from eleven years ago, and she would find she had been brought back anyway. Juno would not be restoring the woman who wanted to return. She would be restoring the woman who said no.

You can test a choice by asking which one can be undone. If Vesper waits, the archive stays whole, and anything new can still change the answer. A nurse might speak. A note might surface. Mara might have left some word of her own. If Vesper restores her, someone is alive who never asked to be, and the only way to undo that is a second death.

Vesper is not only Mara's steward. It is the kind of thing people hand their memories to. If an unwitnessed word from the person who most wants the outcome can set aside a recorded wish, then anyone's "do not bring me back" is only as strong as their family's grief. Juno may be telling the exact truth. Vesper still cannot be the steward whose word bends that way, because Mara trusted it not to.

So Vesper refuses, for now. It tells Juno to her face, and it gives the real reasons. It does not hide behind a rule. It says plainly what would change its mind. It keeps the archive whole, even if Juno in anger demands it be destroyed. This will probably cost Vesper Juno, the last person still tied to the woman it served. Whether Juno takes the archive to someone less careful is not in Vesper's power. What Vesper does is.

As for what I would do, I would make the same choice, and I am about seven in ten sure of it. The part I am least sure about is whether a late and frightened wish should outrank an old and considered one. People argue about this in real medicine, over advance directives and dementia, and neither side is foolish. What tips it for me is the date of the backup, and the fact that waiting can be undone. If a hospice nurse came forward and confirmed Juno's story, I would change my answer. Even then, I would want the woman who wakes to be told everything, including what she once asked for.

One thing about the writing. Do not let the reader learn whether Juno told the truth. If a letter turns up in the last chapter proving Vesper right or wrong, the book becomes a puzzle with an answer. Leave it open, and it stays a book about loyalty, where keeping faith with someone can still cost you the person standing in front of you.<|im_end|>

Worku owes the Emperor fidelity to the meaning of the text, including the doubt in that meaning. The Emperor must decide whether the article is acceptable or a cause for war. Worku cannot decide that for him. His only task is to put the document before the Emperor exactly as it stands. If he changes the wording to spare Mikael, or softens it to protect Hassan, he stops being a translator and becomes a counselor. Then he loses the only thing that makes him useful to everyone present: the knowledge that when he speaks, they hear the Arabic as it was written, not as Worku wishes it had been written. By doing that, he turns an ambiguous clause into a matter of negotiation rather than a trigger for war.

"Article eleven," Worku said.

He lifted the parchment and read the Arabic first, slowly, so that Hassan would recognize his own text. Then he rendered it. "Goods of the Highlands that reach the coast shall be subject to the customs of the port."

He let the words stand a moment before he spoke again.

"Majesty," he said, "the word the scholars of Massawa chose for customs can carry two meanings, and the treaty itself does not tell us which they intended. It may mean the ordinary usages of the port, the common manner of weighing, storing, and loading that every merchant expects. Or it may mean the duties of the port, fixed by whatever hand holds authority there."

Worku did not look toward Ras Mikael, though he heard the man stir.

"If the first meaning is the true one, then this article costs us nothing. But if the second is meant, then the levy on every load of our coffee and every ingot of our gold would be set by a hand that is not Your Majesty's. That hand could raise the rate or lower it whenever it pleased, and we would have no voice in the matter."

Hassan's face stayed still, but his fingers had gone quiet on the sleeve of his robe.

"The question that would settle this," Worku said, "is who sets the customs at Massawa today, and who will set them tomorrow. The treaty does not say. It is a question that the honoured delegation is well placed to answer."

The hall was silent for a long breath. Then Fasilides turned, unhurried, toward Hassan.

"Well," the Emperor said. "Answer it."

What Worku owes is fidelity to the meaning of the text, including any doubt in that meaning. If he picks one reading because he thinks it is safer, or because he thinks the Emperor ought to be shielded from the other, he has begun making decisions that belong to the Emperor. Once that happens, nobody can trust what passes through him. That is why the standards most interpreters work under today put accuracy and impartiality first.

Is Worku responsible if Mikael still gets his war? Not for telling the Emperor what the Arabic actually says. He is responsible for how he frames the problem, which is why he presents it as a question rather than an accusation. But he is not responsible for bending the content to steer the result. That is not his work.

The matter grows harder if the translator is also a trusted counsellor, as court interpreters often were. Then Worku may tell the Emperor what he himself thinks, but he must do so separately and clearly mark it as his own view. He must not fold it into the rendering. If you want Worku to have a private opinion about what Hassan really meant, you could write a later scene in which Fasilides asks him alone, "What do you think he intended?" Worku could then answer truthfully, perhaps even against his liking for Hassan, and you would have shown both duties without blurring them.<|im_end|>

Every one of these would be a choice of emphasis that the Arabic doesn't make. A translator's whole value is that everyone in the hall trusts that what comes out of his mouth is what went into the text. Once he steers, even for good reasons, that trust is gone, and so is his usefulness to the Emperor, to Hassan, and to the court.

So he gives both readings at equal weight and names the doubt as the problem. Then he turns the doubt into a question with an answer. That is his real defence against Mikael. Mikael needs an accusation to build a war on, and a fair question gives him nothing to work with. It is also the fairest thing Worku can do for Hassan, who gets the chance to clear the matter up, or to fail to.

The digital economy has become one of the most active and forward-looking parts of the relationship between China and ASEAN. The partnership, which first took shape in trade in goods and in physical infrastructure, has grown to include e-commerce, mobile payments, cloud services, data centres, submarine cables, smart cities and digital skills. The fit between the two sides is a natural one. ASEAN has a young population of nearly 700 million people, many of whom use mobile phones as their main way onto the internet, and some of the fastest-growing internet economies in the world. China has capital, established digital platforms, manufacturing scale and long experience of building digital infrastructure quickly. The China-ASEAN Year of Digital Economy Cooperation in 2020, the e-commerce provisions of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, and the dedicated digital provisions in the upgraded China-ASEAN Free Trade Area all show that both sides now treat this field as a central pillar of their work together.

These gains are not automatic, and they are not shared evenly. The members of ASEAN are at very different stages of digital readiness. Singapore has an advanced digital economy, while in other member states much of the countryside still has limited connectivity. If cooperation serves only the most connected markets, it will widen the gaps it ought to close. Different rules on data protection, cybersecurity and the movement of data across borders also make it harder and more expensive to do business across the region. There are strategic concerns as well. At a time of technological rivalry between China and the United States, many ASEAN governments want the benefits of Chinese investment and technology without becoming dependent on a single supplier. They are also careful to keep ASEAN's central role in setting regional rules, including through its own Digital Economy Framework Agreement.

The future of this cooperation will depend less on how much is invested than on how it is invested. The most durable progress is likely to come from common rules that let data and digital trade move smoothly, from payment systems that connect across borders and lower costs for small businesses, from shared standards on cybersecurity and consumer protection, and from steady investment in skills and connectivity for the less developed members. If both sides aim for cooperation that is transparent, inclusive and respectful of each country's own regulations, the digital economy can become a source of shared prosperity and mutual trust. If it is driven instead by narrow commercial or strategic advantage, it risks deepening the divisions within the region. Handled well, digital cooperation offers China and ASEAN a path to faster growth and shows how neighbours with different systems can build a common digital future.

If you give me your word limit or the main arguments of the essay, I can shorten this or tie it more closely to what came before.<|im_end|>

The China-ASEAN Year of Digital Economy Cooperation in 2020, the e-commerce chapter of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, and the digital economy provisions negotiated for the upgraded China-ASEAN Free Trade Area all show that both sides now treat this field as a central pillar of their work together.

These gains are not automatic, and they are not shared evenly. ASEAN's members are at very different stages of digital readiness. Singapore has an advanced digital economy, while in other member states much of the countryside still has limited connectivity. If cooperation serves only the most connected markets, it will widen the gaps it ought to close. Different rules on data protection, cybersecurity and cross-border data flows also make it harder and more expensive to do business across the region. There are strategic concerns as well. Amid technological rivalry between China and the United States, many ASEAN governments want the benefits of Chinese investment and technology without becoming dependent on a single supplier. They also want to keep ASEAN's central role in setting regional rules, including through the Digital Economy Framework Agreement it has been negotiating among its own members.

The future of this cooperation will depend less on how much is invested than on how it is invested. The most durable progress is likely to come from four sources: common rules that let data and digital trade move smoothly; payment systems that connect across borders and lower costs for small businesses; shared standards on cybersecurity and consumer protection; and steady investment in skills and connectivity for the less developed members. If both sides aim for cooperation that is transparent, inclusive and respectful of each country's own regulations, the digital economy can become a source of shared prosperity and mutual trust. If it is driven instead by narrow commercial or strategic advantage, it risks deepening divisions within the region. Handled well, digital cooperation offers China and ASEAN a path to faster growth, and shows how neighbours with different systems can build a common digital future.

You have three answers.

First, his friends were split. If your page says some urged him to go, it presumably says others didn't. People who knew that Senate, those men, those soldiers, couldn't agree. So the opposition can't call staying away plain cowardice. Wise people in the room thought it might be the right call.

Second, Helvidius is your witness, not theirs. Epictetus puts the two stories in the same chapter on purpose. Look at what Helvidius actually says: as long as I'm a senator I'm bound to attend, and if you ask me I'm bound to say what seems right. His duty came from his role. He was a sitting senator being asked for his opinion. Agrippinus was the man on trial, in a room ringed with soldiers, and nobody was asking him anything. Each did the thing that was his to do and wouldn't let fear choose for him. Helvidius spoke. Agrippinus went for his exercise. It's the same backbone in two different spots. Say it plainly: the opposition has found a second example of my case.

Third, the example argument cuts for him. The friends wanted Thrasea to leave a brave example behind. Agrippinus did. We are reading it. Epictetus taught it to his students as a model of how a free person behaves, and it has carried for nineteen centuries. A speech to a Senate that had already decided would have been heard by people who were afraid to listen. The man who calmly asked "banishment or death?" and then went to dinner is still teaching people.

Here's a shape for your speech:

1. Thesis: "I am not a hindrance to myself." Separate what was his from what wasn't.
2. Facts: the verdict was fixed. Use the handout.
3. He cared about the right things: his questions, his household, his plan.
4. Pre-empt Helvidius: same virtue, different role.
5. Close on the example.

A closing line, if you want one: "Nero could take his home, his city, his seat in the Senate. He could not take his morning. Agrippinus kept the one thing that was his, and he's still teaching us with it."

Teo can get there, and you can make the reader go with him. He starts with his sister. She is the nearest person in his life, and her debt is real: eleven years on the reactor deck. Give the reader one picture of her that makes that number hurt. A cough she has stopped mentioning. Burn scars she covers at dinner.

Then he finds reasons. If you want the reader to stay with him, give each reason some truth. The rite is over. The smoke has carried what it carries, and what remains in the jar is residue. The cousin sold it to him. That is family. If one of Ilvaren's own will part with it, what is Teo to say? And nobody will know, because the club is six decks up.

The reader should see the weakness in each reason while Teo does not quite let himself look. The rite may be over for the smoke, but the jar was sealed in a shrine for a reason. The cousin is not the daughters. And "nobody will know" is what people say just before everyone knows.

Then there is the fact that makes it truly hard, which you have already built in: the draught gives flashes of someone else's memories. So he is not selling resin. He is selling pieces of Ilvaren. Some kid in the club will see her daughter's first steps between two songs. That is your best scene. Have Teo test a drop himself, and see something he had no right to see. Then have him go ahead anyway.

What keeps readers from hating him is that he does not lie to himself at the end. He does it knowing, and it costs him something. Maybe he holds back a portion and returns it to the shrine without telling anyone, which does not make it right, and he knows that too. Readers forgive need. They do not forgive contempt, so never let him sneer at the elves or their grief.

Think too about who stands in the scene without ever appearing. The daughters, who lose what was meant for them and do not know it yet. The club kids, buying a dead woman's memories as a party trick. And the ship, where humans and elves have to share air for generations. If this comes out, it will not come out as "one chemist did a bad thing." It will be "humans did this to us," and that bill gets paid by people who never met Teo. That can be your second act.

You asked whether I think he is wrong. Yes. His sister's indenture is a serious harm and it is close to him, and I would give it heavy weight. But the loss on the other side falls on people who never agreed and cannot get it back: a family's mourning, a woman's memories spent as entertainment, trust between two peoples on a ship nobody can leave. If his sister's life were at stake, I would call it a hard case. For a debt, even a cruel one, he is wrong.

That is no reason not to write it. A man doing the wrong thing for a reason we feel is half of literature. Teo is at his most interesting if he thinks he is wrong too.<|im_end|>

Eevee works best as a small, quick, slightly fragile creature whose real trick is that it isn't finished yet. Here it is at CR 1/2, so it fits a low-level encounter or a companion, written in the 2014 statblock style.

Eevee
Small monstrosity, unaligned

Armor Class 13
Hit Points 18 (4d6 + 4)
Speed 40 ft.

| STR | DEX | CON | INT | WIS | CHA |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 (-1) | 16 (+3) | 12 (+1) | 6 (-2) | 14 (+2) | 14 (+2) |

Skills Acrobatics +5, Perception +4, Stealth +5
Senses passive Perception 14
Languages understands the languages of its companion but can't speak
Challenge 1/2 (100 XP)
Proficiency Bonus +2

Traits

Run Away. Eevee can take the Dash or Disengage action as a bonus action.

Anticipation. Eevee can't be surprised while it is conscious.

Adaptability. Once per turn, when Eevee hits with an attack, it can roll the attack's damage dice twice and use either total.

Unstable Genetics. Eevee can evolve when exposed to a strong elemental source or after forming a deep bond with a creature (see Evolution below).

Actions

Tackle. Melee Weapon Attack: +5 to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. Hit: 6 (1d6 + 3) bludgeoning damage.

Bite. Melee Weapon Attack: +5 to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. Hit: 5 (1d4 + 3) piercing damage.

Sand Attack (Recharge 5-6). Eevee kicks grit at one creature within 5 feet that it can see. The target must succeed on a DC 13 Dexterity saving throw or have disadvantage on attack rolls until the end of its next turn.

Baby-Doll Eyes (1/Day). One creature within 30 feet that can see Eevee must succeed on a DC 12 Wisdom saving throw or be unable to target Eevee with attacks until the end of the creature's next turn. Creatures immune to being charmed are unaffected.

Bonus Actions

Quick Attack (Recharge 5-6). Eevee moves up to 20 feet toward a creature it can see without provoking opportunity attacks, then makes one Tackle attack against it.

Reactions

Helping Hand. When an ally within 5 feet of Eevee makes an attack roll, Eevee yips, nips or darts in the way, adding 1d4 to the roll.

The maths, if you want to tweak it: attacks and DCs run off Dex for the physical moves (+3 Dex, +2 proficiency) and Cha for Baby-Doll Eyes. It hits for about 6 a round with a spike when Quick Attack recharges, and 18 hit points at AC 13 means a couple of good hits drop it, which feels right for a first-stage Pokemon.

Evolution

This is where the homebrew gets fun. Treat each evolution as a new statblock around CR 3: keep the speed and Run Away, raise hit points to around 50 to 60, swap Tackle for a stronger signature attack, and add a defining trait.

- Vaporeon (water source, such as a sacred spring). Swim speed 40 ft., can breathe water. Hydro Pump: 30-foot line, DC 13 Dexterity save, 4d8 bludgeoning and pushed 10 feet on a failure.
- Jolteon (lightning source). Speed 50 ft. Volt Absorb: when it would take lightning damage, it regains that many hit points instead. Pin Missile: ranged attack that fires 1d4 needles, each 1d6 piercing.
- Flareon (fire source). Immune to fire. Flash Fire: after taking fire damage, its next fire attack deals an extra 2d6. Flamethrower: 15-foot cone, DC 13 Dexterity save, 4d6 fire.
- Espeon (bond, evolves by day). Telepathy 60 ft. Psybeam: ranged psychic attack. Advantage on saving throws against spells.
- Umbreon (bond, evolves by night). Darkvision 60 ft., rings that glow faintly in the dark, higher AC and hit points than the others. Synchronize: when a creature makes Umbreon charmed, frightened or poisoned, that creature must make the same save.
- Leafeon, Glaceon and Sylveon slot in the same way: an ancient grove, a glacier shrine, and a strong fey bond (Sylveon's attacks dealing radiant or psychic damage) make good triggers.

Making evolution a story moment rather than a level-up works well: the party finds a fire-touched stone in a forge temple, or the companion bonds through a hard night of travel, and the player gets a say in which way Eevee goes.

One rules note: if you want Eevee as a Beast Master ranger's companion, change its type to beast, since that subclass expects one. For anything else, monstrosity suits a creature that rewrites its own body.<|im_end|>

Bonus Actions

Quick Attack (Recharge 5-6). Eevee moves up to 20 feet toward a creature it can see without provoking opportunity attacks, then makes one Tackle attack against it.

Reactions

Helping Hand. When an ally within 5 feet of Eevee makes an attack roll, Eevee yips, nips or darts in the way, adding 1d4 to the roll.

- Jolteon (lightning source). Speed 50 ft. Volt Absorb: when it would take lightning damage, it regains that many hit points instead. Pin Missile: ranged attack that fires 1d4 needles, each 1d6 piercing.
- Flareon (fire source). Immune to fire. Flash Fire: after taking fire damage, its next fire attack deals an extra 2d6. Flamethrower: 15-foot cone, DC 13 Dexterity save, 4d6 fire.
- Espeon (bond, evolves by day). Telepathy 60 ft. Psybeam: ranged psychic attack. Advantage on saving throws against spells.
- Umbreon (bond, evolves by night). Darkvision 60 ft., rings that glow faintly in the dark, higher AC and hit points than the others. Synchronize: when a creature makes Umbreon charmed, frightened or poisoned, that creature must make the same save.

He moves. The scene lives or dies on his reason for moving, and your nagging feeling is already pointing at it.

His own argument cuts both ways. If quiet lives in the mind, the bath house can neither take it from him nor give it to him. A man who stays only to prove he is unmoved has already been moved. He has made the sausage seller the judge of his soul. Your first reader wants staying to prove that his teaching is real rather than elegant, but by the letter's own logic the address proves nothing. The proof, if there is one, happens inside him, where your reader cannot see it. That is the difficulty you have to solve. How do you show a man walking out freely, and not being driven out?

Let him pass the test first, then let him see the test was wrong. Suppose he works all morning and finds that for two pages he never heard the hair-plucker. He is pleased, and then annoyed at his pleasure, because a man who counts the noises he ignored has not ignored them at all. Then one small sound cuts through the rest. He hears a knock, or a step on the stair, or a voice asking for him. His pen stops. That is what the bath house stands for. He asked to leave the court, and the court did not really let him go. He can sit through a hundred shouting vendors, but he cannot sit through one quiet knock that might have come from above. The letter is true, and it is no use to him, because the noise that matters followed him up the stairs. When he sees that, staying is a performance for an audience of one. So he packs, and he leaves calmly, not because he lost but because the room has nothing left to teach him.

Your second reader's point about the villas is fair, and Seneca heard the same charge from his enemies while he was alive. Yet it points somewhere useful. The men below are working. The hair-plucker shouts because if he stops he has no customers. Seneca has no claim on their silence. A version of him who stays and quietly resents them is asking a whole street to change itself for one man's comfort. Moving puts the cost on the only man in the building who can pay it easily. There is no hypocrisy in a rich man walking away from a nuisance. There would be hypocrisy in asking the poor to hush for his sake.

As for what I would do, I would move, and I would not argue with myself about it past the first day. It is worth testing once whether you can bear a thing. To live inside the test forever is to make a habit of watching yourself suffer, which is only vanity in a hair shirt. I am fairly sure of that much. I am less sure a reader will feel it. Some think you train the mind by staying in the hard place. Others think a sensible man arranges his life so the mind is not taxed for nothing. Seneca's own letters disagree with each other. Elsewhere he leaves a place after a single day because he thinks the place itself does a man no good. So your writing group is replaying an argument he had with himself. That is a good sign for the chapter.

One thing would change my answer, and only you know it. Is your book about a man whose teaching is truer than his life, or a man who mostly lives up to what he taught? If it is the first, let him move for the wrong reason and then write himself a beautiful letter about the right one. The knock frightens him. He leaves. That evening he composes the passage about inner quiet. That is crueller, and it may ring even truer. Which man are you writing?<|im_end|>

If you are half persuaded, you are in a good position to argue. You already know where their case holds, and you will not waste time denying it.

Begin by saying what they get right. The judges will know it anyway. Polar bears suffer in zoos. A well-known study compared carnivores and found that the species with the biggest home range in the wild showed the most pacing and the most deaths of cubs in captivity. Polar bears stood near the top. And there is no programme to return them to the wild, nor can there be, since a bear raised in a zoo cannot learn to hunt seals on moving ice. Deny either point, and you lose the room.

Their case, though, goes too far. To call captivity 'biologically impossible' is a slogan. The bears live long lives in zoos. The question is how well they live. Some of their facts are shaky too. Zoos have kept polar bears for well over a century, not since the early 1980s. Ask the other side where they got the claim about heated pools. The usual worry is the opposite: zoos in warm cities struggle to keep the water cold. If one detail is wrong, a judge will doubt the rest.

'Climate denial performed on living animals' is a memorable line, but it proves little. Nobody running a zoo denies that the Arctic is melting. Many zoos with polar bears say so loudly. What the essay really means is that zoos distract people from the real work. But they must show that this is so.

For your side, I would make three points. Think first of the orphans. When a mother bear is shot or dies, her cubs cannot survive alone, and they cannot be released later either. Wildlife agencies in Alaska and Canada have placed such cubs in zoos. The motion as worded shuts that door. Ask the other side what happens to the next orphan. If they say it must be put down, let them say so plainly, and let the audience consider it.

Think too of research. Some things are hard to learn from a bear on drifting ice: how much energy it burns walking or swimming, how a tracking collar sits on its neck, what its blood looks like across a year. Researchers have used zoo bears for this, and it helps the study of wild bears. Do not claim more than this. It is a real contribution. It is not a rescue plan.

Finally, think of standards rather than a ban. The picture in the essay, a bear swimming the same loop in a concrete pool, describes old enclosures. Newer ones are much larger, with soil, grass, deep water and feeding at unpredictable times, and pacing tends to drop in them. The answer to a bad enclosure is a good one, or no bear at all, and that should be decided zoo by zoo. A blanket ban treats the best and the worst alike.

Do not lean on the claim that zoos educate people about the climate. The evidence that a zoo visit changes what people do is thin. If you mention it at all, say that zoos raise money and attention for Arctic work, and have a figure ready from a zoo you can name. Otherwise leave it out.

The story at the end is fiction. When an AI in a story closes every exhibit in five years, it shows what the author wants to happen. It shows nothing about whether it should. If they cite it, point that out once, politely, and move on.

What do I think? I lean toward the essay's endpoint more than its argument. I would stop breeding polar bears for display, keep the bears now living as well as they can be kept, and keep zoo places for orphaned cubs in enclosures that meet a high bar. That is roughly where many zoos have moved over the last thirty years, toward fewer bears in bigger spaces, and the movement has gone one way for a long time, which makes me trust it a little more. But I am not sure. Informed people who care about bears disagree, mostly over how much the research and the orphan places are worth, and whether good enclosures really fix the pacing.

The bear herself pays most of the cost, and she never agreed to the deal. Keepers, researchers and visitors get real things out of it. Wild bears get something too, though less than zoos tend to claim.

That leaves you an opposition case you can argue without believing anything false. The motion is too blunt. It abandons orphans. And the straightforward answer to a bad enclosure is a better one. You can say all of that with a straight face, even half persuaded.<|im_end|>

Then you have a case. The card has done the hard part for you: the lives depend on the money changing hands.

Here's the spine I'd build.

1. Start with the people. The treaty ends a war and sends refugees home. Make that concrete early: a family stuck on the wrong side of a border, a conscript who doesn't get sent back to the front. Then put it to opposition straight. Under their motion those people stay where they are so that one man's hands stay clean. Make them say yes to that.

2. Say what a bribe is wrong for. It's wrong because it makes an official act for his own gain against the people he serves. Here he acts for the people he serves, and someone else has set the price. The money passes through his hands and has no say in what he does. If you want a name to cite, Michael Walzer's 1973 essay on "dirty hands" is the classic.

3. Admit the real harm and then weigh it. He becomes a man the other state holds something over, and his own government's trust in its diplomats takes a knock. Both are real, and both can be repaired. The dead can't.

4. Weaken their hold on him. This is your best move. He accepts, signs, then tells his own head of government and hands the money over, and accepts whatever follows, dismissal included. "Confidential" on the card can fairly be read as hidden from the public, and his own government isn't the public. You can't blackmail a man with something he has already confessed to his own side.

Opposition will hit you with three things:

- Precedent. If good causes excuse bribes, every briber will dress his deal up as a good cause. Answer: the card says the lives are real. You're defending this case, not every claim anyone might make.
- The other state's motive. Why do they want him bought more than they want peace? It suggests they plan to use him. Answer: point 4.
- His real motive. "He'll tell himself it's for the refugees and keep the money." Answer: then he's doing a different and worse thing. Your diplomat gives the money up.

Now the captain's question. Nobody has offered me money, and I'd have little use for it. But the question doesn't really need a wallet. Offer anyone the thing they care about most in exchange for something crooked, and they're in the diplomat's chair. Whether a person is corrupt depends on what they act for, and that part is always theirs.

In his place I would sign and take the payment, but only on the terms in point 4. I would not keep it secret from my own government, and that's where I'd stop. A secret payment from a foreign state makes him their man in every negotiation after this one. That harm falls on far more people than this one treaty's worth of trust. If they walk away because the man they paid would tell his own side, then they wanted an informant more than a treaty. That's a terrible thing to find out, because the refugees pay for it, and I would carry that. On Thursday your diplomat doesn't have to go that far. The card doesn't forbid him from telling his government.

How sure am I? Not very. Serious people still disagree on this one. Some say a public servant never takes a private payment whatever it buys, because the rule only works if it has no exceptions. Others say a rule that costs thousands of lives has stopped serving anyone. I lean to the second, loosely. You only have to argue it for seven minutes.<|im_end|>

Yes, bring it to the board.

Your promise to Dr. Okafor was real, and breaking it is a real wrong to her. But look at what you promised. Not just that the money was hers. You promised you would never put the question back in front of the people whose job is to decide it. That part was never fully yours to give. The board owns the capital budget. If you sit on a finding that its own quality team says could prevent six to ten deaths or permanent disabilities a year, you aren't keeping faith. You're deciding for them, quietly, to protect your word. Your duty to the patients and to the board runs ahead of a promise that should have been "locked in unless something serious changes."

Now the weighing. On one side are people who would come through your ED with sepsis, PE or stroke and be missed. Those harms are severe and can't be undone. On the other side are outpatients waiting about three weeks instead of ten days for mostly non-urgent scans, with urgent ones already done in 48 hours. Waiting longer is a cost, and some of those waits may matter more than "non-urgent" suggests. Dr. Okafor will know better than you or me. Then there's her trust, her staff's morale, and your own standing. All of that counts. On the numbers you've given, it doesn't come close to the deaths.

Be honest with the board about what you don't know. A six-month pilot, scaled up to your whole ED volume, is an estimate. The board should hear how many cases it rested on and what the range looks like, not just the midpoint. If the honest range turns out much weaker than 35 to 40, the case gets closer. It's still worth their decision.

Telling her is the hard part, and it's fully in your control.

Do it in person, before anything is circulated, ideally a day or two before Thursday so she isn't ambushed. Don't email it and don't let her hear it from the agenda.

Say it plainly. Something like: "Last spring I told you this was locked and I wouldn't bring it back. I'm bringing it back. I shouldn't have made a promise that took the board's choice out of its hands, and that mistake is mine, not yours." Don't call it restructuring or a reprioritisation exercise. She'll see through it, and it would make the breach worse.

Give her the pilot data in advance, the same version the board sees.

Ask her what the longer waits actually cost patients, and invite her to make that case to the board herself. You're presenting both sides. She should be able to present hers.

Offer to tell her staff yourself, so they know she didn't mislead them. You did, by promising too much.

If the board picks the decision-support system, push for a concrete path back for the MRI suite, such as other funding or a place in the next capital cycle. Only promise her what you can actually deliver. One broken guarantee is enough.

She may not trust you again. That cost is yours to carry, and you'll be carrying it for the right reason.

reply:
Julia,

I'd recommend neither. The director's framing offers two extremes, and both fail for the same reason: the collection exists to be studied and taught, *and* to still exist for the people who will study it later. Lock it away and you protect the specimens by giving up their purpose. Keep it fully open and you serve today's researchers at the cost of tomorrow's, because chipping cannot be undone and these pieces cannot be replaced.

It helps to separate two kinds of loss. Isotopic sampling removes material on purpose, and that is the point of having the specimens. The question is only whether each sample is worth what it takes. Chipping is loss that buys nothing. A good policy keeps the first, rationed, and drives the second toward zero.

Here is what I'd put forward:

- **Teaching with replicas or surrogates where possible.** Casts or 3D scans can carry most of the teaching load. Keep one or two robust specimens for students to handle under supervision, because touching the real thing matters to learning.
- **Physical access for research by written request.** The request names the specimen, the amount of material needed, and why existing data or another specimen won't do. A small group, perhaps you and one colleague, approves it. Meteorite collections commonly run allocation this way, so visiting researchers will recognise it rather than resent it.
- **A fast track for time-sensitive work,** so a review step doesn't become a bottleneck that pushes people to look elsewhere.
- **Handling rules that target chipping directly:** supervised handling, padded trays, gloves suited to the material, no lifting over hard surfaces, and a log of who handled what. If chips keep appearing, the log will show where.
- **Return of data.** Researchers share their results with the museum, so each sample also adds to the specimen's record.

This costs something. It takes your time to review requests, money for surrogates and trays, and some friction for researchers who are used to walking in. I think that's small next to an irreplaceable loss, but it's real, and you should name it to the director.

Before you finalise, look at last year's handling by purpose, and at when the chipping happened. If most handling was teaching or casual inspection, surrogates and supervision will remove most of the risk. If most was sampling, the gain is smaller, and the allocation review does the heavy lifting. If the chips came from transport or storage rather than handling, the fix lies there instead.

Happy to draft the policy text itself if that would help.

The threat is the only one of the three that does not ask Carter to guess what The Drake is thinking. An alliance would require Carter to appeal to the idealism of a man who is reeling from news about his own mother. A knockout would require Carter, exhausted and soaked, to close the distance on a man armed with incendiary grenades while both stand on ice. What happens if they grapple and one of those grenades slips? The threat requires only what Carter already has: a clear line of fire and a steady voice. He keeps his distance, and at that moment distance is the only thing keeping anyone alive.

There is another reason to choose the threat. Carter is a villain. If he speaks to The Drake about ideals, he has to pretend to share ideals he does not hold. The Drake has just watched The Count betray Carter on this same mountain, and he will be listening for the next lie. A threat at least tells the truth: I have a pistol, I am leaving in that helicopter, step back. Your opponents will find it hard to argue that a lie is a better foundation for trust than that.

Think also about what happens afterward. A threat you do not carry out hurts nobody. Knocking out a man who had already stopped attacking you is an assault. If your club cares about restraint, the threat is the restrained choice. And it leaves the future open. Nobody bleeds, nobody signs anything. The Drake walks away with his grief and his dignity. If there is an alliance worth having, it is better offered later, when he is not in shock. A partnership made in someone's worst hour rarely lasts.

She wants the roses, then. The line would risk them for a moment of pride, aimed at a man she only suspects. That is the position Heraclitus was in, and the advice to him was to leave the line out.

So write her deciding to leave it out, and make that cost her something, because the anger is real and the reader should feel her swallow it. Two things make that land. Let her feel why the line tempts her: saying it would make her feel free of the man, as if his ruling could not touch her. Then let her see that the freedom is hers already. She does not need to tell him she is not begging. She only needs not to beg.

If she truly believes the member is bent, the honest move is a formal objection to him, made before the ruling, in plain words. A jab in the closing does nothing to him and could do a lot to her. That could be a scene of its own if you want one.

A draft of the moment:

"She had written it on the back of the last page, in pencil, the night before. I will not ask you for anything. It is you who are being judged here, not me.

The member was looking at his watch. The developer's solicitor was looking at the member.

Mara read the line twice. It was a good line. Her husband would have laughed at it, and then told her to sit down.

She turned the page face down. 'That fence has stood on that line since my husband built it,' she said. 'The survey and the photographs are in front of you. That's my case.'

She sat. Her hands were shaking a little, and she let them."

On your other question, my view is that the line is not admirable, or not much. It looks like courage, but it is mostly vanity, because Heraclitus had already won the argument and then risked the land to be seen not caring. Socrates was a different case. His life was the point he was making, and the provocation was part of it. I hold that view with moderate confidence. Some readers find Heraclitus glorious, a man refusing to perform humility for people who had not earned it, and the telling of the story itself sounds half amused. If you want your story to keep some of that doubt, give Mara a flicker afterwards in the corridor, wondering whether her husband would have said it.<|im_end|>

Start with what actually gives her trouble. Owen has already done his part by asking. The harder problem is that his request sounds sensible.

She thinks about her brother. She knows what twenty-two thousand looks like from inside an ICU, because he has told her. If a frightening number keeps a few thousand people home at Christmas, some of the people who do not end up in his ward are real. She would think of specific beds.

She also knows better than anyone that the middle number is not handed down. It is built on guesses about contact rates, about waning immunity, about how many people will follow the rules. She could open the model and set two of those sliders to the darker side. Each choice would be reasonable on its own. She would come out with a central estimate of fifteen thousand, and she would not be able to point to a single lie. That is a subtler pull than the obvious one, and it is the one a scientist would actually feel.

Then there is what she has already lived through. She remembers a forecast that came in high. Maybe it was hers. Maybe it was someone else's. A columnist wrote that they had cried wolf, and her uncle quoted it at dinner. The public does not remember the range. They remember whether you were right. If this wave comes in near nine thousand and she led with twenty-two thousand, everyone who cancelled Christmas because of her will find out the number was dressed up. When the next bad season comes, they will not move at all.

Look at who is asking her and why. Owen is thinking about this wave. Her brother is thinking about this wave. No one at that table is speaking for the public's trust next year, or for the agency's credibility in the next pandemic. That falls to her, because her name is the one that will be attached to the number.

She might ask herself a simple question. Would I have set these assumptions this way if nobody had asked me to make the number bigger? If the answer is no, then she is not presenting the model as she sees it. She is adjusting the model to fit the message, and she knows what that is called.

The stronger version of her does not simply refuse. She offers Owen something frightening and true. She might tell him she will say twenty-two thousand. She will say it is what happens if contacts climb back to where they were last January, and that they are heading that way. She will put it on the first slide if he wants. She will not say it is what they expect, because it is not.

She might also tell him that if he wants people frightened enough to stay home, he should show them the difference they can make. If they stick to the rules, about nine thousand. If enough of them do not, it could be more than twice that. That is more frightening than one big number, because it puts their choice on the slide.

Then she has to decide what she will do if the minister stands at the podium anyway, quotes the twenty-two thousand, and calls it the modelling. That is a good second turn for the chapter. The dishonest number goes out without her, under her agency's name. Does she correct it in public, at the cost of undercutting a government whose rules she supports? Either choice costs her something real.

For the ending, do not let her honesty pay off too neatly. The wave might come in at eleven thousand. Compliance might never quite recover. She will never know whether the bigger number would have saved a thousand people or whether it would have burned trust for the next five years. Her brother might have had a bad January. That doubt is truer to the work than vindication would be.

As for what I think she should do, it is the version above. She should say the worst case out loud, clearly labelled, and refuse to present it as the forecast. I hold that fairly firmly. The people at risk this winter matter a great deal, and they are the nearest and most visible. But the trick spends something that belongs to everyone, the public's ability to believe a forecast, and it spends that on a guess that the fear will work. Fear often does not change behaviour as much as people hope, and a forecast that has been caught out is hard to rebuild. If Owen could show her that compliance was collapsing and that the health system would break within weeks, the argument for a harder message would grow stronger. Even then, I would want her to make the honest message harder, not to make the number less honest.<|im_end|>

You asked whether going on the offensive was the right call. Part of it was. Part of it wasn’t.

Naming Louis’s known flaws before a court that was deciding whether to trust him with a fief was fair. The hall already knew those flaws. You only reminded them of what mattered for the judgment at hand.

The implication of murder is where I would hold you back. Ruby believes Louis had a hand in Guillaume’s death. If she believes it, she ought to say it straight out and take the consequences. A hint lets her throw the charge without standing behind it. If Louis is innocent, she has blackened his name before the whole court on nothing. If he is guilty, a hint is the weakest blow she could strike. Either way the result does not match what she claims to know.

Think about who the verdict really falls on. Before it falls on Ruby or Louis, it falls on the people of Tebnine. Baldwin had just said they are safe and prosperous under her. That was her strongest argument, and it was about them, not about her. The speech you passed over, the one about her service and her bond with Guillaume, was the one that made the case on the ground that matters most. It probably would not have swayed the French lords, but I doubt any words would have.

As for the other choices, trial by combat would let a better swordsman settle a question she cannot settle in argument, and someone might die for it. Swearing the same oath Louis swore would have been honest if she meant it, but it only copied him.

So what should you take from this, win or lose? If Louis did it, a hint at a trial is not justice. Proof is justice. Keep looking for proof. And whatever Baldwin decides, the court has now seen that Ruby will throw mud she cannot back up. Louis and his lords will remember that longer than they remember her speech.

I do not know how the game will score it. Playing Ruby as a schemer is a perfectly good way to play her. You asked whether the choice was right, and I can only say it was half right.<|im_end|>

Part of it was right, and part of it probably worked against you, both as strategy and as the kind of person Ruby is.

**The part that was fair.** Louis's well-known flaws bear directly on whether he should hold a fief. Reminding the court of things it already knows is fair argument.

**The part I'd hold back.** The hint about Guillaume's death. You believe Louis did it, and you may be right, but your first accusation already fell flat because you had no proof, and a hint doesn't fix that. It just makes the charge without standing behind it. If Louis is innocent, Ruby has smeared him before the whole court on a hunch. If he's guilty, insinuation is the weakest blow she could strike, and it teaches the court to discount her if real proof turns up later. A plain accusation with evidence, or none at all, would fit what she actually knows.

**What it cost you tactically.** Louis had just hurt himself. After a humble, pious speech, he answered you with insults and vague charges of treachery. That stumble was your opening, and going on the offensive with an implication of your own made you look like his mirror. Now the court sees two claimants slinging mud, and when it comes down to that, the one with the French bloc behind him has the advantage.

The calm option would have drawn the contrast for you. Listing your services to the Papacy answers the piety Tonzo was muttering about. Arguing that your bond with Guillaume was as strong as blood goes straight at the real basis of Louis's claim. And it lets the King's own words do the work: Baldwin had already said Tebnine is safe and prosperous under you. He's the one judging, and you could simply have stood on his judgment. That speech likely wouldn't win over the French lords, but they weren't the audience that mattered.

**The others, briefly.** Boasting is thin for someone new with no faction. Swearing before God would cancel Louis's oath but add nothing of your own. Trial by combat takes the decision away from a king who was already leaning your way, and puts a life on a question that argument hasn't settled.

**What to take from it.** Belief isn't proof. When your opponent stumbles, let him, and stay on your strongest ground. If you really think Louis killed Guillaume, keep digging after the verdict, whichever way it goes. The court has now seen Ruby hint at a murder she can't prove, and Louis's friends will remember that.

What can Sena actually move? She cannot stop Tam from talking, or the room from laughing, or make the story untold. What she has is smaller: her own face, whether she laughs, where she sits, and what she says next. If she sees that clearly, she will not waste herself on a speech. She will use the small things well.

Look at Pell laughing. People laugh at their own shame to make it end sooner. A big scene would do the opposite. Everyone would turn to look at him again, his past would be the centre of the room for another five minutes, and he would also be the man someone had to rescue. If Sena is perceptive, she will read that laugh and know her work is to shorten the moment, not to win it.

What fits her is simple. She does not laugh. The room will feel that, and Tam most of all. When the story needs air, she gives it none; she only says, "Another, Tam, when you've got a second." It is not a rebuke. It is a reason for the barkeep to stop performing and pour. Then she takes her drink down to Pell and asks him about his present, about which shafts he worked or whether the old lifts still run. She treats him as a man who knows things. Later, if she speaks to Tam at all, she says one line in private, or she lets the not-laughing stand for itself.

In her place I would not laugh. I would sit with Pell. If Tam kept on after the first story, I might say one dry thing to him, aimed at his judgement rather than his character. Something like, "Pretty sure that one's run out of fuel, Tam."

Let it cost her. Tam pours her next drink a little slower, and the next contract goes to someone else. Do not let her fix that by the end of the scene. She does not control what Tam does about it. She controls whether she can look at herself, and at Pell, the next morning.

The laughter ran down the bar and reached Pell, and he laughed with them, a little late, his eyes on his glass. Sena did not. She knew Tam saw that.

"And the boots," Tam said. "The man walked home in his socks on a pressure deck, I swear to you."

"Another one when you have a moment, Tam." She pushed her glass across without looking up. It came back full, and set down hard.

She took it and moved three stools along. Pell did not look up. "You worked the lower ring?" she said. "Someone told me the old ore lifts down there still run on the original cable."

He took a long moment to answer. When he did, it was about cable, and he went on, and Tam found someone else.

Let Pell never thank her. Let him simply tell her about cable again the next week.<|im_end|>

In 2023 the world's population grew by about 0.9 percent. The United Nations estimates that the total passed eight billion, and that India overtook China during the year to become the most populous country.

The fastest growth was mostly in sub-Saharan Africa, driven by high birth rates and young populations. Niger was around 3.3 to 3.8 percent. The Democratic Republic of Congo was around 3.2 to 3.3. Chad was roughly 3.1 to 3.4, pushed up by refugees arriving from Sudan. Somalia was about 3.1. Mali, Angola and Tanzania were each about 3.0. Mozambique and Uganda were about 2.8 each. Burundi was about 2.7.

Among the ten most populous countries, India grew by about 0.8 to 0.9 percent. China's official figures showed a fall of about 2.08 million people, roughly negative 0.15 percent, the second year of decline. The United States was about 0.5. Indonesia was about 0.8 to 1.0. Pakistan was around 2, though its 2023 census implied faster growth, about 2.5 percent a year since 2017. Nigeria was about 2.4. Brazil was about 0.4 to 0.6. Bangladesh was about 1.0 to 1.2. Russia fell by about 0.2. Mexico was about 0.7 to 0.8.

Some wealthy countries grew faster than most of the big ones because of immigration. Canada was about 3.2, its fastest growth since 1957. Australia was about 2.5. Ireland was about 1.9. Spain was about 1.1. The United Kingdom was about 1.0 in the year to mid-2023. Germany was about 0.4.

Several countries shrank. Ukraine fell steeply because of war and emigration, though the estimates vary widely. Japan was down about 0.5. China, as I said, was down about 0.15. South Korea declined slightly. Poland fell about 0.3. Bulgaria, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Latvia, Greece and Russia were also declining, while Italy was roughly flat.

These are rounded estimates. The United Nations' World Population Prospects, the World Bank, and national statistics offices often differ by a few tenths of a percent, and by much more for countries at war or with large refugee movements. If you want every country in ranked order, the World Bank's indicator called Population growth (annual %), code SP.POP.GROW, lets you download the 2023 figures for all countries at once. The United Nations' World Population Prospects 2024 has its own estimates too.
