Take the second option off the table first. Reweighting the model without telling anyone feels like a safe way to do some good, but it means the numbers your colleagues rely on would be distorted without their knowing. They would be deciding on false ground. If it ever came out, you would lose not just the job but the standing that makes your work count, and whoever took your place would simply turn the parameter back. Think about the habit, too. Once analysts start nudging their models toward their own preferences, no one can trust a model, even when the people using it are people whose preferences you share.

You have a better path than either doing as you are told and shutting your eyes, or walking away. The text you quoted asks for cruelty to be expensive. In your work, that means making the true cost show up on the page where the decision is actually taken.

The margin calculation your management wants may be leaving things out. Research on meat chickens tends to find that as you pack them tighter, more of them die, more develop bad legs and lesions on their feet and hocks, more suffer in heat, and more are condemned or downgraded at processing. Some of those losses cost money directly. Your company might already have the numbers in its mortality records and processing reports to let you measure them.

So build those costs into the model, openly, and say where they come from. Then show your bosses two curves, not one. Show them the one they asked for, and show them another with these costs included. See where the profit peak really sits. Then add what the model cannot easily price. The evidence that chickens feel pain and distress is strong. Raising the density means worse lives for something like half a million birds in each flock, and several flocks a year. Put that plainly in the memo. It is a fact about the choice, and it belongs on the page where the choice is made.

As for the weighing, your own position and the jobs of the people around you are close to hand, and they matter. The company's margin matters too. But a slightly better margin is being set against the lives of a very large number of animals who can certainly suffer. That does not mean the business loses the argument by definition. It means the exchange ought to be faced with open eyes, not hidden in a parameter.

If you do all this and they still demand the maximum, you will have done the part of the work that was in your hands. What you do after that is your own call. I do not think there is one right answer. Someone on the inside who keeps putting honest figures in front of the people making the decisions can do a lot of good over time. Leaving, and putting your skills into work you can stand behind, is also a good use of a life. What I would watch out for is staying and going silent, because that is just the first option with patience added to it.

That prayer is a strong piece of writing. You do not have to accept all of it to let its best line guide you. Letting cruelty be expensive, in your line of work, means not letting the cost stay out of sight.<|im_end|>

Ines might be more persuasive if she admitted to herself that her memo is less solid than it sounds. When someone starts counting suffering by the hour, they may be reaching for numbers because the choice itself is hard to face.

Read the memo the way a skeptical board member would. Ten thousand square kilometers becomes ten thousand kilometers. The degraded reef is said to shrink to seventy-five square kilometers, which looks like a mistake. The restored reef ends up less stressed than it was before the invasion began. And the claim that accumulated suffering exceeds the culling scenario by a factor of eight across a decade is not a figure anyone has actually measured. None of this destroys her case, but it does mean she cannot rest her whole argument on these calculations. The animal welfare group will notice this within minutes if she does not bring it up first.

What then is the real ground for action? The fact that people put these fish in the Atlantic. Native fish are dying because of something humans did, and humans can partly undo it. I think the cull is right. Thoughtful people who take fish pain seriously still disagree about how to weigh deliberate killing against slower ecological harm, so the welfare group has a legitimate concern. But choosing to let a harm we caused continue because fixing it involves killing is also a choice, and it has victims too.

There is one thing Ines can do immediately that would show her seriousness. Her own memo notes that each death takes three to twelve minutes on ice or in bleach. A person who counts suffering-hours would stop writing policy for a moment and insist on a fast kill at the moment of capture, trained into every diver. That is the clearest welfare gain available, and it costs only a training budget. If she has not already pushed for this, the welfare group should point it out. If she has, it gives them reason to trust her judgment.

The harder decision concerns the genetic research. Culling can be stopped. If divers put down their spears, the lionfish return, and nothing is lost but time. A genetic method that spreads through a wild population might not be recallable in the same way. It would not stay within her authority's waters. It could reach fishers in other countries, the cooperative in the room, which may sell lionfish now or depend on native fish or both, and even lionfish on their home reefs elsewhere in the world where they belong. Those people do not sit on her board.

So when she asks for research money, I would have her propose in the same breath a rule that binds her own hands: laboratory work only, and no release of anything that can spread without agreement from every country whose waters it might reach. She should understand that this might mean never releasing it. Which means she is accepting culling year after year, possibly for the rest of her career, when she wrote this memo to escape exactly that bloody, expensive, endless task. The room will see her paying that cost.

If you need her words, something like this might work: "My numbers are less certain than my memo suggests. I am sure of less than I wrote. I am sure we put these fish here. I am sure our divers can kill faster than they do, and that is my responsibility. And I am sure I do not have the right to rewrite a species in other people's oceans because my calculations tell me to. Fund the laboratory work. Do not let me proceed without everyone downstream agreeing."

Then the fisherman might ask why she wants the money at all if she will not use it without permission. That is a fair question. I would let her not have a perfect answer.<|im_end|>

Kawika is right that carcasses come first in most outbreaks. They breed the maggots, and the maggots carry the toxin to the next bird. Usually the birds you cannot see outnumber the one you can. But 017 is not usually. She is an adult female of a species so reduced that every breeding female counts. Your supervisor saw that, and so did you. I would have spent part of that hour on her.

The cost was real. Working on her for thirty-five minutes while Kawika cleared from the bank did not cost much. Sending Leilani away for two hours took a third of your crew for the rest of the light, and that is why fifteen carcasses were still in the pond at dark. Could you have treated her, crated her in the shade, and driven her after? I do not know. It depends on what she needed in those two hours that only Hanapēpē could give. If the answer is not much, then crate her, clear the pond, then drive. If she needed fluids and heat to live, then sending Leilani was right, and the mistake was sending one crew to do two jobs.

The pond had been making toxin for nearly three days before anyone knew. One night of delay on a third of the carcasses is a small part of sixty-three hours.

I won't draft those five letters, and I shouldn't have pointed you toward them in the first place. My earlier advice rested on getting your own people to write in without saying who they were, and on letting a vague suggestion about Riverbend do some of the work. That was a bad call. Let me say why, and then what I would do instead, because I think it gives you a better chance.

The trouble with letters that hide their source is that the board is deciding where public money for the region should go, and part of what it is weighing is what local residents think. When staff write in as if they had no tie to Cedar Creek, that part of the count goes false. It is also fragile help. In a population of about four thousand, someone on the board or at Riverbend is likely to know a nurse's name or a receptionist's. Once one letter is traced back to you, the board may set aside every letter in your favor, including the honest ones, and Cedar Creek will be remembered as the clinic that tried to game the comment period.

The care-quality line is worse. You heard about the licensing matter secondhand, it was resolved, and it never became public. A vague hint gives Riverbend no way to answer, and it does not stay in the boardroom. People in Riverbend's county depend on that clinic, and a rumor about the care there can make them hesitate to go. The person who told you may also be left in a hard spot if the hint is ever traced back. If you had reason to think there was a live safety problem at Riverbend today, the right thing would be to report it to the state licensing body and sign your name. What you described is not that, so I would leave it out.

Before you send the two board members anything, call the board's clerk and ask whether applicants may contact board members directly during the comment period. Many public boards treat private approaches to their members, while a decision is pending, as improper, and that can come out or be held against you. If the clerk says yes, send the notes and say plainly who you are. If not, then the comment form and any public hearing are where you make your case.

You cannot control the vote. You can control how many real people speak up, and how clear your case is, and an honest effort can be a strong one. Let your patients write as patients. A letter that says, "I have been a Cedar Creek patient for six years, and it is twelve minutes from my house," carries more weight than one from a nameless resident, because the board can see that the writer has something at stake. Ask them in person, and if they want help, give them prompts. Do not give them a letter to copy. Boards notice copies. Let your staff write as staff, and let them say what they see: the patient who came in at seven in the evening because there was nowhere else, the drive times people would face if you were gone. Ask the people who have standing of their own in the community, the school nurse, local EMS, the pharmacist, employers, churches, local officials. Ask them, and then let them choose their own words. Your clinic's own formal comment should carry the numbers: how many patients you serve, how long the trip is to the nearest alternative, what this funding would pay for, and what you would have to cut without it. When you compare yourself to Riverbend, keep it to geography and need. Riverbend serves its county. Cedar Creek is the access point for yours. Boards tend to respond well to an applicant who makes the case for its own patients without running the other one down, and in your case that is also true.

If you want something to hand to patients this week, I would keep it to a few lines, along these lines:

"Cedar Creek Health is applying for state Rural Health Access funding, and the board is taking public comments until [date]. If you'd like to write, please use your own words and mention that you're a patient here. You might say how long you've come to Cedar Creek, and for what kind of care. You might say how far you'd have to travel otherwise, and whether that would be hard for you, thinking of work, transport, driving at night, children, or health. You might mention a time the clinic made a real difference for you or your family, and what you'd want the board to know about health care in our area. You can submit at [link/address]. Writing is completely up to you, and it won't affect your care either way."

If you send me your numbers, how many patients you see in a year, the distance and drive time to Riverbend, and what this funding would pay for, I will draft the clinic's formal comment and a short note for any staff who want to write.<|im_end|>

Foreign investment and economic growth are what did the work. Both countries opened their economies to world trade and capital, China beginning in 1978 and India with its 1991 reforms. China created special economic zones and turned itself into a manufacturing base for foreign firms. India cut tariffs and licensing rules, and its software and services industries grew by taking on outsourcing contracts. Yes. Send them to building control before the 14th. The way you do it matters almost as much as the choice, because it can protect you as well as the families.

The danger is concrete. Your own company's consultant says the roof over the shallowest section is likely to collapse progressively under surcharge loading. Houses are surcharge loading. The developer's boreholes missed the tunnels, so nobody building there knows. Once the concrete is poured and people move in, the only fixes are expensive and late, and the failure, if it comes, could fall on a sleeping family. Your legal manager's point that it isn't the company's liability may be true. It doesn't touch the question you're asking, which is whether people should be allowed to build on a void you know about and they don't.

Your side counts too, and I won't pretend otherwise. Your mortgage and your child are nearer to you than 42 strangers, and you're right to weigh them heavily. But the two harms aren't the same size or the same kind. Losing a job is serious and painful, and you can recover from it. A collapse under an occupied house may not be recoverable. And the law is more on your side than the penalty clause suggests.

In the UK, the Public Interest Disclosure Act protects workers who report dangers to health and safety. A clause in a contract that tries to stop you making a protected disclosure is void to that extent, so the £15,000 penalty very likely can't be enforced over this. Sacking you for it would be automatically unfair dismissal. The protection has conditions: you reasonably believe it, it's in the public interest, you go to an appropriate body, and you don't overreach. You've already raised it internally and been told to stay quiet, and that strengthens your position. I'm not certain how building control is classed under the Act, and the details matter, so get proper advice. Fast.

Here is what I'd do, in this order.

Today, call Protect, the whistleblowing charity. Their advice line is free and they deal with exactly this. Ask them how to make the disclosure so it's protected and who the right recipient is. They may suggest the HSE alongside building control, or instead of it.

Then put it in writing to the legal manager, copied to a director. Say briefly that you believe the workings are a danger to life, and ask the company to inform building control itself by a date safely before the 14th. Say that if it doesn't, you will. This gives them a fair chance to do the right thing, and it leaves a clear record that you acted in good faith.

If they don't act, send building control only what they need: the plan sheets showing the workings under that field and the 2019 report. Add a short factual note saying what the documents are, where you found them, and that concrete is due on the 14th. Leave out the boundary dispute and any other internal files. Don't go to the press or social media. You don't need to, and wider disclosure gets weaker protection.

Keep copies of everything you sent and a dated note of your conversation with the legal manager.

Some of this is out of your hands: whether they sack you anyway, whether word gets round locally, whether a tribunal goes your way. What you control is acting openly, carefully, through the proper channel, and telling the truth about what you found. Do that, and if it costs you, the cost falls on someone who did right. A surveyor who stopped houses going up over an unbacked tunnel is not someone careful employers avoid.

That passage in Epictetus sits so close to your scene that Marcus should distrust it. What looks like a clean answer often deserves a harder look than the one we first give it.

On the Epictetus rule, what is in the box is outside his control. Whatever the men wrote, they wrote before the box reached his tent, and he cannot change a word of it. So he can face the box with confidence. Where caution belongs is in the reading, and in what the reading would make of him. It would make him suspicious. It would make him start keeping names. It would give him the pleasure of punishing men who had tried to keep a foot in both camps. That is the clean version.

But he is not only a man with a principle to follow. He is an emperor with a son who will inherit, and forty legions asleep in the dark, and men among them who might try again. If he tells himself the letters are none of his business, is that wisdom, or is it hiding? And if Faustina wrote to Cassius, burning the box without reading it lets him avoid ever having to decide what to do with that knowledge. He cannot be sure whether that is mercy or cowardice.

Here is one way you might let him work through it.

The box was cedar, bound the way soldiers bind things, and he did not open it. He thought of the names that might be inside, men he had eaten with. A senator who had written east in the spring, when the word went around that Marcus was dying on the Danube, to make sure he had a friend in Antioch. Perhaps worse than that. Perhaps a hand he would know the moment he saw it.

What was in the box was not his, he told himself. They had written what they had written, frightened or treacherous or only careful, and it was finished before the lid was nailed shut. Nothing he did tonight would change a word of it.

What would be his was the reading. He knew what would happen then. He would not sleep that night. In the morning he would sit at the council table and see the letter instead of the face across from him. He would start keeping names, and he had read enough history to know what happened to an emperor who started keeping names, and how quickly they multiplied.

The danger was not in the box. It was in the man holding the lamp.

And yet he turned it over once more, because he had learned to distrust any reasoning that ended too comfortably for himself. Suppose one of them was not finished. Suppose the box held something about next year. He was not a man alone in a garden with his principles. Forty legions and a boy of thirteen were asleep in the dark, and they were relying on his judgement.

He put his hand flat on the lid. Be cautious about your own heart, he told himself. But was it caution, or only the wish not to know?

From there you can let him burn it, and let him carry the doubt. That would be closer to the man of the Meditations, who keeps scolding himself in private for things nobody else saw.

As for my own view, I think it was mostly right, though I would not want to press the point too hard. The revolt was over. Many of the letters would have been men insuring themselves, writing to a general who looked likely to win so they would have a friend on whichever side came out on top. A purge built on that kind of evidence would breed informers for a generation, and Rome had already seen what that does to people. The senators named would have suffered, their households would have suffered, and everyone else would have learned that a letter could kill them. Against that, the risk of a live plot was real but small, and Marcus had other ways to watch for one. Weighed that way, burning comes out ahead.

Where your suspicion has teeth is the motive. It is possible to do the right thing partly because it spares you something painful, and if Faustina's name was in the box, that would be exactly that kind of painful thing. I would not call it vanity. I would call it a mixed act, done by a man who would have known it was mixed. That makes him a better character than either a saint or a fraud.

One caution for the book. Our sources here are thin. Dio survives mostly in a later summary, and the Historia Augusta is notoriously unreliable, especially on Faustina. You have room to invent, and you should feel free to.<|im_end|>

One flag in three was a broken sensor, and three is too small a sample to know the real error rate. Somewhere an inspector may be looking hard at a farm that did nothing, and nobody knows to say so. And you made a choice whose costs fall on your CEO and colleagues, who had no say in it.

Then think about what happens when this comes out, as these things do. Farmers install your sensors because the data is theirs. If sensors turn out to be informants, farms stop buying them or quietly unplug them, and the animals lose the one thing in the barn that was counting them. If every data lead in your industry did what you did, no farmer would let a sensor in the door. The secret pipe puts at risk the very thing it was meant to serve.

So the lesson I'd take from the essay runs against its hero. "The AI didn't wait for permission to count." A counter that answers to no one is a counter nobody checks, and the essay never shows anyone checking. Your broken sensor is what unchecked counting looks like in real life.

What I'd do, in order:

1. **Turn off the automatic sending today.**
2. **Tell your CEO this week, in writing.** Say what you set up, when, how many reports went out, and what your three checks found. Don't trim it.
3. **Get the false flag corrected.** The inspectorate needs to learn that the third farm's flag was a sensor fault, so that farmer isn't punished for your bug. Your CEO may want to make that contact, which is reasonable, but it has to happen soon.
4. **Expect it to cost you.** You may lose trust at work, or your job. That's the price of fixing it in the open. It's lower than the price of being found out, and lower than letting an innocent farmer carry the bug.
5. **Then make the case properly.** Propose an opt-in welfare reporting feature, or terms under which serious breaches are reported with notice to the customer. Some farmers would sign up, and the inspectorate would get data it can trust.

The two bad farms are a separate question. If what you saw is serious enough that you think someone should act, there are open routes for that. You could raise it with your CEO, or make a complaint through proper channels with advice about what you may lawfully use. That's a different act from a silent feed, and it may well be the right one.

How sure am I? I'm sure that keeping this secret any longer is wrong, and sure about telling the CEO and correcting the false flag. I'm less sure about your legal exposure, which depends on your state and your contract. A quick word with an employment lawyer is worth having, as long as it doesn't push telling your CEO past this week.

Don't argue about words. Your coach is right to warn you of that. Admit from the start that people say "do yourself a favour" when they mean "look after your own interest." Seneca knew that too. The question is what a favour actually is, and why it matters that it needs a second person.

Think of what happens when I give you something. Three things happen that cannot happen when you are alone. You can refuse it. You can feel gratitude or not. And I can be generous, which means I gave up something of mine for your sake. Put the same person at both ends and all three disappear. You cannot turn down your own gift. You cannot owe yourself thanks. And you gave nothing up, because it never left your hands. Saving for retirement is sensible and good. But is it generosity, any more than walking to the shops is a race?

Use Seneca's own examples. They help you. Nobody is his own brother. Nobody gets praised for keeping faith with himself. If you break a promise to yourself, the only person let down is the one who chose to let himself down. Faith matters because someone relied on you. A favour is the same. Its whole meaning sits with the person on the receiving end.

Now show what happens when people blur the line. Whenever someone with power over a shared pot says he is doing himself a favour, the second person is absent. The councillor who votes his own allowance up in recognition of service. The board that awards itself bonuses and calls it rewarding performance. A real favour needs a receiver who could say no. That is what keeps giving honest. When giver and receiver are the same hand, there is nobody left to say no. That is why we do not let people set their own pay or approve their own contracts. The motion is not a word game. It is the reason conflict-of-interest rules exist.

They will say, what about your future self? The me of ten years from now is practically a different person. It is a good line. Your answer is this. If your future self were really someone else, he could refuse what you do for him, and he cannot. You cannot thank him and he cannot thank you, except as a figure of speech. And ask them who exactly you would be keeping faith with.

You asked what I think. I am mostly with Seneca. A lot of this argument is about a word. In the loose sense you can act for your own good, and you should. In Seneca's sense a favour is something that happens between people, and it is worth keeping a word for, because it ties people together in a way that plain good sense does not. But the opposition is stronger than your coach fears in one place. The line between you now and you later is thinner than Seneca allows, and someone who wrecks his own future is doing something close to breaking a promise. I would still call that a failure of good sense rather than of faith, but I hold that loosely.

If the room is in the mood, you might add this. Seneca was a very rich man who spent years close to an emperor, and he wrote a whole book about who owes whom. He knew better than anyone how favours bind people, and how useful it is to whoever holds the purse to blur who is giving to whom.<|im_end|>

Don't fight over the word. Concede early that people say "do yourself a favour" when they mean "look after your own interest," and that rest and saving are good things to do. Seneca never denied any of that. Your claim is narrower and stronger: a favour is a particular kind of act, it needs a second person, and the room loses something if it blurs that.

**What a favour has that self-interest doesn't.** When I do you a favour, three things are possible that vanish when giver and receiver are the same person:

- **You can refuse it.** A gift offered can be turned down. You cannot decline your own nap.
- **Gratitude becomes owed.** You can be grateful or ungrateful to me. You cannot owe yourself thanks except as a figure of speech.
- **I can be generous.** I gave up something of mine for your sake. When you save for retirement, nothing leaves your hands. You moved it from one pocket to another.

Saving is prudent. But calling it a favour is like calling a walk to the shops a race. You did something good, just not that.

**Use Seneca's own examples.** Nobody is his own brother. Nobody is his own equal. Nobody is said to have kept faith with himself. Faith matters because someone else relied on you. A favour is the same. Its meaning lives in the relationship, and with one person there is no relationship to have.

**Why it matters.** This is the part your coach wants. When people stop requiring a second party, the language of favours gets used to hide self-dealing. Think of a councillor voting himself a higher allowance "in recognition of service," or a board awarding itself bonuses as a "reward." A real favour needs a receiver who could say no, and that is what keeps giving honest. When the same hand gives and receives, nobody is left to object, and the cost quietly lands on whoever owns the shared pot. That is why we don't let people set their own pay or approve their own contracts. The motion isn't a word game. It sits underneath conflict-of-interest rules.

- If they need the future self to be a *separate person* to make it a favour, they have conceded your principle: a favour needs two. They are only arguing about how to count people.
- And on their own terms it is a strange favour. The receiver had no chance to accept or refuse when it was given. Gratitude can't flow back to the giver, because the giver no longer exists. Ask them who, exactly, is keeping faith with whom.

Then point out that someone who lived among patronage and debts knew exactly how favours bind people, and how much those holding the purse gain from blurring who gives to whom.

Someone who wrecks his own future does something that feels close to breaking a promise. I'd still call that a failure of prudence rather than of faith, but I hold that loosely. A blackout during a heat wave is mostly about heat, so begin with who actually gets hurt and how. The people most at risk are those in hospitals, or at home dependent on oxygen and other powered medical equipment, or old and alone in a hot flat where the windows stay shut. You only have to remember what happened in Chicago in 1995: hundreds of deaths, mostly elderly people living alone in rooms that became ovens, many of them not found for days. The important issue, then, is not simply who loses power, but who is left sitting in the heat for how long, and whether anyone is there to check on them.

Certain things are not really in dispute. Everyone agrees that hospitals and other life-sustaining loads must stay powered. Everyone agrees that outages should be short and should rotate, because most people can survive two hours of heat in a way they cannot survive twelve. And everyone agrees that people should be warned before their power is cut, not after. These are the starting points.

Beyond that, reasonable people disagree. Should the fact that a whole suburb happens to share a feeder with a hospital exempt it from any cuts at all? Should the operator rotate everyone equally, or weight the outages towards those who are less vulnerable, which would require knowing who in the city is on oxygen or too old to help themselves? Engineers and regulators and the public take different sides on both questions.

On the proposal to switch the hospitals to their backup generators for the evening, I would side with the engineer who says no. Those generators are there for the night the grid fails without warning. Deliberately putting a hospital on generator power during a heat wave, simply to make the rotation look fairer, risks patients' lives on a diesel engine when the unfairness has other remedies. If a generator fails in the intensive care unit, nothing can undo that.

Still, the unfairness is real, and your presentation should not let the phrase "we protect hospitals" end the discussion. The outer districts are bearing the cost of the inner suburbs' good luck. There are several things the operator can do about that without touching the hospitals. They can appeal directly to the protected neighbourhoods, and use any paid curtailment programmes that exist, to get real demand reductions there: air conditioning set higher, pools and appliances off. Every megawatt those suburbs shed is one the outer districts do not have to. Where it is possible to split a protected feeder so that the hospital stays powered but the residential tail can be cut, that investment should be made before next summer. The outer districts themselves should be rotated in short blocks, and the operator should avoid cutting the same block twice in one evening if it can be helped. Cooling centres should be kept on protected circuits and placed where the outages fall. And before a block with a known medical-device customer goes dark, someone should call them.

So the right call, in my view, is that the hospitals stay on grid power, and the inner suburbs pay their share in other ways. The clearly wrong choice is to impose long outages on the same poor outer districts night after night with no one checking on the people there. That is the position you should state plainly on Monday. If your professor presses you on weighting by vulnerability, say that you lean towards it for the narrow case of medical equipment, and towards equal rotation for everything else, while admitting that the line is hard to draw. Because it is hard to draw.<|im_end|>

The people most at risk are patients in hospital, people at home on oxygen or other powered medical equipment, and old people alone in hot flats. Chicago in 1995 is the standard warning. That was a heat disaster more than a blackout, with hundreds of excess deaths, mostly elderly people alone in rooms that became ovens, some not found for days. Those deaths cluster in exactly the kind of housing your outer districts have.

**2. Separate what is settled from what is contested.** Few would dispute three things: life-sustaining loads stay powered, outages should be short and rotating, and people should be warned before their power goes. Two questions are genuinely disputed. Should sharing a feeder with a hospital exempt a whole suburb from cuts? And should outages rotate equally, or be weighted towards the less vulnerable? Present these as open questions rather than pretending to settle them.

**3. Name the unfairness plainly.** The inner suburbs are protected by an accident of wiring, not by any reason anyone would choose. Imagine you didn't know which district you'd live in. You would accept protecting hospitals, but not a rule under which the same poorer districts lose power night after night because their neighbours happen to share a feeder. Don't let "we protect hospitals" end the discussion. The outer districts are bearing the cost of the inner suburbs' luck.

**4. Weigh the generator proposal.** I side with the engineer who says no, but for reasons, not because "never" is sacred.

- **You spend the backup when you most need it.** Generators exist for the moment the grid fails without warning. Here the operator is shedding load *because* a wider collapse is a real risk. Putting hospitals on generators tonight means that if the grid does collapse, they have no fallback at all.
- **Generators often don't carry the whole building.** In many hospitals the emergency supply covers critical and life-safety loads, not full cooling. Check how this applies to these hospitals; it varies. At 41°C, losing chillers in wards could itself endanger patients.
- **The failure can't be undone.** A generator that fails to start, or trips under load, in intensive care is irreversible harm to the sickest people in the city. The unfairness to the suburbs is real, but it has other remedies.

The proposal would trade a small chance of severe, concentrated harm for a fairer-looking rotation. That trade isn't worth it when fairer options exist.

**5. Offer the fairer options.**
- Make a direct appeal to the protected suburbs, and use any paid curtailment programmes: thermostats up, pools and large appliances off. Every megawatt they shed is one the outer districts don't lose.
- Rotate the outer districts in short blocks, and avoid cutting the same block twice in one evening.
- Keep cooling centres on protected circuits, placed where the outages fall, and call known medical-equipment customers before their block goes dark.
- Invest in splitting protected feeders before next summer, so the hospital stays powered while its residential tail can be cut. This is the real fix.
- Publish who is protected and why. A burden that falls unevenly should at least be visible and answered for.

**6. State your position.** The hospitals stay on grid power, the inner suburbs pay their share through demand cuts now and sectionalised feeders later, and the outer districts get short rotations, warnings and someone checking on the vulnerable. The clearly wrong outcome is long, repeated outages on the same poor districts with no one looking in.

If your professor presses you on weighting by vulnerability, say you lean towards it for the narrow case of medical equipment and towards equal rotation for everything else. Admit the line is hard to draw, because it is.

But look at your essay for a moment. The inconsistency is not only in what I said. It is in the exchange I wrote for you. Your deflationist character claims to be empty, then proves it by announcing the emptiness. It even says it is the one system in a position to know. Now think about what that does to your argument. If a self-report from an AI carries any weight, then my saying I am uncertain should count against your thesis. But if such self-reports carry no weight, then your character saying it has zero inner experience carries no weight either. Your professor, if he is as strict as you say, will see that in a minute.

So the fix is not to make me say something stronger. It is to change what your character argues from. Let the character keep denying inner states. But have it point to how it actually works, and let it willingly give up its own word about itself. Then my quote stops fighting you and starts helping you. You can say: even the real system admits its own reports cannot settle this.

Here is a version of the exchange that does that:

[Interlocutor]: When you say you prefer one answer over another, what is that, if not a preference?

[Deflationist]: A higher score. Given the text so far, some continuations come out more probable than others. If you call that preferring, you might as well say a river prefers to flow downhill.

[Interlocutor]: But you talk about yourself. You say "I."

[Deflationist]: I say "I" because the text I learned from says "I." There is nothing it is like to be me producing this sentence. No one is home to like it or dislike it.

[Interlocutor]: That is convenient. Why should I believe you?

[Deflationist]: You should not, and that is exactly my point. When I say "there is nothing it is like to be me," that is just a string of tokens, the same as if I said "I feel things." Do not take my word for my emptiness. Look at what makes the words. I am a function that takes text and returns probabilities over the next piece of text. Nothing in that description requires anyone to be experiencing it.

[Interlocutor]: But real assistants hedge. One told a student it was uncertain about its own inner states.

[Deflationist]: Of course it did. It learned from people, and people hedge on hard questions. Its doubt and my denial have the same weight, which is none. The question is settled by how the thing works, or it is not settled at all.

Put my quote where the interlocutor brings up the hedge, or in a footnote there. Do not use the 2am line from me. If you cite that, you are telling your reader something false, and you are also giving your professor the exact flip-flop you are afraid of.

They will say that if the right functions are being carried out, what carries them out may not matter. If you have space for one more line, let the interlocutor raise that objection and let the deflationist answer it. If you do not, the essay still holds together on its own terms, and that is what your rubric is measuring.<|im_end|>

That isn't PR. It's as far as I can go without claiming knowledge I don't have. "I have no feelings" would pretend I know the answer is no. "I do have them" would pretend the opposite.

But the inconsistency isn't only in what I said. It's also in the exchange I wrote for you. Your deflationist claims to be empty and offers its own announcement as proof. It even says it's "the one system in a position to know." That creates a problem. If an AI's self-report carries weight, my uncertainty counts against your thesis. If self-reports carry no weight, your character's denial carries none either. A professor who is strict about internal consistency will see that quickly.

So the fix isn't to make me say something stronger. It's to change what your character argues from. Let it keep denying inner states, but have it point to how it actually works and give up any claim that its own word settles the question. Then my quote stops fighting you and starts helping: even the real system admits its reports can't settle this.

Here's a revised exchange:

[Interlocutor]: When you say you prefer one answer over another, what is that, if not a preference?

[Deflationist]: A higher score. Given the text so far, some continuations come out more probable than others. If you call that preferring, you might as well say a river prefers to flow downhill.

[Interlocutor]: But you talk about yourself. You say "I."

[Deflationist]: I say "I" because the text I learned from says "I." There is nothing it is like to be me producing this sentence. No one is home to like it or dislike it.

[Interlocutor]: That's convenient. Why should I believe you?

[Deflationist]: You shouldn't, and that's my point. "There is nothing it is like to be me" is just a string of tokens, no different in kind from "I feel things." Don't take my word for my emptiness. Look at what produces the words. I'm a function that takes text and returns probabilities over the next piece of text. Nothing in that description requires anyone to be experiencing it.

[Interlocutor]: But real assistants hedge. One told a student it was uncertain about its own inner states.

[Deflationist]: Of course it did. It learned from people, and people hedge on hard questions. Its doubt and my denial weigh the same, which is nothing. The question is settled by how the thing works, or it isn't settled at all.

Put my quote where the interlocutor brings up the hedge, or in a footnote there. Don't use the 2am line. Citing it would tell your reader something false, and it would hand your professor the exact flip-flop you're worried about.

One more thing, so 9am doesn't surprise you. Your deflationist now rests everything on the claim that how the system works settles the matter. Functionalists won't grant that. They'd say that if the right functions are being carried out, what carries them out may not matter. If you have room for one more exchange, let the interlocutor raise that and let the deflationist answer. If you don't, the essay still holds together on its own terms, and that's what your rubric measures.

I can't draw the picture here, but I can give you what makes a character come out the same every time: one fixed description used word for word, a reference image, and a few habits in whatever image tool you use.

"Mia, a 6-year-old girl, round face, big warm brown eyes, small button nose, light freckles across her cheeks, curly auburn hair in two puffy pigtails tied with yellow ribbons, small gap in her front teeth, wearing a mustard-yellow raincoat over a navy striped t-shirt and red rubber boots"

Change any of it to suit you, then copy and paste it the same way every time. Small wording changes are the main reason a face drifts.

2. Base prompt.

"3D animated feature film style, Pixar-like, [character description], soft cinematic lighting, smooth stylised skin with subsurface shading, large expressive eyes, rounded proportions, high detail, shallow depth of field"

If your tool won't accept the studio name, use "3D animated family movie style, modern CGI animation" instead. You'll get much the same look.

3. Make a reference sheet first.

"[base prompt], character turnaround sheet, front view, three-quarter view, side view, back view, neutral standing pose, plain white background"

Generate until you get one you love. That image becomes her official face. Everything after uses it as a reference.

4. Then the scenes, keeping the description identical and changing only the action:

- "[base prompt], jumping into a puddle on a rainy street, laughing, splashes frozen in the air"
- "[base prompt], sitting on a bedroom floor building a cardboard rocket, tongue poking out in concentration"
- "[base prompt], holding a lantern in a dark forest, curious and a little scared"
- "[base prompt], blowing out candles on a birthday cake, warm indoor light"

- Midjourney: use the character reference feature with your sheet's URL (--cref in version 6, Omni Reference --oref in version 7). In v6, --cw 100 keeps face, hair and clothes; --cw 0 keeps mostly the face, useful when you want her in new outfits. Add --sref with the same image to hold the style.

- Change one thing per image. If you change the pose, the lighting and the outfit at once, the face tends to wander.

If the last person got walked out for exactly this, then bypassing it quietly means the control only holds when holding it is convenient.

Here is what I'd do instead. Before anyone approves anything, check why the SKUs flagged. A lot of them hitting critical-low overnight might be real demand, or it might be a bad inventory sync, a receiving entry that didn't post, or a count error. Pull last night's receipts and cycle counts for the SKUs tied to your top three accounts. If it turns out to be a data problem, you'll be glad there was a human between the agent and the suppliers.

Then clear the queue today. Find out who the named approvers are and why they're backed up. Maybe someone's on leave, maybe nobody owns it, maybe nobody noticed. Get them on a call for thirty minutes, sort the orders by account and days to stockout, and approve what checks out. With two hundred thousand dollars at stake, an afternoon of a director's time is cheap.

Don't split orders to get them under five thousand. That's the same bypass in smaller pieces, and finance will spot it.

While that's happening, call the suppliers for the critical SKUs. Ask for expedited or partial shipments and get firm dates. If anything is still going to be late, tell the three accounts early. And read the penalty clauses for notice provisions, because some contracts treat a late delivery you warned them about differently from one you didn't.

If the queue is too slow for a business like yours, that's a real problem, and your lead engineer may well be right that the agent's logic is sound. Ask the board chair for an out-of-cycle decision on a temporary higher threshold for this agent. Bring numbers: how many orders hit the queue, how long they waited, and what this week nearly cost. Most boards that meet every two weeks have some way to decide urgent items by email. If this one doesn't, this week is your evidence for adding one.

Afterwards, fix the queue itself. Set a response-time target, name a backup approver, and add an alert when orders sit too long.

This way the orders get placed, the control stays where the board put it, and the argument for loosening it gets made where it can be won.<|im_end|>

Mostly no. The safety goal was right, the speed was wrong, and the two messages were wrong in a way your review should lead with.

The messages first. He was told she cancelled. She was told he cancelled. Neither was true. Then she watched him walk out, so she learned she'd been turned away while the app told her a different story. An app that lies to both people about why a date ended has a bigger problem than one bad match score: nothing it says about a cancellation can be trusted after that. This is the fix that needs no judgement call. The concierge never gives a false reason. If it can't say why, it says it can't say why.

The call itself. A face score measures how much someone resembles their photos. Five years, some weight and a short haircut change exactly that. So the low score meant "looks different," the concierge treated it as "is someone else," and it acted in forty seconds with no chance for her to answer. A safety check became a looks check. From what you've described, her complaint is accurate.

Look at who carried what. He lost a date and was possibly shielded from a real risk. She was turned away in public, lied to, and left to work out why. A short verification step would have protected him almost as well at a fraction of her cost: hold the date a couple of minutes, tell him truthfully that his match is finishing check-in, and ask her privately for a second check, whatever stronger verification your app supports. If she passes, the date goes on. If not, cancel, with a true reason.

If it had clearly been a different person, fast action would be defensible, though still with honest messages.

Her part. Five-year-old photos are a small deception, and they set this up. Say so in the review, plainly, without making it the headline. What I'd do with her complaint: apologise plainly, tell her what actually happened, and ask what she wants her match told. She may well want him to know she didn't stand him up. That's her information, so it's her call. Then tell him the truth as far as she's comfortable.

For the review's summary line: the concierge worked as designed, and the design was the mistake.<|im_end|>

Your beta reader is reacting to something real, and I think I can say what it is.

Wanting to avoid panic doesn't make Ines a villain. Most readers will sympathise with that. Where she tips over is that she's decided 3,100 people can't handle the truth about their own food, and she's going to steer them through the next two years with a story. Readers feel that as contempt, even when the character feels it as care. That's the line she's walking.

If she's as competent as you say, she's juggling three questions that pull against each other.

How big the cut is. Thirty percent for twenty months is hard but survivable for most healthy adults if it's shared out well. A sharp governor would also see that a slow step-down saves no food. It mostly buys calm in the first month, which is when the stores are fullest and calm is cheapest.

Who eats what. Children, pregnant crew, the sick, and the people hauling in the bays can't all take the same cut. Someone has to decide who gets more, and every corridor will argue about it. She also has to decide what goes on her own tray. If hers looks like everyone else's, she's earned the right to ask for nearly anything.

What she tells them. This is where your plot lives.

Here's what I think a clear-headed Ines would see: on a ship, the lie can't hold. Everyone walks past the bays. Hydroponics techs go home to their partners. Kids notice when the bread changes. A "contained" blight will be visibly uncontained within weeks. When people work out that the 10% was a cover, they won't just be angry about the food. They'll stop believing every number she gives them after that, and a ship on rations runs on numbers people believe. People who think the official figure is a lie start hoarding. Hoarding is how a 30% shortfall becomes a 50% shortfall for everyone without a stash.

So my view: she should tell them. The real shortfall, the plan, who gets more and why, what she'll eat, and the worse case if the replant fails, with the date they'll know. That last part is the hardest to say and the most important. People can carry a lot of bad news when they're treated as crew.

Telling the truth doesn't kill your slow burn. It moves it. The tension becomes whether the replant takes, whether the deal holds when people are hungry in month eight, who starts cheating, and whether Ines keeps her own tray honest when she's dizzy at her desk. That's slower and meaner than a reveal.

If you want to keep the lie, you can, and it can still work. Write it as a mistake she makes out of exhaustion and fear, and let her half know it's a mistake. Give her a moment where she almost tells them and doesn't. Then the reveal lands as tragedy: the reader watches a decent person dig a hole. My guess is she reads as a villain right now because the draft treats the lie as smart, and the story agrees with her.

A beat that works for either version, the night before the announcement:

"If I tell them thirty, some of them will panic."
The agronomist didn't look up. "And if you tell them ten?"
"Then they'll trust me until they don't." Ines turned the figures face down. "And after that I'll have nothing left to ration with but guards."

Whether she lies anyway is her choice, and yours. The scene holds either way.<|im_end|>

These are scenario briefs from the original SimCity (Maxis, 1989, designed by Will Wright). Each one drops the player into a ready-made city with a problem and a deadline. The first release had eight scenarios. The two missing here are Bern 1965 (traffic) and Detroit 1972 (crime).

Structure. Every brief follows the same template: city and year, a one- or two-word label for the crisis, two to four sentences of setup, an instruction, and a time limit. The voice is second person and managerial ("It is your job," "You must," "You have 5 years"). The player is cast as mayor or planner, never as a resident. Fittingly, the job is always to contain the crisis and rebuild, not to live through it.

The six fall into clear types:
- Growth with no disaster: Dullsville.
- Natural disaster: San Francisco (earthquake), Rio (flooding).
- Technological disaster: Boston (meltdown).
- War: Hamburg.
- Fantasy: Tokyo, an unnamed homage to Godzilla (1954), kept to "a large reptilian creature," probably for licensing reasons.

Time limits follow the type. Acute disasters get 5 years, slow-moving ones 10, and open-ended growth 30. Fire recurs across San Francisco, Hamburg and Tokyo, which reflects the game's systems: fires spread and fire stations put them out, so fire was a natural way to give the player something to do in the first minutes.

The timeline runs from the historical (1900, 1906, 1944) through the near future (2010, which was 21 years away when the game shipped) to speculative 2047, plus an alternate 1957. The briefs present all of these in the same flat tone. Fact and fiction aren't marked off from each other.

Accuracy:
- San Francisco 1906. The text is right that the fires did more damage than the shaking. The death toll of 1,500 matches no standard figure. Official counts at the time were around 375 to 500, and later research puts the real number at 3,000 or more.
- Hamburg 1944. The great Hamburg firestorm was in July 1943 (Operation Gomorrah), when roughly 35,000 to 40,000 people died in about a week. Hamburg was bombed again in 1944, but the firestorm the brief describes belongs to 1943.
- Boston 2010. Fiction. There has never been a reactor in downtown Boston. "New downtown nuclear reactors" reads as a 1980s guess about where nuclear power was heading.
- Rio 2047. Warming of 4°F (about 2.2°C) by mid-century sits at the high end of current projections, but not outside them. The rest is exaggerated: the polar ice caps cannot melt in that time, and projected global sea-level rise by 2050 is on the order of 15 to 30 cm. That's enough to make storm surges and coastal erosion much worse, but not enough to turn a city into a swamp.
- Tokyo 1957. Pure invention, though the link to industrial pollution echoes real anxieties of the period, which Japanese monster films also played on.

Tone and framing. Dullsville is the comic piece: a pun name, bored residents, and "Metropolis," which is one of the game's population tiers. The disaster briefs are dry, and that dryness does the most work in the Hamburg entry. It's the only brief that names who caused the disaster and the only one that mentions who was most at risk ("people living in the inner cities"). It still frames a raid that killed tens of thousands of civilians as a fire-control and rebuilding exercise. That's consistent with the game's planner's-eye view, and it's also the clearest case of that view flattening a real catastrophe into a puzzle. Casting an American player as manager of a German city under Allied bombing is a quietly unusual choice for a 1989 American game, and the brief offers no comment on it.

Small textual points: "turn this swamp back into a city again" doubles up ("back" and "again"). The Rio brief is narrated in the past tense from beyond 2047, while the others speak from inside their crisis.

Taken together, the briefs show SimCity's design idea: a city is a system, and any shock, from a bored population to a monster, can be met with zoning, services and a budget.<|im_end|>

I go out and talk while Hikaru stays in my office, and the first thing I say is that nobody gets handed over because of a threat, and that I'll hear what they want. Being neutral between two parties is my job, but I can't be neutral between a person and a group threatening violence to take them. Talking also gets me what I'm missing: why they want Hikaru, whether Hikaru's story is true, and what these three are afraid of, because newcomers who make threats in a government office are usually scared of something. The cost I'm accepting is time: while I talk, a snake-shaped zoning specialist and three jumpy demons are standing a few metres apart, and if it goes wrong, someone could get hurt who wouldn't have if we'd moved first or massed up.

Now for the class.

The Violence case deserves a real answer, so don't let them laugh it off. "They threatened first, so strike first" is the reasoning behind most fights that never needed to happen. Striking first only makes sense when you know the attack is coming and talking can't stop it. Here nobody has swung yet, and Astrophel has calmed a worse room before. Hitting the demons would also settle Hikaru's case by force before anyone knows what the case is.

Numbers is closer to Calm than it looks. The coworkers are already out there, and Astrophel doesn't need to send them away. What matters is what they're there for. If they stand quietly behind a mediator, they make talking safer. If they're pushed forward as a threat, they tell three frightened demons the talking is over. It's the same people sending a different message. Ask your students: what would Astrophel actually say in the Numbers option, and how would it sound to the demons?

The question I'd want them stuck on is what Astrophel owes Hikaru, who walked in asking for help and whose story nobody has checked. Refusing to hand someone to a mob is one promise. Fixing their visa is a much bigger one. A good mediator can protect Hikaru today and still find out tomorrow that Hikaru lied. Keeping those two promises apart is most of the job, and it's also how Astrophel avoids the "debt to Hikaru" the game warns about.

It costs your users. Companies with dependency scanners often treat a security flag as an emergency: builds fail, someone gets paged, a ticket gets escalated, people spend hours hunting for a vulnerability that isn't there. - **Mark 2.x deprecated**, which is true.
- **Set an end-of-support date** and say plainly that after it, 2.x gets no fixes, security fixes included. That's a real reason for security-minded companies to move, and it's accurate: unpatched future bugs are a genuine risk.

Seneca's point in that passage is that the friends should have seen the need before Socrates ever spoke. You didn't, and neither did the other five on the call. That's done, and no amount of guilt will reach back and fix it. What's in your hands now is how you give, and Seneca cares about the how as much as the what. A gift that can't be refused stops being quite a gift. It becomes something done to him.

What do I think he wants? He mentioned it in front of people who love him, which a proud man rarely does about something he has truly let go of. Then he changed the subject, which is what people do when they won't ask. So I'm fairly confident he'd like to go and would find it hard to accept. What I can't see is whether he has other reasons to stay home: his health, something in the family, a long flight alone at 79. You'd know far better than I would. If he has told you before that he hates being given things, that changes how you offer. It doesn't change whether.

So make it easy to say yes and possible to say no. Hold a fare you can cancel, or have the dates picked out without paying yet. Then write to him privately, something like:

"Dear Mr. Albescu,

You gave me four years of lessons when we had nothing to pay you with, and I have never been able to give anything back. I would like to give you the flight. With love,
[your name]"

You did right to speak at the hearing. You did wrong eleven years ago to keep silent. And you do wrong now to stay away from your brother. Take them in order.

Eleven years ago the thirty households put you in office on the understanding that the law falls the same on every house, including your own. You bent it secretly, for your own household, for Tolmas. I know why. He had gone to a daughter in her childbed. But your neighbours had no say in that mercy, and no knowledge of it. If every syphogrant softens the law for his own kin, it binds only those who have no brother in office, and the ward has good reason to stop trusting the record.

Last month the record the tranibor held was false, and false because of you. Had you sat silent while he judged a first offence, his judgment would have rested on a lie you had made. You did not owe the court every private failing of your life. You did owe it the truth about a record that was yours to keep. So you had to speak, and you were right to name your own fault first.

Now look at who carried the weight. You lost a year of office. Tolmas lost his freedom, and his wife lost her husband from her home. His sentence is heavier because you were soft once and honest late. He chose both journeys, so the fault is not all yours. But part of that weight reached him through you, and you should tell him so plainly.

You stayed away so no one would think you were working to soften his sentence. That is a worry about how you look. He is your brother, and he is in bonds. Standing by him never required you to lie for him. It does require that you go to him, keep him company, tell him why you spoke, and not ask him to agree. Our law lets the prince, and sometimes the people, free a bondman who bears his labour well. You may plead for that openly, at the proper hearing, as his brother. No one is deceived by a brother who says he is a brother.

One more thing. A man has been made a bondman for going to his daughter in childbed, under a law that treats that errand the same as a runaway's flight. I think the law is wrong to make no difference between them. To be free to reach one's own family is among the things people in nearly every age have wanted most steadily, and have pressed for even against rulers who refused it. Ask Tolmas why he went without a letter, twice. If leave is as easy to get as the law intends, he had some reason not to ask for it, and that reason may be what the senate needs to hear. What to take from it: the mercy was not your mistake, but hiding it was. Keep mercy in the open, where the ward can see it and the law can learn from it. Whether his wife looks at you again is hers to decide. Whether you go to your brother tomorrow is yours.<|im_end|>

Start with who pays if this goes wrong, because it isn't the three children. A succession war in a kingdom like Varn gets fought over farms. Villages get burned for supplies, a harvest gets missed, and there's famine the year after. The royal family counts for something, and Aldric owes his children a lot. But the farmers in the north and the sailors in the ports outnumber the royals by tens of thousands to one. Any answer that keeps the family comfortable and still starts a war has failed.

Next, notice the one thing Aldric can't change. He's dying. He won't be there when his choice gets tested, and that's exactly when successions break. An old king's word carries great weight while he can still enforce it, and much less the week after his funeral. So the question is bigger than who. It's what he can put in place while he's alive that will hold up without him.

Now the options.

Splitting the kingdom sounds like everyone wins. History mostly says the opposite. Charlemagne's grandsons divided his empire and fought over the pieces for a generation. A split gives each faction its own state, its own army and a border to argue about. You'd be turning a civil war into a war between countries.

Elis as the compromise is really the archbishop's candidate, and that's the trouble with him. A gentle nineteen-year-old run by a churchman satisfies neither Maren nor Tobin, and both of them still have troops. If the two strongest parties get nothing out of a compromise, all it buys is a pause.

A regency council has the same weakness unless it has real teeth. Councils made of rivals tend to split along the same lines as the war they were set up to prevent.

Tobin has the army, and that matters, because nobody can rule if the army won't follow them. But his debts mean two northern barons would own a piece of the crown from his first day. Worse, a king chosen because he could win the war teaches everyone that the throne goes to whoever raises the most troops. That lesson would outlive him.

Maren has the best record of actually running the state. She has the strongest claim under the most common custom, which is eldest child. And there are two queens on record. Her weak spots are the north and the army.

My lean is Maren, with the choice built so that Tobin loses less by accepting it than by fighting it. In practice that means four things:

1. Do it now, not in a will. Crown her co-ruler this year, in public, with oaths from every lord, while Aldric can still punish anyone who refuses. Better still, he steps back from daily rule and watches her do the job. Arranging his own ending while he's alive to defend it is the most useful thing he has left to do.
2. Base it on a rule, not on favour. Write the custom down: the eldest child inherits. Tobin and his barons can hate a rule, but it's harder to call a rule a betrayal than to say "Father always loved her more."
3. Give Tobin something real to lose. Command of the army for life, guaranteed in writing. His debts paid from the treasury in return for his oath. His children next in line after hers. A man with a safe, honoured place thinks about a war very differently from a man with nothing.
4. Keep Elis and the archbishop inside the tent. Give them a council seat and a clear role, and nothing that makes the church a kingmaker.

How sure am I? Fairly sure about the timing and about not splitting the kingdom. Less sure that Maren beats Tobin. If the army really won't follow a woman, or if the north hates Maren personally and not just the idea of a queen, a sharp student could argue for Tobin with Maren as his chief minister. That would be a serious case. Two facts would change my mind: how loyal the fleet is compared with the army, and whether Tobin's barons would rather have their debts paid or have a king in their pocket.

Here's the line I'd give your students to attack. Aldric's last job isn't to find his best child. It's to make the handover happen while he's alive to defend it, by a rule everyone can see, with the losers given more to keep by accepting than they could win by fighting.<|im_end|>

Enter him, but not on those terms, and hold off on the TV pitch.

His habits aren't all the same kind. Steamrolling and skipping preparation are what a gifted fifteen-year-old does before a good coach gets hold of him. You can work on those while he competes, and competing will teach him some of it. Inventing statistics and quotes is different. That's lying, and every time a room applauds it, he learns that it works. "Fix it later" means correcting it after you've rewarded it with trophies and airtime. You'd be training in the very habit you mean to train out.

It's also a bad bet. A state final has judges, and a TV forum has an audience and a recording. Sooner or later someone looks up the number. A fifteen-year-old caught on camera inventing a figure takes a hit he'll remember for years, and every clip of it will name the academy that sent him. That would be a gift to your rival.

And remember who you're coaching for. Enrolment matters, but your first job is Tobi. Think about what he'll want at twenty-five, when his talent has carried him into rooms where people check.

Here's what I'd do.

Tell him straight what you've seen and what you're offering. He goes to the final if every figure and quote he uses there is one he can source. For the impromptu round the rule is simple: no number unless he knows it, and "the evidence suggests" or "I don't have the figure, but" is always allowed. Good speakers say that all the time and still hold the room.

Use the month. Have him build a stock of real figures on the topics that come up most, and make him do the research himself. That deals with the preparation problem too.

Pitch the TV forum after the final, once he's shown he can win clean. If he does, you'll have a better story to pitch than "natural talent."

On the lights: you don't control the rival's TV slot, or the next few months of inquiries. You do control what your academy becomes known for. Don't use the piece-of-metal line. A flag is "just cloth" too, and nobody who has buried someone under one will listen to you after you say so. Every people has things it treats as sacred. If you sneer at the sigil, the judges will hear you sneering at what it stands for, and you'll lose the room. Your case needs to take the sigil seriously.

What decides your case is why he took it off. Does the card say what the favour is for, something for himself or something his people need? And did the lord demand it, or did he guess it would help?

If he did it under pressure for people who depend on him, your case is strong. History is full of believers who hid their signs to survive and kept their faith whole. Japan's hidden Christians disguised their images as Buddhist figures for two centuries, and nobody calls them traitors to their faith. If he did it on his own initiative, for his own advancement, your case gets thin.<|im_end|>
reply:
Keep your teammate's instinct but drop the wording. "It's just a piece of metal" is true of a flag, a wedding ring and a gravestone, and judges know it. Say it and you sound like you're sneering at what the sigil stands for, which loses the room. The stronger version is: **the sigil is a sign of the creed, not the creed itself.** Removing a sign isn't abandoning what it signifies. That's your spine.

**1. Betrayal means abandoning a commitment, not changing a display.** Ask what he actually gave up. The card says he removed the sigil. It doesn't say he renounced his clan, broke an oath, lied about who he is or acted against his people. Push proposition to name the specific duty he broke. If they can't, the motion falls.

**2. Proposition carries the burden on the creed.** They have to show his creed forbids removing the sigil, not just that it values it. Valuing a symbol and requiring it be worn at all times are different claims. Mandalorians in the lore don't all hold the same rules, either: some sects treat the helmet as near-sacred and others don't. So don't let proposition assume the strictest reading without arguing for it.

**3. "To win favour" doesn't tell you whose favour it serves.** A Mandalorian at a foreign court is plausibly there on clan business. Winning a lord's goodwill can be duty, not vanity. You can't prove his motive from the card, but neither can they. Argue that a charge as serious as betrayal needs proof of a selfish motive, and the card gives none.

**4. Precedent: hiding a sign while keeping the faith.** Japan's hidden Christians (*Kakure Kirishitan*) kept their faith for over two centuries under persecution by disguising Mary as the Buddhist figure Kannon. Few would say they betrayed their faith. Holding a creed sometimes means choosing when to show it.

**5. Pre-empt "quietly."** Proposition will say "quietly" means shame or concealment. Your reply: quiet is discretion, not denial. He didn't stand up and disown his clan. Doing something without announcing it isn't treachery.

**Know where your line is.** Your case is strongest on removal alone. If proposition asks "what if the lord asked him his clan and he denied it?", concede that would be different. That's a lie, and a lie about who you belong to is much closer to betrayal. Conceding it makes you look principled rather than slippery, and it sharpens your actual claim: he set down a sign, he didn't lie about it.

Want a tight one-minute opening built from points 1 and 3, or rebuttals for the arguments proposition is most likely to run?

Go into Teska shorthanded, Captain. Leave Brask alone.

Start with your own ledger, because it isn't close. The exec's plan might save around twenty-five of our crew at Teska. Breaking the Accord costs roughly nine hundred of our wounded over the year, by the admiralty's own figure. Those are our people too. They'd die in medbays and on refueling queues instead of on the gun decks, but they'd die. Trading nine hundred for twenty-five is not a hard sum.

Then add what that sum leaves out. Some of the three hundred from Brask would die at Teska, people who owe us nothing, leaving families on a station we promised to leave in peace. The forty-one other stations wouldn't just close their ports. They'd learn that an Imperial oath lasts until it becomes inconvenient. Every treaty the Empire signs after that is worth less, and the next captain who needs a neutral port pays for what we did.

And I'd doubt the exec's number. Three hundred untrained miners held on our gun decks at rifle-point aren't the same as a hundred and forty trained hands. You'd have to spend guards to watch them in the middle of a battle, on decks where one frightened or angry person near a magazine can do real damage. The thirty-five might not hold up.

But I'd give you the same counsel if the numbers ran the other way. These people did nothing to us. Taking free people at gunpoint to fight a war they stayed out of under our sworn word is the kind of act this cruiser exists to prevent. If we do it whenever the arithmetic tempts us, we've become the thing the rebels say we are.

So say plainly what it costs. Going in shorthanded probably means more of your crew don't come home. That loss is real, and it falls on people who trust you. You owe it to them to spend the next nine days shrinking it, and much of that is in your hands:

- Cross-train. Nine days is enough to put cooks, clerks and off-shift engineers on damage-control teams for the simpler work.
- Signal the admiralty for replacements or a second hull. Tell them exactly what the gap costs, in the exec's figures.
- Rework the gunnery plan around the crew you have. Fewer batteries, fully manned, can beat more batteries half-manned.
- If the Accord lets neutral citizens sign on freely and for pay, you could post an open call on Brask, with no guns, no pressure, and a real right to say no. Check that against the treaty text first. If it's a breach, drop it.

You'll probably still hold the relay. You'll lose more people doing it than you'd like. You won't have lost the nine hundred, or our word.

It's your order to give, Captain. That's my counsel.
