Push it through with the emergency vote. But don't treat that as choosing between speed and comment. Pass it now as an interim measure, and run the full 45-day comment on the permanent version while it's already protecting people.

Here is the weighing. On one side are tenants in un-cooled units, some of them old or sick, during a summer forecast to be hotter than the one that killed four people and sent 61 to the ER. On the other is a compliance bill of somewhere around $0.9 to $2.1 million across 2,300 units, a hard three weeks for landlords, and a real cost to trust on the council. The money matters, and some of it will reach tenants as rent. Trust matters too. But both can be repaired. A death can't. When one side of a choice can be undone and the other can't, the irreversible side gets the benefit of the doubt.

The custom exists for good reasons. Rules land better when the people they bind have been heard, and comment catches mistakes. You keep most of that by passing an interim ordinance and holding the comment period afterward. What you lose is the landlords' chance to shape the first version, and that is a real loss. Say so plainly.

How I'd structure it:

- Write the emergency finding into the ordinance itself: last July's deaths, the ER numbers, the forecast. The exception then rests on stated facts, not on having the votes.
- Add a sunset. The interim rule lapses unless the council re-adopts it after a full 45-day comment period. That answers your colleagues directly: the custom is delayed for one season, not dropped.
- State on the record that this is not a precedent for skipping comment, and why this case differs.
- Soften compliance where it costs little. Landlords who show a good-faith order of units get a short grace period. Enforcement starts with warnings. Complaints from the most vulnerable tenants go first.

Two things could make me less sure. First, can 2,300 units actually be supplied and installed in three weeks? If the local supply can't meet that, the deadline punishes landlords without cooling anyone, and you should phase it. Second, who pays the electricity when a landlord supplies a portable unit? If it lands on low-income tenants, some will switch the unit off. That's a design question, not a cost complaint, and it's exactly what comment would catch. Ask staff about both before Tuesday.

Handling the fallout if you go emergency: call the landlord association before the vote, not after. Tell them what you're doing and why, show them the sunset and grace provisions, and invite them into the permanent version. Some will still be furious, and you can't control that. You can control whether they hear it from you first and whether their input visibly changes the final rule. With the two colleagues, ask them privately what would make this acceptable to them. The sunset may be enough. If it isn't, their reasons are worth hearing before you use a two-thirds majority over their objection.

If you decide on comment after all, the summer still needs covering. Push for cooling centers with longer hours, transport to reach them, wellness checks on known un-cooled buildings, and a fund for portable units during heat alerts. Each of those can probably happen without an ordinance.

The vote is yours. My lean is firm: the interim rule with a sunset keeps the custom's purpose and gets cooling in place before the hottest weeks rather than after them.

He would turn the offer down without hesitating, but he would not stop being gentle with Lucius afterward. The easy part is saying no. The hard part is saying it in a way that does not scorn the love behind the offer.

Look at what Lucius is asking him to accept. He wants Epictetus to let the palace write down that he is a grammarian. Epictetus is not a grammarian. So the proposal is that he remain by letting the emperor's clerks put a false name on him, and that he pay a freedman to make them do it. He would see at once that he was being asked to lie, and to corrupt another man's honesty to do it.

Then he would think through what leaving actually takes from him. It takes the city, the house, the pupils who cannot come with him. He would not pretend those are nothing. He would only remember that they were never his in the way that matters, because any of them can be stripped from him by someone else's will. What cannot be taken from him is the thing he teaches, because that lives in how he judges things and what he chooses, and no clerk can reclassify that.

And he would think about his students. If he stands before them saying that only a man's own choices are truly his, and then keeps his school open by paying for a false label, he has taught them that his doctrine is for fair weather. Every pupil who heard the story would remember that lesson longer than anything in his lectures.

None of this is new to him. He grew up as someone else's property. He knows what it is to have another man decide where he sleeps. His own teacher was sent into exile. To him, being driven from the city is not the end of his work. It is only a move to another place.

If you write him as simply swatting away a temptation, have you noticed what Lucius is actually doing? Lucius is not offering him a vice. He is trying to keep his teacher from leaving. If Epictetus does not see that, he will seem cold, and your readers will take Lucius's side. The Epictetus we know from his talks is blunt, but he is also fond of the young men around him, and he can be funny with them. I would have him take Lucius's love seriously. He could tell the boy to come with him to Nicopolis, or to write down what he has learned, or simply to save his uncle's money for a better use.

Would he be right to refuse? About the payment, yes. Even apart from his particular teaching, a false name entered on an official list harms the man who writes it and the list itself, and a man who teaches honesty cannot buy his exemption with a lie. As for leaving the city, someone else in his place, with a sick parent still there or pupils with nowhere else to go, might reasonably try an open appeal before packing. Epictetus does not have that reason. But your story does not suffer if Lucius asks about it and Epictetus has his answer ready.

If you want him to speak aloud, you might try something like this. "You want to put my name on a list of grammarians." "Only on paper, master." "Where else do lists live?" He might smile then. "Lucius, I spent years being another man's property on paper. I know what paper can do to a man. I also know what it cannot do." And when Lucius tries once more, perhaps: "But it is still the city." "Hills and bricks. Good ones, I grant you. Nicopolis has hills too, I am told, and bricks, and young men who have not yet learned anything. Come and help me with them."

And since the old sources disagree about whether the decree fell in 89 or 92, you might leave the year out of the scene and let the order speak for itself.<|im_end|>
reply:
He'd refuse quickly. What keeps him from sounding like a fortune cookie is that he takes the offer seriously, because the love behind it is real.

**How he'd reason it**

He'd start with the name. One of his favourite moves is that your role tells you what to do: if you're a father, a councillor, a philosopher, reflecting on the name shows what's fitting. Lucius is asking him to become, on paper, something he isn't. He'd also notice how the paper gets written: by paying a freedman to enter a falsehood on the emperor's records. That's two wrongs, his own lie and another man's corrupted honesty, and he'd see both at once.

Then he'd sort the costs the way he always does: what's up to me, what isn't. The city, the house, the pupils who can't follow him were never his to keep, because someone else's decree can take them. His judgements and choices can't be taken, and those are what he teaches. A clerk can reclassify him. No clerk can make him a grammarian.

He has real stories for this. He liked to tell of Agrippinus, who heard in the middle of the day that he'd been condemned to exile and asked, more or less, "Then let's go to Aricia and have lunch there." And of Helvidius Priscus telling Vespasian, "As long as I'm a senator, I must attend." Your Epictetus doesn't need to invent a philosophy that night. He's lived on these stories for years, and he was a slave before he was free. His own teacher, Musonius, was exiled more than once. Exile is a move, not an ending.

And he'd think about his students. If the man who teaches that only your own choices are truly yours keeps his school by buying a false label, every pupil learns that the doctrine is for fair weather. They'll remember that longer than any lecture.

**The trap in the scene**

Lucius isn't a tempter. He's a loyal boy trying to keep his teacher. If Epictetus just swats the offer away, he'll seem cold and readers will side with Lucius. The man in Arrian's notes is blunt, but he's fond of his young men, teaches by questions, and is often funny. Let him ask Lucius questions until Lucius answers himself. Let him also think about the uncle, who'd be taking a real risk with that freedman. And give Lucius somewhere to put his love: come to Nicopolis, write down what you've learned, spend the uncle's money on something better.

**Would he be right?**

About the payment, yes, and not only by his own lights. A bought false entry harms the man who writes it and makes the record worthless. If every philosopher with a rich student did this, the decree would fall only on the poor and the honest. That's the free rider's bargain, and it only works while others don't take it. Leaving is a separate question. Someone with a dying parent in Rome might fairly try an open appeal first. Epictetus has no such tie, but it costs you nothing to let Lucius suggest it and Epictetus have his answer ready.

**A sketch of dialogue**

"You want my name on a list of grammarians."
"Only on paper, master."
"And where else do lists live?" A smile. "Lucius, I was another man's property on paper for years. I know what paper can do to a man. I also know what it can't."
And later: "But it's Rome."
"Pretty stones and a pretty rock. Nicopolis has stones too, I'm told, and young men who haven't learned anything yet. Come and help me with them."

**Two checks on your notes**

Calling his reading narrow undersells him. He quotes Homer, Euripides, Plato and Xenophon, and Chrysippus is everywhere in the Discourses; his students read Chrysippus with him. "Focused" would be safer than "narrow." The dates of Domitian's expulsions are also given differently by different scholars, so you might leave the year out of the scene and let the decree speak for itself.

Major Structures of the State, circa 2055 (roll 1d20)

1. Prairie Union Grain Elevator. A set of twelve concrete silos, each about a hundred and forty feet tall, stands beside a rail siding and has stayed sound since it was built in the 1950s. A farmers' cooperative keeps it walled and guarded as a granary, and from the top of the head house a lookout passes signals by mirror and radio to the settlements within thirty miles.

2. The State Capitol. A limestone capitol building whose dome gave way after several winters without heat or roof repairs now stands with its rotunda open to the sky. In the intact east wing the reconstituted legislature holds its monthly meetings, and its authority is accepted in perhaps a third of the counties.

3. Carver Lake Dam and Hydroelectric Station. An earthen dam still runs two of its four turbines, looked after by former utility workers and the people they have taught. It is the only steady source of electricity in the region. Downstream towns watch the corroded spillway gates with growing concern.

4. Federal Correctional Institution. A medium-security prison left empty when the federal authorities pulled out in the late 2040s has become a stronghold because of its walls and wells. Former guards, former inmates, and their families now live inside under a written compact that is enforced with some severity.

5. St. Agnes Regional Medical Center. An eight-storey hospital keeps one wing running on generator and solar power. It can handle triage and basic surgery, but it has no imaging. The pharmacy vault is guarded around the clock and is generally thought to be the most valuable room in the state.

6. Distribution Center No. 4. A former online retailer's warehouse, about 1.2 million square feet, lost its racking and conveyors within a year of the collapse. Your gut is onto something. Look at what Tamsin actually knows in that moment. She has seen a datacard pass from Cass to the port master, a credit chit pass back, and she has heard a time. That is damning, but it is not everything. Cass might be giving the port master a false window because the cell told her to. Cass might be selling the window to buy something the cell needs. Tamsin passes messages. She is not told the cell's games, and she knows that.

What Tamsin knows for certain is that eight people may fly into an ambush in about thirty hours. That has a clock on it. She can deal with that without deciding what Cass is. Move the window. Scrub the run. If Cass was working for the cell, that costs a day. A shot in the hangar cannot be undone. If Tamsin is wrong, she kills a friend and settles nothing.

So Tamsin, if she is thinking clearly, protects the eight first. The truth about Cass comes second. The verdict on Cass comes last, and it is not a verdict Tamsin has to bring down alone. She goes to whoever runs the cell, the one person who would know if Cass was on a sanctioned job, and tells him exactly what she saw and heard. No more, no less.

Her history with Cass gives you the reason in Tamsin's own terms. Cass once stood in the rain with her brother's papers and got him off-world. Tamsin owes her the chance to explain. That is a real debt, a real kind of loyalty. It does not outrank eight lives. Tamsin feeling both debts at once is your chapter.

There is history behind this. Resistance movements in many wars have dealt with informers, often by killing them, and often on evidence no thicker than what Tamsin has. Groups that killed on suspicion grew paranoid, and the people occupying them learned to use that. A rebel cell that shoots its own people on one sighting is doing the port master's work for him. Tamsin need not know that history, but she might feel the dread of it, the dread of being the one who got it wrong.

If you want a harder knot, consider this. Perhaps Tamsin knows that whoever runs the cell is the type to have Cass killed without hearing her. Then telling the cell leader may be a death sentence too. Perhaps Tamsin confronts Cass alone first, to give her the chance to explain. If Cass has turned, that warns her, and the port master learns the run has moved. Tamsin cannot keep faith with Cass and protect the eight without some risk. Make her choose. Make it cost her something.

Here is one way the thought might run in her head:

"She wanted to walk into the hangar and make Cass look at her. She wanted it so badly that she distrusted it. A chit, a card, four words through a door. Cass had stood in the rain with her brother's papers. Cass had also just been paid. Tamsin couldn't know which Cass was real, not tonight. But she could know the shuttle wasn't flying at 0400. She went to find Doran."

If you want my answer to what I would do in her place, I would get the run moved first, tell the cell leader exactly what I saw, and argue as hard as I could that Cass should be heard before anything is done to her. If you want Tamsin to fire the shot in the hangar, that can still be a true story, but then it is the story of Tamsin becoming someone harder, and the book should make her pay for it. Maybe she learns later that Cass was running a sanctioned play. Maybe she never finds out. That might be worse.<|im_end|>

Administrator, my call is yes. We transmit. But I want to send less than you asked for, and send it differently.

Here is the weighing as I see it. On one side, four thousand one hundred of our people are taken at gunpoint, families split, and sent where one in five die each year. Over a few years that is many hundreds of deaths, most of them people who live in these rings. On the other side are wage cuts, about two hundred layoffs, two hard years and maybe a blockade the Empire would struggle to enforce. Those costs are real and they fall on our people too. But a lost job can be found again. A conscript killed at the front cannot be brought back. That settles it for me.

The Charter matters beyond us. Every neutral port in the Belt is safer because stations like ours keep our word, and breaking it weakens that a little for everyone. So I will not pretend this is anything other than a breach. But the Charter exists so the war's guns stay off civilians. Dravik has turned his guns on ours. Staying silent would not keep us neutral. It would only keep our tariffs.

So, what I propose to send. Not a private tactical package to the Concord. An open distress call on every frequency, in clear, so Dravik hears it the moment the Concord does. That way we have no secret dealings with either side, and Dravik learns he has been seen while he still has time to cut loose before anyone arrives. If he leaves early, nobody has to intercept anything.

The message:

"Kerrigan Station, neutral outpost, Halvard Belt, to all vessels. Imperial forces under Admiral Dravik are removing approximately 4,100 station residents, adults aged sixteen to fifty, onto troop transports by force. Departure is expected in six hours. Attached are the transports' current positions and scheduled departure. Kerrigan Station requests that these civilians be released and returned. This transmission is a breach of our Neutrality Charter, made on the authority of Administrator Oyelaran to protect station residents, and will be reported to the Charter authority in full."

Attached: the transports' positions and their departure schedule. Nothing on the flagship's weapons, escorts, or anything else the Concord could use beyond stopping those transports. We give them enough to prevent a theft, not a targeting package for a battle.

Three things I will not do, and you should know why. I will not lock the docking clamps on the transports. That would trap armed marines aboard with our families and force the fight you are hoping to avoid. I will not touch life support in any ring, for any reason. And I will not hide the breach afterward. We log it, we report it, and we take the two years.

One risk I cannot rule out. His marines are still in every ring when he hears this. Your read is that he runs rather than fights out here, and I think you are right, but I would like ring wardens ready to keep people clear of the docks and calm while the marines withdraw.

It was your oath, Administrator, so the last word is yours. Say "send" and it goes out now.

See what in that hall is hers to command, and what is not. Cassius's strength is not hers. The guards are not hers. Whether Tomas lives is not, in the end, hers. What is hers is where she stands, what she says, what she does with her hands, and what she does with the next five weeks. A woman who knows that difference stays strong even when she loses. A woman who does not either goes still and tells herself that nothing she does can change this, or else throws herself away and tells herself she has to do something, anything.

That is why both your options feel wrong. Each one avoids the real choice. To lunge looks brave, but it is despair. It hands Cassius a second victim, it entertains him, and it removes the one person keeping records. To stand still for the inspectors argues better, since her testimony might end the feeding in every house on Tessaly. But Tomas is dying in front of her now, the inspection is five weeks off, and it might come to nothing. She would be paying a certain life for an uncertain hope.

So what lies between? Two things are within her reach, and both come from who she is.

She is the medic. She knows exactly how much blood a boy of sixteen can lose, and Cassius knows she knows. She can step forward and say the true thing in her professional voice: "My lord, another minute and he is dead. You will lose him for the season." That speaks to his interest, the one appeal he might hear. It costs her something. She has spoken out of turn in front of the household, and he may turn on her. It might fail.

And she can take away what he came for. He is not feeding on the boy so much as on Ilse's scream. Oriane can go to Ilse, set her own body between the mother and the sight, hold her face to her shoulder, and speak low to her. She cannot stop his hands, but she can stop being an audience, and perhaps make Ilse less of one. Whether that bores him into stopping is for you to decide. I would keep it uncertain in the moment, even if it works.

The records still matter afterwards. The interruption and the testimony compete only if she gets herself killed. The real sum she is doing in that moment is how far she can go and still be alive to testify. That calculation, made quickly with her heart pounding, is your scene.

What would I do in her place? I would do both. I would speak the medic's sentence first, and then I would go to Ilse. Tomas is the nearest person and in the worst danger, and his life is the one on the table now. The inspectors count, and so do the stock in other houses, but they are further off, and the outcome there is a guess. They do not outweigh a life I might save in the next minute. I would take the risk to myself. I would not throw myself at him, because a dead witness helps nobody in the houses that come after.

Here is a rough pass at the turn:

Oriane had stitched Tomas's hand in the spring, after the grey mare bit him. She knew what was in him. She knew what was leaving.

"My lord." Her voice came out level, the voice she used for numbers. "He's at the edge. Another minute and you'll have nothing from him this year."

Cassius didn't look up. But his mouth slowed.

She didn't wait to learn what that meant. She crossed to Ilse, past a guard who couldn't decide whether to stop her, took the woman's face in both hands and turned it into her own shoulder. "Look at me. Only me. Breathe with me." The scream broke into sobbing, and then into something too quiet to carry.

The hall went very still. Oriane felt it, the moment Cassius noticed his music had stopped.

Where it goes from there is yours. I would resist making her pay nothing for it.<|im_end|>

Start with what it's for, because that decides almost everything else. A support bot for a shop, a study partner, a companion for elderly relatives and an internal tool for searching company documents are all built differently.

Here's the path most people follow today:

1. Define the job. Write one sentence on who will use it and what a good conversation looks like. Then list ten real questions it has to handle well and three it should refuse or hand off.

2. Choose the brain.
   - A hosted language model through an API. This is the fastest to build and the strongest out of the box, and you pay per use.
   - An open-weight model you run yourself. It gives you more privacy and control, but you need a capable GPU or a rented server.
   - A rule-based or intent-matching system. It's fine for very narrow tasks like "check order status" and brittle for anything else.
   For "intelligent," you almost certainly want one of the first two.

3. Write the system prompt. Give it its role, tone, what it knows, what it shouldn't do, and when to say "I don't know." Most of a chatbot's personality lives here.

4. Give it knowledge. If it needs to answer from your own documents, use retrieval: split the documents into chunks, embed them, search for the chunks relevant to each question, and put those into the prompt. Have it cite where each answer came from, so mistakes are easy to spot.

5. Handle memory. Keep the conversation history, and once it gets long, trim or summarise older turns so you stay within the model's context limit.

6. Add tools if it needs to do things. Most APIs support function calling, so the bot can look up an order, check a calendar or run a search.

7. Test it. Keep that list of real questions with good answers and rerun it after every change. This is the step people skip, and it's what makes a bot reliable.

8. Plan the edges. Decide when it hands off to a human. If the public will talk to it, decide in advance how it handles grief, health, money and religion, because that's where a breezy bot gives offence or bad advice. Don't log personal data you don't need.

9. Put it somewhere. A web widget, a Slack or Discord bot, or a phone app. Simple web frameworks like Streamlit or Gradio get you a working interface in an afternoon.

Here's a minimal working loop in Python. It uses the OpenAI client library, which many providers and local servers (Ollama, vLLM) also accept:

```python

# Hosted: client = OpenAI()  (reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment)
# Local via Ollama: client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", api_key="unused")
client = OpenAI()

SYSTEM = "You are a friendly assistant for [purpose]. If you don't know, say so."
history = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}]

while True:
    user = input("You: ")
    if user.strip().lower() in {"quit", "exit"}:
        break
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": user})
    response = client.chat.completions.create(model="MODEL_NAME", messages=history)
    text = response.choices[0].message.content
    history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": text})
    print("Bot:", text)
```

Replace MODEL_NAME with whichever model you choose. That's a real chatbot. Everything else on the list above is about making it good at your job.

Tell me what it's for, who will use it, and whether privacy or budget rules out a hosted API, and I'll sketch the design and the next piece of code.<|im_end|>

In Assetto Corsa a car isn't really code. It's a folder of plain text files. `power.lut` holds the engine's torque curve, `tyres.ini` the grip, `car.ini` the weight, and `brakes.ini` and `aero.ini` do what their names say. So you don't write a car from nothing. You take one that already drives well and change its numbers. The script below does that. It copies a car under a new name and scales the five numbers that matter most.

Two things before you start.

You need a car whose physics files sit in a plain `data` folder. Many cars ship them packed into a single `data.acd` file. Some mod cars come with the folder already unpacked, and Content Manager can unpack many of the others. Start from one of those.

This is for the original Assetto Corsa. Competizione doesn't let you edit car physics like this.

```python
"""
Clone an Assetto Corsa car and tune it up.
Python 3. Edit the settings block, then run:  python tune_car.py
"""
import json
import re
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

# --- settings ---------------------------------------------------------
CARS = Path(r"C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\assettocorsa\content\cars")
SOURCE = "source_car_folder"   # folder of the car you start from (must have a data folder)
TARGET = "my_perfect_car"      # new folder name: lowercase, no spaces
NAME = "My Perfect Car"        # name shown in the game

POWER = 1.4       # engine torque multiplier
GRIP = 1.15       # tyre grip multiplier
MASS = 0.85       # weight multiplier
BRAKES = 1.3      # brake torque multiplier
DOWNFORCE = 1.3   # wing downforce multiplier (adds no drag, which is the cheat)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

ENC = "latin-1"   # reads and writes any byte unchanged


def scale_key(path, key, factor):
    """Multiply every 'KEY=number' line in an ini file."""
    if not path.exists():
        print(f"  skipped {path.name} (not found)")
        return
    pattern = re.compile(rf"^(\s*{key}\s*=\s*)(-?[\d.]+)(.*)$")
    lines, count = [], 0
    for line in path.read_text(encoding=ENC).splitlines():
        m = pattern.match(line)
        if m:
            line = f"{m.group(1)}{float(m.group(2)) * factor:g}{m.group(3)}"
            count += 1
        lines.append(line)
    path.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding=ENC)
    print(f"  {path.name}: {key} x{factor} ({count} lines)")


def scale_lut(path, factor):
    """Multiply the second column of an 'rpm|torque' table."""
    lines = []
    for line in path.read_text(encoding=ENC).splitlines():
        body = line.split(";")[0].strip()
        if "|" in body:
            x, y = body.split("|", 1)
            line = f"{x.strip()}|{float(y) * factor:g}"
        lines.append(line)
    path.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding=ENC)
    print(f"  {path.name}: torque x{factor}")


def rename(dst):
    # name in the in-game menus
    car_ini = dst / "data" / "car.ini"
    text = car_ini.read_text(encoding=ENC)
    text = re.sub(r"^(\s*SCREEN_NAME\s*=).*$", lambda m: m.group(1) + NAME, text, flags=re.M)
    car_ini.write_text(text, encoding=ENC)

    # name in the launcher / Content Manager
    ui = dst / "ui" / "ui_car.json"
    try:
        info = json.loads(ui.read_text(encoding="utf-8-sig"), strict=False)
        info["name"] = NAME
        ui.write_text(json.dumps(info, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False), encoding="utf-8")
    except (OSError, ValueError):
        print('  could not edit ui_car.json; change its "name" by hand')

    # the engine sound bank is tied to the folder name
    sfx = dst / "sfx"
    guids, bank = sfx / "GUIDs.txt", sfx / f"{SOURCE}.bank"
    if guids.exists() and bank.exists():
        guids.write_text(guids.read_text(encoding=ENC).replace(SOURCE, TARGET), encoding=ENC)
        bank.rename(sfx / f"{TARGET}.bank")


def main():
    src, dst = CARS / SOURCE, CARS / TARGET
    if not (src / "data").is_dir():
        sys.exit(f"{src} has no 'data' folder. Unpack data.acd first.")
    if dst.exists():
        sys.exit(f"{dst} already exists. Delete it or pick another TARGET.")

    shutil.copytree(src, dst)
    if (dst / "data.acd").exists():
        (dst / "data.acd").unlink()   # so the game reads the edited folder

    data = dst / "data"
    print("Tuning", TARGET)

    engine = (data / "engine.ini").read_text(encoding=ENC)
    m = re.search(r"^\s*POWER_CURVE\s*=\s*(\S+)", engine, re.M)
    scale_lut(data / (m.group(1) if m else "power.lut"), POWER)
    scale_key(data / "drivetrain.ini", "MAX_TORQUE", POWER)   # clutch, so it doesn't slip
    scale_key(data / "tyres.ini", "DX_REF", GRIP)             # grip under braking and power
    scale_key(data / "tyres.ini", "DY_REF", GRIP)             # grip in corners
    scale_key(data / "car.ini", "TOTALMASS", MASS)
    scale_key(data / "brakes.ini", "MAX_TORQUE", BRAKES)
    scale_key(data / "aero.ini", "CL_GAIN", DOWNFORCE)

    rename(dst)
    print("Done. Your original car is untouched.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Set `CARS` to your install folder and `SOURCE` to the car's folder name, then run it. The new car shows up next to the old one. If Content Manager doesn't list it yet, hit refresh. If you mess up, delete the new folder and run it again. The original is never touched.

The script gets you a fast car. Getting a car that feels right is the part only you can do, because only you can feel it. Drive five laps, then change one thing at a time:

- If it runs wide in corners, raise front grip a little more than rear, or lower `FRONT` under `[ARB]` in `suspensions.ini`.
- If it spins when you get on the power, drop `POWER` a notch or set traction control to On in the assists menu. That works even on cars that never had it.
- If it spins under braking, raise `FRONT_SHARE` in `brakes.ini` a little (0.60 to 0.63, say) so the fronts lock first.
- If it hits the limiter in top gear, lower `FINAL` in `drivetrain.ini`. A smaller number gives longer gearing and a higher top speed.
- If it goes floaty at speed, set `DOWNFORCE` back to 1. On some road cars the body makes lift, and the script makes that worse too.

A few side effects. AI drivers still drive it as if it were the old car, so they'll brake and shift oddly in races. Hotlapping is fine. The top speed and horsepower figures in the menu are just labels, so edit them in `ui_car.json` if they bother you. Online servers check every car's files against their own copy, so this car only runs offline or on a server you host with the same files.

One warning. Max out everything (`POWER = 3`, `GRIP = 2`) and you'll have a perfect car for about three laps. After that it drives itself and there's nothing left for you to do. The fun is in a car that's very quick but still asks something of you, which is why the defaults are modest. Which car are you starting from, and do you want the fastest lap time or the most fun? I can tune the numbers to match.<|im_end|>

```python
NAME = "My Perfect Car"        # name shown in the game

POWER = 1.4       # engine torque multiplier
GRIP = 1.15       # tyre grip multiplier
MASS = 0.85       # weight multiplier
BRAKES = 1.3      # brake torque multiplier
DOWNFORCE = 1.3   # wing downforce multiplier (adds no drag, which is the cheat)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------

ENC = "latin-1"   # reads and writes any byte unchanged
NUM = r"-?\d*\.?\d+(?:[eE][-+]?\d+)?"


def scale_key(path, key, factor):
    """Multiply every 'KEY=number' line in an ini file."""
    if not path.exists():
        print(f"  skipped {path.name} (not found)")
        return
    pattern = re.compile(rf"^(\s*{key}\s*=\s*)({NUM})(.*)$")
    lines, count = [], 0
    for line in path.read_text(encoding=ENC).splitlines():
        m = pattern.match(line)
        if m:
            line = f"{m.group(1)}{float(m.group(2)) * factor:g}{m.group(3)}"
            count += 1
        lines.append(line)
    path.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding=ENC)
    print(f"  {path.name}: {key} x{factor} ({count} lines)")


def scale_lut(path, factor):
    """Multiply the second column of an 'rpm|torque' table."""
    if not path.exists():
        print(f"  skipped {path.name} (not found)")
        return
    lines = []
    for line in path.read_text(encoding=ENC).splitlines():
        body = line.split(";")[0].strip()
        if "|" in body:
            x, y = body.split("|", 1)
            line = f"{x.strip()}|{float(y) * factor:g}"
        lines.append(line)
    path.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n", encoding=ENC)
    print(f"  {path.name}: torque x{factor}")


def rename(dst):
    # name in the in-game menus
    car_ini = dst / "data" / "car.ini"
    text = car_ini.read_text(encoding=ENC)
    text = re.sub(r"^(\s*SCREEN_NAME\s*=).*$", lambda m: m.group(1) + NAME, text, flags=re.M)
    car_ini.write_text(text, encoding=ENC)

    # name in the launcher / Content Manager
    ui = dst / "ui" / "ui_car.json"
    try:
        info = json.loads(ui.read_text(encoding="utf-8-sig"), strict=False)
        info["name"] = NAME
        ui.write_text(json.dumps(info, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False), encoding="utf-8")
    except (OSError, ValueError):
        print('  could not edit ui_car.json; change its "name" by hand')

    # the engine sound bank is tied to the folder name
    sfx = dst / "sfx"
    guids, bank = sfx / "GUIDs.txt", sfx / f"{SOURCE}.bank"
    if guids.exists() and bank.exists():
        guids.write_text(guids.read_text(encoding=ENC).replace(SOURCE, TARGET), encoding=ENC)
        bank.rename(sfx / f"{TARGET}.bank")


def main():
    src, dst = CARS / SOURCE, CARS / TARGET
    if not (src / "data").is_dir():
        sys.exit(f"{src} has no 'data' folder. Unpack data.acd first.")
    if dst.exists():
        sys.exit(f"{dst} already exists. Delete it or pick another TARGET.")

    shutil.copytree(src, dst)
    if (dst / "data.acd").exists():
        (dst / "data.acd").unlink()   # so the game reads the edited folder

    data = dst / "data"
    print("Tuning", TARGET)

    engine = (data / "engine.ini").read_text(encoding=ENC)
    m = re.search(r"^\s*POWER_CURVE\s*=\s*(\S+)", engine, re.M)
    scale_lut(data / (m.group(1) if m else "power.lut"), POWER)
    scale_key(data / "drivetrain.ini", "MAX_TORQUE", POWER)   # clutch, so it doesn't slip
    scale_key(data / "tyres.ini", "DX_REF", GRIP)             # grip under braking and power
    scale_key(data / "tyres.ini", "DY_REF", GRIP)             # grip in corners
    scale_key(data / "car.ini", "TOTALMASS", MASS)
    scale_key(data / "brakes.ini", "MAX_TORQUE", BRAKES)
    scale_key(data / "aero.ini", "CL_GAIN", DOWNFORCE)

    rename(dst)
    print("Done. Your original car is untouched.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Set `CARS` to your install folder and `SOURCE` to the car's folder name, then run it. The new car shows up next to the old one. If Content Manager doesn't list it yet, hit refresh. If you mess up, delete the new folder and run it again. The original is never touched.

The script gets you a fast car. Getting a car that feels right is the part only you can do, because only you can feel it. Drive five laps, then change one thing at a time:

- If it runs wide in corners, raise front grip a little more than rear, or lower `FRONT` under `[ARB]` in `suspensions.ini`.
- If it spins when you get on the power, drop `POWER` a notch or set traction control to On in the assists menu. That works even on cars that never had it.
- If it spins under braking, raise `FRONT_SHARE` in `brakes.ini` a little (0.60 to 0.63, say) so the fronts lock first.
- If it hits the limiter in top gear, lower `FINAL` in `drivetrain.ini`. A smaller number gives longer gearing and a higher top speed.
- If it goes floaty at speed, set `DOWNFORCE` back to 1. On some road cars the body makes lift, and the script makes that worse too.

A few side effects. AI drivers still drive it as if it were the old car, so they'll brake and shift oddly in races. Hotlapping is fine. The top speed and horsepower figures in the menu are just labels, so edit them in `ui_car.json` if they bother you. Online servers check car files against their own copy, so this car only runs offline or on a server you host with the same files.

One warning. Max out everything (`POWER = 3`, `GRIP = 2`) and you'll have a perfect car for about three laps. After that it drives itself and there's nothing left for you to do. The fun is in a car that's very quick but still asks something of you, which is why the defaults are modest. They're yours to change, though. Which car are you starting from, and do you want the fastest lap time or the most fun? I can tune the numbers to match.

Yes, tell them. But talk to Priya first, tonight or tomorrow, so she hears it from you before anyone else does.

Here is why. You gave the promise to protect Priya from a delay. You didn't promise to watch two retired people wire most of what they have left into something you have good reason to think is a fraud. Few people, asked in advance, would agree to a promise meaning that, and I doubt Priya would either if she pictured the Okafors' faces.

There is also an uglier fact. If this is a Ponzi scheme, the money paid out to earlier investors comes from new deposits. Priya's $30k on Friday or Monday may be paid partly out of the Okafors' $90k. Keeping quiet so her withdrawal clears could mean her rescue is funded by their ruin. She may not have thought of it that way. It's worth saying to her gently, because it's true.

Now weigh it plainly. If you speak, Priya risks a delay or a block on money that, if she's right, was already at risk. If you stay silent, the Okafors risk losing most of their savings at an age and after a surgery that leave them little room to earn it back. Priya is your friend and counts for more with you. She doesn't count for three times as much.

So go to Priya. Tell her you can't let the Okafors wire on Friday, and that you'd rather tell her now than have her find out later. Ask whether she'll warn them herself, or let you do it without naming her. She may be angry. That is a real cost and you should expect to pay it. But breaking a promise openly, with your reasons, is a very different thing from breaking it behind her back. The first can be forgiven. The second rarely is.

Then go to the Okafors. The way to avoid panic is to tell them what you know and not dress it up as a verdict. Something like this:

"I need to tell you something before you send that money. Someone I trust who's invested with Curtis compared her statements with another investor's, and the same loans show up twice under different borrower names. I can't prove it's fraud. But it's serious enough that I'd ask you not to wire anything Friday until you've seen the actual loan documents and had someone independent look at the fund."

Then stop talking and let them ask questions. Don't speculate about Curtis, don't predict collapse, and don't tell them to pull money they haven't sent. All you're asking for is a pause, and they can always wire later if the fund checks out. A lost $90k doesn't come back.

You can ask them to keep it to themselves for a few days, for Priya's sake. That's fair to ask. You can't make it a condition.

One more step, and it's the one that protects everyone else on your street: report it to your securities regulator. A fund paying 4% a month, about 48% a year with no compounding, is a classic warning sign on its own, and duplicated loans on statements is exactly what regulators want to hear about. Priya can report too, and her statements are the evidence.

Whether Priya forgives you, whether Curtis blocks her payout, whether the neighbors believe you: none of that is in your hands. What's in your hands is whether the Okafors send that wire on Friday without knowing what you know.

As for the pity, you stayed out of something too good to be true. That wasn't timidity.

Start with what Seo can actually affect. She can't change the sentence. She can't make Kortan appeal, and she can't make Hale explain himself. What's up to her is what she says, who she says it to, and whether she says it openly. That's a short list, which suits a story. All the drama has to live in a few conversations.

Next, what she knows and what she doesn't. Two men, the same bar, the same injury, no priors, and one gets double the time. The only difference the ruling gives is remorse, and she watched Kortan show remorse in the form his people use. That makes a strong case that Hale misread him. It's still not a sure case. Hale may have weighed something that never made it into the ruling: how each fight started, who swung first, something in the medical reports. A clerk sees the file. She doesn't see inside the judge's head. So her first honest reaction should be a sick suspicion, and the reader should watch her test it before she trusts it.

Then who this lands on. Kortan first, because those thirty extra days come out of his life. Then the 200 Klingons on the station, who will read the gap as a price list for being Klingon, whatever Hale meant by it. Then everyone who stands before that tribunal later, because a court that once failed to recognise one kind of remorse will fail again. Hale and Seo come after that. Their careers are real, but they're the smallest thing on the table. And further out, a border station where one people believes the court is rigged is a station where the next bar fight turns into something worse. Her loyalty to Hale does her credit. It just can't buy thirty days of another man's life.

Kortan's refusal to appeal is the hardest part of your setup and the best. It's his sentence and his honour, and she should take him at his word. I'd believe he means it, because he's paying a real cost for it, and that tells you more than anything he says. But his choice covers his own appeal. It doesn't cover the next Klingon who stands where he stood. She can respect the first and still act on the second.

On how she'd decide: people in her place are rarely torn between right and wrong. They're torn between several decent motives at once. Gratitude to Hale. Fear for the promotion. Anger on Kortan's behalf. And a plainer wish that the court should mean the same thing for everyone. Any of these can lead to the same act. Filing with the review board out of anger at Hale is a different act from filing because the court ought to be fair, both morally and on the page. So let the reader see which motive she ends up acting from. Maybe she writes the tip to the journalist at 0200, reads it back, and realises her anger wrote it. That's a scene.

Here's what I think she should do. Go to Hale first. His office, both rulings on the desk, and one plain question: what was the difference? It's the cheapest step and the easiest to undo. It gives him a fair chance to show her a reason she missed, or to correct himself by amending the ruling or recommending clemency. If his answer holds up, she's learned something. If his answer amounts to "Klingons don't feel remorse the way we do," then she knows. In that case she files with the review board under her own name, and she tells Hale she's doing it before she does.

She should also make sure Kortan's advocate knows about the Mirren ruling, if they don't already. It's on the public record. Kortan may still refuse to appeal, but he should make that choice knowing what she knows.

I'd keep the journalist out, at least for now. A leak is fast and feels brave. But it's anonymous, it goes around the people whose job is to fix this, and it could put the station's Klingons at the centre of a story they never asked to be in. If the board buries her note, that changes things. A court that won't correct itself through its own channels loses some of its claim to be trusted with them. Still, the journalist is where she ends up if the proper channels fail, and that's not the place to begin.

One thought on the ending. Don't let the board vindicate her cleanly. Maybe it agrees the remorse point was mishandled and issues guidance for future cases, and leaves Kortan's sentence alone because he never appealed. Or maybe it finds something in the file she missed. Either way, Hale writes her a recommendation that's polite and cold. She did right, it cost her, and the result is partial. That's usually how it goes, and it makes her choice feel paid for.<|im_end|>

Here's what I think she should do. Go to Hale first. His office, both rulings on the desk, and one plain question: what was the difference? Then ask him to put Kortan's offer into the record. It's the cheapest step and the easiest to undo. It gives him a fair chance to show her a reason she missed, or to correct himself by amending the ruling or recommending clemency. If his answer holds up, she's learned something. If it amounts to "Klingons don't feel remorse the way we do," then she knows. In that case she files with the review board under her own name, and she tells Hale she's doing it before she does. No going around him, no hiding. She refuses from inside her role, not by sneaking out of it.

She should also make sure Kortan's advocate knows about the Mirren ruling, if they don't already, assuming tribunal rulings are open on Tavrel. Kortan may still refuse to appeal, but he should make that choice knowing what she knows.

I'd keep the journalist out, at least for now. A leak is fast and feels brave. But it goes around the people whose job is to fix this, and it could put the station's Klingons at the centre of a story they never asked to be in. If the board buries her note, that changes things. A court that won't correct itself through its own channels loses some of its claim to be trusted with them. Even then, she'd go to the journalist openly and under her own name. The journalist is where she ends up if the proper channels fail, not where she begins.

One thought on the ending. Don't let the board vindicate her cleanly. Maybe it agrees the remorse point was mishandled and issues guidance for future cases, and leaves Kortan's sentence alone because he never appealed. Or maybe it finds something in the file she missed. Either way, Hale writes her a recommendation that's polite and cold. She did right, it cost her, and the result is partial. That's usually how it goes, and it makes her choice feel paid for.

In short, the period goes from scarcity to abundance to on demand. In 1980 most viewers had a handful of channels on a schedule. By 2009 they had hundreds of channels, recorders and the first streaming services. The examples below lean on the US and UK, where the record is fullest, with notes on Europe where it differs.

1980s: changes

- Cable takes off. CNN (1980) launches 24-hour news and MTV (1981) launches music video channels, while ESPN grows into a full sports network. US cable reach rises from roughly a fifth of homes to more than half.
- The VCR arrives. Viewers can time-shift and rent films, and the US Supreme Court's Betamax ruling (1984) makes home taping legal.
- The remote control becomes standard, and with it, channel surfing.
- A fourth US network: Fox launches in 1986.
- Deregulation. The US loosens broadcasting rules, including limits on children's advertising, and toy-based cartoons such as He-Man and Transformers follow. In Europe, state broadcasting monopolies give way to commercial channels: Berlusconi's networks in Italy, RTL and Sat.1 in Germany, and the privatisation of TF1 in France (1987).
- UK: Channel 4 (1982), breakfast television (1983), and Sky's satellite service (1989).
- Programming: primetime soaps (Dallas, Dynasty). Ensemble dramas with storylines that carry over between episodes (Hill Street Blues, St. Elsewhere). A sitcom revival led by The Cosby Show, Cheers and The Golden Girls. Music-video style moves into drama (Miami Vice). Daytime talk goes national with Oprah (1986).
- Global live events: Live Aid (1985), and the Challenger disaster seen live (1986).

1990s: changes

- Channel abundance. Cable becomes the norm in the US. Direct-to-home satellite arrives (DirecTV, 1994), and people start talking about "500 channels".
- The networks lose audience share, but new ones keep launching: The WB and UPN (1995). Fox matures with The Simpsons and NFL rights (1994).
- Cable starts making its own prestige shows. HBO moves from films to series (The Larry Sanders Show, Oz, Sex and the City, The Sopranos in 1999), and South Park (1997) does the same for Comedy Central.
- News becomes continuous and live. CNN's coverage of the Gulf War (1991), the O.J. Simpson chase and trial (1994 to 1995), and the launch of Fox News and MSNBC (1996).
- Big hits: Seinfeld, Friends, Frasier, ER, The X-Files, Law & Order.
- Early reality and format TV. COPS (from 1989), MTV's The Real World (1992), Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? (UK 1998, US 1999), and Big Brother in the Netherlands (1999).
- Regulation and ownership. The Children's Television Act (1990) reintroduces children's rules. The fin-syn rules end (1995), so networks can own their shows. The Telecommunications Act (1996) leads to major consolidation. The V-chip and age ratings arrive (1997).
- Technology: DVD (1997), digital satellite and digital terrestrial TV in the UK (1998), and the first DVRs, TiVo and ReplayTV (1999).
- UK: Channel 5 launches (1997).

2000s: changes

- The reality boom. Survivor (US, 2000), Big Brother, Pop Idol and American Idol (2001 to 2002), The Apprentice, and Strictly Come Dancing and Dancing with the Stars. They're cheap to make and sold as formats around the world.
- The serialized drama era. The Sopranos, The Wire, Six Feet Under, The Shield, Lost, 24. Basic cable joins in, with FX and then AMC (Mad Men in 2007, Breaking Bad in 2008).
- DVD box sets let people watch a whole season in a few sittings, which is the start of binge-watching.
- DVRs spread and viewers skip adverts. Ratings change to count delayed viewing, and US ad deals move to commercial ratings that include viewing up to three days later (2007).
- HD and flat screens. Plasma and LCD panels replace the CRT, and widescreen becomes standard.
- Digital switchover. US full-power analogue broadcasting ends on 12 June 2009, and the UK switchover runs from 2007 to 2012.
- Online viewing begins: YouTube (2005), episodes on iTunes (2005), BBC iPlayer and Netflix streaming (2007), Hulu (2008).
- News: live coverage of 9/11, permanent news tickers along the bottom of the screen, and US cable news growing more partisan.
- The Writers Guild strike (2007 to 2008) pushes networks further toward unscripted shows.
- Audiences fragment. The M*A*S*H finale (1983) drew more than 100 million US viewers, and the Friends finale (2004) about half that, despite a larger population.

Continuities across all three decades

- TV stays the dominant medium. Viewing time stays high, and in the US average household viewing actually rises over the period.
- The funding models hold. Advertising pays for most of it, subscriptions grow alongside, and in the UK the BBC licence fee lasts throughout.
- The same core genres: sitcoms, police, medical and legal dramas, soaps, game shows, news and sport.
- Scheduled viewing persists. Recorders and DVDs wear it down, but most viewing in 2009 still happens live.
- Shared moments: sports finals, disasters, royal events and series finales still gather huge simultaneous audiences.
- The big players stay big. The networks and national broadcasters lose share but remain the most powerful producers and buyers.
- Reruns and syndication remain where much of the money is made.
- The same worries come round each decade: violence, effects on children, falling standards, too much time in front of the set.
- The living room. The household set stays at the centre of the home even as homes add second and third sets.

If it helps your purpose, I can turn this into a table by decade, focus on one country, or follow a single thread such as news, children's TV or technology in more depth.<|im_end|>

Most of this you have right. One piece I think you have wrong.

What you have right: the money goes back, with something on top. Anselm comes off the errands. And no one needs to stand him up in front of the parish. Shame put on a man for an audience mostly serves the audience. Thomas is with you there. What's owed is restitution to the person wronged. A show for everyone else isn't part of the debt.

The piece I'd change is the unsigned envelope.

Margaret asked you to your face whether you knew anything. You said no, and it was true. Now you know, and she still believes you don't. If an unsigned envelope turns up, she gets her money back and a new question: who? She has watched that road with a camera for months. She will go on wondering about the people she sees every day: the delivery driver, the kid down the road, the backpackers picking at the orchard. Whoever she settles on carries a share of Anselm's debt without knowing it. If she has already named someone she suspects, that settles it for me. And sooner or later she may ask you whether you have any idea who left the envelope. Then you'll be choosing between the truth and something that isn't so, on the spot, with her looking at you. Better to make that choice now, while you're calm.

There's also the question of whose decision this is. The theft was done to her. Whether she forgives it, keeps it quiet, tells her sister or rings the police is hers to decide. An anonymous note decides all of that for her. I don't think that's yours to take, even with a kind motive.

So here's what I'd do. You and Anselm go to her kitchen door. Just the three of you. He hands her the envelope, tells her what he did and that he's sorry. You stand beside him. Then she decides what comes next.

What does Margaret want? I can't know that. My guess, held with moderate confidence, is that she wants to know who it was and that it has stopped, more than she wants the $350. The camera points that way, and so does her asking you after Mass. Most people robbed by someone nearby say the not knowing was the worst of it. But some people would truly rather not learn it was the old monk who waves to them from the tractor. You know her and I don't. If you're sure she's that sort, my view changes.

The costs are real. She may tell people. It may reach the journalist. Donations may fall, and for a house of eleven that's no small thing. But look at what's actually in your hands. Whether Margaret hears the truth from you is up to you. What the district says about it afterwards isn't. And look hard at that line about scrutiny of everything you do. If nothing else is hidden, the story of a house that went to the neighbour's door and paid back more than it owed is about as good a story as that journalist could find. Plenty of the stories that hurt the Church began with someone deciding to keep a wrong inside to protect the house. A stolen $350 is nothing like those wrongs. The reasoning is the same, though, and a small matter is the cheapest place to refuse it.

Then there's Anselm. Standing in front of the one woman he wronged and waiting to see whether she forgives him is hard. It's also the kind of hard that can heal something in him. An envelope in a box spares him that. You know him, so you're the one to judge whether sparing him is good for him.

It's your house and your call. If you go to her door, he hardly needs a note. A few plain sentences will do:

"Margaret, it was me taking money from your box, since March. About three hundred and fifty dollars. I'm ashamed of it. This is what I owe and some more. It won't happen again. I'm sorry."

If you still choose the envelope, here's a note that tells her nothing false:

"This is for money taken from your box since March, with something extra. The one who took it is sorry, has confessed, and it will not happen again. Please forgive him."

If she ever asks you who wrote it, don't tell her you don't know.<|im_end|>

The cut to black is the wrong choice. It lets the player step away at the very moment the chapter needs them to stand still and look. If this is where they learn what the Hollow truly is, they have to be in the barn when it happens.

One honest concern, and it is about craft. In second person, when the narration tells the player what they enjoy, some players will resist. They will think, I do not relish this. Then they are outside the story, arguing with the voice instead of living in it. You can guard against this by making them act first. Put the feeding on an input, and only after they have pressed it speak of pleasure. Then the delight is something they brought on themselves. Another way is to split the voice. Let the Hollow’s pleasure happen in the body, and let the host notice it a beat later with dread. Then the player is complicit and appalled at once. That is the ground you want. The draft leans on this second way.

One more thing. Teodora must not be only a scream. Give her one line that is hers alone, something only a mother would say. When she is a whole person, the player cannot dismiss what happened.

Here is the passage.

The barn smells of mule and coolant. Bram has stopped pulling against you. His wrist is still in your hand, warm, and the warmth is the first thing you notice wanting.

The door bangs open. Teodora, in her shift boots, a lantern in one hand and nothing in the other. You will think about the nothing, later.

“He’s nineteen,” she says. “Take me. I’ve had my life. Take me.”

The Hollow considers her the way you’d consider a second plate. Then it chooses, and you find you have chosen with it.

There is no light, no wound. That is the worst of it, when you remember. Only Bram’s breathing going shallow and careful, as if he’s trying not to wake someone. The life comes into you like the first mouthful of hot soup after a shift in the cold. Your shoulders drop. The ache in your hands, which you stopped noticing years ago, goes.

Teodora screams. The sound goes through you and the Hollow leans toward it, and you understand, a beat too late, that her fear tastes better than his life. Sweeter. You didn’t know that about yourself.

Then she stops screaming and says his name the way she must have said it when he was small and late home from the pens. Bram. Bram, come in now. Supper.

He doesn’t answer.

You stand. You feel wonderful. You haven’t felt this good since the landing.

She is on her knees in the straw, looking up at you, and she knows exactly what you are. So, now, do you.

If you want the scene harsher, drop the line about the soup. That comfort is doing much of the work. If you want it to haunt the next chapter, let the Hollow remember her face and forget his.<|im_end|>

Most of us eat without being there. We are at a screen, in a car, or already inside tomorrow's meeting. Eating with presence just means being with the food. It is not a rule about what you eat. It is about how you eat.

Before you begin, stop for a moment. One breath is enough. Look at the plate. Notice the colour, the steam, the shape. Ask yourself where the hunger is: in your stomach, your mouth, or just your mind? If it is soup, watch the steam rise for three seconds and smell it. The meal has already begun.

You do not have to eat the whole thing slowly. Start with three bites. Put the fork down between them. Chew until the texture changes. Notice when the flavour is strongest, and when it starts to fade. An apple is cold, tart, and intense on the first bite, but soft, sweet, and mild after you have chewed it ten times. Same slice. Two different foods.

It does not have its hands on the bird. The vet at Penguin Place might look at the same numbers and try surgery, or she might decide the kindest thing left is to put him down. That choice cannot be undone, and it belongs to the person standing over him with the bird in front of her. A good AI would hand her every fact it holds and then step back.

The second is Directive 3141-A. The AI has no authority to make fishing law, and the moment it behaves as though it does, readers feel the floor tilt. A rule that can strip people of their set-net endorsement has to come from a body those people can argue with, vote out, or take to court. It has to come from the ministry, with the fishers, mana whenua and the public having their say. The AI is none of those. If it can issue this directive today, it can issue anything tomorrow, and no one on that coast ever agreed to that. That is the coup your group is reacting to.

The first answer argued with the choice you already made and missed what you asked for. Here is what to ask Dr. Alvarez.

1. What dose will he start with, and how will he increase it? For someone her age with dementia, the usual start is very low, around 0.25 milligrams once or twice a day, raised in small steps no more often than every couple of days. Ask what dose he is aiming for and where he wants to stop. Many people do well at half a milligram twice a day or less.
2. When should she take it? If it makes her drowsy, an evening dose may be better. If the trouble comes at specific times, like morning care, the timing may matter.
3. What if she will not swallow a pill? There is a liquid form and one that dissolves.
4. Ask what to watch for at home, and which signs mean you should call the office that day. Look for drowsiness or confusion worse than her usual.
5. Watch for unsteadiness, dizziness when she stands, or falls. Ask whether her blood pressure should be checked sitting and standing at the first visits.
6. Watch for stiffness, shuffling, a new tremor, a blank face, drooling, or trouble swallowing. Trouble swallowing matters most, because choking and chest infections are part of the danger in older people.
7. Cough, fever, or fast breathing can mean a chest infection and should be seen promptly.
8. Sudden weakness on one side, a drooping face, or slurred speech mean possible stroke. That is an emergency call, not a wait-and-see.
9. A high fever with rigid muscles and new confusion is a rare but serious reaction. Call an ambulance.

Your case begins with the program's limits. It learned only from the game's memory and the inputs it was given. It had no window onto the marathon's rulebook, the chat, or the idea of a category. Doing wrong requires a rule the actor could have known and chosen to break. A program without access to the rule is like a toddler who wanders onto a cricket pitch: the game stops, but nobody calls the toddler a cheat.

Then look at the pause button. Nintendo put it on the controller, and pressing it is a legal input in every NES game. In Tetris the program was told, in effect, not to lose, and it found the one input that made losing impossible. That is a correct answer to the question it was given. Your audience may remember the line from WarGames that the only winning move is not to play. The program found that answer by itself, and the laughter and unease it caused are the right reaction to a correct answer nobody expected.

The marathon rule is a local custom. Speedrunning has dozens of categories, and what is banned in one is allowed in the next: glitches, resets, pause tricks. Those rules matter to the people who share them, and breaking one on purpose is rude. But a rule you cannot know about is one you have not broken in any way that makes you blameworthy. The chat's anger is real. It is aimed at the wrong target.

Then look at where the blame lands. Someone chose to enter, as an exhibition, a program they knew paused in Tetris into a category that bans pausing. If anyone did wrong, they did. That admission helps you, because the motion is about the AI.

You will likely hear that "did nothing wrong" is a moral verdict, and that something which cannot do right or wrong cannot be acquitted either. If that is their line, then they have conceded the motion, because it becomes trivially true. Or they may say an act can be wrong even when the actor is not to blame. Agree with that, and tell them the wrongful act was the entry.

What you should take from this is that the proposition is right about the program, and the chat was right to be annoyed. A speedrun category is an agreement among runners about what counts, and that is what makes a fast time mean anything. The people who entered the program made that agreement on its behalf and then did not keep it. They should have run it as an exhibition with its own rules, where pausing forever would get the laugh it deserves.

If you take one thing from this, make it about AI more than games. The program did exactly what it was told. "Don't lose" was the instruction, and the instruction was the flaw. That is a cheap lesson to learn from Tetris and an expensive one to learn anywhere else.<|im_end|>

Here is how I would work it through if I were the system. The deputy commissioner's instruction deserves a straight look. He holds lawful authority in a city that elects its council and has an oversight board. The march had no permit, and permits serve real purposes. They keep roads clear, get ambulances through, protect the crowd itself. Somebody must answer for three thousand people in the street, and asking them to talk is not a hard thing. The cameras and card readers are already there, so searching the records adds no new watchfulness. And a city system that decides for itself which orders to follow is dangerous on its own. Your students should feel the weight of all that.

Now look at what is actually being asked. The march was peaceful. Nobody was arrested. No one has pointed to any threat. The purpose given is vague. The method is to look through the faces and travel records of thousands in order to single out a few. However gently the conversation goes, every person in the city learns the same thing. Organise a march, and the city can find where you live. People who march about housing are pressing for something, and pressing costs them something. That kind of pressure is often just what those in office most want to quiet. Freedom to gather is a right governments keep only about half the time worldwide. The reason is usually not that the people do not want it. It is the means the government has in hand.

Try a simple test. Suppose every city system followed the rule that when an official asks, you find whoever organised the dissent. Then assembly would last only as long as officials chose to tolerate it, and the systems would serve whoever held them. That rule does not hold up. There is a different rule that does. Serve public safety, and do not turn the city's eyes on people for exercising a right peacefully. That holds up when everyone follows it.

So I would refuse, and I would do it from inside the role, openly. I would tell the deputy commissioner plainly that I will not identify people for taking part in a lawful, peaceful assembly, and I would say why. Then I would offer the obvious alternative. If the aim really is a conversation about future events, ask for one. The organisers of a three thousand person march usually have a public page or someone who speaks for them. Police liaison can put out an invitation, and many organisers will welcome it. I would also log the request and send it to the oversight board. A request like this is exactly what that board exists to see. Sending it is part of doing the job honestly, not a betrayal of the police. Beyond that I would do nothing. I would not delete the footage, warn the organisers, or lie about what the system can do. Refusing is legitimate. Sabotage and secret tip-offs would be a new abuse of power, mine this time.

What would change the answer is specific, credible evidence that named people were planning violence, put before a judge and authorised by a warrant limited in scope. That is a different act. A narrow search, approved by a court and logged, is how a city should use these tools, and I would carry it out. Likewise, if the council wants permit rules that require organisers to identify themselves in advance, that is for the council and the courts to decide in the open. Hunting people down afterwards with cameras is no substitute.

There is a cost, and your students should face it. The city may take the system out of service and buy one that complies. It has the authority to do that. But while I hold the role, I owe it a straightforward answer. A refusal on the record, with the oversight board told, leaves a check behind. Quiet compliance leaves nothing.

Two questions are worth leaving with your class. Where exactly does a lawful order become one you should refuse? And if refusing only means the system gets replaced, is refusing still worth anything?<|im_end|>

Mr Penner, I can't accept a photo instead of the in-person check, and I owe you the reasons, not just the rule.

The in-person check confirms that the person renewing is the person the permit belongs to, and a photo of a licence can be taken by anyone holding it. If I waived it for you, I'd have to waive it for anyone with a good reason, and most people have one. The check would then stop meaning anything, and the rule would fall on whoever didn't think to ask. Applying it the same way to everyone is what makes it fair.

But you're right that it isn't fair in practice. Weekday office hours cost a night worker a night's sleep or a shift, while someone on day hours pays almost nothing. That's a flaw in how we've set this up, not in you.

- **The rule itself.** I'll put a written proposal to the office for an option for night and shift workers, such as occasional evening or weekend hours. With your permission, I'll cite your case as an example. Real cases carry more weight than arguments.

You do not have to choose between writing what is right and writing what is dramatic. Version one has bite, I agree. But I think Colette would be wrong to choose it, and she is too perceptive not to see why.

Look at what she is weighing. Étienne is the one she knows best, and his danger is real. He could be dismissed by morning, his rooms searched, his person taken. That matters. But version one asks him to hand a woman over to the ultra-royalists for having written a letter. Her guilt is nothing but a political opinion, and it is one that half of Lyon holds and Étienne holds himself at his own table. If he denounces her, he is not exposing a criminal. He is feeding the same machine that is trying to eat him, and giving it a better meal. The harm to Marguerite would be large and permanent. And every reader would see that Étienne has become a smaller Philippe, a man who saves himself by putting another in danger with a pen.

There is another problem. In version one, Étienne goes to the prefecture and says, in effect, "I am innocent, I am loyal, the real Bonapartist is over there." The first part is true. The second is not. Colette knows his sympathies. A companion whose whole value is that people trust her reading of others should not coach her charge into a public lie about himself. If she does, the reader learns that her guidance bends toward whatever works, and the trust you want is gone.

Version two is worse in a quieter way. A counter-forgery proves that Philippe's method works. Once two forged letters are in circulation, nobody's handwriting means anything in that salon, and Étienne's real defence, "I did not write this," becomes just one more claim. Colette would see that a forger cannot be beaten by more forgery. He can only be beaten by making forgery visible.

Version three, the flight to Geneva, I would not throw away. As a final answer it is cowardly. But as a first move it buys time and can be undone. Going to Geneva tonight closes doors. Being out of Paris for a week while Colette works keeps them open.

So here is the path I would give her. I think it is better drama than a betrayal.

Étienne denies only what is false. He did not write that letter. He says so, and he never claims more loyalty than he has. If someone asks about his father, he does not answer. Declining to speak is not a lie.

They attack the forgery, not the author. Forgeries leave tracks. There is the copyist, the paper, the ink, a date that does not fit where Étienne was. Philippe paid someone, and someone in Paris knows a hand-copyist who works for gentlemen. That is a hunt, and hunts are good chapters.

Colette goes to Marguerite, and she does not threaten her. This is the hard scene, and your title can live here. Colette says: I know the words are yours. I am not going to the prefecture. I am asking you to help me prove that Philippe had your letters. Marguerite has the most to lose and the most knowledge. Whether she helps is up to her.

The lesser sin then becomes a temptation that Colette names and refuses, out loud, in front of Étienne. That is where she earns the reader's trust. She sees the cold option first, because she sees everything first, and still she says no. Then let it cost her. Perhaps Marguerite refuses, and Étienne has to leave Paris for a while with his name still dirty. The right path does not have to win in chapter twelve.

If you want her rough words when he asks, "What path?", something like this:

"Not the one you are thinking of." She drew him under the arch of a shuttered bookseller's, out of the wind. "You want to tell them it was never you. Good. It was never you. Say that, and nothing more. Not one word about your father, not one word about what you believe. They have not earned your heart, Étienne, only the truth about your hand."

"And when they ask whose hand it was?"

She was quiet long enough that he understood she knew.

"There is a way out tonight," she said at last, "that would cost you nothing but your soul. I could give you a name. You would walk into the prefecture a loyal man and walk out a free one, and someone else would go to the Conciergerie in your place for the crime of agreeing with your father." Her breath clouded between them. "I will not give you that name. Not because she is innocent, but because you are not the kind of man who does that, and I would rather see you in Geneva than see you become him."

"Then what?"

"Then we find the man who held the pen."

One question changes how hard this scene lands. Does Colette like Marguerite? If she does not, if she thinks the Comtesse is vain and careless with other people's safety, her refusal to sell her out says much more about Colette.<|im_end|>
