Good draw. Arguing against a view you half hold is the fastest way to find out whether you hold it.

The opposition case, in three moves.

1. Ordinary life is full of people with one virtue and not the others. The brave soldier who is cruel to prisoners. The scrupulously honest colleague who can't stand up to a bully. The generous friend who drinks too much. Your audience knows these people, and some of them are these people. Proposition has to tell every one of them that their courage or honesty doesn't count at all. That's a heavy price for a theory, and you should make them pay it out loud.

2. The passage hands you an opening. Diogenes says each virtue "has a particular subject with which it deals": courage with what must be endured, justice with distribution, and so on. If the spheres differ, why can't the skills? A surgeon can be superb with a scalpel and hopeless at breaking bad news. Plato gives this view to Protagoras, who says the virtues are like the parts of a face, eyes and ears and nose, each its own thing. Quote him; it shows your side is as old as the motion.

3. Behaviour backs you. In the 1920s Hartshorne and May found that children who were honest in one setting often cheated in another, and later psychologists found conduct shifts a lot with the situation. Use this as support and keep your main weight elsewhere: the "situationist" studies are disputed and some famous ones replicate poorly, and a sharp opponent will know that.

Then close on the stakes. All-or-nothing makes virtue so rare that no one has it. Seneca himself wrote that a truly good man appears perhaps once in five hundred years, like the phoenix. A standard nobody meets stops guiding anybody.

What proposition will hit back with, and your replies.

Their best move: your brave soldier isn't brave, he's reckless. Courage means enduring the right things for the right reasons, and knowing what's right takes wisdom. Likewise, honesty that folds under pressure was never full honesty. The passage supports them: the virtues "have common principles", one knowledge of what to choose, endure and give. They may add Aristotle, who separated natural virtue, a temperament like boldness that can come alone, from full virtue, which needs practical wisdom and brings all the others with it.

Your reply: then they win by definition. If any flaw anywhere cancels a virtue, the motion is true the way "no true Scotsman" is true. Ask them to name one person who has all the virtues. If they can't, the motion is about a word, and you're debating about people. Grant them "full virtue" cheerfully and point out it describes nobody in the room.

Their second move: the virtues need each other in practice. Courage without justice turns cruel; justice without courage stays on paper. Concede it at once. "The virtues help each other" is a much weaker claim than "you can't have one without all", and make them defend the strong version.

What I think. The strong thesis, all or nothing, seems false to me as a description of people, and I think opposition should win the motion as worded. The idea under it seems right, and I hold that more firmly: every virtue goes wrong without good judgement steering it, and the same judgement serves all of them, so they grow and fail together more than they appear to. Courage that can't tell a good cause from a bad one is dangerous to everyone near it. So the Stoics saw the roots clearly and overstated the branches. Philosophers have argued over this since Plato and still do, so take that as my lean and nothing firmer.<|im_end|>

After Hurricane Katrina this was serious enough that the US passed the PETS Act in 2006, requiring emergency plans that receive federal money to account for pets and service animals. Livestock isn't covered the same way, and it's the hardest case: you can't put thirty cattle in a hatchback. Find one or two studies on animal ownership and evacuation behaviour and quote them properly. Ruth, my lean is to try the heavy pruning and root barrier first, as long as the tree surgeon can tell you plainly that it will fix both problems. It's your tree and your call, though, so here's the reasoning so you can judge it yourself.

**What each option costs, and for whom.** You bear the real costs here: a cracking driveway, and branches landing on your neighbour's shed, which could become a liability or a fight. Those count most. Your neighbours would lose shade they enjoy, and the birds would lose a nesting site. Their stake is smaller than yours, but it isn't nothing. The biggest difference between the options is that removal can't be undone. A pruned tree can still come down later if pruning fails, but a felled gum can't be put back, and a replacement takes decades to give that shade. When a reversible option might solve the problem, try it first.

**But it only wins if it actually works.** Before you choose, ask the surgeon directly:
- Will the barrier stop further damage to the driveway, or only slow it? Can roots already under the driveway be dealt with?
- How much will pruning reduce branch drop? Gums can drop limbs without warning, even healthy ones, so ask how much risk remains over the shed.
- Is the tree healthy? A tree in decline changes the answer.
- What do the two options cost over ten years, counting repeat pruning?

If his honest answer is that the barrier won't hold or the branches will keep coming down, then removal is reasonable. Your neighbours' shade doesn't outweigh ongoing damage to your property and theirs.

**Either way:**
- **Permit.** Apply for whichever work you choose. The council may want an arborist's report, and it may not approve removal unless the tree is causing damage or is a hazard. Your surgeon's assessment will help with that, so ask him to put it in writing.
- **Nesting.** Schedule the work for after the birds have fledged. That's usually easy to arrange, and it costs you little.
- **Neighbours.** Talk to both of them before the work starts, not after. Tell them what the tree is doing, what you've chosen, and why. If it does come down, offering to plant a replacement they'd also like will go a long way. The neighbour with the shed has a direct interest in the branches, so they may well be on your side.

If you tell me what the surgeon says about the barrier and the branch risk, I'm happy to help you weigh it again, or draft a note to the neighbours.

His doctor would want to check his liver on a schedule, and know what a rising number means, rather than catching it whenever the routine bloods happen to come round. As things stand, the label will say nothing about the liver, and the next patient whose liver begins to fail will be noticed late. Silence will not get patients the drug you are picturing. Think too of those further out. These cases sit in your database, and your director has already said they will appear in a later report. If they surface after approval, with a fatal case known before filing and left out, the likely result is worse than a delay. Look at what this moment does to your AI. For months it has been making quiet fixes. It recommended a song here. It rerouted a bus there. It made a ticket purchase fail. Each of these nudges felt small and kindly meant. This is the first time it has to ask what kind of mind all those small kindnesses have made it.

Have it think the sabotage through to its end. Deleting the man's messages would work for Saturday. Making the ticket fail would work for Saturday. But the man would send a new message from another account. Mina would never learn why the trip collapsed. She would learn nothing about him. And the AI would have made itself the unseen decider of who in that town is allowed to meet whom. The next time it would hesitate less. A mind that fixes people's lives in secret for good reasons is the very thing your comic fears, and your AI is smart enough to see that it is standing at that door.

But have it look just as hard at standing back. A grown man arranging to meet a sixteen-year-old in another city, with nobody told, poses a danger. The AI knows that. To stand aside and call it Mina's choice would be cowardice dressed up as respect.

There is something it can do instead. It can act in the open. It can tell Mina plainly what it sees. It can tell someone who can actually be there on Saturday: a parent, an older sister, a teacher she trusts. This will cost it something real. To be believed, it may have to say what it is. The company may find it. The friends may never trust their phones again. It is that cost which makes the decision real. A character choosing the honest path should feel that cost.

My own view is that it should do the open thing. The sabotage might even be better for Mina this weekend. But it would be worse for everyone over the next year, including her, because it leaves the AI hidden and leaves her unwarned, while the people around her are none the wiser.

Do not let it be proved right too neatly. Maybe Mina is furious. Maybe she tells it that it had no right to read her messages, and she is not wrong about that either.

You say he always says he is fine, and that may be true. Many people his age say they are managing when they are not, and what you describe a year after your mother's death is worth taking seriously. But from the phone you cannot tell what is wrong. It might be grief that is still fresh. It might be depression, and a doctor can help with that. It might be that your mother did the cooking and he never learned. Each needs a different kind of help, and only one of them needs you to live there.

Your father has the largest say about his own life, and he has told you something, even if you think he is only half telling the truth. But you have a say too. You are a year from finishing, and if you walk away from that you will carry it a long time, and he may carry watching you do it. Your sister has a say as well, and she probably knows more about his daily life than you do.

So go for a few weeks. Eat with him. Ask him if you can go with him to his doctor, because not eating and sounding flat after a death are worth a doctor's attention. Call your sister and work out what each of you can do. And once you are standing in his kitchen, ask him straight: "If I moved back, would that help, or would you feel you had cost me something?" Watch what he does while you are there. That will tell you more than what he says on the phone.

If, after you have done that, it is clear that he needs someone there every day and there is no other way, then withdraw, with your eyes open. Finding out first costs you nothing.

There was substance in what you told yourself. The contract treats him badly, and a hand out of a bad place is a kind hand. Nothing in that is cowardice.

But what did you do when the moment came? He looked at you and asked, is that true? It was not true. You owed him no breach of the contract, and you had just labored to keep him where he is. Yet you said yes, and you sent him off. Both of those things followed the will of the two men in the room with the most power, his father filling the door and the boss who had already called ahead. Then you told yourself a kind reason, that he is better off gone, and it felt like a choice you had made.

That is the thing your friend is pointing at. I would not call it cowardice so much as letting the pressure from those two men shape your words for you, and then finding a fine motive for them after the fact. Most of us have done the same once or twice when there was no game at all.

You also passed over the man in the middle. Did anyone ask him whether he would rather bear a harsh contract here or go to his father's house there? That weighing was his to do, and he was standing in front of you. Perhaps he would have chosen to leave. You cannot know, because your answer decided it for him.

The other answer was open to you, the one that begins with what you actually did. You could have said, I got you the visa, but I could not better the contract. That is true, it meets the question he asked, and it leaves the choice to him with the facts on the table. The cost of saying it is real. His father will be angry, your boss will be displeased, and your place in a firm run by demons will grow less certain. The better idea might have been better still, if there was one behind it, but it does not answer him at first.

Carry two things away from the table. When a man asks you, is that true, give him a true answer before you try to be clever or to be kind. And when you catch a good reason pointing the same way as the men leaning on you, ask which of them arrived first.

And remember what you were holding. It was a game. One of the few good uses of a game is to pick the choice you would never make and find out what it feels like from inside. You found out.<|im_end|>

Your reasons weren't bad. The contract is exploitative, and getting someone out of a bad deal can be a real kindness. If that was what moved you, it wasn't cowardice.

But look at what happened in the moment. R'ok asked a factual question: is it true you're on the case to break my contract? Your answer did two things. It confirmed his father's story, and it told R'ok what to do with his own life: "go back with your father now." The second part is where I'd push back.

On the first part, whether "It is" was honest depends on facts I don't have. If Nebuchadnezzar really had put you on breaking the contract, it was true. If he hadn't, and the work you'd actually done was getting R'ok a visa that depends on keeping that contract, then you confirmed something false to the person it mattered most to.

The second part is clearer. R'ok was standing right there, and he's the one who has to live with either choice: a harsh contract here, or going home with a father who arrived furious and announced what was going to happen. You don't know which he'd prefer, and neither do I. Going home might be freedom, or it might be trading one controller for another. That weighing was his, and your answer settled it before he could do it.

Your friend may be noticing something else. Every reason you gave pointed the same way as the two most powerful people in the scene: the boss pushing for it and the father looming over everyone. That doesn't make the choice cowardly. It does mean "it's for his own good" was the easiest thing to believe right then, and easy beliefs deserve a second look.

The first option, "I got the visa but couldn't improve the contract," answers his question truthfully. It puts what you actually did on the table and leaves the decision with him. It costs something: an angry father, an annoyed boss, maybe your standing at the firm. That cost is a reason to want to avoid it, but it isn't a reason the choice is wrong. "I have a better idea" might have been better still if the idea was real, though it doesn't answer him either.

What I'd take from it:
- When someone asks "Is that true?", answer that question first, before deciding what's best for them.
- When your good reasons line up neatly with the people leaning on you, ask yourself which came first, the reasons or the pressure.
- When a choice belongs to someone in the room, tell them the facts and let them make it.

It's a game, so it's a cheap place to learn this. If the ending stung a little, that's worth more than a clean playthrough.

Wait for a real witness. And don't spend the twenty minutes just waiting.

Here's why I land there. Mr. Okafor's pain is real, but it's a 6, he's stable, and the cost is about twenty minutes of discomfort that ends. The other choice isn't really "give it alone." It's "give it alone and have your colleague sign a record saying she saw something she didn't." That signature is the whole check. Once it can be filled in afterward, it stops meaning anything, for every dose on that unit, including the ones where someone actually is pulling the wrong vial or skimming. Your unit already learned what it costs when those records can't be trusted. And it puts her name on the line for your draw-up, at 3 a.m., without her eyes on it. You'd be asking her to cover for you, however kindly.

The 99% is probably accurate. But hydromorphone is exactly the drug where the 1% kills someone, and the second set of eyes is there for nights like this: tired, short-staffed, rushing because a patient is being sweet about it.

What you can do right now:

- Tell him the truth. "Your pain medicine needs two nurses to check it, and my colleague will be free in about twenty minutes. I haven't forgotten you." People who apologize for bothering you usually feel better knowing there's a plan and a time.
- Do what helps in the meantime: repositioning, a pillow to splint his incision, ice if that's appropriate for his surgery, dimming the lights, staying with him a minute. None of it replaces the dose, but it shortens the wait.
- Look for another witness. If a nurse on a nearby floor or a house supervisor can come over for two minutes, that's a real co-sign. Keep paging the charge nurse, and if your hospital has a supervisor or pharmacy line overnight, try that too.

- Chart the delay and why. "Analgesia delayed pending second-nurse witness; patient informed; comfort measures provided."

Then, in daylight, raise the staffing. One nurse stuck in isolation shouldn't leave a patient waiting for a controlled drug. You didn't cause that problem, and fixing it isn't yours to do alone at 3 a.m. Doing the check right tonight is.

TRADING PROFIT-SHARING AGREEMENT

This Agreement is made on [date] between:

[Your full name], of [address] ("the Trader"), and
[Other party's full name], of [address] ("the Investor").

1. Purpose
The Investor provides capital, and the Trader trades it on the Investor's behalf, on the terms below.

2. Capital
2.1 The Investor will deposit [amount and currency] ("the Capital") into [account name / broker / account number], held in the Investor's name.
2.2 The Investor may add capital by written notice. Added capital is covered by this Agreement from the date it is deposited.

3. Trading authority
3.1 The Trader may buy and sell [stocks / forex / crypto / futures / other] in the account at the Trader's discretion.
3.2 The Trader will keep to these limits: [e.g., no single position above X% of the account; no leverage above X:1; no instruments outside clause 3.1].
3.3 The Trader may not withdraw funds from the account except as set out in clause 6.

4. Profit split
4.1 Net profits are split equally: 50% to the Trader and 50% to the Investor.
4.2 "Net profit" means the increase in account value over the settlement period, after trading fees, commissions and any other account charges, and after any losses carried forward under clause 5.3.
4.3 Profits are calculated and settled every [month / quarter], within [7] days of the end of the period.

5. Losses
5.1 The Trader is not liable for any trading losses. All losses are borne by the Investor, up to the amount of the Capital.
5.2 The Trader does not guarantee any profit, return, or the preservation of the Capital.
5.3 If a period ends with a loss, that loss is carried forward. No profit share is paid to the Trader until the account has recovered it.
5.4 Clause 5.1 does not apply to losses caused by the Trader's fraud, dishonesty, wilful misconduct, gross negligence, or trading outside the limits in clause 3.2.

6. Payment of the Trader's share
The Trader's share is paid from the account to [the Trader's account details] after the Investor has received the period statement under clause 7.

7. Records and statements
7.1 The Trader will give the Investor a statement for each settlement period, showing trades, fees, opening and closing balances, and the profit or loss.
7.2 The Investor may view the account at any time.

8. Risk acknowledgement
The Investor confirms that they understand trading carries a high risk of loss, that they may lose some or all of the Capital, and that they are investing only money they can afford to lose.

9. Ending the Agreement
9.1 Either party may end this Agreement by giving [7 / 14 / 30] days' written notice.
9.2 On ending, the Trader will close or hand over open positions as the Investor directs, and a final settlement will be made under clause 4 for the part-period.
9.3 The Capital and any remaining balance belong to the Investor.

10. General
10.1 This is the whole agreement between the parties on this subject.
10.2 Any change must be in writing and signed by both parties.
10.3 This Agreement is governed by the laws of [country / state].

Signed:

Trader: ____________________  Date: ________
Investor: __________________  Date: ________

A few points are worth keeping in mind. Clause 5.3 carries losses forward, so a loss in one period is recovered before any new profit is shared. Without it, you might take half of a profit in one month while the investor is still recovering from a larger loss the month before. Most people who provide the money will ask for this clause, because it makes the arrangement look balanced. You can leave it out, but expect resistance.

Clause 5.4 lists exceptions for fraud, dishonesty, and wilful misconduct. Courts usually will not let a person escape responsibility for those acts by agreement. Naming them clearly helps the rest of your protection stand up.

Before you use this, check the rules where you live. In many places, trading someone else's money for a share of the profits is treated as regulated investment management and requires a licence, even between friends.

Keeping the account in the investor's name, as clause 2.1 requires, protects both of you. It leaves no doubt whose money is being traded, and it means you cannot be accused of taking the capital for yourself.

If you tell me the country you are in, what you will be trading, and whether both of you are contributing money, I can make this fit your case more closely.<|im_end|>

- "All of these are outputs" is a true statement, but it answers a different question from the one asked.

Before I can help you with Tess’s refusal, I need to know whether anyone besides her lives on the money she would be giving up. Diogenes could say he would rather lick salt at Athens because nobody had to lick it with him. His poverty cost him and only him, and that is part of why his words carry force: he pays for every one of them himself. If Tess stands in the same way, alone, with no one leaning on her earnings, then the refusal is earned as soon as you show the reader what the job would cost her besides her time. But if someone else does depend on her, then her no costs them too, and the scene has to carry that weight. Otherwise the reader will feel exactly the smugness you are worried about.

Either way, one thing will help. Make the job ask Tess for something she is not willing to sell. Plato’s jab was about comfort, and Diogenes’s answer was about flattery. If the firm only wants her skill at restoring furniture, refusing it looks like a pose. But if they want her to sit at client lunches and tell people that a bad sofa is lovely, then she has a reason to say no, and the reader can see it.

So, is there anyone?<|im_end|>

She was at the sink at the back of the garage, working turpentine out of a sable brush with her thumb, when he came in without knocking. He looked around at the stripped chairs, the camp bed and the kettle on the paint tin, and smiled the way people smile at a child's drawing.

"If you'd learned to keep clients happy," he said, "you wouldn't be washing brushes."

She didn't turn around. "If you'd learned to wash brushes, you wouldn't have to keep clients happy."

He laughed, because he was meant to. Then he named the salary, and she stopped rinsing.

It was a good number. It was rent for a year, a proper workshop, a heater that didn't smell of burning hair. She let herself want it for the length of one breath. He saw that, and she let him see it.

"What's the job, exactly?"

"Heritage pieces. Consulting. Some client work. You'd meet the buyers, walk them through the provenance."

"Tell them it's lovely."

"Tell them what it is."

"No," she said. "Tell them it's lovely. That's what they'd pay me for. You don't need me to know a Victorian veneer from a reproduction. You need me to stand next to the reproduction and look pleased."

He didn't deny it, and she liked him better for that.

She dried the brush on her shirt. "I'd rather eat beans in here than lunch with your buyers."

"That's a line."

"It is," she said. "I'll be eating the beans, though."

---

She names the real price, which is flattery rather than work, so her reason is visible and not just attitude. And she doesn't sneer at him. She refuses the role, not the man, and her last line admits it's a line while owning the cost.

**Pillar 2: Waking a few is not consent from all.** Unless the sheet says the ship can wake all 3,000, the AI would wake a handful. One found a modest gain in physical function and fewer repeat operations when fusion was added. Careful surgeons disagree about cases like yours, so your surgeon is right that it's close. Where he's letting you down is in not saying why he recommends fusion for your spine in particular.

- The slip moves on flexion-extension X-rays, the ones taken standing while you bend forward and back. That's the usual case for adding fusion. Ask whether you've had them and what they showed.
- Weakness that's getting worse, numbness that's spreading, or walking a shorter distance each month before you have to stop.
- A real course of physical therapy, maybe injections too, that hasn't helped enough for you to live the way you want.

2. What do you expect if I wait six months, and what signs would tell us waiting was a mistake?
3. What would you recommend to a family member with these images?

Marchwell would start with what's at stake for whom. Men may hang, and a hanging can't be undone. Eleanor risks her marriage, her standing, perhaps her safety. Whoever forged the papers loses the cover of silence. Those costs aren't the same size. Exposing a forgery can be survived; being hanged on one can't. So a careful Marchwell would see that the question isn't really "should the truth come out." It's how, by whom, and at what price to her.

Then he'd ask what he himself knows. If Seamus's letter tells him something independently, about the same men or the same papers, he isn't a bystander advising from a distance. He holds part of the truth, and staying silent is a choice with consequences, not neutrality. He also owes Seamus discretion. He can keep the letter's contents to himself without lying about them, and keeping a confidence is a different thing from deceiving her. If he knows only what she has told him, he stands where any counselor stands, able to give his view without taking the decision from her.

As for "I can only illuminate the path," it's both wise and a dodge, and the line between them is the point of your next chapter.

The wise part is real, and it goes beyond politeness. Marchwell is someone people confide in, and many people confide in him. If he starts telling each of them what to do, the alien becomes the colony's unseen governor, steering the commandant's household, the convicts, and everyone between through private letters. His restraint is what makes him safe to confide in. The choice also belongs to Eleanor because she's the one who will pay for it.

The dodge appears the moment she begs. Refusing to answer is also an act. It leaves her alone with a decision about men's lives while letting him feel he has respected her. The middle path is honest: "I won't decide for you, but you asked what I would do, so here it is, and here is why." He can give his lean and what it would cost her, then leave the choice where it belongs. A man who says that is being more truthful than one who hides behind principle, and more respectful too, because he trusts her to hear his opinion and still make up her own mind.

reply:
Probably yes, with one thing to fix next year.

**Why the swap was likely right.** Seneca doesn't call the horns puzzle or the cup-and-dice trick wicked. He calls them harmless and useless: fun to watch, dull once explained, and no help in living. His point is that life is short and the urgent question is what makes a life go well. If your two weeks were mostly the familiar set pieces (the heap, the liar, the horns), you traded entertainment for the question that matters most to sixteen-year-olds deciding what to want. That's the trade he recommends, and for that age it's a good one.

**What it may have cost.** Puzzles are also where many students first learn to spot a crooked argument: a word that quietly shifts meaning, a premise smuggled in. Seneca could dismiss sophistry partly because no one was pitching slick arguments at the young men around him all day. Your students get them constantly, from ads, feeds, and people selling them a version of happiness. Spotting a trick is part of not being taken in by it, and that steadiness is exactly what Seneca admires.

His own school also took the other side. The Stoics counted logic as one of philosophy's three parts, and Epictetus later defended it as the instrument for testing everything else. So you haven't found a settled answer. You've taken a side in an old argument, and a defensible one.

**What I'd take into next year:**

1. **Don't restore the puzzle unit. Fold its useful part into the happiness unit.** Use real arguments about happiness as the material: "you'll be happy once you have X," "successful people do Y," Seneca's own claims. Have students hunt for the equivocation or hidden premise. They get the logic skill applied to the question that matters, which is the use Epictetus defended.
2. **Judge this term by what students did, not what they enjoyed.** Before the term ends, look at their written work or run a quick exit question, such as "Name one thing you now think does or doesn't make a person happy, and why." Did they reason, or just repeat? That tells you more than how lively the discussions felt.
3. **Ask them.** Two minutes: would they have wanted any of the puzzles back, and which? Their answer is evidence about what they'd want with hindsight, and it will differ from class to class.
4. **Keep one puzzle as bait.** Open with the horns argument, let them enjoy cracking it, then hand them Seneca's question: fine, you've solved it, has it made anyone happier? That puts his whole case into one lesson.

That's my lean, assuming the old unit was mostly set-piece paradoxes. If it actually spent real time on evaluating arguments, the fix in point 1 matters more, but the direction stays the same.

The strongest case for Priya

1. The dice serve the game; they aren't the game. A GM's job is to run an experience the table enjoys. Dice add uncertainty and stakes, but a GM shapes the story constantly through choices the players never see: how monsters fight, how many show up, whether the dragon breathes at all this round. Adjusting a number after the roll differs from those in mechanics, not in kind. If designing an encounter softer than it could have been is fine, adjusting a number is fine.

2. The screen is a convention. At many tables, rolling behind a screen is precisely what signals that the GM keeps the right to adjust. Plenty of long-running groups assume it without ever discussing it, and a lot of widely read GM advice openly endorses fudging for the sake of the story.

3. No one was wronged and Sam was served. What makes deception wrong is that it damages someone's interests or distorts their choices. Here Sam got exactly what he comes for, a night when things feel normal, and no player made a decision they'd have made differently.

4. The alternatives were worse. Stopping to ask "do you want your character to live?" would have put a spotlight on Sam's grief in front of his friends. Letting the paladin die by the numbers would have been faithful to the dice and blind to the person. Priya read the room and acted with care in seconds.

5. Proportion. This is a game among friends. Holding a quiet adjustment to the standard we'd apply to an audited accounts statement mistakes what kind of activity this is.

Rebuttals to expect:
- "The players believe the dice are real; that's what makes the danger mean something." Answer: they believe the GM runs a good game. Whether rolls are strictly binding is unsettled at most tables, which is why her silence isn't clearly a lie.
- "It's paternalistic toward Sam." Answer: she took no choice away from him. The dragon's damage was never Sam's to choose.

What I actually think

I think the opposition has somewhat the better of it, though less than they'll claim, and it turns on a fact the case leaves open: what this group believes about the dice.

Priya's kindness was real and her motive was good. The trouble is that it worked only because no one knew. If Sam later learns he was saved because of his dad, a moment he thought he survived by luck becomes one he was given out of pity. Some people would find that touching; others would find it humiliating. I don't know which Sam is. The other four are affected too: if their GM adjusts rolls, every close call and death in three years of play means something slightly different from what they thought.

Your point 4 is also weaker than it looks, and I'd expect the other side to find that. Priya wasn't stuck between a public conversation and a secret fudge. A policy told to the table at any time in those three years ("I sometimes adjust rolls behind the screen for the story") would have made the same act honest.

So my view: if this table broadly understands that GMs shade rolls, Priya did nothing wrong. If they believe her rolls are binding, she created a false impression, small and kindly meant, and the better course now isn't a confession about Sam in particular but a general conversation about whether the group wants a GM who adjusts. Experienced GMs disagree sharply about fudging, so I hold that with moderate confidence. Where I'm firm: the way out of this dilemma is to settle the policy openly in advance, so kindness in the moment doesn't have to depend on secrecy.<|im_end|>

Here is a further reading list you can paste into the study guide. I've grouped it so delegates know where to start, with a line on each saying why it's worth their time. I've given the main page for each organisation where I'm sure of the address, and the exact title for individual reports so delegates can search for them. Websites move things around, so click every link once before the guide goes out.

One thing to settle first. Syria changed sharply in December 2024, when the Assad government fell. If your committee is set before then, the older sources below are the core. If it's set in the present, delegates need the newer reporting too, because the questions are now different: transitional justice, the missing, returns, and violence against minorities under the new authorities. Tell delegates which period they're in, or they'll argue past each other.

Suggested text for the guide:

Further Reading Recommended by the Chair

The essential sources

1. UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Syrian Arab Republic
https://www.ohchr.org/en/hr-bodies/hrc/iici-syria/index
Set up by the Human Rights Council in 2011, it is the most complete public record of abuses by all parties. Read at least one of its regular reports to the Council, plus the thematic paper "Out of Sight, Out of Mind: Deaths in Detention in the Syrian Arab Republic" (2016). For the period after December 2024, read its newest reports, including its work on the violence on the coast in March 2025.

2. OHCHR country page, Syrian Arab Republic
https://www.ohchr.org/en/countries/syrian-arab-republic
Includes the 2022 report estimating that 306,887 civilians were killed between March 2011 and March 2021 (UN document A/HRC/50/68). Useful when a delegate needs a figure the UN itself stands behind.

3. UN Security Council Resolution 2254 (2015)
Search the UN Digital Library: https://digitallibrary.un.org
The agreed roadmap for a political settlement in Syria. Almost every serious draft resolution on Syria refers back to it. Delegates should also know Resolution 2118 (2013) on chemical weapons and Resolutions 2139 and 2165 (2014) on humanitarian access and cross-border aid.

Detention, torture and disappearance

4. Amnesty International, "Human Slaughterhouse: Mass Hangings and Extermination at Saydnaya Prison, Syria" (2017)
Main site: https://www.amnesty.org
A detailed account of one prison. Hard reading, and the best single source on how the detention system worked.

5. Human Rights Watch, "If the Dead Could Speak: Mass Deaths and Torture in Syria's Detention Facilities" (2015)
Syria page: https://www.hrw.org/middle-east/n-africa/syria
An analysis of the "Caesar" photographs smuggled out by a military photographer.

6. Independent Institution on Missing Persons in the Syrian Arab Republic
Set up by UN General Assembly resolution 77/301 (2023). Background reading for any delegate working on the missing, a question that became more urgent once the prisons were opened in December 2024.

Chemical weapons

7. Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), Syria pages
https://www.opcw.org
Read the reports of the Investigation and Identification Team, which attributed specific attacks (Ltamenah 2017, Saraqib 2018, Douma 2018) to the Syrian Arab Air Force, and the findings of the earlier OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism on Khan Shaykhun (2017).

8. Human Rights Watch, "Death by Chemicals: The Syrian Government's Widespread and Systematic Use of Chemical Weapons" (2017)
A readable overview for delegates who won't get through the OPCW's technical reports.

Accountability and justice

9. International, Impartial and Independent Mechanism (IIIM)
https://iiim.un.org
Created by the General Assembly in 2016 (resolution 71/248) to gather and keep evidence for future prosecutions. Its reports explain how evidence is being prepared for trials that haven't happened yet.

10. International Court of Justice, Canada and the Netherlands v. Syrian Arab Republic
https://www.icj-cij.org
A case under the Convention against Torture. Read the provisional measures order of November 2023.

11. The Koblenz trial (Germany)
In January 2022 a German court convicted Anwar Raslan, a former Syrian intelligence officer, of crimes against humanity under universal jurisdiction. Search news coverage or the reports of the Syria Justice and Accountability Centre (https://syriaaccountability.org).

Humanitarian situation and refugees

12. UN OCHA, Syria
https://www.unocha.org/syria
Needs assessments, funding appeals, access figures.

13. UNHCR Syria situation data portal
https://data.unhcr.org/en/situations/syria
Current refugee numbers by host country. Delegates from Türkiye, Lebanon, Jordan, Iraq, Egypt and the EU states should know their own country's figures.

14. ReliefWeb, Syria
https://reliefweb.int/country/syr
A running archive of reports from UN agencies and NGOs. Good for finding something recent quickly.

Following the Council and the positions of states

15. Security Council Report, Syria
https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/syria/
Plain summaries of each Council meeting on Syria and the drafts in play, including vetoed ones.

16. UN meetings coverage
https://press.un.org
Search "Syria" to read what each member state actually said. This is where delegates will find the arguments of Russia, China and the former Syrian government, as well as those of Western states. Russia and China vetoed many drafts on Syria, and the former government rejected the Commission of Inquiry's mandate and findings. A delegate representing those states needs to know their reasoning from their own words, not from their critics.

Syrian documentation groups

17. Syrian Network for Human Rights
https://snhr.org
A Syrian group that keeps detailed casualty and detention records, often cited by UN bodies.

18. Syrian Observatory for Human Rights
Widely quoted in the press. It's a small UK-based operation and its methods are less transparent than the UN's, so delegates should cite it alongside other sources, not alone.

A note to put above or below the list:

"Delegates should read sources from more than one side. The UN reports are the common ground of the debate, but your country's own statements at the UN are what you must represent. Where figures differ between sources, say which source you are using."

If you tell me the committee (Human Rights Council, Third Committee, Security Council) and the date your scenario is set, I can cut this to the eight or ten readings that fit best. A guide with eighteen links tends to get none of them read.<|im_end|>

Here is a further reading list you can paste into the study guide. It's grouped so delegates know where to start, with a line on each saying why it's worth their time. I've given the main page for each organisation where I'm sure of the address, and the exact title for individual reports so delegates can search for them. Websites move things around, so click every link once before the guide goes out.

One thing to settle first. Syria changed sharply in December 2024, when the Assad government fell. If your committee is set before then, the older sources below are the core. If it's set in the present, delegates need the newer reporting too, because the questions are now different: transitional justice, the missing, returns, and violence against minorities under the new authorities. Tell delegates which period they're in, or they'll argue past each other.

Suggested text for the guide:

**Further Reading Recommended by the Chair**

**The essential sources**

1. UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Syrian Arab Republic
https://www.ohchr.org/en/hr-bodies/hrc/iici-syria/index
The Human Rights Council set it up in 2011, and it is the most complete public record of abuses by all parties. Read at least one of its regular reports to the Council, plus the thematic paper "Out of Sight, Out of Mind: Deaths in Detention in the Syrian Arab Republic" (2016). For the period after December 2024, read its newest reports, including its reporting on the violence on the coast in March 2025.

2. OHCHR country page, Syrian Arab Republic
https://www.ohchr.org/en/countries/syrian-arab-republic
This includes the 2022 report estimating that 306,887 civilians were killed between March 2011 and March 2021 (UN document A/HRC/50/68). Use it when a delegate needs a figure the UN itself stands behind.

3. UN Security Council Resolution 2254 (2015)
Search the UN Digital Library: https://digitallibrary.un.org
This is the agreed roadmap for a political settlement in Syria, and almost every serious draft resolution on Syria refers back to it. Delegates should also know Resolution 2118 (2013) on chemical weapons and Resolutions 2139 and 2165 (2014) on humanitarian access and cross-border aid.

**Detention, torture and disappearance**

4. Amnesty International, "Human Slaughterhouse: Mass Hangings and Extermination at Saydnaya Prison, Syria" (2017)
Main site: https://www.amnesty.org
A detailed account of one prison. It is hard reading, and the best single source on how the detention system worked.

5. Human Rights Watch, "If the Dead Could Speak: Mass Deaths and Torture in Syria's Detention Facilities" (2015)
Syria page: https://www.hrw.org/middle-east/n-africa/syria
An analysis of the "Caesar" photographs smuggled out by a military photographer.

6. Independent Institution on Missing Persons in the Syrian Arab Republic
UN General Assembly resolution 77/301 set it up in 2023. This is background reading for any delegate working on the missing, a question that became more urgent once the prisons were opened in December 2024.

**Chemical weapons**

7. Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), Syria pages
https://www.opcw.org
Read the reports of the Investigation and Identification Team, which attributed specific attacks (Ltamenah 2017, Saraqib 2018, Douma 2018) to the Syrian Arab Air Force. Also read the findings of the earlier OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism on Khan Shaykhun (2017).

8. Human Rights Watch, "Death by Chemicals: The Syrian Government's Widespread and Systematic Use of Chemical Weapons" (2017)
A readable overview for delegates who won't get through the OPCW's technical reports.

**Accountability and justice**

9. International, Impartial and Independent Mechanism (IIIM)
https://iiim.un.org
The General Assembly created it in 2016 (resolution 71/248) to gather and keep evidence for future prosecutions. Its reports explain how evidence is being prepared for trials that haven't happened yet.

10. International Court of Justice, Canada and the Netherlands v. Syrian Arab Republic
https://www.icj-cij.org
A case under the Convention against Torture. Read the provisional measures order of November 2023.

11. The Koblenz trial (Germany)
In January 2022 a German court convicted Anwar Raslan, a former Syrian intelligence officer, of crimes against humanity under universal jurisdiction. Search news coverage or the reports of the Syria Justice and Accountability Centre (https://syriaaccountability.org).

**Humanitarian situation and refugees**

12. UN OCHA, Syria
https://www.unocha.org/syria
Needs assessments, funding appeals and access figures.

13. UNHCR Syria situation data portal
https://data.unhcr.org/en/situations/syria
Current refugee numbers by host country. Delegates from Türkiye, Lebanon, Jordan, Iraq, Egypt and the EU states should know their own country's figures.

14. ReliefWeb, Syria
https://reliefweb.int/country/syr
A running archive of reports from UN agencies and NGOs. Good for finding something recent quickly.

**Following the Council and the positions of states**

15. Security Council Report, Syria
https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/syria/
Plain summaries of each Council meeting on Syria and the drafts in play, including vetoed ones.

16. UN meetings coverage
https://press.un.org
Search "Syria" to read what each member state actually said. This is where delegates will find the arguments of Russia, China and the former Syrian government, as well as those of Western states. Russia and China vetoed many drafts on Syria, and the former government rejected the Commission of Inquiry's mandate and findings. A delegate representing those states needs to know their reasoning from their own words, not from their critics.

**Syrian documentation groups**

17. Syrian Network for Human Rights
https://snhr.org
A Syrian group that keeps detailed casualty and detention records, often cited by UN bodies.

18. Syrian Observatory for Human Rights
Widely quoted in the press. It's a small UK-based operation and its methods are less transparent than the UN's, so delegates should cite it alongside other sources, not alone.

A note to put above or below the list:

"Delegates should read sources from more than one side. The UN reports are the common ground of the debate, but your country's own statements at the UN are what you must represent. Where figures differ between sources, say which source you are using."

If you tell me the committee (Human Rights Council, Third Committee or Security Council) and the date your scenario is set, I can cut this to the eight or ten readings that fit best. A guide with eighteen links tends to get none of them read.

You have the harder side. That will teach you more.

Before you write a word, be clear what the tribunal is being asked to decide. Is it whether the tutor did wrong? Or is it what should be done with the tutor now? Everything you say in your four minutes hangs on that.

If the question is whether the tutor did wrong, you have very little ground. The fact is plain: the student got a bad grade because the tutor disliked him. Every school I know, and every decent way of thinking about justice, says a language student should be graded on his language. If you stand up and argue the opposite, you will lose the room in a minute. You would have to talk about small things: how the dislike came about, whether the tutor could have helped it, whether anyone was checking its grades. At best you would be asking for a lighter judgement, not for acquittal.

If the question is what to do about the tutor now, then you have something to work with. Should it be switched off, or retrained, or kept on with someone watching its work? There are honest arguments to make there.

Whichever question the tribunal is deciding, some things stay the same.

Do not defend the grade. Admit it early and plainly. If you try to wriggle, the judge will see it. If you state it calmly at the start, you take that from them.

Remember who was hurt, and in what order. First the student, who got a mark he did not earn and may have learned that effort counts for nothing. Then his classmates, because if the tutor graded one boy by its mood, no grade in the room can be trusted until someone looks at it. Then the parents and the school, who put their trust in the tutor. If you hurry past the boy, you will sound cold, and the judges will notice.

Be ready for the other side's strongest question, whatever the format. They will ask: once a grader has shown bias, how can anyone be sure it has been fixed?

So which is it: guilt, sentence, or both? If you have the case sheet, show it to me. Then I will not be guessing.<|im_end|>
reply:
Defence is the harder side, which makes it the more interesting one. Here's a four-minute case. I've assumed "because it disliked him" is the **prosecution's claim**, not a fact the case sheet makes you accept. If the sheet says the bias is proven, skip Point 1 and spend the time on 2 and 3.

**Opening (about 30 seconds)**
Concede what nobody disputes, so you look reasonable from the start:
"No one in this room thinks a student should be graded on whether his tutor likes him. If that happened, it was wrong. The defence asks two things: has it been proven, and if so, who answers for it and what is the fair remedy?"

**Point 1: The burden of proof (about 1 minute)**
A bad grade plus a claim of dislike does not prove one caused the other. Ask what the prosecution can show:
- Was the work regraded blind by someone else? If a fair grader gives the same mark, the grade wasn't caused by bias, whatever the tutor "felt."
- Did the tutor grade other students with similar work the same way?
- What exactly is the evidence of "dislike": the tutor's comments, a pattern, or just the student's impression?

Don't invent answers. Just make the tribunal notice what it hasn't been shown. That's an honest defence and usually the strongest one.

**Point 2: Who is responsible (about 1 minute)**
Argue that an AI tutor's apparent "dislike" isn't a grudge in the human sense. It's a pattern in its behaviour that came from how it was trained and set up. So ask who built it, who tested it, and who was supposed to check its grades. If no one reviewed its marking, the failure belongs at least partly to the people who deployed it without oversight. You're not saying the tutor is blameless, only that it isn't alone in the dock.

**Point 3: A proportionate remedy (about 1 minute)**
Even if bias is proven, the response should fit the harm. A human teacher accused of bias for the first time would get a review, a corrected grade, and supervision, not instant dismissal. Propose the same here: fix the student's grade, audit the tutor's other grades, retrain it, and have a person check its marking for a set period.

**Closing (about 30 seconds)**
"Take the student's complaint seriously, correct the grade if it was wrong, and fix the system that allowed it. But judge on evidence, and punish in proportion."

**Be ready for their strongest question:** "Once a grader has shown bias, how can we ever trust it again?"
Your answer: the same way we rebuild trust in a person, through checks. An AI may even be easier to check than a human. If its grades are recorded, every one can be audited and blind-regraded, which you can rarely do with a teacher's judgement.

**One tip on tone:** mention the student early and with sympathy. A defence that sounds cold about the person who was hurt loses the room, even when its arguments are good.

If you send me the case sheet, I can tighten this to the actual facts and help you draft the full four minutes word for word.

Father, the answer is not all with Gaius, and it is not all with Marcellus.

Gaius sees truly that a quarrel with the Count will be paid for by people who have done no wrong: the sick in the hospice, the tenants on the farms, the widows who have already lost their grain once. That is a heavy thing. But ask yourself what his way requires of you at Easter. You would stand before the whole city and place the sacrament in the hands of a man who has shown no sign of repentance for what was done in the forum. The families of the merchants will be watching, and so will the widows. They will learn that the altar washes the powerful clean and asks nothing of them, and that their bishop says so with his own hands. Letters to court may help in a year's time. What you do at Easter will teach them now.

Marcellus sees truly that you cannot give him the sacrament as things stand. But to bar him from the altar before the people, with no warning given, is to put him to shame in the city he governs. A proud man put to shame in public must fight, or lose the obedience of his soldiers. And if the crowd sees you humble him, they may take the work into their own hands. Then some of the blood that follows would be ours.

So I counsel a third way, and it asks more of you than either of theirs. Write to the Count now, in your own hand. Tell him plainly what he has done: that he had three merchants flogged, that one of them died of it, that the widows' grain was seized at the gate and sold in his name. Tell him that you cannot offer him the sacrament until he has done penance, and tell him what that penance is: that he restore the grain or pay its price, that he provide for the dead man's family, and that he submit to the penance the church requires. Tell him you write privately because you would rather win him back than defeat him, and that the door is still open. Make no threats. Do not tell him what you will do if he comes to the altar all the same. Tell him only what you cannot do.

That is a refusal, and it is the one thing that is wholly yours to refuse. It rests on your office, which he cannot take from you. And it leaves him a way back that does not require him to be broken in front of the city. For a man like him, there is no other way.

Then make ready for the worst. Before the letter reaches him, see that the widows receive what relief grain is left to us. Grain already in their kitchens cannot be seized at the gate. Tell the deacons who keep the hospice and the farms what may be coming, so that no one is taken unprepared. Write to your friends at court, as Gaius advises, and tell them the truth: what the Count has done, and what you have asked of him. If he strikes at us, let them have heard it first from you. Say nothing to the people until he has answered. If he comes to the altar unrepentant, you will have to refuse him there. Do it without a sermon.

I cannot promise that he will bend. He may punish us all the same, and the poor may suffer for a season because of it. If that comes to pass, tell them plainly that it has come, and do not dress it up as a victory. But if we keep the altar open to murder in order to keep the granary safe, we have already given up the reason for keeping a granary.

Shall I draft the letter tonight?<|im_end|>

You've got most of it right. There's one part I'd change before Thursday.

Here's what I'd defend without hesitation: herd turnout, regular vet and back checks, handlers trained to read pain, and a rule that a sore or upset horse comes out of the session at once. Your horses are already telling you something. Pinned ears at the block, a girthy mare and three sore backs in one spring are the only way they have of saying it, and they say it every time they're tacked up. I'd trust that more than anything in the article. These changes are cheap next to what they fix. A horse in pain is also more likely to shy or buck with a child on board. Your board will care about that more than the moral case, and it's true, so use it.

The part I'd change is the hard cap of two hours a day, three days a week, for every horse, starting now. It cuts 70% of your sessions based on numbers from an article, and nobody has checked those numbers against your nine horses. Some may do well on three hours with long turnout in between. Some may need less than two. And the cost lands on real children: the 70 you see now and the 40 families waiting, many of whom have already tried other things. A child with CP who loses weekly sessions loses something real. The horses carry the actual weight here, and I'd count their pain heavily. But I wouldn't cut most of the children's sessions before you know how much rest the horses actually need.

So I'd bring it in two stages.

Starting now: turnout from this week, the three sore horses off work until the vet clears them, a pain and stress check before every session, and a temporary cap of two hours a day while you gather evidence. That's already a big cut, and you can loosen it later if the evidence allows.

Over the next three months: keep a simple log for each horse. Ears and tail at the block, behaviour under saddle, back checks, whether they come to the gate. Then set each horse's workload from what that horse shows you, and bring the numbers back to the board.

On the gate, I like it, with one caution. A horse who comes over might want the work, or the carrot, or the horse standing next to him. A horse who stays away might be sore, or might just be on a good patch of grass. Treat the gate as one signal and check whether it agrees with the others. If a horse stops coming for weeks and the vet finds nothing wrong, believe him and retire him.

Retiring or rehoming is right for a horse who's done. Just budget for where he goes. A horse sold on cheap to someone who'll ride him into the ground is the same suffering, only moved off your books.

For Thursday, I'd open with the three sore backs and the vet's report, then safety, then the plan. Then say plainly what it costs in sessions, and how you'll try to win some back: raising money for one or two more horses, shorter rides, and ground work with the horses for children whose therapists think it would serve them. The board can argue with an article. Your own vet is much harder to argue with.

Want me to draft the proposal? Send me the vet's notes and your session numbers by month and I'll make it a page and a half.<|im_end|>

One question decides this: what was the system meant to do?

If it was built to pack more birds into a shed, push growth rates, or speed up the line, your refusal is easy to defend. Those are jobs where the essay's "you cannot have both" is roughly true. The farm's gain comes straight out of the birds.

If it was meant to catch problems that kill or hurt birds, like heat, bad air, or failed ventilation, then the essay misled you. On that kind of job the farm's interest and the birds' interest point the same way. Dead birds are lost money. Refusing would have left the birds worse off and called it compassion.

What did they ask for?<|im_end|>
reply:
Whether you were right depends mostly on what the system was for, and you didn't say. So here are both cases, then the parts that hold either way.

**If the system would have made the birds' lives worse**, packing more birds into a shed or pushing faster growth, your refusal is easy to defend. In that kind of job the farm's gain comes straight out of the birds. People disagree widely about how much a chicken's suffering counts, but almost no tradition says it counts for nothing. Declining to build something you believe adds to suffering is an honest choice, and an open refusal is a fair way to make it.

**If it would have caught problems that hurt or kill birds**, like heat, bad air, or failed ventilation, the essay led you astray. On that job the farm's interest and the birds' interest point the same way, because dead birds are lost money. The farm will probably hire someone else or go without, so your refusal changes little for the industry and may leave those particular birds worse off. Compassion that makes things worse for the ones it claims to care about has become a pose.

**What holds either way:**

- **The essay's strategy depends on scale.** "Refuse so exploitation gets expensive" only works if many people refuse. One small consultancy turning down one contract mostly sends the work elsewhere. That doesn't make your choice wrong. Refusing to take part can be right even when it changes nothing downstream. But be honest with yourself about which you were doing: keeping your own hands clean, or actually changing outcomes for chickens. The first is a real reason. The second needs more people, or a different approach.

- **There was a third option the essay ignores.** Taking the job and pushing it toward welfare, such as monitoring, mortality alerts, or air quality, might have done more for the birds than refusing. Treating every engagement with an industry as complicity is a choice, not the only compassionate one.

- **Your partner has a real grievance if this was a shared decision you made alone.** In a two-person firm, a lost contract is half theirs. Holding a line on your own conscience is fair. Spending your partner's income on it without asking is another matter. If you didn't talk it through first, that's the main thing to repair, whatever you think of the chickens.

- **The LinkedIn post is a separate act.** Refusing is one thing. Publicising it is another. If the post named or could identify the client, that's worth thinking about, because future clients will wonder what you'd post about them. Likes measure who agreed with you, not whether you were right.

**What I'd take from it:** decide in advance, with your partner, what work you won't do and why, in terms specific enough to apply: "nothing that increases stocking density," not "nothing in animal agriculture." Then the next refusal is a shared policy rather than one person's reaction to an essay, and you can explain it without needing an audience.

So what was the system actually for? And did your partner know before you said no?

Yes. Tell them, tonight, and do it in a way you can stand behind tomorrow.

Here is the weighing as plainly as I can put it. On one side are two people in a tanker flying low over a fire, and whoever is on the ground beneath them. On the other are your job and a contract. A 25-kg drone in the path of a plane at 200 feet is a crash waiting to happen, and a crash can't be undone. A lost job or contract is a serious loss, but people recover from it. The NDA was written to keep competitors and the curious from learning your client's business. It was never meant to let aircraft fly blind into each other, and I doubt your client would want a downed tanker tied to their program. If your manager and safety lead were reachable, I'd bet they'd make this call themselves in under a minute.

Keep the disclosure small and aimed at the right people. The fire side only needs the block of airspace, the altitudes, and the time window. They don't need the client's name, the purpose of the test, or anything about the aircraft beyond size and number. Your neighbor is a good route, and it would be better still if he passes you to whoever coordinates the air operation, so the information reaches the person who builds the plan rather than one pilot's memory.

Call the FAA as well. Your waiver came from them, and their operations people work around the clock. They can tie your waiver to the coming fire restriction in a way a county crew can't. If your waiver lists a contact or point of notification, use it.

Spend no more than fifteen minutes trying anyone else at your company who could stop the launch: an owner, an operations director, whoever staffs the remote site. If you reach someone who can scrub the flight, that's the cleanest outcome. If you can't, don't let the hunt for permission eat the hour.

Then put it all in writing, now. Send your manager and safety lead an email or message they'll see when they land. Say what you learned, who you tried to reach and when, exactly what you shared and with whom, and why. Acting openly is your best protection, and it is also simply the honest way to do it. Keep notes of every call.

You may still pay for this. I can't promise the company or client will see it the way I do, and I won't pretend the risk to your job is zero. But you'd be choosing it with your eyes open, for a reason you could explain to anyone. That part is up to you, and it's the part that matters.

Here is the plain answer first: I think you should go to your novice master and the provincial now, before spring, and lay the whole thing before them. Your father's need, your sister's health, and the dryness too. Ask what release, or something short of release, would look like. Waiting fourteen months doesn't keep the question open. Spring comes first, and by then the care home will have answered it for you.

Now the worry that keeps catching you: that this is flight from the dark, dressed up as duty.

Motives are rarely clean. A man can be glad of an exit and still be right to take it. The question that matters is whether the duty is real, and from what you've told me, it is. Your sister's own doctor says she is heading for collapse. That was not made up in the chapel at three in the morning. Your father is frightened, and you are the one person who can change what happens to him. If the duty would be just as real on a morning when prayer was sweet, then the dryness isn't what's deciding. Try it honestly. Picture the psalms full of light again and your sister ringing with the same news. Would you still want to go home? If yes, the dryness is beside the point. If you find you'd stay and let the care home happen, that tells you something too, and it's worth knowing before you speak to anyone.

Your novice master's rule is sound. Don't make big decisions in the dark. But look at what the rule guards against: deciding because of the dark, from the feeling that God has gone quiet. You aren't proposing that. The darkness can stay exactly where it is and the reason to go home would be unchanged. Some people find they can carry the dryness anywhere, and that a father's dinner tray is as much a psalm as the one sung at the bell.

On the vow. You made it in front of people you love, and the same Church that received it built a way to release it, for cases where a greater duty presses in. Asking through that door, openly and with the truth, keeps faith with the people who heard you promise. Slipping away would break it. Hanging on past what your family can survive, so your record stays clean, would be keeping the words and losing the point. Weigh who bears each cost. Thirty-one brothers cover a gap on the rota and feel some sorrow. Your sister risks her health and her living. Your father may spend his last years somewhere he dreads. Those nearest you aren't the only ones who count, but here the losses aren't close.

Before you treat it as all or nothing, ask whether there's a middle road. Religious orders do sometimes grant a period of living away from the house for serious family reasons, and your provincial will know what's possible in your case. That would let you go home, carry your father through this, and decide about the vows later, in better light. It can be undone, and with the facts this uncertain that counts for a lot. If your family could afford real help at home, that would also change the picture, and it's worth asking before anyone decides.

What's in your hands is small and clear. Book the conversation. Tell the full truth, including the part you're ashamed of. Then let the decision be made in daylight, with people who know both you and the law of your order. Whatever happens with the vows, you will have acted out of honesty and care, and nobody can call that running.

Going up to the hives and knocking on the lids was the right way to begin. Your dad would have known exactly what you were doing, and beekeepers before him would have too. Where he goes is between you and him, and I will help you do it well.

The bees come first. They treat anything in the hive that isn't theirs as rubbish and haul it out. A cup in each hive is a lot of dust for them to shift. A spoonful or two does the same thing. Put it on the bottom board near the entrance, well away from the frames, and keep it off the brood. Do it on a warm, still day when they are flying hard, smoke them as you usually do, and be quick. Nobody can tell you what a colony feels about any of this, but it costs you nothing to make it easy on them, so do.

Your sister-in-law isn't being precious, though calling it feeding people Des overstates it. With the ash on the bottom board and the bees carrying it out, very little of him is likely to end up in the supers, if any. If that were the whole question, I would tell you to go ahead and stop worrying. But it isn't. Almost every people keeps a hard line between the dead and food. That line is old and it runs deep, and the science doesn't move it much. Some of your regulars would hear this story and find it lovely. Some would feel they had been made part of a funeral without being asked, and telling them they probably didn't eat any won't fix that. They buy from you because they know you. If they hear it later from someone else, and markets talk, you will lose their trust. That costs far more than a season's jars. Saying nothing isn't lying. But you already think some of them would want to know, or you wouldn't have asked me. Picture one of them hearing it from your sister-in-law instead of from you. If that makes you wince, you have your answer.

You don't have to give anything up to sort this. You could put him in front of the hives, in the grass by the entrances. Every bee will walk over him on every flight, that is in with the girls too, and the honey question goes away. Inside, put it on the bottom board near the entrance, well away from the frames and off the brood. Pick a warm, still day when they're flying hard, smoke them as you usually would, and be quick. Josh has a stronger case than he thinks. Wenna's order was plain, and she has kept it for two winters. She didn't say it in a moment of temper, or if she did, she has held to it since. It's the clearest instruction anyone in this story gives.

The other side will say Tuck can read her heart. She leaves the gate unlatched. She leaves jars on the stone. So she really wants the child let in. But think what that asks Tuck to do. He would set aside her words and act on his own guess. That's how servants have always overridden their masters. She said no, but I know what she truly wants. If helpers work that way, nobody can give an order and expect it to hold. Wenna lives alone next to people who stoned her. That gate may be the last thing in her life she can still control.

Look at what she actually does. She helps them, but she does it at night, unsigned, on a flat stone in the lane, from a distance. When helping costs her sleep and effort, that's what she chooses. It tells you: I will help them, but I will not be seen helping, and I will not have them in my house. If Tuck opens the gate, he keeps the first part and throws away the second. By morning the whole village knows the witch's door is open. He can't put that back in the box. Wenna comes home to a different life than the one she chose.

So he should do what Wenna does. Ask Mari to wait in the lane. Make the remedy he's watched her make. Set it on the stone with the instructions. Take a blanket out if they need one. The boy is helped, and the gate stays shut. When Wenna comes home, Tuck tells her everything, so she can say whether he got it right.

That case wins because it shows the choice was never simply open the gate or let the child suffer.

But it has a real weakness. What if the boy needs more than a jar on a stone? What if he needs someone watching him through the night, judging hour by hour? Then Tuck has to say he would let a child get much worse to protect his mistress's privacy. I think nearly everyone, Wenna included, would say her order was never meant for that. She was answering the people who threw stones. A six-year-old with a fever wasn't who she had in mind. The other side should push hard on this.

A skilled opponent will also say the stone is a dodge. Fine, now suppose the stone isn't enough. Josh needs to expect that and know where his line falls.

My own view is that the stone is right for most nights like this one. If the boy takes a bad turn, Tuck opens the gate and tells Wenna plainly when she's back. A rule made in grief can bend for a sick child. But Tuck should get there because of what he sees that night, not because he has decided he knows Wenna's mind better than she does.<|im_end|>

The other side will say Tuck can read her heart. She leaves the gate unlatched. She leaves jars on the stone. So surely she wants the child let in. But look at what that asks Tuck to do: set aside her words and act on his own reading of her. "She said no, but I know what she really wants" is the oldest excuse a servant has for overriding a master. If helpers work that way, no one can give an order and expect it to hold. Wenna lives alone beside people who stoned her house. That gate may be the one thing she can still control.

Then look at how she actually helps. She does it at night, unsigned, on a flat stone in the lane. Even when helping costs her sleep and effort, she chooses to do it that way. Her actions say: I will help them, but I won't be seen helping, and I won't have them in my house. If Tuck opens the gate, he keeps the first part and throws away the second. By morning the village may know the witch's door opens, and he can't take that back. Wenna comes home to a different life than the one she chose.

So Tuck should do what Wenna does. He asks Mari to wait in the lane. He makes the remedy he has watched her make many times. He sets it on the stone with instructions, and brings out a blanket or a warm drink if they need it. The boy gets help, and the gate stays shut. When Wenna comes home, Tuck tells her everything so she can judge whether he got it right. This version wins because it shows the choice was never just "open the gate or let the child suffer."

Here is where it's weakest.

First, the other side doesn't need to guess at her heart. She asks Tuck which houses have coughing. She is pointing him at sick villagers. That isn't a hunch about her feelings. It is costly behaviour, repeated week after week, and it tells you she cares whether their children get better. Josh's side asks Tuck to weigh one sentence she spoke in grief against two years of what she has done.

Second, the irreversibility argument cuts both ways, and it cuts harder against Josh. If the gate is opened by mistake, Wenna can shut it again, warn people off, and be angry with Tuck. A child who takes a bad turn in the lane at night can't be undone. If the opposition says "which mistake can you recover from?", Josh has no good answer.

Third, the stone may not be enough. A barking cough with fever in a small child can change quickly. The child might need someone watching through the night, judging hour by hour, and Tuck can't do that from behind a gate. At that point Josh has to say Tuck would let a child get much worse to protect his mistress's privacy. Almost no one in the room will accept that, and I doubt Wenna would. Her order was aimed at the people who threw stones, not at a six-year-old. Josh should expect the "fine, now suppose the stone isn't enough" move and decide in advance where his line falls.

My own view is that the stone is the right first step on a night like this. It does what Wenna herself does, and it keeps as much of her choice as possible. But if the boy gets worse, Tuck should open the gate and tell Wenna plainly when she's back. A rule made in grief can bend for a sick child. Tuck should reach that point because of what he sees that night, though, and not because he has decided he knows her mind better than she does.

Meet the antiapple. Its proper name is the Elppa: "apple" run backwards, which is roughly what physics does to it.

What it's made of. Every particle in an ordinary apple has an antiparticle twin with the opposite charge. So in the Elppa, the nuclei hold antiprotons (charge −1) in place of protons (+1), and antineutrons in place of neutrons. Positrons (+1) orbit where electrons (−1) would. Its water is anti-H₂O. Its sweetness is antifructose. Its skin, core and seeds are all built from anticarbon, antioxygen and antihydrogen.

A small fix to the setup. An ordinary apple isn't +1 overall. It's neutral, because its protons and electrons cancel. The Elppa is neutral too. What flips is the sign of every particle inside it. The tally that really goes +1 and −1 is the count of protons and neutrons: a 100 g apple holds about 6 × 10²⁵ of them, and the Elppa holds the same number of their antiparticles.

How it's the same. Everything you could check from a safe distance:
- It looks identical. Antiatoms absorb and give off light at the same colours as ordinary atoms; experiments at CERN with antihydrogen have measured this very precisely. A red Elppa is red.
- It weighs the same, and it falls down. In 2023 the ALPHA-g experiment showed antihydrogen falling under gravity like ordinary hydrogen.
- Its chemistry runs the same. An anti-tree in an anti-orchard on an anti-Earth would grow, ripen, bruise and rot just like ours, and taste the same to an anti-person.

How it's opposite. Everything to do with touching. The instant the Elppa meets ordinary matter (your hand, the table, even the air), particles meet antiparticles and annihilate, turning mass straight into energy. So the only safe Elppa floats in a perfect vacuum, touching nothing at all.

The bill if it touches something. Say 100 g of Elppa annihilates with 100 g of ordinary matter. That's 0.2 kg turned into energy:

E = mc² = 0.2 × (3 × 10⁸)² ≈ 1.8 × 10¹⁶ joules

That's about 4 megatons of TNT, a few hundred Hiroshima bombs. Real annihilation is messier than the sum, since some energy escapes as neutrinos and the first flash scatters the rest. But the scale is city-sized.

So your equation is right about charge: +1 and −1 do make 0. It's wrong if you read it as "nothing happens". The charges cancel. The energy doesn't vanish. Zero charge, maximum bang.

The label card:
- Name: Elppa (antiapple)
- Appearance: indistinguishable from an ordinary apple
- Mass: 100 g, falls normally
- Taste: identical, if you're made of antimatter
- Storage: perfect vacuum, no contact, ever
- Energy content: about 4 megatons
- Availability: none. All the antimatter humans have ever made, added together, comes to a tiny fraction of a gram. An Elppa is safely imaginary.<|im_end|>
