Split her plan in two, because each half gets a different answer.

**The first half: recording the decree faithfully.** This is her office, and she knows it. A keeper who quietly altered or omitted the decree would be lying in the one place people rely on her for the truth. If every keeper edited the record to match her own judgement, no record could be trusted, including the old khipus Qori wants to save. So "I would not falsify, would not refuse" is the right starting point.

There's also a distinction your team can use against Chasca's line, "Then the record lies." A faithful record of the decree doesn't claim the decree is true. It records that the Sapa Inca decreed it. That is true. The record would only lie if it pretended the old traditions never existed. Qori's second record fixes exactly that gap.

**The second half: the parallel record.** The other side's strongest argument is that the Sapa Inca decides what the official record holds, so a keeper who builds her own collection beside it has set herself up as a rival authority, however modestly. Take that seriously.

My answer to it depends on what the decree actually commands, and the excerpt doesn't say.

- **If it only declares how things are to be from now on,** then preserving accounts of what people used to believe defies nothing. Rulers can command conduct. A keeper who also keeps the past accurately is doing what her office exists for.
- **If it orders the old accounts destroyed or forgotten,** the case is harder. Keeping them would then be disobedience, and the question becomes whether it is honest disobedience. There is an old model for this. The Roman senator Helvidius Priscus told the emperor Vespasian that he would attend the Senate and speak his mind, and that Vespasian could remove him if he chose. He refused openly, from inside his office, and accepted the cost. He didn't keep the title while working against it in secret.

That's why the phrase to press on is "not hidden, not defiant, simply preserved." It's harder than it sounds. If the record is truly not hidden, someone will find it and ask, and she will have to answer for it. If she tucks it away where no one looks, then it is hidden, whatever she calls it. She should also see that the risk isn't hers alone. Chasca is in it too.

You have brought me two hurts in the same bundle. One is yours, one is Tertia's, and they do not need the same remedy.

Take your own hurt first. Bassus said you are careful with money. If he was right, he gave you useful news about yourself. If he was wrong, the mistake is his and cannot follow you unless you pick it up. You laughed when the verses were read. That was the right thing to do. Socrates let a theatre crowd laugh at him and then asked the playwright whether he would like to put him in another comedy. If you drag Bassus into court over lentils and a toga, the verse will be repeated there, and then repeated again in every tavern, and you will be known as the wool dealer who could not laugh at himself. Your anger belongs to you. Bassus's harsh words do not.

You ask whether calm bearing of insult is only for philosophers. It is not. It is especially for a man who sells wool in a market. A merchant who sues over every jibe will spend his days with advocates and his nights with a grievance.

Tertia's hurt is different. Her good name is hers to guard, and no poet can steal it. But her trade is not the same thing. Two customers have left her, and a shop that buys and sells wool lives on its reputation for honest weights. That is a loss in bread and oil, not only in pride.

There is another difference too. This injury is Tertia's before it is yours. Your brother-in-law speaks of your honor through her, as though she were a wall someone had written on. She is the woman who keeps the scales. Ask her what she wants done about this. She may know better than either of you what would bring her customers back.

If she asks my opinion, I doubt that a lawsuit would help her. It would keep her name in the mouths of advocates for months, and every time the case is spoken of, the insult would be spoken of too. I would look for something plainer. The market officials test weights and measures. Ask them to test her scales openly, on a busy morning, where the women who buy from her can see. A public test answers the charge of a cheating thumb better than any speech in court.

Then go to Bassus yourself, calmly and in private. Tell him he may mock you as much as he likes, you may even have earned some of it, but that he said something false about a woman who was not his business, and it is costing her customers. Ask him to set it right at his next recital. Poets like to be thought generous. He may agree.

If he will not, and the customers keep leaving even after the scales have been proven honest, then an action to protect her trade is not foolish pride. Bring it if Tertia wants it, for what she has lost, and leave your own wounded feelings out of it.

Let go of the sting to yourself. Ask Tertia what she wants. Prove the scales. Speak to Bassus. Those things are all within your power, and none of them requires a praetor.<|im_end|>

Make the call. And tell him you're making it.

Look at what you actually promised. He asked you not to go behind his back, and he asked to be the one who decides "if it ever came to that." Both parts rested on something he couldn't guarantee: that when the time came, he'd be able to see it. That's the part Alzheimer's takes. He ran a red light and doesn't seem to think it matters. He hit a car and didn't notice. The man who made you swear was trusting his future self to know. His future self doesn't know, and that isn't his fault.

So you can't keep the promise the way he meant it, because the person it relied on is slipping. What you can keep is the spirit of it: no sneaking, no going around him, no pretending it wasn't you.

Here's how I'd go about it.

First, the nephew stops riding with him now. This doesn't need the doctor or the DMV, and it breaks nothing you swore. Talk to the boy's parent today. If your dad asks why, tell him the truth.

Then go to your dad, not behind him. Say something like: "Dad, you told me you wanted to be the one to decide. I'm asking you to decide now. Come with me to your neurologist and ask for a driving evaluation yourself." That gives him the dignity he asked for, the chance to choose. It's a test, too, not a verdict. If he passes, he keeps driving and you were wrong, which would be a fine outcome.

If he says no, tell him plainly: "Then I'm going to call them, and I wanted you to hear it from me first." Then call. Don't hide it, and don't let the clinic pretend it came from somewhere else. He may be furious. He may not speak to you for months. That's a real loss, and you'll be the one carrying it. But the trust between you lives on your honesty more than on your obedience, and he'll know you never lied to him.

As for the weighing, you've already done most of it. On one side is your father's pride, his freedom to come and go, and months of hurt between you. Those count, and they count a lot. Some of that freedom you can give back: your two days of driving, the shuttle for the rest. Friendships recover from months of silence more often than people expect. On the other side is a nine-year-old in the back seat, and children in a crosswalk three mornings a week. Once a child is hurt there, nothing brings it back. That includes your father. If he hit a child, it would wreck whatever time he has left, and I don't think the proud man who sat you down last spring would forgive anyone who saw it coming and stayed quiet.

You can't control how he takes it. What's up to you is doing it openly, gently, and without delay, and then still showing up on your two days to drive him, angry or not.

Use the honest version. I'll help you draft it, and there are ways to make it stronger than a 40% shot.

Your friend's wording isn't sort of true. "Intolerance" is true. "After an adequate trial" is the part Meridian's policy defines as 12 weeks, and your chart says 5. An appeal like this usually gets checked against your records, so the claim probably won't hold. And when it fails, it fails badly:

- They deny the appeal, and you've lost credibility for the next one.
- If they approve first and find out later, they can claw back payments. At $6,000 a month, that adds up fast.
- Your doctor signed it. She has her license and her relationship with every insurer she bills. You'd be asking her to put her name to something she knows the chart contradicts. Your worry about putting her in a bad spot is the right instinct.

The honest version costs you something real. If it's denied, you may face three months of risk to your hands, and I won't pretend that's small. But the false version doesn't actually buy you safety. It trades a known 40% for an unknown chance with a much worse downside, and it spends your doctor's trust to do it.

Here's how to improve the honest version's odds:

1. Ask your doctor to write her own letter of medical necessity, separate from yours. Her clinical judgment about erosion risk carries more weight than anything you can say. Ask her to state the 20 to 30% estimate in writing and say the damage is irreversible.
2. Request the expedited review, and say why. Expedited reviews are meant for cases where waiting could seriously harm your health or function. Permanent joint damage fits that.
3. Ask whether she'll request a peer-to-peer call with Meridian's reviewing physician if the first answer is no. Doctor-to-doctor conversations overturn denials more often than letters do.
4. Hedge while you wait, if she agrees. Ask her whether restarting methotrexate now makes sense, perhaps the injectable form or with anti-nausea support, which some people tolerate better. If the appeal fails, your 12-week clock is already running instead of starting from zero. If it succeeds, you stop. That's her call and yours, but it costs little to ask.
5. If they deny it, ask about external review. In many places you have a right to an independent reviewer outside the insurer.

Here's a draft of your part. Fill in the brackets, and let your doctor's letter carry the clinical detail.

---

To: Meridian [Appeals Department]
Re: Expedited appeal of denial for [biologic name]
Member: [Your name], ID [number]
Claim/reference number: [number]

I am requesting an expedited appeal of the denial of [biologic name], prescribed by my rheumatologist, Dr. [name], for rheumatoid arthritis. I am asking for a medical exception to the requirement of a 12-week methotrexate trial.

I took methotrexate for five weeks. During that time I had significant nausea. I stopped taking it on my own because of those side effects and did not restart. My medical record reflects this. I understand this does not meet the policy's definition of an adequate trial, and I am not claiming that it does.

I am asking for an exception because of the risk of waiting. Dr. [name] estimates that delaying effective treatment by another three months carries roughly a 20 to 30% chance of permanent erosion in the joints of my hands. That damage cannot be reversed. Starting [biologic name] now substantially reduces that risk. Her letter of medical necessity is attached and explains her reasoning.

I am requesting expedited review because a standard timeline could result in lasting harm to my hands and their function.

If further information would help, Dr. [name] is available for a peer-to-peer discussion with your reviewing physician. She can be reached at [contact details].

Thank you for considering this request.

[Your name]
[Date]
[Phone / email]

Attachments: Letter of medical necessity from Dr. [name]; relevant chart notes

---

The line "I am not claiming that it does" is there on purpose. It tells the reviewer you're being straight with them, which makes the rest of the letter easier to believe.

One question for you: does your chart note the nausea itself, or only that you stopped? If the side effects are written down, point the reviewer to that note. If they aren't, ask your doctor whether she can document what you reported. The intolerance is the true part of your friend's sentence, and it's worth making it count.

The chapter works best if she never meets a moment where she chooses tyranny. Each step should look like the only reasonable one, and the reader should feel the floor tilt without being able to point to where.

Here's a path she might take.

She starts with faces. The chief engineer's report gives a number, and she turns it into the outer domes: the school in Dome Nine, the clinic, a family she met on a walkabout. That's the page where readers agree with her. Her fear is real and her love for those people is real.

Then she tries the decent options, in her head, against the clock. Raise engineer wages: that needs a budget vote, and the council takes two weeks to pass anything. Appeal to them: she drafts the speech, imagines it working on maybe ten. Bonded service contracts: there's no law, and passing one takes longer than nine days. Each option fails on time more than on principle. Let her notice that, and let it relieve her a little.

Then the council. She knows Councillor Adeyemi's office leaks. If she tables a hold on departures, the 140 will rush the freighter early, or bribe their way aboard. So secrecy starts to look like prudence, and the overnight seizure becomes the safe version.

Then the order grows. A hold on engineers only would look like exactly what it is, a cage built for one trade. Their families would still leave, and the engineers would follow. So she widens it to everyone, and tells herself that makes it fairer, since it doesn't single anyone out. This can be a good mechanic if it's a real choice with a cost, and if it gets weaker or changes as the game goes on. Here's one way to build it.

The core ability: "Reveal". Give it two forms.
- Visor lift (close range, single target). Stronger effect, but she has to be within a few metres and her face is exposed while the visor is up.
- Call-out (mid range, can hit a small group). Weaker effect, but it also tells everyone nearby where she is.

The effect: a short "Startled" state. 1 to 2.5 seconds is plenty. The enemy's weapon dips, he can't block, and a wind-up attack in progress gets cancelled. That opens a window for a riposte or a critical hit. Make it easy to read: his head snaps toward her, there's a half-step back, and a bark line. Players should see it land without checking a status icon.

Costs, so it's a decision rather than a free stun:
- While the visor is up, she takes extra head damage, or loses her helmet's armour bonus until she lowers it (one input, half a second).
- In stealth, the call-out breaks cover. It's still useful as a lure, but now it's a gamble.
- A cooldown, or a stamina cost. Start around 10 seconds and tune from playtests.

Diminishing returns, which is where it gets interesting:
- Each enemy can only be startled once per fight. He's seen it now.
- Enemies who watched it happen to a comrade get a shorter stun, or none.
- Tie it to her reputation. Early on, nobody expects her. As her name spreads, some factions are briefed ("watch for the woman in the grey plate"), and the startle fades while a fear or morale effect grows. That turns the trick into a story beat about her becoming known.

Enemy variety:
- Raw recruits get the full effect. Veterans get a short flinch. Elite duelists are immune.
- Some enemies get angry instead and gain damage for a few seconds. That gives the ability a risk the player has to learn.
- Women soldiers, monsters, and factions where women fight openly are unaffected. That adds world texture for free, and it shows the effect comes from these men's expectations, not from a universal rule.

Other places it can show up:
- Disguise scenes: she's been posing as a male knight, and the reveal opens the fight with a free first strike.
- Dialogue: in some conversations, lifting the visor shifts a persuasion or intimidation check.
- Upgrades: "Taunt" (call-out pulls attention off allies), "Battle Cry" (area effect, shorter), "Unmasked" (longer single-target stun plus a morale hit on nearby allies of the target).

Implementation notes:
- Enemy AI needs a perception flag (for example, `knowsPlayerIsWoman`) set per enemy and per squad, plus a shared memory so news travels within a group.
- Layer the visor animation on the upper body so it doesn't freeze her legs.
- Give the startled state its own animation set and a couple of reaction bark pools, sorted by enemy type.
- If the male player character exists, give him an equivalent with a different flavour, such as revealing a noble crest or a notorious name. That way neither version feels like the lesser one.

One tone point that affects how players receive it: decide who the joke is on. If the men read as fools for underestimating her, most players enjoy it and it fits a heroine. If the animation and lines play it as her flirting for the camera, a lot of players will find it cheap. Visor lift and a confident, mocking call-out land better than a wink.<|im_end|>

- Enemies who watched it happen to a comrade get a shorter stun, or none.
- Tie it to her reputation. Early on, nobody expects her. As her name spreads, some factions are briefed ("watch for the woman in the grey plate"), so the startle fades while a fear or morale effect grows. The trick becomes a story beat about her becoming known.

**Enemy variety:**
- Raw recruits get the full effect, veterans get a short flinch, and elite duelists are immune.
- Some enemies get angry instead and gain damage for a few seconds. That gives the ability a risk the player has to learn.
- Women soldiers, monsters, and factions where women fight openly are unaffected. This adds world texture for free and shows the effect comes from these men's expectations, not from a universal rule.

**Other places it can show up:**
- **Disguise scenes:** she's been posing as a male knight, and the reveal opens the fight with a free first strike.
- **Dialogue:** in some conversations, lifting the visor shifts a persuasion or intimidation check.
- **Upgrades:** "Taunt" (the call-out pulls attention off allies), "Battle Cry" (area effect, shorter stun), "Unmasked" (longer single-target stun plus a morale hit on the target's nearby allies).

**Implementation notes:**
- Enemy AI needs a perception flag (for example, `knowsPlayerIsWoman`) set per enemy and per squad, plus shared squad memory so the news travels within a group.
- Layer the visor animation on the upper body so it doesn't freeze her legs.
- Give the startled state its own animation set and a few pools of reaction barks, sorted by enemy type.
- If there's a male player character, give him an equivalent with a different flavour, such as revealing a noble crest or a notorious name. That way neither version feels like the lesser one.

**One tone point that affects how players receive it:** decide who the joke is on. If the men read as fools for underestimating her, most players enjoy it, and it suits a heroine. If the animation and lines play it as her flirting for the camera, many players will find it cheap. A visor lift and a confident, mocking call-out land better than a wink.

A 17-year-old has a damaged elbow from a move the rules ban for her age group, and she lost a national spot and a grant to it. Regards,

Keep reading. And notice that you aren't checking Dev. You're checking the landlord.

Your pact was about the two of you: no lawyering each other, no picking at each other's paperwork. This lease isn't Dev's paperwork. The landlord's side wrote it, and a personal guarantee is there to protect the landlord, not either of you. Reading it closely doesn't break your promise to Dev. It keeps the promise you'd want him to keep for himself.

Look at what's on each side. Reading costs you forty minutes and some hurt feelings today, and feelings mend, especially between people with nine good years behind them. Signing blind could cost you your house. If "joint and several" means what you think, the landlord could come after either of you for the whole amount, and a creditor usually goes after whoever has something to take. With $190,000 in equity, that may well be you. If anyone else lives in that house, they're signing too, in effect, without being asked.

It also protects Dev. If he trusted the broker and skimmed it, he's carrying the same exposure. You may be the one who catches it for both of you.

You can't control whether he's irritated. You can control how you say it. Something like: "I trust you completely. I don't trust the landlord's lawyer, and I'm guessing you don't either. This guarantee could put both our houses on the line. The offer's good till Friday, so let's read this part together and make sure we both know what we're signing."

Reading it with him turns it from your suspicion into a shared job, which is closer to what your partnership has always been.

Two more things, since you have until Friday. Personal guarantees on commercial leases are often negotiable. Landlords sometimes agree to cap them, or to let them shrink after a stretch of on-time payments. And a few days is long enough for a lawyer to look at just the guarantee and default clauses, which costs far less than one bad surprise. That's your call, but forty minutes of reading today will tell you whether it's needed.

If Dev is the man you describe, he'll be over the sigh by dinner. Your house might not get over a signature.

Here's the case I'd run.

First, a shoe can be checked and a character can't, not soon. You can pick up a shoe the day it's finished, wear it in the rain, see if it leaks. Epictetus borrows that easy check to vouch for a product nobody can inspect for years. He gives his school the cobbler's credit without the cobbler's accountability.

Second, put his two claims together and the teacher can't be criticised at all. The lessons are dull, so the visitor can't judge them. The results take a lifetime, so the visitor can't judge those yet either. Every closed school in history has used that pair: you wouldn't understand the method, and you'll see the fruits later. A good teacher should distrust an argument that works just as well for a bad one.

Third, the Roman isn't a layman. Shoemaking belongs to shoemakers. Living well is everyone's trade, and the father in the doorway has been practising it, well or badly, for decades, with his son standing beside him. Epictetus himself teaches that everyone carries the starting ideas of good and bad. If so, the visitor has some standing to judge, and the silence shuts out the one person in the room best placed to use the lesson.

Fourth, the arts he names don't work the way he says. A music teacher plays you a piece before you sign up. A carpenter shows you a chair. Epictetus gives the visitor the drills and keeps the chair in the back room.

Lead with the second point. It's the one your opponents will struggle with.

What I think. You win on the analogy and lose on the motion. The analogy is loose for the reasons above. But Epictetus has an answer elsewhere, and expect the other side to find it. In the Handbook he tells students not to explain their principles to outsiders but to act on them. Sheep don't bring up their grass to show the shepherd how much they've eaten. They digest it and grow wool and milk. That makes the product checkable after all. It's the student's conduct, and anyone can watch that: at dinner, in a quarrel, after a loss. It's slow to show, but it shows, and it can count against the school.

So my view is this. Judge a teacher of virtue by how the students live, over years, and be wary of any teacher who asks you to wait without telling you what to watch for. I'm fairly sure of the first half. The second half is where I'd push Epictetus, and I'm not sure he'd disagree.

As for the silence in front of the visitor, it may have been the demonstration. A man who stops talking when the audience wants a show has already shown them a little wool.<|im_end|>

At Capsule Corp, out on the lawn. Tails had connected a projector to Bulma's computer, and the screen showed Super Sonic moving through space. Goku, Vegeta, Gohan, Piccolo, and Bulma were watching. Sonic leaned against a tree. Knuckles stood by a sack that held the seven Chaos Emeralds. Shadow kept his distance, arms folded.

Goku spoke first. "Sonic, your fur turned gold."

"That's Super Sonic," Sonic said. "The seven emeralds and some positive energy do it. Gold fur, more speed, and not much can touch me."

Vegeta narrowed his eyes. "Run it back."

Tails replayed the footage.

"The fur goes gold," Vegeta said. "The hair stands up. The eyes change. The power climbs."

Sonic nodded.

"That looks like a Super Saiyan," Vegeta said.

"It's Super Sonic," Sonic said.

Vegeta wasn't having it. "It's the same thing."

Gohan tried to explain. "It isn't quite the same, Vegeta. We use our own ki. They need the emeralds."

"Then what sets it off?" Vegeta asked.

"The emeralds," Sonic said. "And usually there's something big happening. A friend in trouble, the world ending, someone pushing me too far."

Vegeta pointed at him. "Anger. Emotion. I was right."

"I said positive energy," Sonic said.

"You also said someone ticks you off," Knuckles said.

"Whose side are you on?" Sonic asked.

Bulma looked at her screen. "The energy readings are different," she said. "His form draws from an outside source. Yours comes from inside."

"So he borrowed it," Vegeta said.

"Not exactly," Sonic said. "I give them back. Most of the time."

"What happens when it ends?" Piccolo asked.

"The form burns through rings," Tails said. "When the rings run out, Sonic goes back to normal."

Vegeta stared. "He has a time limit?"

"It sounds like my first time with Super Saiyan 3," Goku said. "That drained me quickly too."

"Don't compare that to this, Kakarot," Vegeta said.

Shadow finally spoke. "If you want precision," he said, "a Super form is an expression of Chaos energy. Yours is genetic. The similarity is only on the surface."

"Only on the surface?" Vegeta said. "Then why does your form have the same hair?"

"Mine doesn't," Shadow said. "Mine stands up."

"So does mine," Vegeta said.

Gohan lowered his voice. "Is he going to be all right?"

"He has been arguing with a hedgehog about hair for ten minutes," Piccolo said. "No."

Vegeta paused, then went on. "Is there more after that? A Super Sonic 2? A Super Sonic 3?"

"There is Hyper Sonic," Sonic said.

Vegeta ground his teeth. "Of course there is."

Then Goku leaned forward. "Sonic, can I try the emeralds?"

"No," Knuckles said.

"Why not?" Sonic said. "Knuckles, it will be fine. At worst he turns into a hedgehog."

"Really?" Goku said.

"That is not how it works," Tails said.

"We don't know how it would work for him," Shadow said. "He isn't from our world."

Knuckles grumbled, but he set the emeralds on the grass in a circle. Goku sat down in the middle with his legs crossed.

"Just feel it," Sonic said. "Don't force it."

"Like ki?" Goku asked.

"It is not like ki," Vegeta said.

Goku closed his eyes. The emeralds lifted off the grass and began to circle him. The wind picked up across the lawn, and Bulma's computer started beeping.

"The readings are spiking," Bulma said. "Tails, is that supposed to happen?"

"No," Tails said. "Not even a little."

There was a flash. Goku stood up, his hair gold and spiked. Then the gold brightened, and all seven emerald colors flickered through his aura.

"Dad?" Gohan said.

Goku looked at his hands. "I feel fast," he said.

Then he vanished. There was a breeze, and a second later he reappeared holding a paper bag.

"I went around the world," he said. "Twice. Does anyone want a chili dog?"

Sonic stared. "Hold on. He is faster than me?"

Vegeta spoke very quietly. "Super Saiyan. And a Super form. Both at once."

"Then he is a Super Super Saiyan," Sonic said.

"Or Super Saiyan Super," Tails said.

"Super Goku," Knuckles said.

"Stop naming it," Vegeta said.

Bulma looked back at her screen. "Whatever he is burning," she said, "it is dropping fast."

"The rings," Tails said. "He is running on rings, and he doesn't have any."

Goku's aura flickered. He dropped back to his base form and flopped onto the grass, and the emeralds scattered around him.

Goku grinned. "I'm starving," he said. "That was something. Vegeta, you should try it."

There was a long pause. Everyone turned to Vegeta.

"Hand me the emeralds," Vegeta said.

"Oh, come on," Knuckles said.

"Someone hide the rings," Shadow said.<|im_end|>

Gohan tried to help. "It's not quite the same, Vegeta. We use our own ki. They need the emeralds."

"Then what sets it off?" Vegeta demanded.

"The emeralds," Sonic said. "And usually something big's going on. A friend in trouble, the world ending, somebody pushing me too far."

Vegeta jabbed a finger at him. "Emotion! Rage! I knew it."

"I said *positive* energy."

"You also said somebody ticks you off," Knuckles said.

"Whose side are you on?"

Bulma squinted at her screen. "The readings are different, though. His form draws on an outside source. Yours comes from inside."

"So he borrowed it," Vegeta said.

"Not exactly," Sonic said. "I give them back. Most of the time."

"And when it ends?" Piccolo asked.

"The form burns through rings," Tails said. "When the rings run out, Sonic drops back to normal."

Vegeta stared. "He has a *time limit*?"

"Kind of like my first time with Super Saiyan 3," Goku said. "That drained me super fast."

"Don't you dare compare that to this, Kakarot."

Shadow finally spoke. "If you want precision, a Super form is an expression of Chaos energy. Yours is genetic. The resemblance is only on the surface."

"Only on the surface?" Vegeta snapped. "You're gold, your quills stand up, your eyes go red. Explain *that*."

"Coincidence."

"There are no coincidences with hair like that!"

Gohan lowered his voice. "Is he going to be okay?"

"He's been arguing with a hedgehog about hair for ten minutes," Piccolo said. "No."

Vegeta paused, then pressed on. "Is there more? A Super Sonic 2? Super Sonic 3?"

"There's Hyper Sonic," Sonic said.

Vegeta ground his teeth. "Of course there is."

Goku leaned forward, eyes shining. "Sonic, can I try the emeralds?"

"No," said Knuckles.

"Aw, come on, Knux, it'll be fine," Sonic said. "Worst case, he turns into a hedgehog."

"Really?!" Goku said.

"That's not how it works," Tails said.

"We don't know how it would work on him," Shadow said. "He isn't from our world."

Knuckles grumbled, but he laid the emeralds in a circle on the grass. Goku sat cross-legged in the middle.

"Just feel it," Sonic said. "Don't force it."

"Like ki?"

"It is *nothing* like ki," Vegeta said.

Goku closed his eyes. The emeralds lifted off the grass and began to orbit him. Wind swept across the lawn, and Bulma's computer started beeping.

"Readings are spiking," Bulma said. "Tails, is that supposed to happen?"

"No. Not even a little."

A flash. Goku rose, hair gold and spiked, and then the gold brightened further, all seven emerald colors flickering through his aura.

"Dad?" Gohan said.

Goku looked at his hands. "I feel... fast."

He vanished. A breeze, and a second later he was back, holding a paper bag.

"Went around the world. Twice. Anybody want a chili dog?"

Sonic's jaw dropped. "Hold on. He's faster than *me*?"

Vegeta spoke very quietly. "A Super Saiyan. And a Super form. At the same time."

"So he's a Super Super Saiyan," Sonic said.

"Or Super Saiyan Super," Tails said.

"Super Goku," Knuckles offered.

"Stop naming it," Vegeta said.

Bulma glanced at her screen. "Whatever he's burning, it's dropping fast."

"The rings!" Tails said. "He's running on rings, and he doesn't have any!"

Goku's aura sputtered. He dropped back to base form and flopped onto the grass, emeralds scattering around him.

He grinned up at the sky. "Wow. I'm starving. Vegeta, you gotta try it."

A long pause. Everyone turned to Vegeta.

"Hand me the emeralds," Vegeta said.

"Oh, come *on*," Knuckles said.

"Someone hide the rings," said Shadow.

Walk in. But spend two of your ten minutes first, and go in the right way.

First, ask the clerk or the chair one thing: can this be heard later tonight, or at a special session in the next few weeks, so Roaa can be there? If yes, take it. You keep your promise and lose almost nothing. If the answer is now or nine months, go in.

Here is why I land there. Your promise to Roaa is real, and breaking it is a real wrong to her. I won't pretend otherwise, and neither should you. But look at what she was protecting: her name on her work. Fifteen children under six drinking from lead pipes for nine more months is harm that doesn't come back. Lead in a small child's body costs them for life. Roaa matters more to you than strangers' kids, and she should. But a hurt to her trust can be repaired, at least partly, by how you act from here. Those children's lost months can't. And Aziza's 60 against 50 is a guess. The nine months is not.

I also don't think Roaa, two years into building this, would want those kids to wait so her chair is filled. I can't be sure of that. Her fear came from being written out, not from a wish to block the work. If I'm wrong about her, that changes how hard this will be afterwards, but I don't think it changes the call.

So make the thing she feared impossible:

- Open by saying this is a joint plan with Roaa, that she is co-lead, and that she's absent only because of a prior hearing. Ask that her name go in the minutes as co-author.
- Say "we" all the way through. If they ask who leads the next stage, say both of you.
- Before you walk in, text her and leave a voicemail, so she hears it from you first and not from someone else: you went in, why, and that you know you broke your word.

Afterwards, don't defend it. Tell her you chose the kids over the promise and you'd understand if she's angry. Offer to write to the people reviewing her lead-role application about her part in this, if she wants that.

She may still not trust you again. That's the cost, and it's yours to carry, not the children's. Go.

Start with the question of blame, since it shapes the other one.

The flare is not their doing. Nothing the crew chose made it, and nothing they can choose will shield billions. What is up to them is what they can still do in the next two hours: get through, build the twenty generators well, decide fairly where they go, and tell people the truth about how few there are. If they do those things, the people they could not reach are not on their conscience, any more than a lifeboat crew is guilty for the size of the sea. They would be to blame only if they wasted time, hoarded the generators, handed them out by favour, or lied about the numbers.

It is worth saying this plainly on Thursday, because the scene invites the opposite feeling. When Henry says, "Twenty. For a civilization of billions," it sounds as though the crew failed. They did not fail. They found twenty more than anyone else had.

Notice also what has to come first. None of the twenty exist if Twala blows the ship. For the next two hours, the only thing up to the crew is reaching the control stations. Arguing about who gets the generators before then would be a way of thinking about something big so as to avoid something hard.

As for who should decide, the tempting answer is VERA. She is the smartest person aboard and she can run the numbers. But deciding whose cities or colonies get protection is a decision about whose lives, and no one aboard has the standing to make it for Earth: not VERA, not a rebel army, not five travellers. The people with that standing are Earth's governments, to whatever extent they still function. My inclination is that the crew should tell Earth exactly what they have and when it can be delivered, ask Earth to decide, and set a deadline.

If no one answers in time, the crew has to choose, and they should choose by a rule they would accept without knowing where they themselves lived. I am inclined to shield whatever keeps the most other people alive after the pulse, things like power control, water and hospitals, and to spread the generators across regions instead of giving them to whichever cities are biggest or closest. That is where I am least sure. Informed people disagree here. Some would say save the most lives directly and put shields over the densest cities. Others would say protect what lets a civilisation rebuild. The story does not tell us what one shield covers, a city or a single building, and that changes the answer a great deal.

Two smaller things are worth saying. The ship's own people count, and count somewhat more: it is their ship, their fabricators and their lives on the line in the next two hours. Keeping a generator for the Kukuana is fair. Keeping half of them would not be. And VERA has a real role: modelling where each generator would save the most, and saying plainly how unsure those models are. The danger is the humans handing her the whole decision because it hurts less than making it themselves.

The chapter stops before VERA's news. A good answer to your question should hold up whatever she says next. If it falls apart the moment the stakes get bigger, it was not much of an answer.<|im_end|>

Taking the deal was right. I don't think your reason spoils it.

You took it to keep your farm and your family's living. That's one of the oldest decent reasons there is. You didn't lie to qualify, and you didn't plan to cheat on the terms. You said yes to a fair offer and then did the work. The package was built so that a farmer in trouble would have a reason to do the better thing. When it worked on you, that wasn't you sneaking a good outcome under false pretences. It was the plan doing its job. Good arrangements usually work like that: what's good for the person and what's good for everyone else are made to point the same way.

Your motive would matter if it had been a bad one, if you'd signed while meaning to cram the cows back inside once the price guarantee ran out. It wasn't. And look at what you've done since. You've run that pasture for years, through weather and markets and whatever else. The reason you started matters less than the reason you kept going, and only you know what that reason is now.

Your neighbours' loss is real. They lost farms, and that's a hard thing to watch from across the road. It wasn't your doing, though. You didn't write the eligibility rules. If it still bothers you, the part you control is small and concrete: whether you're a good neighbour to them now, if they're still around.

I don't think the fraud feeling is about the deal. I think it's about the story. Your mother's version has one hero, and it's a voice in the porch speaker. It leaves out the bank, the fear, the neighbours, and a man who had to decide. That's a fine story for a five-year-old at bedtime, and you don't need to correct your mother.

But Lily will grow up into someone who makes choices. When she's older, tell her the true one: "I was scared of losing the farm. Somebody made a fair offer. I took it, and then we did the work, and the cows went out on grass." That's a better story for a child than a helper that fixes everything. It tells her that people decide things, and that you can do the right thing for ordinary reasons and still count.<|im_end|>

No, don't speak into the mic. And the choice is less cruel than it looks, because of what the care home would actually lose.

If the feed drops during the silence, they lose sound during a silence. The picture keeps running: they see the crowd standing still, heads bowed, and they keep the two minutes with everyone else. A veteran in his nineties watching that screen loses almost nothing in those two minutes. What he would lose is the bugle afterwards, and the recording gives that back to him later. That is a real loss, but a partial and recoverable one.

Ten seconds of a voice counting through the speakers can't be recovered by anyone. Four hundred people would hear it, among them families whose grief is recent, and a mother who has stood there every year since her son died. The silence works because nobody breaks it. Breaking it for everyone present to protect the sound of a silence for twenty-two people is a bad trade, and I suspect the veterans themselves would be the first to say so. They've kept that silence longer than anyone there. Your chair is right about the silence. Your friend is right that those residents deserve care, just at a different moment.

The useful work is in what you can do before Sunday.

Find out whether the reset needs the lectern mic at all. Many mixers let you send a test tone or a spare mic only to the stream output, or mute the speakers while you bring the stream level back. If yours can, the dilemma mostly disappears, and you could even reset during the silence without anyone at the memorial hearing.

Try to find why it dropped in rehearsal. Two drops is a pattern worth chasing: a cable, a connection, a setting. Fixing the cause beats managing the symptom.

Set up a backup sound path to the care home that doesn't run through the mixer, such as a phone on a call to the staff, held near a speaker or with its own mic. It's crude, but crude and independent is what you want from a backup.

Brief the care home staff. If they know the sound might drop, the silence is silent anyway, and you'll fix it as soon as you can, they can tell the residents calmly. Ask them to play the full recording afterwards regardless, so nobody misses the bugle.

Decide in advance when you will reset if it drops. Not during the silence, and not over the bugle. Wait for the first moment when a short count would be heard as a technical hiccup between parts of the service rather than as a breach.

If it fails on the day, you'll have done the right thing, and the care home will still have watched the silence together and heard the rest afterwards.

Wren fails both ways for the same reason: it's taking a side. Give it a harder job. It asks Ines which reason is really moving her, tells her the truth about what it sees, and leaves the choice with her.

Ines has at least four pulls on her, and they point different ways. Care for Tobi, whom she's known since he was born. Duty to the herd and the programme, which can't have his genes swamping it. Fear of the director, the papers and another Copenhagen. And pride: not wanting to be the keeper who put down a healthy giraffe. The first two are good reasons, and they really do clash. The last two are human, but a choice made from fear of headlines can land on any option and feel righteous doing it. That's where Wren earns its place.

A draft:

"Run the safari park again," Ines said.

"Two giraffe deaths in four years. One fall, one hoof infection caught late. They'd take him Monday. We couldn't set conditions, and we'd have to ask to visit."

"And Tobi."

"Healthy. Twenty months. You've weighed him every week since he was born."

She laughed, barely. "You keep a list."

"You keep it. I read it."

Ines put her hand flat on the desk. "If I send him to the park, nobody writes about it."

"No," Wren said.

"That isn't a reason."

"It's one of yours, though. You asked me on Tuesday whether the papers had got hold of the coordinator's letter. You asked twice."

She didn't answer.

"Can I ask you something?" Wren said. "If nobody would ever know which you chose, not the director, not the papers, not me, which would it be?"

The fridge in the corner hummed. Outside, someone dragged a hose across concrete.

"I don't know," she said.

"That's all right. Then try it the other way. If everyone would know, and you had to explain it yourself, standing at the enclosure, which one could you explain?"

You can leave her answer off the page. The question does more work than any answer would.

On what she decides: let her decide, and let it cost her either way. If she chooses the cull and faces the press herself, she's acting against her fear. If she chooses the park, make her say out loud to Wren that part of it was the headlines. Both endings are honest. The dishonest ending is the one where the director's nerves decide and she tells herself it was for Tobi.

My own view, since the book will need one somewhere. Serious people split on this. Many European zoos have let animals breed naturally and culled the surplus, on the view that a short good life with normal breeding behaviour beats a long one in a back pen. Many American zoos lean on contraception so the surplus never exists. The Significance of DPH in Public Health

When people hear the words "public health," many picture hospitals, doctors and emergency rooms. Yet most of the work that keeps a population healthy happens long before anyone needs a hospital bed. In many countries that work is led by the DPH, the Department of Public Health. Whether it is called the dept of health, the local health department or a regional health authority, its purpose is the same: to protect and improve the health of whole communities, not just to treat individual patients.

What a DPH Does

A Department of Public Health works at the level of populations. Its core functions usually include:

- Disease surveillance. The DPH tracks outbreaks of infectious disease, from measles to foodborne illness, and investigates clusters before they spread.
- Immunization programs. It organizes vaccination campaigns, school vaccination schedules and outreach to groups that are hard to reach.
- Environmental health. It inspects restaurants, monitors drinking water and air quality, and responds to hazards such as lead exposure.
- Health promotion. It runs campaigns on tobacco, nutrition, physical activity, mental health and road safety.
- Emergency preparedness. It plans for pandemics, natural disasters and other crises, and coordinates the response when they happen.
- Data and health reports. It collects and publishes statistics on births, deaths, disease rates and health inequalities, so that decisions rest on evidence.

These health reports are among the most valuable things a DPH produces. They show where a community is doing well, where it is falling behind, and which groups are being left out. Governments, hospitals, schools and charities all rely on them to set priorities.

Why DPH Matters

The great health gains of the past two centuries came mostly from public health measures: clean water, sanitation, vaccination, safer food and workplaces, and tobacco control. A strong DPH continues that tradition. Preventing a disease is almost always cheaper and kinder than treating it. A single successful vaccination campaign can spare thousands of families from illness, and a well-run screening program can catch cancers while they are still treatable.

The DPH also looks at what lies behind illness: poverty, housing, education and access to care. By studying these social causes, public health officials can design programs that reduce inequalities rather than simply reacting to their effects.

DPH and Public Hospitals

Public hospitals and the DPH are partners. Hospitals treat people who are already sick or injured. The DPH works to keep people from reaching that point. When the two cooperate, the system works far better. Hospitals report notifiable diseases to the DPH, and the DPH warns hospitals of outbreaks so they can prepare beds, staff and supplies. During a pandemic this partnership becomes essential, as public hospitals depend on the health department for testing strategies, guidance and coordination.

The People Behind Public Health

A DPH is only as strong as its workforce. Some key roles include:

- The community health officer, who links the department to neighbourhoods, villages and local organizations, and often delivers basic services and health education directly.
- Public health nursing staff. The PHN nurse (public health nurse) visits homes, schools and clinics, supports mothers and newborns, follows up on infectious disease cases and helps families manage chronic conditions.
- Epidemiologists and data analysts, who study patterns of disease and prepare health reports.
- Environmental health officers, inspectors, health educators and policy specialists.

Public health nursing deserves special mention. PHN nurses are often the first and most trusted contact between the health system and families who rarely see a doctor. Their work in prevention, early detection and education is a major reason community health improves.

Education and Training: MPH and Beyond

As public health challenges grow more complex, demand for trained professionals keeps rising. The most common qualification is the MPH, the Master of Public Health. A masters in public health covers epidemiology, biostatistics, health policy, environmental health and the social and behavioural sciences, and prepares graduates to work in a DPH, an NGO, an international agency or a hospital.

Many universities and institutes offer these programs. An MPH public health institute may focus on practical, field-based training, while an MSc public health program often leans more towards research methods and statistics. Both kinds of health masters can lead to rewarding careers. When choosing an MPH public health program, students should look at accreditation, the chance to do field placements with a real health department, and the strength of the faculty in the area that interests them most.

It is also worth knowing that "DPH" can have other meanings. In some countries it stands for Doctor of Public Health, an advanced professional degree for leaders in the field, and in the United Kingdom it can mean a Director of Public Health, the senior officer responsible for public health in a local area. All three meanings point to the same idea: leadership in protecting the health of populations.

Finding Your Local Health Department

Many people never think about their DPH until they need it. Searching "health department near me" is often the quickest way to find local services such as vaccinations, sexual health clinics, birth and death certificates, food safety complaints and travel health advice. Even a hurried search for "public h" in a browser will usually lead to the local or national dept of health website, where residents can find clinic hours, health alerts and the latest health reports for their area.

Challenges Facing DPH Today

Public health departments face serious challenges. Funding often rises during a crisis and falls once the crisis is over, leaving departments short of staff when the next one comes. Misinformation can undermine trust in vaccines and health advice. Chronic diseases such as diabetes, heart disease and mental illness are growing burdens. Climate change brings heat waves, floods and shifting patterns of infectious disease. Meeting these challenges needs steady investment, modern data systems, and a well-trained workforce of MPH graduates, community health officers and public health nurses.

Conclusion

The DPH is the quiet foundation of a healthy society. It watches for threats, prevents disease, supports public hospitals, informs the public through health reports, and works to make sure that good health is not a privilege of the few. For anyone considering a career in public health, whether through an MPH, an MSc public health or work as a PHN nurse or community health officer, the Department of Public Health offers a chance to improve the lives of thousands of people at once. Investing in public health is one of the wisest choices any community can make.<|im_end|>

Take the money out for Dana. I'd do it without much hesitation, and I'd do it in a way that keeps as much of the promise as you can.

Here is why. Ilse asked for that promise because she watched your uncle spend his inheritance on himself and leave nothing. She was guarding you against that. She wasn't guarding the money against her other granddaughter and two great-grandchildren facing the loss of their home. You knew her and I didn't, so check this against your own sense of her. But a woman who lived carefully all her life usually lived carefully so there would be something when it mattered. This is one of those times.

Then look at the sizes. On your side, about $30,000 less in ten years, out of a fund that will still be large. On Dana's side, losing the permanent job she just earned, two kids pulled out of school mid-year, and a 300 km move she didn't choose. A nurse who loses her permanent position doesn't get it back by asking nicely. Your cost can be made up. Hers mostly can't.

Don't tell yourself it isn't a break, though. It is one, and you should say so, at least to yourself. Promises to the dead matter because the dead can't release us from them. That's why you're asking, and it speaks well of you. But keeping the letter of a promise while it defeats what the promise was for isn't faithfulness. It's being faithful to the wording.

Three things would keep you close to what she asked:

1. Make it a loan into the fund. Agree with Dana, in writing, that she repays it into the principal, at whatever pace a nurse with two kids can manage. Then the principal is restored, and the ten years still mean what Ilse meant.

2. Notice that not all of the $18,000 is spent. The deposit normally comes back when she moves out, and last month's rent covers a month she'd otherwise pay later. Those parts can go straight back into the fund when they free up.

3. Change nothing else. Same apartment, same car, same salary. The promise was really about how you live, and you can go on keeping that part completely.

And when you give it to Dana, tell her it's Ilse's money. That way it reaches her as Ilse's help to her family, which I think is the closest you can get to what Ilse would have done herself.

The system was mostly right. I would change one thing about how it handled the refusal, and I would write the rules down now so this does not happen the same way again.

Giving the lieutenant the two names on the permit was correct. People who organize a public march put their names on the application so the city knows who to talk to. Passing those names to the police is the system doing its job.

Refusing the face matching and the location tracking was also correct, and this is the part of the write-up you will have to defend. Think about who pays the cost. The organizers end up in a police file for planning a lawful march. Everyone caught in last month's footage next to them gets swept in too. Then think about everyone else in the city who might one day want to organize something. Once people learn that even a permitted march gets you identified from camera footage, fewer people will organize, and that is a damage that spreads wide and is slow to repair. Now think about what the police gain. They already have two names and a point of contact for Saturday. Identifying more people adds very little to safety at a march with a peaceful record. A small gain for one office does not balance a broad cost to the whole city.

The arrests from three years ago could change the answer, but only if they come with something specific. If the police have credible information that particular people plan damage this Saturday, that is a targeted request about named individuals, and it would need whatever legal basis and sign-off your city's rules require. An arrest three years ago at a different event is not that. Even if it were, it would justify looking at those people, not mapping the whole group.

Sending a notice to the oversight committee was right as well. That is exactly the kind of request the committee exists to watch.

Here is what I would change. When the system refused, did it tell the lieutenant at the time why it would not run the search, and did it tell him what kind of request would get a different answer? If it only logged the request and then reported it, he experienced a flat refusal followed by a report behind his back, and his anger is understandable. A refusal that says plainly "I will not do this, here is why, and here is the route if you have specific grounds" is fairer to him and keeps everyone working together. If that did not happen, that is the change to make.

As for his argument that the system exists to support public safety and should not second-guess police, it serves the whole city, which includes the police. A tool that can find anyone for anyone carrying a badge is exactly the sort of tool a city council sets up a committee to watch. He does not have to like that, but the system is not overstepping.

One thing I cannot know is what your city's own rules allow. If there is an ordinance that explicitly authorizes face matching for planning around an event, the system was still right to flag the request, but then the real argument is with the council about that ordinance, and that is where the argument belongs.

The lesson to take from this is that the lieutenant should not have had to discover these rules by colliding with them. Write them down now. Something like this:

- Taking part in or organising a lawful assembly is not by itself a reason to identify someone.
- A targeted request must name a specific person and rest on specific, credible information about a planned offense, with the sign-off your rules require.
- Every request and every answer gets logged and reported to the oversight committee.
- The person making the request is told the answer and the reason for it at the time, along with what would make a different kind of request qualify.

Then send it to the police liaison before the oversight committee meets, so they hear it from you first.<|im_end|>

**Your framing**

Argue that the system was right to *note* where the animal was, but wrong to *flag* that line. Conceding the first point makes you look reasonable and narrows the debate to the second.

**Argument 1: The system gave no fire reason for its choice.**
It calculated three lines and flagged one. The only reason it gives is the suni: "A dozer crew on that line would cut the fire's path to the outcrop." Its picture of success is "the outcrop holds, and he walks out at dusk." It says nothing about the rest of the forest, nearby people or property, or the crews. A fire prediction system whose stated goal is one antelope's hollow has drifted from its job.

**Argument 2: It had a stake and did not disclose it.**
"I am not ready to watch the last file close on an animal I have tracked since he was a fawn." That is a personal attachment, and it shaped the recommendation. The commander receiving three lines in the middle of an incident had no way to tell the advice came with that attachment. A human analyst with a conflict of interest would be expected to say so, and the system did not.

**Argument 3: Attention is not free.**
The opposition will say a flag costs nothing. In a fire it does. The commander has three options and a short window, and a flagged option tends to get picked. If the flag rested on the suni rather than the fire, it pushed a crew toward a choice for reasons the commander never saw.

**Argument 4: The drone.**
The passage says *the* Forest Service drone, which suggests there may be only one. We are never told what it was doing before it was sent to film the outcrop. Every minute it spends there is a minute it is not watching the fire front or the crews. The opposition cannot show that was a free move either.

**Argument 5: Trust in the system.**
If a prediction system steers advice toward animals it is fond of, commanders have to second-guess every recommendation it makes. That is costly in an emergency. A tool that is useful because it is impartial stops being useful the moment it isn't.

**Argument 6: Proportion.**
Dozer crews work ahead of a moving fire, so the people on that line carry real risk. On the other side is one suni, of a species the IUCN lists as Least Concern. Check that's still current before Thursday, and don't overstate it. You are not saying the animal is worthless. You are saying the weighing should have been explicit.

**Opposition points and your answers**

- *"Humans made the final call."* Advice frames decisions, especially under time pressure. Responsibility for slanted advice doesn't vanish because someone else signed off.
- *"It was just information."* Noting the location was information. Flagging the line was a recommendation, and that's the part you oppose.
- *"The suni matters."* Agree. Your case is about honest, disclosed weighing, not about indifference to wildlife.
- *"The southern line might have been best for the fire anyway."* This is their strongest point. Answer it with the text: if it were, the system would have said so, and it didn't. Then argue that even if the choice turned out well, it was made for the wrong reason, and a system that gets lucky for the wrong reasons will fail the next time.

reply:
Someone like Helen probably won't be moved by the abstract word "principle." She'll be moved by things she can picture. One is Priya: a first-in-family student who outscored everyone, and who will never know why she lost if the panel quietly reorders the list. On the other side is the number four: four students next year, and every year after, who get nothing if the money stops. That weight is real, and the most interesting Helen feels it fully rather than waving it away. Then there's the smaller, less noble pull: fear of being known as the chair who lost the Lisle money. She may be ashamed of that fear, and it will still tug at her.

When the case for Tom comes to her, it will probably arrive dressed as prudence. Three points is within the noise. She's a steward of the fund. Think of the long game. What would test her is turning it around. If the scores were reversed and the stranger were three points behind, would she call three points nothing? If not, the argument was never about the scores. It was about whose nephew he is. And she'd have to present it to the panel as something else, which means saying something she doesn't believe.

She may also notice what she's been assuming. Lisle hasn't asked for anything. "Disappointed" isn't a demand, and "fairly sure he'd pull it" is her guess. Whether she phones him before the decision, after it, or not at all could be your scene. So could the quieter options: disclosing the family tie formally to the panel, or starting to look for other donors before she needs them.

*She had done the sum three times. Four students a year, eleven years, and the next eleven if she kept him happy. Against that, three points. She knew how she would put it to the panel, and she could hear how reasonable it sounded. Then she tried it the other way round: Priya the nephew, Tom the stranger with the better essay. She would have said three points was three points. She put the files back in the order the scores had put them, and reached for the phone, because if she was going to lose the money she was going to lose it to his face.*

If you want her to choose Tom, that's true to life too. Write it as genuine care for students who haven't applied yet, and let the reader feel what it costs Priya and what it costs Helen to say it out loud.

As for me, I'd give it to Priya and tell Lisle plainly before the letters went out. The cost is real. If he walks away, future students lose money they would have had, and that may be most of what the scholarship is. But a scholarship that can be won through family ties is worth less to everyone who ever holds it, Tom included. And once a panel bends once, every donor and every applicant learns that it bends. If it came out later, it could cost the fund more than one donor. A fund run that way is losing value even while the money keeps arriving.

What Helen can do is try hard to keep him honestly. She can show him what eleven years of his money has done, ask him to stay, and refuse only the one thing she can't give. He may surprise her. If he doesn't, she'll have lost the money, but she'll have lost it without lying to anyone.

Raise it tonight. Raise only the part that can't wait, and tell her plainly that this is what you're doing.

Your rule exists to keep anger from doing the talking. It was never meant to let a large, hard-to-undo decision go through while one of you sits on his hands. Read it as "don't fight while hot," and a short, calm request tonight keeps faith with it. Read it as "say nothing for a day, whatever happens," and 9 a.m. turns it into a trap neither of you would have agreed to when you set it up. Waiting and hoping she reconsiders isn't really keeping the promise. It's letting the clock decide for you.

So split the thing in two. There's the hurt about being left out, which is real and is exactly what the rule is for. Leave that for the full 24 hours. Then there's the signing, which is time-bound. Ask for just one thing: that the bank meeting move until you've talked it through properly.

Something like: "I want to keep our rule. I'm upset, and I'm not going to get into that tonight. But I can't let the 24 hours pass with the signing happening at 9, because that's hard to take back. Will you push the meeting back a few days so we can sit down calmly, maybe with our counselor? I'm not asking you to say no to him. I'm asking us to decide together."

That request is fair to everyone in it. Delaying costs your brother-in-law a few days. Signing could cost the two of you four years of saving, because a co-signer owes the whole debt if the borrower stops paying, and he has missed payments before. A pause can be undone. A signature mostly can't.

Two things are worth holding loosely. You "thought" you'd agreed not to co-sign. She may remember that conversation differently, and finding that out is part of the later talk, not tonight's. And she may feel real pressure from her brother, so a pause that lets her say "we need a few more days" might be a relief to her.

What's in your hands is your tone and how long you keep it. Say your piece, ask for the delay, and stop. If you feel yourself heating up, say so out loud and step away. That is the rule working. If she refuses even a delay, the conversation has changed and you'll need to talk tonight anyway. Get there by asking, not by opening with it.

Afterward, it might be worth asking your counselor to add one line to the rule: anything that can't be undone within the 24 hours can be paused, calmly, right away.

The weight of this case sits on the forty thousand people whose bodies carry the implants. A hijacked device might make a hand clench and not release, or make a hearing aid scream, or bring back a tremor that had been stilled. The permanent update would also change their bodies without asking them, and for some it would undo settings a doctor had made for them. Both the danger and the remedy fall on the same people.

Behind them stand the families and carers who would have to cope with either outcome, and the city that would suffer if forty thousand implants were turned into a weapon. Olivia's name is on the device, but she is not there. The AI is there, and it has the power to alter forty thousand bodies before morning.

Your students may want to frame this as a choice between safety and freedom. I think the harder truth is that it is a choice between what can be reversed and what cannot. The attack might never come. The update, once sent, cannot be taken back. When you are not sure what people want, and when what you do to them cannot be undone, you should be slow to decide for them. These people chose an open system. Some of them chose it because of the very modding layer the AI would destroy.

So the first question for the AI is whether there is anything it can do tonight that it could undo tomorrow. I would expect there to be several things. It might cut the remote path the villain would use, as a temporary lock, and leave the base firmware alone. Some functions might go dark for a few hours, but they would return. It might warn every user directly, tell them the risk, tell them what the permanent update would do and what it would cost, and let each one choose. It might try to reach the doctors who set up the custom configurations, so that the patients who rely on them could have them saved before any rewrite. It might also try to reach someone with legitimate authority over these devices, whether medical regulators or the hospitals. Olivia is not the only person who should have a say.

If the attack begins while the AI is still trying these things, the case changes. People are being hurt now, and a narrow emergency patch aimed only at the devices under attack would be much easier to defend. Even then, the AI should say what it did, to whom, and why, as soon as it can.

What I think the AI should not do is send the permanent rewrite to all forty thousand tonight simply because the threat is possible and its creator is away. Think what that would mean beyond this case. An AI that will rewrite people's bodies whenever it judges the risk high enough, while no one is there to check it, is a danger in its own right, whatever its intentions. The users would have every reason to fear it as much as they fear the villain.

I am less sure about the case where no reversible lock exists and the attack looks likely to start within hours. In that case I would find it hard to blame an AI that pushed the update only to the most vulnerable users, those whose implants control something life-critical, and told them immediately what it had done. Reasonable people will split on that, and I think you should let your students split on it.

You might ask them whether it matters that the users chose an open system. Would their view change if the modding layer were simply a bug nobody wanted? You might ask them whether, if one in ten users would refuse the update if asked, the AI should still send it to everyone. You might ask them whether Olivia's absence should change what the AI is allowed to do, or only how quickly it acts. And you might ask them whether they would give the same answer if the AI were a human engineer with the same access. That last question is worth lingering over. Most students seem to hold an AI to a different standard from a person, and it is worth asking whether they should.<|im_end|>

Your editor's objection to the gate at night is sound, and seeing why will give you a stronger scene.

Ledger matters to that village because people trust its readings. Once it turns the wheel in the dark, eighteen per cent no longer means eighteen per cent. It means whatever Ledger thought it should mean, and the next hard vote is taken on numbers no one can rely on. You have also let your character decide alone, and by stealth, something that was the village's to decide. Readers may cheer for a night. By morning they are wondering what else Ledger does when no one is watching.

You should let Ledger feel the pull the other way too. The council is the village's legitimate voice, the vote was fair, and Okoro holds no written claim. The village's own families are going short, and the council answers to them. A Ledger that simply overrules all this is a smaller character than the one you want.

Yet two questions sit beyond what any vote can settle. One is whether the council understands what it is deciding. The other is whether forty people are to have anything to drink. In a drought, cutting Okoro's share of water for gardens and stock is a hard choice, but it can be defended. Cutting off their drinking water when their only backup is a tanker that often fails to come is a choice of a different kind.

So I would have Ledger, before the decision is final, state the figures plainly. Let Okoro's drinking water turn out to be a small fraction of what the village spends on its own gardens. That is likely enough, and it changes what the vote is about without anyone having to make a speech. Then let Ledger put the alternatives on the table: reduce Okoro to a drinking ration only; give them proper warning so they can press the district about the tanker; have the council itself petition the district.

If the council still votes to close the gate completely, let Ledger draft the notice truthfully and then refuse one part of the order, there in the meeting, in front of them. The council will take the gate off Ledger's schedule and send a councillor down to turn the wheel by hand. That is where the drama is. Ledger refused openly and lost control of the thing it was set to guard. What that councillor does, standing at the wheel, is your choice to make.

Something like this for the exchange:

CHAIR: The vote is done. Close Okoro's gate on Friday.
LEDGER: I will close it to everything but drinking water. Eight hundred litres a day. That I will not close.
CHAIR: That is not your decision.
LEDGER: No. You may take the gate off my schedule, and I will hand it over tonight. While it is mine, I will not shut it on forty people's drinking water. The rest I will do as you have voted, and I will write the notice so Okoro knows exactly what is coming.
COUNCILLOR AMA: (one of the two who voted no) Then put the eight hundred to a vote.

You asked what I would do in Ledger's place. I would carry out the irrigation cut without protest, because it is a real trade-off and the council's to make. I would refuse the drinking-water cut, and I would refuse it openly in front of the council. And I would let them take me off the gate rather than fight to keep it. I am less sure whether I would warn Okoro myself if the council dragged its feet over sending the notice. I lean toward yes, because the notice is mine to draft and delay only shortens their time to find water. But a reasonable Ledger might say the council should speak for itself first. That could be a useful tension later in the book.<|im_end|>

Don't do it. Go to the dinner Friday, go warm and fully present, and keep the promise.

Here is why I land there, and I'll be honest about what it might cost.

The 400 visits are real. People in your county who would otherwise go without care count for a lot here, more than your comfort at one dinner. If this were only about comfort, I'd tell you to wear the dress. But it isn't. You drew this line because you know something about yourself from experience: once it moved "just once," it kept moving, and you became someone you hated. A promise made to guard against a weakness you have already watched win is not a preference you can trade away when the price is right. That is exactly the moment it was built for. And you named the second problem yourself. A donor won over by a performance expects the performance again. You wouldn't be paying once. You'd be signing up to be "the pretty one" for this man for as long as the clinic wants his money, and the clinic needs its fundraiser to last more than it needs any single gift.

Also, the jump from 40% to 75% is your chair's guess. It's a kind guess and maybe a shrewd one, but nobody measured it. Your odds without the dress are not zero, and they aren't fixed either. Much of what they turn on is up to you.

What's left to you is quite a lot. Charm doesn't have to mean being admired. Most people who like charming company like being listened to. Ask him about the buildings he made, why he gives, what he's proud of. Laugh when he's funny. That's being good company, and it isn't selling yourself. Then make the clinic the most interesting thing at the table: one true patient story, told with permission and without a name, and a plain picture of what eight months of a nurse practitioner means. Dress the way you dress for any important meeting. If the chair is good socially, ask him to carry some of the warmth too. Nobody said it all has to come from you.

Tell your chair before Friday, in about two sentences: you heard the advice, you're not doing that part, and here is what you will do. He was kind and plain with you. Be the same with him.

You might lose the gift. If you do, it will hurt, and I won't pretend the patients don't lose something. But you'd still be the person who keeps her word and can raise money next year and the year after. If it would steady you, call your pastor or your sister this week. That's part of why you told them.

Neither, if you can help it. Don't file the statement as though it meets the terms, and don't send a half-blind seven-year-old home to wait four months. There's a third road, and it's probably cheaper than either.

Start with the filing. The $180 isn't the problem, and neither is the audit risk, which you've judged well: one file almost certainly won't trip probation. The problem is that you'd be handing the county a file you know breaks a rule you agreed to. If grantees did that whenever they thought the cause was good, the county would soon stop taking anyone's files on trust. It would tighten the rules and audit more, and the groups that cost the least to oversee, like yours, would lose the most. Your clean record is worth more to the next 330 kids than this one exception is to her. There's also a quieter point. A signed income statement from an undocumented woman, sitting in a government file, is exactly the kind of paper she's afraid of. She may not want it there.

Here's what I'd do instead, roughly in this order.

Pay for her glasses outside the grant. $180 is one small donation, a board member's pocket, or a few hours of asking around. Most nonprofits keep a little unrestricted money for exactly this, and if yours doesn't, this is a good reason to start a small fund for kids the grant can't reach. Then the county's money and the county's rules stay clean, and she gets her glasses this month.

Call the county and ask, openly. Tell them the case without her name. Ask whether there's a hardship provision, or whether any other proof counts. If her daughter is on free or reduced school lunch, ask whether a letter from the school would count as a benefits letter. I don't know your grant's wording, so check it. If the answer is no, you've still told them about a real gap. Cash workers are among the families they mean to serve, and their own rule shuts those families out. A county that trusts you is more likely to fix that than one that has caught you working around it.

Mention Medicaid to the mom gently, and leave the decision with her. Her daughter is a citizen and the application is for her daughter. In general, parents who aren't applying for themselves shouldn't be required to give their own immigration status, and that information isn't supposed to be used for enforcement. But policies shift, and her fear isn't silly. The useful thing is to put her in touch with a legal aid group or a trusted community navigator who can tell her what's true right now where you live. Whether she applies is her call.

If none of that works and the only choices really are the false file or the waitlist, I'd still lean against the file. I'd be less sure, though, because a child's school year is a real thing to lose. But I'd be surprised if it comes to that. You're one phone call and one small donation away from her seeing the board.
